News.title: DWP state pension age rule clarified in new ‘entitlement’ update
News.content:
DWP state pension age rule clarified in new ‘entitlement’ update

The Department for Work and Pensions has explained the rules around an aspect of the state pension after a question from a prominent new MP

View 2 Images Treasury minister Torsten Bell has issued a new update on an aspect of the UK state pension rules (Image: Parliament TV)

The Department for Work and Pensions has issued an update on the rules around the state pension. The DWP issued has put out a new statement to clarify the rules after it received a question from a high-profile new MP.

‌



‌



It comes as the state pension age rises as the UK government deals with the rising cost of the state pension and people live longer. The age started to rise from 66 to 67 on May 6 this year and will complete this process on April 6, 2028.

‌



Another rise from 67 to 68 is scheduled for 2044 to 2046. The current guidance shows that if you were born between April 6, 1960 and April 5, 1977, the rise up to 67 will probably affect you. If you were born later than this, the current government timetable shows your state pension age may be 68.

‌



The My Pension Expert website says: “There is also ongoing discussion about whether the rise to 68 could be introduced earlier, though no decision has been made.” However, it notes that “any change would require further government legislation.”

In a question lodged with the DWP about these changes, Green Party MP Hannah Spencer asked the department about the “potential impact of the State Pension age increase on widowed women who expected to inherit some of their deceased partner’s State Pension at the age of 60.” Former plumber Ms Spencer is the Green MP who won a by-election in February in Gorton and Denton after then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer blocked Andy Burnham from standing as the Labour candidate. Within four months, Starmer resigned and Mr Burnham became PM.

View 2 Images The matter was raised with the DWP by new MP Hannah Spencer, whose election preceded the end of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership (Image: Parliament TV)

‌



Current rules say that you may be able to inherit an extra payment on top of your new State Pension if you are widowed. There are several caveats and rules around this policy, however. In a new statement issued this month, the DWP responded to Ms Spencer’s question.

Pensions minister Torsten Bell said: “The new State Pension, for people reaching State Pension age on or after 6 April 2016, is based on an individual's own National Insurance record. In general, it is not possible, as it was under the old State Pension system, for a person to increase their State Pension or qualify for a State Pension based on their spouse or civil partner's National Insurance record, although there is some protection under the transitional arrangements for the new State Pension.

‌



It remains the case that a person cannot become entitled to inherit State Pension until they reach their own State Pension age.” The gov.uk website explains the rules around such payments and when they would apply.

You may be eligible to inherit a portion of your deceased partner's Additional State Pension if your marriage or civil partnership commenced before 6 April 2016 and one of the following conditions applies: your partner reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016; or they passed away before 6 April 2016 but would have reached State Pension age on or after that date. This will be paid alongside your State Pension.

‌

You will inherit half of your partner's protected payment if your marriage or civil partnership began before 6 April 2016 and they reached State Pension age on or after 6 April 2016, or they died on or after 6 April 2016. This will also be paid alongside your State Pension.

Article continues below

You may inherit some or all of your partner's extra State Pension or lump sum if: they passed away while deferring their State Pension (before claiming) or had begun claiming it following a deferral; they reached State Pension age before 6 April 2016; and you were married or in a civil partnership with them at the time of their death.

News.title: Heating oil update as 6 ‘steps’ to protect households this winter confirmed
News.content:
Heating oil update as 6 ‘steps’ to protect households this winter confirmed

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has issued details of support for eligible households

View 2 Images Government minister Polly Billington has explained steps that are being taken to help heating oil consumers (Image: Parliament TV)

The government has confirmed ‘steps’ it is taking to protect households this winter that use heating oil. The oil is used to heat more than 1.5 million homes in the UK. Prices have more than doubled in the last year, mostly due to Donald Trump's Iran war - and there is no price cap as there is for many gas and electricity customers.

‌



‌



Kerosene is the most widely used fuel in domestic central heating systems in the UK. It is typically used in homes not connected to the mains gas grid - often in rural areas.

‌



The government has been pressed over what steps are being taken to protect users of heating oil from rising prices this winter. Now it has issued a response explaining six measures that could support households that are eligible.

‌



View 2 Images Tom Gordon MP raised the issue of heating oil challenges facing UK households with the government (Image: Parliament TV)

The matter was raised by Lib Dem Harrogate MP Tom Gordon, who asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero what steps it is “taking to protect households that use heating oil from price rises this winter.”

Polly Billington, a minister in the department, has now set out six steps that the government says it is taking to offer help. They provide a recap of what support it has announced.

‌



These are:

A £100 payment for eligible households

£100 million to councils that can offer support to homes struggling with energy bills

£53 million of targeted support for heating oil users

The extension of an energy VAT cut

Measures that cut £150 from energy bills

And plans to regulate the heating oil sector

‌



Ms Billington said in a response issued on Wednesday, November 18: “The Government recognises the significant pressures heating oil price increases place on rural households, and given the volatility of global fossil fuel markets, provided breathing space for off-grid households through the measures announced at the Autumn Budget.

“The £100 Household Energy Payment will reach eligible households in England living in their main home in Council Tax bands A to D from January 2027. It supports eligible households regardless of heating source as eligibility does not depend on having a gas account. Therefore, households who use heating oil can also receive this support if they meet the criteria.

‌



“Furthermore, an additional £100 million enables councils to provide discretionary support to households struggling with energy bills who are ineligible for the core payment. This comes on top of the £53 million of targeted support announced in March for heating oil users, with £27 million made available to local authorities in England via the Crisis and Resilience Fund.

“Off-gas-grid households with domestic electricity meters also benefit from the extension of the existing VAT cut on electricity to 1 July 2027, and last year’s Budget measures removing an average of £150 of costs from household energy bills.

‌



“The Government also published its formal response to the Competition and Markets Authority’s heating oil report on 13 October and is taking forward proposals to regulate the heating oil sector for the first time, ensuring households are treated fairly.”

The government announced in October that there would be stronger protections for heating oil consumers in new codes of conduct for the industry. It also said minimum order volumes as high as 500 litres for some customers would be reviewed.

Article continues below

At the time of the announcement, the government also said: “Heating oil customers are also eligible for extra support to get onto homegrown clean energy, after the government increased its discount off the cost of a heat pump to £9,000 for households who use heating oil.” For more on the heat pump scheme, see the gov.uk announcement here.

News.title: Chilling moment dad excuses child abuse in police interview that 'shocked officers to the core'
News.content:
Chilling moment dad excuses child abuse in police interview that 'shocked officers to the core'

Both the father and mother have been convicted of child neglect at court in Essex - and the dad's reaction 'shocked police to their core', officers said

View 2 Images The dad, whose identity has been obscured by police, had a 'shocking' reaction

The chilling moment where a father excused ‘degrading’ his children and ‘shocked police to their core’ has been caught on camera. The father, from Essex, has now been jailed for more than four years for neglecting his two vulnerable children.

‌



‌



Their mother, a woman from Essex, has been handed a two-year community order for failing to report the abuse when she knew about it. Neither parent has been named by Essex Police in order to protect the identity of their child victims.

‌



Police said they found evidence they repeatedly physically abused the young children who have additional complex care needs.

‌



In a police interview, DC Scott Cameron showed the father a video of him ‘continuing to whip with a towel’ a child ‘five, six, seven times’ after they started crying. Discussing another video clip, DC Cameron added: “It looks to me like you are using one of your children’s hands to hit the other one whilst they’re already crying.”

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

The man excused his behaviour initially. He chillingly told detectives: “Since they’ve been little, they’ve not been overly close.”

‌



His comment prompts an incredulous reaction from cops. Later in the interview, DC Cameron tells the abuser: “I thought I'd seen most things in social care and in the police that I wouldn't be shocked anymore.

“But I'm not lying to you. That has shocked me to my core. The only thing that shocks me a little bit more is your reaction, or your lack of reaction watching that.”

‌



View 2 Images A general view of Basildon Crown Court in Basildon, Essex (Image: Getty Images)

The man subsequently pleaded guilty to two counts of child cruelty and one count of intentional suffocation. He was sentenced to four years and nine months in jail, at Basildon Crown Court on Monday (November 23).

‌



The children's mother admitted two counts of child neglect which related to a delay in reporting what she knew to be happening to the police when she came forward in December 2025. She was given a two-year community order, with 150 hours of unpaid work to carry out.

His Honour Judge Collery KC said the father was ‘almost sadistic’ in his treatment of the youngsters. He told the defendant: “This was gratuitous degradation, which could almost be said to be sadistic. You are dangerous – you present a substantial risk of causing serious harm to children in the future.”

‌



While DC Courtney White would have been pleased to see the defendants jailed, she said her main focus is on the children. Both infants are now in a safe, loving home.

‌



DC White added: “What happened to them was deeply upsetting, including for experienced officers investigating the case. But our focus throughout has been on those children. They are safe, and the people responsible for harming them have been held accountable.

“Investigations such as this require our detectives to examine distressing evidence in painstaking detail, build a case and sometimes sit across a table from someone accused of causing serious harm to a child. We do that because children who are being abused may not always be able to tell somebody what is happening to them.”

News.title: Forehead sign could be a 'red flag' for heart disease risk, scientists say
News.content:
Forehead sign could be a 'red flag' for heart disease risk, scientists say

A study discovered that a crucial indicator of potential heart problems can be detected in the forehead

View Image Signs of a serious heart condition could show in the forehead (Image: Getty)

Research has indicated that hardening of the arteries may become obvious in signs in the forehead, as the blood vessels there are particularly sensitive.

‌



‌



A study discovered that a crucial indicator of potential heart problems can be detected in the forehead. Researchers have suggested that individuals with deeper forehead wrinkles than would be expected for their age may face a significantly higher risk of dying from cardiovascular disease (CVD).

‌



While furrows in the brow are not considered a superior method of assessing cardiovascular risk compared to established techniques such as blood pressure monitoring and lipid profiles, they could serve as an early warning sign at a glance and at minimal cost. The study, presented at the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Congress in Munich, Germany, in 2019, did not establish a definitive cause for the link, but theorises it may be connected to atherosclerosis, or the hardening of arteries caused by plaque build-up.

‌



Atherosclerosis is a significant contributor to heart attacks and other cardiovascular events, with alterations in collagen protein and oxidative stress appearing to play a role in both atherosclerosis and the formation of wrinkles. Furthermore, the blood vessels in the forehead are so minute that they may be particularly susceptible to plaque build-up, suggesting that wrinkles could be amongst the earliest indicators of vascular ageing.

The study examined a group of 3,200 healthy working adults aged 32, 42, 52 and 62 at the outset, who were assessed by physicians and given scores based on the number and depth of wrinkles across their foreheads. A score of zero indicated no wrinkles while a score of three indicated "numerous deep wrinkles".

The participants were monitored for 20 years, during which period 233 died from various causes. Of these, 15.2% had score two and three wrinkles, 6.6% had score one wrinkles and 2.1% had no wrinkles.

‌



The researchers discovered that individuals with a wrinkle score of one had a marginally elevated risk of dying from cardiovascular disease compared with those who had no wrinkles. Those who had wrinkle scores of two and three faced almost 10 times the risk of dying when compared with individuals who had wrinkle scores of zero, following adjustments for age, gender, education, smoking status, blood pressure, heart rate, diabetes and lipid levels.

Study author Yolande Esquirol, associate professor of occupational health at the Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Toulouse in France, said: "The higher your wrinkle score, the more your cardiovascular mortality risk increases.

‌



"You can't see or feel risk factors like high cholesterol or hypertension. We explored forehead wrinkles as a marker because it's so simple and visual. Just looking at a person's face could sound an alarm, then we could give advice to lower risk."

She explained that such advice could include simple lifestyle modifications such as increasing exercise or adopting a healthier diet. The risk of heart disease rises as individuals age, though lifestyle and medical interventions can reduce the danger.

‌



The difficulty lies in identifying high-risk patients sufficiently early to make a meaningful difference. Dr Esquirol added: "Of course, if you have a person with a potential cardiovascular risk, you have to check classical risk factors like blood pressure as well as lipid and blood glucose levels, but you could already share some recommendations on lifestyle factors.

"This is the first time a link has been established between cardiovascular risk and forehead wrinkles so the findings do need to be confirmed in future studies, but the practice could be used now in physicians' offices and clinics.

Article continues below

"It doesn't cost anything and there is no risk." Earlier research has examined various visible signs of ageing to determine whether they might predict cardiovascular disease, identifying a connection between male-pattern baldness, earlobe creases, xanthelasma (cholesterol deposits beneath the skin) and an elevated risk of heart disease, though not with a heightened risk of mortality.

News.title: Mum accused of 'faking daughter's leukaemia diagnosis' in sick series of lies
News.content:
Mum accused of 'faking daughter's leukaemia diagnosis' in sick series of lies

The mother allegedly lied about her four-year-old daughter's cancer diagnosis, forcing her to suffer from unnecessary medical treatments and faking doctors reports

View 2 Images A mugshot of Danielle Rowan, an Ohio mother accused of faking her 4-year-old daughter’s leukemia diagnosis.

A mum allegedly faked her four-year-old daughter's leukaemia diagnosis, forcing her to undergo unnecessary medical treatments in a series of lies told to family, friends and medical professionals.

‌



‌



Danielle Rowan, 32, from Ohio, faces endangering the welfare of children charges after reportedly lying to her friends, family, and even her own husband for months that her 4-year-old daughter had leukaemia, according to a probable cause arrest affidavit seen by Law and Crime.

‌



The police rushed to the Rowans' home on November 10 due to a domestic dispute after her husband allegedly demanded to see the daughter's medical records. The husband took the four-year-old and her sister to Rowan's parents' house; however, according to the outlet, the 32-year-old showed up and claimed she needed to give her daughter medication.

‌



View 2 Images Police attended the domestic dispute at the property (stock image)

The police attended the property, and Rowan's husband and parents informed officers that Rowan had informed her family and friends in May that their daughter had leukaemia.

The statement obtained by the outlet said that Rowan had even administered a series of steroid injections which made the girl gain weight and become irritable.

‌



The complaint continued to reveal that the mother said her daughter needed a semi-permanent IV line, but the treatment kept getting delayed, which caused concern within the family.

She even produced a cancer diagnosis report from the Cincinnati Children’s Hospital’s oncology department, but a doctor confirmed that this was fake. Examinations carried out by doctors also showed that the girl did not have cancer.

‌



The mum also allegedly told the daughter’s paediatrician that the child could not eat solid food, leading to her being prescribed three to four bottles of high-calorie PediaSure a day.

The statement shows that the prescription caused the girl to suffer from constipation and pain.

Article continues below

Court documents claim that Rowan denies telling anyone her daughter had cancer. When asked about social media posts she shared about her diagnosis she said “did not remember making the posts".

Danielle Rowan has been released on bond, according to Law and Crime.

News.title: Boy, 2, fatally attacked by alligator at Disney World as parents watched
News.content:
Boy, 2, fatally attacked by alligator at Disney World as parents watched

Lane Thomas Graves was just two years old when he was fatally attacked by an alligator during a family holiday at Disney World's Grand Floridian Resort and Spa in Florida in 2016

View 2 Images Lane Thomas Graves was dragged off by an alligator (Image: Orange County Sheriff's Office)

Lane Thomas Graves was just two years old when he was fatally attacked by an alligator while on a family holiday - after the creature "took off" with him.

‌



‌



The toddler tragically lost his life at Disney World's Grand Floridian Resort and Spa while his parents watched helplessly. According to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission's final investigative report, Lane had been building sandcastles along the water's edge at around 8:30pm in June.

‌



While standing in ankle-deep water to fill a bucket, the little boy, who was approximately 37 inches tall and weighed roughly 30 pounds, was suddenly grabbed by an alligator which clamped onto his head and pulled him under the water.

‌



His father, Matt Graves, who was nearby, witnessed the animal surface and attempted to rescue his son by prising open the jaws of the roughly 8ft reptile. The alligator briefly resisted before breaking free and vanishing into deeper water with the youngster, according to the Mirror US.

View 2 Images A decade after 2-year-old Lane Thomas Graves was killed by an alligator at Disney World's Grand Floridian Resort & Spa, his parents are ensuring the little boy is never forgotten (Image: Lane Thomas Foundation/YouTube)

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



In his statement to investigators about the heartbreaking incident, the father noted that the gator "just took off" despite his desperate rescue efforts.

"I saw it come out to get him," Matt Graves told investigators, according to the report. The father's attempts to save his son proved futile after the gator "just took off" after, he said.

‌



His mum and dad remain committed to honouring Graves' legacy. On the anniversary of his passing, his parents, Matt and Melissa Graves, told The Today Show: "Lane had a special light about him and cared for his family deeply. We simply want to shine a light on our beautiful, blue-eyed boy at this very difficult milestone."

The couple unveiled a nine-minute memorial film to Today, crafted as a tribute to Lane on the 10th anniversary of his death. The touching homage will be accessible through the Lane Thomas Foundation's website.

‌



"We promised him at his wake, we would turn this tragedy into good for many families," Matt revealed in footage for the foundation, as reported by the publication.

On June 14, 2016, Matt, Melissa, their son Lane, and their then four year old daughter Ella, were holidaying from Nebraska when the devastating event occurred. Lane was paddling in a lagoon close to the resort at Lake Buena Vista when an alligator struck. His dad's frantic efforts to ward off the animal were unsuccessful, resulting in hand injuries, The Associated Press documented at the time.

‌



Lane's remains were discovered by a diving squad the following day. Following the catastrophe, his parents founded the charity to assist families facing emergencies.

"We know that we can never have Lane back, and therefore, we intend to keep his spirit alive through the Lane Thomas Foundation," Melissa and Matt stated in a 2016 announcement. "It is our hope that through the foundation we will be able to share with others the unimaginable love Lane etched in our hearts," they added.

‌



The foundation offers financial support to families whose children are in need of transplants, while also championing awareness of the vital importance of organ donation. "Melissa and Matt Graves know what it's like to go through a very traumatic experience," the foundation's website states.

"They want to provide resources so that you can focus solely on your child and keep your family together."

‌



Two years on from Lane's heartbreaking death, Melissa and Matt welcomed their third child into the world, a baby boy named Christian Lane Graves.

"Although we know the pain of losing Lane will never go away, we feel God has blessed our family with this precious miracle of life," the couple said in a statement shared with PEOPLE in 2018. "We know Ella and Christian have their brother, Lane, watching over them as their guardian angel."

Article continues below

In the aftermath of Lane's tragic death, wildlife authorities culled 250 alligators from Disney properties in 2021.

News.title: Boy, 16, charged after 'chasing mum with chainsaw for taking away Xbox' after GTA 6 release
News.content:
Boy, 16, charged after 'chasing mum with chainsaw for taking away Xbox' after GTA 6 release

The alleged incident occurred just days after the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, but officers did not establish whether the game had any connection to the incident

View 3 Images A teenage boy has been charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly chased his mum with an electric saw (Image: Volusia Sherriff's Office)

A teenage boy from Florida has been charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly chased his mum with an electric saw. It is understood that the alleged incident occurred after the mum took away the 16-year-old's Xbox.

The Volusia Sheriff's Office deputies responded to the incident on Monday after they received a report that the teenager had cowed his family over this minor issue, blackmailed the family and said he would hurt the family's pets. The incident occurred just days after the release of GTA 6 which is focussed on violence.

The teen was later transported to the Volusia Family Resource Center for help. The authorities have shared the photo of the 18-inch cordless Greenworks chainsaw, believed to be used in the incident.

View 3 Images The alleged incident occurred just days after the release of GTA 6 (Image: Leon Neal, Getty Images)

The alleged incident took place a few days after the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on November 19, but the officers did not establish whether it had any connection with the incident.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

The GTA series allowed players to wander fictional cities, nick vehicles, dodge police and commit crimes. Some people have blamed the game for the terrifying incident.

One person said: "That's GTA withdrawals. Worse than drugs."

Another wrote: "They said once GTA6 came out, people would start ruining their lives over it and here we are. It has begun," another said.

View 3 Images GTA 6 was released last week

The game, released on Thursday, November 19, is the sixth in the GTA series and Rockstar's first new game in 13 years.

It is set in Vice City, Rockstar's imaginary take on Miami, which has appeared in earlier editions of the franchise.

The game centres on two main characters, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, who become entangled in a criminal plot within the fictional state of Leonida.

No further updates have been issued by the police force since the initial post.

News.title: Chris Mason: Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate?
News.content:
When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.

It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader, promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe.

And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.

Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.

All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.

Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.

But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."

So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.

News.title: Pip benefits review to suggest quicker payment for some disabled people
News.content:
Alicia Cartwright in Preston receives the higher rate of Pip for both the daily living and mobility components, which she says equates to about Â£500 every four weeks.

The mum-of-two, a trained benefits adviser, told the BBC that even she found the current assessment process "intimidating and confusing".

"Trust disabled people to know what their needs are. Of course, have some checks in there, absolutely, but we really need to start from a place of trust.

"Currently, in any dealings with the benefits system, you feel like you're on trial, and for a lot of people, asking for help is difficult in the first place."

Cartwright is a power wheelchair user and works several part-time jobs at a university. She says the costs of her disabilities run to a further Â£1,500 a month which she has to pay out of her wages.

"The mobility part of it, that goes on paying for my wheelchair. And then the rest of my Pip goes entirely on paying someone to help me around the house," she said.

Matt Ryder from the Adam Smith Institute, a free-market think tank said disability claims had risen fastest amongst young people "who are the least likely to be become seriously ill as a result of the pandemic".

"We need to target lower-level mental health claims. That seems to be the root cause of the rising claims, so we need to restrict eligibility for that," he said.

Research last month from the Resolution Foundation, a think tank focused on lower and middle earners, suggested about one in six Pip recipients said they didn't incur any extra costs due to their disability.

It suggests removing Pip from this group would save up to Â£4.4m a year.

Lindsay Judge from the Resolution Foundation said although the Timms Review did not set out to cut costs, this "should be possible nonetheless" and that "major change is needed".

She said improvements should include assessments that "better understand disabled people's needs" as well as awards in the form of cash or services that "better reflect the actual costs that disabled people face" as well as "more regular light touch check-ins so that changes of circumstances are fully understood".

Ryder meanwhile said fewer reassessments for people with deteriorating conditions, and a more accessible process, were "individually the right thing for disabled people" but that the think tank was concerned abut rising costs.

"It's where the cost is heading... According to the OBR, we can expect that spending on Pip will rise to Â£47bn in five years' time. And there's no reason why it would stop at that point. Why wouldn't it continue on growing?" he said.

The review's proposals will be put forward by a steering group, led by Sir Stephen, which the government will respond to.

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales, but the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

News.title: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
News.content:
When Shahira Sadat received an invitation for a Chevening Scholarship interview, she felt a rare glimmer of hope.

The software engineer in Kabul had spent three years battling Taliban restrictions, jumping through hoops and working through power and internet outages to prepare her applications for UK universities and grants.

"I was so happy. I can't describe it because I allowed myself to dream about studying in the UK," she says.

But in March this year, the UK's Home Office announced an "emergency visa brake" on study visas for applicants from Cameroon, Myanmar, Sudan and Afghanistan. Skilled work visas for Afghans were also paused. It said the move was a response to widespread visa abuse and had been triggered by a sharp rise in asylum claims from these visa routes.

At the time, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she was "taking the unprecedented decision to refuse visas for those nationals seeking to exploit our generosity". The US barred all visas for Afghan nationals earlier in the year.

Sadat had three acceptance letters to study a masters in AI and machine learning from Sussex, Bradford and Northeastern University London. Now with a shot at getting funding from the UK government-funded Chevening scheme, she felt the education she'd been denied in Afghanistan was finally within reach.

Then came an email saying she would no longer be considered to study in the UK because she was from Afghanistan.

"It was really heartbreaking. I lost all my motivation. I cried for hours and hours," says Sadat, her eyes welling up with tears. "It was not just about education for me; it was the opportunity to resume my career and to build a future for myself."

In Afghanistan, diktats from the Taliban's supreme leader have severely restricted the lives of women. They cannot attend secondary schools or universities, and are barred from most forms of work.

In the western city of Herat, Alia - whose name we have changed - received a similar rejection to Sadat. Her offers to do a digital media masters in the UK were withdrawn, which she says left her feeling trapped.

"Everything is banned just because I am an Afghan woman," she says, her voice cracking with emotion.

News.title: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic
News.content:
Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her.

"It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.

A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.

Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.

Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.

But the world of work has proved more challenging.

For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.

In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."

One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.

Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities.

"I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."

She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.

News.title: 'Life is not infinite': Catherine talks about 'mortality' in new documentary clip
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has said cancer made her confront her own vulnerabilities, in a new clip from her upcoming documentary, Heal.

"When you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite," Catherine says.

In March 2024, Catherine revealed that she had a cancer diagnosis and was receiving chemotherapy.

In a previously released trailer for the documentary, Catherine is seen hugging her children and her husband, the Prince of Wales, as she completed the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year.

Heal will air on BBC One on Sunday, 29 November.

News.title: Coldest spell of autumn continues with risk of hill snow, ice and heavy rain
News.content:
As the coldest spell of the autumn so far continues, parts of the UK could see some hill snow, ice or heavy rain this week.

With Arctic air to the north and east of the UK, Scotland, northern and eastern England will experience temperatures below the average with some hill snow, freezing rain and ice.

Meanwhile, milder air to the west of the UK will bring heavy rain to parts of Northern Ireland, Wales and south-west England with temperatures around average.

The battle between colder and milder conditions is likely to continue through the week.

News.title: State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner
News.content:
The victims' commissioner for England and Wales has said the state is failing to keep the public safe, as she urged Andy Burnham to put the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government.

Claire Waxman told the BBC that she would press the prime minister to commit to reforms in the decade-long blueprint, which he is set to unveil next month.

She warned that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding in jails, along with long waits in the courts, had eroded the trust of crime victims to come forward.

It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice.

Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled.

Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point".

The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan.

"It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added.

She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting."

News.title: BBC secret filming shows dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each
News.content:
When Katie Thornton paid Â£2,000 for a nine-week-old puppy for her son, she knew it was a premium price - but was happy to be doing business with a "legit", council-approved breeder.

But Ozzy the Dobermann pup started coughing in the car on the way home, and within 48 hours he was in a veterinary hospital receiving urgent treatment for pneumonia.

Since then, his ongoing health problems mean Katie has racked up more than Â£5,000 in vet bills.

A BBC investigation has found the breeder had been stripped of his five-star rating two months before selling several sick puppies, but continued to advertise as five-star.

We have also found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than it really is.

An expert reviewing our findings - including undercover footage we recorded at the breeder's home - said the investigation exposes a nationwide "wild west" of dog licensing, making it "easy for consumers to be scammed".

The breeder has not responded to our request for comment.

News.title: Property firm told to repay customers thousands over 'unfair' sales tactics
News.content:
A property sales company has to pay back more than Â£277,000 to customers across the UK after a watchdog found it had treated buyers unfairly by misrepresenting rental incomes.

Let Property is facing "unprecedented" levels of repayments after the UK Property Ombudsman received nearly 200 complaints.

Customers paid the company upfront fees of about Â£3,000 each to reserve buy-to-let properties - but deals later fell through after valuations and rental income projections were found to be misleading.

Glasgow-based Let Property said customers had "experienced difficulties" during transactions in England, but it remained committed to improving its service and treating customers fairly.

The Property Ombudsman said most of the complaints about the company were about its use of buyers' premiums, which were paid upfront to reserve properties.

It described the firm's failings as "systemic" and said Let Property would repay a total of Â£277,725 to customers.

The BBC understands this is the biggest ever overall repayment of its type.

The repayments range between Â£100 and Â£12,300, with average payments of more than Â£3,200. The BBC further understands the average average compensation award in sales cases is just over Â£1000.

Trading standards said complaints about the company were being referred to its local offices.

News.title: Vote on Irish schools law set to fall after Stormont veto
News.content:
A proposed law on Irish-medium education is expected to fall on Tuesday during a vote in the Northern Ireland Assembly after unionists deployed a Stormont veto.

The bill, brought forward by Sinn FÃ©in assembly member Pat Sheehan, would require Stormont's Department of Education (DoE) to prepare a workforce plan on schools in the sector.

A vote during its final stage was postponed a fortnight ago after the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) tabled a petition of concern with the support of other unionists.

It means the legislation will require cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the Stormont assembly chamber.

First Minister Michelle O'Neill earlier this month accused the DUP of "blatant disrespect" and "sectarianism" over seeking to block the bill.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson had said the move was an outworking of his party's response to Sinn FÃ©in's "arrogance" over the Drumcree parading dispute.

News.title: Vapes seized in schools spiked with drugs, Met says
News.content:
One in eight vapes seized from pupils in south-west London schools contained illicit drugs, a Metropolitan Police scheme has found.

Officers tested 32 confiscated devices using specialist equipment, detecting substances including THC, the psychoactive ingredient in cannabis, and Spice, a synthetic drug.

The Met said a further three devices were expected to test positive following laboratory analysis.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Ben Russell said the initial findings were "surprisingly high" and highlighted the risks to children who may believe they are inhaling ordinary nicotine products.

"We've seen a number of cases of children getting quite unwell from taking a vape, thinking it was just going to give them some nicotine and a nice smell, and actually they've really become quite unwell from consuming something they didn't expect to," he said.

The pilot scheme was carried out with schools across south-west London following reports of pupils becoming seriously unwell after using shared vapes or devices they believed contained nicotine.

News.title: US rapper postpones two arena shows after Manchester evacuation
News.content:
The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.

"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.

One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.

A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.

Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out".

"It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".

There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."

Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.

Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat.

"[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.

Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking â it was really distressing."

Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.

"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."

Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.

Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".

Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."

Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".

It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures.

"A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.

Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".

Venues are currently focused on keeping out items â such as explosives â that could cause mass casualties, she added.

News.title: Andrew received £750,000 from Turkish millionaire, court told
News.content:
A Turkish millionaire has told the High Court she was misled over a Â£750,000 payment she made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.

Nebahat Isbilen is alleging her former business adviser, Selman Turk, misappropriated Â£38m of her assets, including a payment to the then-Duke of York which she believed was for help with her passport.

Turk has rejected the allegations, saying the 81-year-old Isbilen knew the money was actually being paid in the hope that Mountbatten-Windsor could help her husband, a politician who is in prison in Turkey.

Mountbatten-Windsor repaid the Â£750,000 and is expected to give evidence to the High Court in December. He is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Isbilen's lawyers also told the court on Monday that Turk had instructed a separate Â£15,000 payment to Mountbatten-Windsor's ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, purportedly for the former Duchess of York's 60th birthday party in 2019, and an unquantified "wedding gift" payment for their daughter Princess Beatrice.

Isbilen's family founded a major soap and cosmetics firm in Turkey.

But when her husband, Ilhan, a former member of the Turkish parliament, was arrested in 2015, she wanted help moving her assets out of Turkey. Her lawyers said the charges were "politically motivated" and that in 2017 she was facing "political persecution".

She left Turkey for Greece in 2017 and moved to London in 2018.

Simon Colton KC, representing Isbilen, said she met Turk in January 2017 and gave him control of most of her financial assets.

But Turk "deliberately and systematically abused" her trust and transferred the money to companies he owned or controlled, Colton added.

Colton added that Isbilen approved the Â£750,000 payment to Andrew, but that Turk "lied to her" about its purpose, which was "a further example of his dishonesty".

The court heard that Isbilen had a private dinner with the then Duke and Duchess of York at Turk's flat in December 2019 where she discussed her husband's case.

Turk's lawyers told the court that Isbilen understood and directed the management of her own affairs.

Joshua Hitchens, representing Turk, said in written submissions: "In circumstances where the claimant dined with the duke and duchess and discussed her husband with them, she cannot have believed that the Â£750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa."

The trial before Mr Justice Adam Johnson is due to conclude in March, with a written judgment at a later date.

News.title: Two men admit sex offences in drugged wife case
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

Two men have pleaded guilty to sexual offences against a woman who was drugged and raped by her husband without her knowledge.

Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport admitted rape and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

In a separate hearing at Manchester Magistrates' Court, Tommy Golden, 59, pleaded guilty to sexual assault involving the same woman in June 2025.

Golden appeared via video link from HMP Risley, where he is serving a prison sentence.

District Judge Simon Blakebrough said his offending was too serious to be dealt with by magistrates. His case was sent to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court, where he is due to appear in December.

During the hearing, Golden said that he had not spoken to a solicitor before entering a guilty plea.

News.title: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
News.content:
Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.

AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.

Recruitment to the EDITH trial , externalhas already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.

Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.

At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.

About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.

It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

News.title: Court clears Army to blow up tons of toxic bomb chemicals in Iowa as Trump pressures incoming governor
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A federal appeals court has granted permission for the U.S. Army to detonate tons of degraded explosive materials at an ammunition plant in Iowa.

The order from the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals was one of two rulings President Donald Trump indicated he was awaiting after directing the military on Monday to pause the chemical disposal pending judicial review.

The president noted that his determination remains contingent upon agreement from incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand, warning that federal authorities would otherwise be forced to proceed with the planned detonation.

Initial plans to destroy 68 barrels of lead azide were set for last Friday, but the Army postponed the operation three times following significant public concern regarding potential health and environmental hazards.

The revised plan aimed for a Wednesday detonation ahead of Thanksgiving to take advantage of favorable weather.

President Donald Trump announced on Monday that his administration would defer to a federal appeals court prior to moving ahead with the disposal of the degraded bomb-making material at the Iowa facility.

The scheduled neutralization of the 68 lead azide drums has been delayed three times after sharp public apprehension over environmental and health risks.

open image in gallery A sign at the US Army Iowa Army Ammunition Plant ( Reuters )

While military personnel sought a Wednesday timeline due to weather conditions, the Army did not immediately comment on the president's statement.

"At the same time, have ordered the military not to do so until such time as the 8th Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation," Trump said.

He warned that if consent is withheld, the administration will halt the procedure, holding Sand responsible for "any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation."

Sand responded in a social media post, writing that past administrative choices meant "No good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been."

He raised questions over why a contract intended to eliminate the hazard was canceled and "why we are rushing to demolition now in late November."

open image in gallery Residents taped up windows in hopes of stopping them from shattering during the explosion ( Getty )

The delay follows a legal challenge from environmental groups, who secured a stay from the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals to review an emergency permit granted by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

Trump indicated a preference for quick disposal via a controlled explosion, describing it as the safer option.

However, he confirmed that the operation remains paused pending judicial and state clearance.

Sand stressed, "The safety of Iowans should be the top priority of everyone involved," adding that "All relevant federal, state and local government resources should be focused on protecting everyone that could be impacted."

Near the Middletown facility, some residents have taken preventive steps by sealing windows and doors against potential lead dust, while others expressed worry online about wind carrying potential plumes.

Officials acknowledged the toxicity of lead, advising residents to stay indoors during any explosion and to wash down outdoor surfaces with water.

In court documents, Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency specialist, explained that reduced liquid inside the barrels leaves the substance susceptible to freezing, raising the sensitivity of crystals near the lids.

open image in gallery Incoming Gov. Rob Sand ( AP )

"Even a small amount of friction can break the crystal formation, causing an explosive chain reaction," he stated.

The barrels were initially discovered in March.

Although EPA records show chemical neutralization options were evaluated, officials determined that moving the drums posed a severe risk of an accidental blast. Environmentalists contend that alternative methods were overlooked, while officials warn that the danger of an explosion grows as temperatures fall below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius).

News.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Moscow threatens Nato member with ‘open war’ over plans to close border
News.content:
