"I did it to plenty of people," he laughed, but always "people who wouldn't arrest me!"

- Family -

"The Only Living Pickpocket in New York" follows Harry, a pickpocket who spends his days caring for his bed-bound and comatose partner, Rosie (Karina Arroyave), and his nights eeking out a living on the streets.

But the city where he once found a decent enough keep has changed: hardly anyone carries cash and the iPods and phones they do have are practically worthless.

Even his one-time nemesis, Detective Warren ("Breaking Bad's" Giancarlo Esposito), finds himself sidelined within a police force that now prioritizes cybercrimes.

The plot thickens when Harry robs the wrong person. Backed into a corner, he decides to stake everything on one final, grand trick.

To prepare for the role -- which has generated Oscar buzz as a potential Best Actor -- Turturro sought to understand how someone falls into a life of larceny.

"A lot of these people came from difficult circumstances," he said, but they lived within a code of honour and usually worked in teams which formed a kind of family.

"The people who were really good could do it by themselves, but... they had to graduate to that.

"They have this moral code that they don't rob from people who are drunk or really old or handicapped."

- Changing -

Written and directed by Noah Segan, "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York" has a nostalgic feel that highlights how fast technology is changing our society.

Turturro, 69, says as the son of a seamstress and a construction worker he has a respect for his character's facility with his hands, and understands his sense of unease in the modern world.

"I understand technology, but I don't understand it as a replacement for relating to other human beings," he said.

A lifelong New Yorker, the actor, seen recently in Apple's cult hit "Severance," embraced a production that highlights the changes in the city where he was born.

"When I was younger, I could see anything I wanted to see," he said of the range of live performances available in America's theater capital.

"I could sit in the back, but I could see it."

"New York is safer now," he said. "But it was more affordable when it was more dangerous."

"The Only Living Pickpocket in New York" is in select US cinemas now.

By Paula Ramon

World.title: Overberg fire leaves trail of destruction as residents count losses
World.content:
MALGAS - A devastating fire in the Overberg region, which broke out on Thursday, has been contained.

But the destruction is extensive, with at least 24 homes and more than 33,000 hectares of land destroyed.

Authorities say the scale of the damage and its emotional impact on residents and landowners have been immense.

Although the major fires have been contained, flare-ups remain a concern, particularly for properties along the river.

“Diepkloof and Riverine area is where all the devastation took place," said Reinard Geldenhuys of the Overberg Municipality Emergency Services.

"In the process, it spread over an extended area like 33,000 hectares and fire services were spread dealing with a fire line of 96 kilometres we had to attend to, which spread us incredibly thin.”

Thick smoke hampered firefighting efforts, preventing helicopters from operating. Firefighters also came close to losing some of their fire engines.

For homeowners and farmers, the fire has left behind extensive losses and devastation.

ALSO READ | Overberg and Garden Route wildfires quelled

Thankfully, no lives were lost.

While some residents lost almost everything, others managed to salvage some of their belongings.

Residents are being urged to remain vigilant as firefighting teams continue to monitor the affected areas.

Although the major fires have been contained, flare-ups could still threaten individual properties.

World.title: Madlanga Commission mulls referring Carrim’s lawyer to LPC
World.content:
PRETORIA - Suliman Carrim's lawyer, Ulrich Roux, is in serious trouble.

The Madlanga Commission is considering referring Roux to the Legal Practice Council (LPC) over his conduct, after he accused the inquiry of issuing a malicious statement intended to damage his client’s reputation.

The controversy centres on a statement issued by the Commission concerning Carrim’s alleged breach of his bail conditions.

Carrim’s legal team had been given 48 hours to appear in person before the Commission to make arrangements for him to testify.

However, instead of attending, the lawyers reportedly sent an email informing the Commissioners about the bail condition.

Roux subsequently accused the Commission of acting with malicious intent during court proceedings last Friday.

But the Commissioners are standing firmly by their statement, taking issue with Roux’s allegations and describing his conduct as something that “boggles the mind” and amounts to a “gratuitous insult”.

World.title: South Korea says Russian jets entered air defence zone
World.content:
SEOUL - South Korean authorities said Wednesday several Russian military aircraft had breached its air defence zone, correcting an earlier alert that reported a North Korean plane had made an incursion.

A breach of South Korean airspace by a North Korean military plane would mark a significant escalation in tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.

The inaccurate alert came following heightened tensions along the heavily fortified border, after a recent mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

An emergency alert was issued on Ulleungdo in North Gyeongsang Province at 8 am Tuesday (2300 GMT Monday), saying a "suspected North Korean aircraft has left the danger zone".

"The air raid alert for Ulleung County was lifted at 7:58 am. Please resume normal activities," it added.

Around 40 minutes later, provincial authorities issued a correction.

"It was Russian aircraft that violated the airspace. We inform that it was Russian aircraft," they said, without explaining the cause of the error.

Several major South Korean news outlets issued breaking news alerts based on the initial warning before later correcting their reports.

South Korea's military later clarified that the Russian aircraft had not violated the country's airspace and that no North Korean aircraft were involved.

"Some media reports that 'a flying object believed to be a North Korean aircraft violated South Korean airspace' are not true," it said in a brief statement.

The Russian aircraft entered South Korea's air defence identification zone (KADIZ) over the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, and "departed as our forces were taking military measures", including deploying fighter jets, according to Seoul's defence ministry.

It later said the Russian military aircraft "flew right up to the edge of our airspace" and the alert was issued as a proactive measure.

The ministry said it plans to summon the Russian defence attache in the afternoon to lodge a "stern protest" over the incident, its spokesperson Chung Binna told reporters.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area in which countries identify approaching aircraft for security purposes.

Military aircraft are generally expected to notify the relevant country before entering its air defence zone, although such notification is not legally required.

World.title: New Zealand Rugby give 'full' backing to Rennie after defeats
World.content:
TWICKENHAM - New Zealand Rugby has given its "full support" to All Blacks coach Dave Rennie after damaging back-to-back defeats including a first loss to Wales in 73 years.

With the World Cup less than a year away, the All Blacks suffered a record 37-12 defeat by England at Twickenham on Saturday.

That followed a stunning 35-28 Nations Championship loss to Wales in Cardiff.

With the All Blacks and England facing off again this weekend, NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster moved to dampen any speculation about Rennie's future.

"I've told Dave that and I'm happy to state that publicly that Dave has our full support," Lancaster told Radio New Zealand.

"We're confident that we have the right person coaching this team, no question in our minds."

Speaking on Monday, Lancaster added: "There's clear leadership. The team are behind Dave but they know what they have to achieve.

"The last two weeks' performance is really disappointing and we need to understand how that's come to pass, but no question over Dave being the right person to lead the team."

Speaking after the defeat at Twickenham, which was England's biggest margin of victory over New Zealand, Rennie said he took full responsibility.

The All Blacks have lost five of their 12 Tests under Rennie, equalling their worst run in the professional era.

"As a coach, you're responsible for the results," Rennie, who was appointed in March, told reporters.

"I'm not going to hide that we weren't good enough and I'm a part of that. We were miles off and this is not where we want to be."

World.title: Corruption haven: How Boda boda riders, mama mboga's lose daily earnings to bribes
World.content:
A new World Bank report shows that 48 per cent of mid-sized businesses face demands for bribes. [AFP]

Kenya wants to attract investors, but corruption is blocking that goal.

Medium-sized businesses are hit hardest, with nearly half of them saying they are forced to pay bribes to get basic public services. Around the world, these firms are known as engines of growth, innovation and job creation, but in Kenya, corruption is killing many of them.

World.title: Ruto backs Didmus Barasa for Bungoma governor in 2027
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kimilili MP Didmus Barasa with President Ruto at a political rally in Mt Elgon during the President’s development tour in the Western region. [PCS]

President William Ruto has thrown his weight behind Kimilili MP Didmus Barasa in the race to succeed Bungoma Governor Kenneth Lusaka in 2027, setting the stage for a contest over the county's political leadership.

During his ongoing tour of Western Kenya, the President rallied support for Barasa, signalling his preference for the legislator in the battle for control of Bungoma County after the next General Election.

Barasa has expressed confidence in securing the United Democratic Alliance (UDA) party nomination, citing his development record and grassroots mobilisation in Kimilili as the foundation of his gubernatorial bid.

The MP has urged Bungoma leaders aligned with Kenya Kwanza to unite behind his candidature, arguing that a common political front would strengthen the region's bargaining power within the national government.

He said he intends to replicate his development model in Kimilili across the county's 45 wards, prioritising healthcare, education and youth empowerment.

“I want to take the development model we have implemented in Kimilili and extend it to all the 45 wards in Bungoma. Our people deserve better healthcare, improved education infrastructure, functional vocational training centres and quality early childhood education facilities,” he said.

The legislator pledged to strengthen county hospitals, improve the availability of medicines and expand access to healthcare services at the grassroots.

He also promised to invest in vocational training centres to equip young people with practical skills for employment and entrepreneurship, while improving Early Childhood Development and Education (ECDE).

Barasa identified agriculture, trade, infrastructure and youth entrepreneurship as key sectors requiring investment to unlock Bungoma's economic potential. He said his proposed administration would prioritise accountability, efficient use of public resources and improved service delivery.

His bid has received backing from a section of county leaders, including Senator Wafula Wakoli of Ford Kenya and Webuye East MP Martin Pepela.

However, Ruto's apparent preference for Barasa has attracted opposition from Sirisia MP John Waluke, who has questioned the endorsement and instead declared support for Westlands MP Tim Wanyonyi, who is associated with the Linda Mwananchi Movement (LMM).

Waluke argued that Bungoma residents should determine their next governor without external political influence.

“Bungoma belongs to its people, and the people must decide who will lead them in 2027. We cannot allow the gubernatorial contest to be determined through political endorsements from outside. Residents must be given the freedom to choose a leader who represents their interests,” he said.

The contest is also unfolding amid political differences between Barasa and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang'ula, adding to the competing interests shaping Bungoma's succession politics.

World.title: Shun leaders inciting you to cause chaos, PS Omollo tells youth
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Internal Security Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo. [File,Standard]

Internal Security Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo has warned young people against political violence, saying the destruction of public property costs lives and diverts resources meant for development.

The warning comes amid concerns over political violence in Embu following the September 12 incident at Nembure Stadium, where a meeting attended by Deputy President Kithure Kindiki was disrupted, leaving one person dead, six vehicles torched and three others vandalised.

Speaking during a Mass at St Thomas More Kairuri Parish in Embu County, Omollo challenged young people to question leaders who ask them to disrupt meetings, block roads or destroy property.

“Before you leave home to disrupt a meeting, ask that leader whether they would allow their own child to do what they are asking you to do,” he said.

“Ask them what they are doing to help you access education, training and employment.”

Omollo said young people should also question what political leaders were doing to improve their access to education, technical training and employment.

He said the Government was working to expand opportunities for young people through education, technical training and employment.

The PS welcomed efforts in the technical and vocational education and training (TVET) sector to equip young people in Embu with skills to pursue their ambitions.

At the same time, Omollo commended county leadership for working with the national government to combat illicit alcohol and drug abuse.

Omollo said proposed legislative changes targeting the sector had passed the first reading in Parliament and urged residents to participate in the next stages of the legislative process.

On security, the PS acknowledged calls for more police vehicles, saying the Government was investing in personnel, vehicles and equipment.

However, he challenged residents to help protect public investments, citing reports that 10 police vehicles had been burned in Embu.

“We use our taxes to buy police vehicles, build markets and construct roads. We cannot pay for development and then allow a few individuals to destroy what belongs to all of us,” he said.

Omollo warned that anyone suspected of destroying property would be taken to court in accordance with the law, where the judiciary would determine their cases.

He maintained that political differences should not be used to justify vandalism, endanger lives or disrupt public services.

“The Constitution protects the right to express ourselves peacefully and unarmed. Political differences cannot be an excuse to vandalise property, endanger lives or disrupt the services our communities depend on,” he said.

Those present included Public Service, Human Capital Development and Special Programmes Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku, Embu Governor Cecily Mbarire, Senator Alexander Munyi and Deputy Governor Kinyua Mugo, among others.

World.title: Narok Senator under fire after threatening to shoot auctioneers in Sh1.2m dispute
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Narok Senator Ledama ole Kina is at the centre of a national uproar after a viral video captured him threatening to shoot individuals during a volatile confrontation involving auctioneers and a former Senate office employee.

The dramatic standoff erupted when court-backed agents attempted to seize a milk delivery truck over an unresolved legal dispute and has since ignited intense public debate regarding political accountability and the rule of law.

The controversy surrounds long court battle after Zakayo Rotiken, who served sacked as Narok North Constituency Coordinator between 2017 and 2020, was sacked.

According to records, the claimant was illegally dismissed amidst unpaid salary arrears.

On October 31, 2023, the Employment and Labour Relations Court ruled in Rotiken's favour , a decision that was subsequently upheld when the Senator lost his appeal.

With accrued interest, the court decree now stands at Sh 1.2 million.

Consequently, when the debt remained unsatisfied, licensed auctioneers moved in to execute lawful warrants which in turn provoked a furious reaction from Senator Ole Kina, who fiercely framed the entire episode as a political witch-hunt.

The lawmaker argued that Rotiken was hired by the Narok Senate office rather than his personal capacity, maintaining that any resultant liabilities ought to be handled by the Parliamentary Service Commission (PSC) rather than attaching his private property.

Defending his harsh words in the widely circulated footage, the senator dismissed the agents as trespassers and asserted action against them.

"Anybody who trespasses will get a bullet in their head or leg because that is trespass," said Ole Kina.

“Nitakupiga Risasi!” Senator Ledama Ole Kina embroiled in confrontation with alleged auctioneers over unpaid car loan https://t.co/k4OSXpNsdi November 21, 2026

The claimant's legal team condemned the threats made against statutory court officers emphasizing that a court judgment is an enforceable command rather than a mere suggestion, calling upon the Inspector General of Police of Police and the Director of Criminal Investigatons to urgently investigate the alleged death threats.

Rotiken noted that he merely sought justice through proper judicial channels and should not be penalized or intimidated for pursuing his lawful entitlements.

"When I was illegally dismissed with unpaid salary arrears, I did not resort to violence or politics—I went to the Employment and Labour Relations Court. Nobody is above the law, and I appeal to the police to protect the officers doing their job so that justice can finally be served," he said.

Ultimately, as pressure mounts on security agencies to look into the firearm threats, the unfolding saga highlights a tense intersection between public office obligations and the absolute sanctity of judicial decrees.

While the senator maintains that his assets were unjustly targeted by political rivals, legal experts and the public continue to demand that the rule of law must prevail without exception.

World.title: Ruto defends IEBC, challenges rivals to present alternative policies
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his tour of the Western region. [PCS]

President William Ruto has launched a scathing attack on opposition leaders over their demands on the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), accusing them of attempting to interfere with the electoral agency because they fear losing the 2027 General Election.

The President challenged opposition leaders to allow IEBC to prepare independently for next year's elections, saying they should instead focus on identifying their presidential candidate, developing a manifesto and presenting alternative policies to Kenyans.

Ruto accused his competitors of attempting to play the roles of both contestants and referees by seeking to influence decisions on the procurement of election materials and equipment.

He spoke a day after opposition leaders walked out of a meeting convened by IEBC, alleging bias by the commission.

“Please give IEBC a chance to arrange the elections next year. The people of Kenya will decide. You go and first look for your candidate, find your policies, agenda and plans and sell them to the wananchi. We shall meet at the ballot,” said Ruto.

Speaking during his development tour of Western Kenya, Ruto questioned why opposition politicians were concentrating on determining how IEBC should procure election materials instead of preparing to face voters.

“How can somebody who is in a competition want to decide where the pitch will be, who the referee will be and where the ball will be placed? Leave IEBC alone. Those who will vote are the citizens, and they are the ones who will decide,” he said.

The President accused his opponents of lacking a clear political agenda and capacity to deliver, claiming their campaigns were centred on slogans and personal attacks against him.

He challenged them to explain what they would do differently in agriculture, education, healthcare, infrastructure and employment rather than mobilising Kenyans around the slogan 'Kasongo Must Go'.

“The reason why my competitors cannot develop a plan is that they have no capacity. The reason why they have no agenda is that they have no knowledge. The reason why they cannot develop anything is that they know they have no capacity to deliver on anything that they will say,” he said.

His remarks were echoed by Kakamega Governor Fernandes Barasa and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang'ula, who rallied Western Kenya leaders behind his re-election bid and defended IEBC against what they termed unnecessary political pressure. President William Ruto during his tour of the Western region. [ Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Speaking in Butere, Barasa said the region's political leadership, including Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, Cabinet Secretary Wycliffe Oparanya, Wetang'ula and trade unionist Francis Atwoli, was united behind Ruto's development agenda.

“IEBC will conduct the elections according to the law. Opposition leaders should leave IEBC alone and allow it to do its work,” he said.

Wetang'ula maintained that IEBC was independent of both the government and the opposition and should be allowed to conduct its work without interference.

“IEBC is independent of the government and independent of the Opposition. You stand there to do your work fairly, truthfully and equally,” he said.

He added: “Just as Arsenal supporters cannot dictate what uniform the referee should wear, the referee's responsibility is to ensure the game is played fairly and the winner emerges through a legitimate process.”

The exchanges underline the growing political contest over the management of the 2027 elections, with the government side accusing the opposition of undermining the electoral agency before campaigns gather momentum.

Beyond the political exchanges, Ruto used his Western Kenya tour to highlight development projects, saying his administration was committed to correcting years of neglect and unequal distribution of national resources.

He also announced plans for a second phase of the Nyota programme targeting an additional 200,000 young people, each expected to receive Sh50,000 to establish or expand businesses.

The government is also targeting 100,000 college graduates for internships from January, with each expected to receive a monthly stipend of Sh20,000.

Ruto's tour comes amid growing competition for Western Kenya's support ahead of the 2027 General Election, with emerging opposition alliances seeking to challenge his influence.

World.title: Ruto sustains attacks on Gachagua, dares Opposition to name 2027 flagbearer
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto launches Matisi-Bokoli-Milani-Teremi road in Webuye West on November 19, 2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

President William Ruto has challenged Opposition leaders to name their presidential candidate and unveil a clear political agenda, accusing them of wasting time hopping from one hotel to another and holding meetings in private residences in search of a flagbearer and campaign manifesto.

The President said the Opposition was yet to settle on a flagbearer or agree on a common agenda despite the clock ticking towards the 2027 General Election.

He dismissed the rival camps' political engagements as endless consultations and manoeuvres, arguing that their leaders were more preoccupied with political meetings than developing policies to convince Kenyans.

Speaking in Bungoma during his development tour of Western Kenya, Ruto challenged his opponents to stop what he termed political confusion and present an alternative development agenda, insisting he was ready to face them in the 2027 contest.

"These people do not have a candidate. They are struggling, moving from one hotel to another and from one person's house to another, trying to find an agenda and a manifesto before they can start campaigning. Time is running out, yet they are still struggling to agree on an agenda," he said.

Ruto also launched a fresh attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, accusing him of promoting tribalism and hatred while questioning his remarks about relocating to Texas, United States.

The President mockingly referred to Gachagua as "Mr Chuki wa Texas", questioning why he would allegedly acquire a house in the US while engaging in politics that could divide Kenyans and fuel hostility.

"Mr Chuki wa Texas has gone to buy a house in Texas. He wants to know whether he will flee our country after spreading tribalism and hatred, dividing people and turning them against each other, before boarding a plane to Texas and leaving others to deal with the consequences," Ruto said.

He accused the former Deputy President of attempting to turn communities against one another for political gain, warning that he would not allow anyone to undermine national unity through ethnic mobilisation.

Ruto said he was ready to confront his political opponents directly but insisted that political competition should not become an avenue for spreading hatred and inciting Kenyans against one another.

The President also questioned Gachagua's allies over their reported visit to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) offices in Kizirani, accusing the Opposition of picking unnecessary fights with the electoral agency ahead of the 2027 General Election.

He suggested that politicians who begin questioning the electoral commission before elections could be preparing grounds to reject the results should they lose.

"Whenever you see someone picking a fight with IEBC, that person is already looking for an excuse to fail. Now they are coming up with all sorts of excuses, asking whether it is IEBC that votes. Is IEBC responsible for the votes?" He posed.

Ruto urged politicians to stop harassing the electoral agency, maintaining that the power to elect leaders rests with Kenyans and not the commission.

"I want to tell Kenyans to stop harassing IEBC. IEBC does not have votes. The votes belong to the people of Kenya," he said.

The President maintained that his administration was focused on delivering development, challenging the Opposition to explain its alternative plans on electricity connectivity, education, healthcare and infrastructure.

He questioned what the Opposition considered its development agenda, dismissing what he described as recycled political slogans and simplistic promises.

The President particularly took issue with promises centred on providing porridge to Kenyans, questioning whether such pledges could constitute a credible national development agenda.

He urged voters to interrogate the policies and development track records of politicians seeking their support instead of being swayed by political rhetoric and personal attacks.

The latest attack marks an escalation in political exchanges between Ruto and his rivals as competing camps intensify mobilisation ahead of the 2027 General Election.

It also comes amid efforts by Gachagua and other Opposition figures to consolidate their political formations and build a formidable challenge to Ruto's re-election bid, with Western Kenya emerging as a key battleground.

World.title: Ruto lists measures to lower cost of living, put more money in Kenyans' pockets
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during his State Of The Nation Address at Parliament, Nairobi. November 18th, 2026. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

President William Ruto has outlined a raft of government interventions aimed at reducing the cost of living, increasing household incomes and creating more employment opportunities for Kenyans.

Addressing Parliament during the 2026 State of the Nation Address on Wednesday, Ruto said his administration had prioritised lowering the cost of essential goods and services while increasing earnings across key sectors of the economy.

“Our economic proposition was simple: Reduce the cost for families and increase the income from what they do,” he said.

On food prices, the President cited the government’s fertiliser subsidy programme, which has reduced the price of a 50-kilogramme bag of fertiliser from Sh7,500 in 2022 to Sh2,000 this year.

He said the government had distributed 38.5 million bags of subsidised fertiliser to farmers, contributing to an increase in maize production from 44.3 million bags in 2022 to 71 million bags last year.

Consequently, maize imports declined from 9.9 million bags to 3.3 million bags, while the average price of a two-kilogramme packet of sifted maize flour dropped from a high of Sh230 in September 2022 to Sh152 in September this year.

Ruto also highlighted gains in the tea, coffee, dairy and sugar industries, saying government interventions had helped improve production and increase farmers' earnings.

He said the Cherry Advance Revolving Fund had disbursed Sh15.07 billion to 684,000 coffee farmers, while tea export earnings increased from Sh163 billion in 2022 to Sh187 billion in 2025.

In the dairy sector, milk production rose from 4.5 billion litres to 5.52 billion litres, while average earnings for farmers increased from Sh32 to Sh60 per litre last month.

Sugar production, he added, increased by 60 per cent between January and October, with cane crushing rising by 57 per cent. The industry is projected to produce more than 900,000 tonnes by the end of the year, with Sh1.2 billion in bonuses expected to be paid to sugarcane farmers.

On healthcare, Ruto said the Social Health Authority (SHA) was designed to ease the financial burden of medical expenses on households through a shared health financing system.

In education, he said the government had employed 100,000 teachers and was preparing to recruit an additional 20,000 to address staffing shortages and reduce the burden on parents who pay teachers hired through Boards of Management.

He added that 23,000 classrooms had been constructed, while 1,600 laboratories were being built and equipped.

The President said the annual education allocation had increased from Sh521 billion in the 2022/23 financial year to Sh784 billion in the current financial year.

"These investments improve the quality of education while progressively reducing the need for Kenyans to finance education," he said.

On affordable housing, Ruto said more than 313,000 homes were at different stages of construction across the 47 counties, with over 1.37 million Kenyans registered on the Boma Yangu platform and more than 18,000 homes already allocated.

He said households could work towards homeownership through monthly payments starting at Sh4,000, which he argued would help ease the burden of rent.

The housing programme, according to the President, had also generated more than 1.1 million employment opportunities and reserved orders worth over Sh61 billion for Jua Kali artisans.

On employment, Ruto said 350,000 Kenyans had secured jobs through the digital economy programme, while another 707,000 had obtained employment abroad through international labour mobility initiatives.

He also cited the Hustler Fund, saying more than seven million Kenyans had established credit records through the programme, with cumulative borrowing reaching Sh94 billion.

Under the NYOTA programme, more than 133,000 young entrepreneurs had received training, mentorship and Sh50,000 each in start-up capital, he said.

The President further announced proposed tax measures aimed at increasing disposable incomes, including exempting workers earning Sh32,333 or less per month from Pay As You Earn (PAYE).

Other proposals include scrapping stamp duty on land transactions valued at Sh1 million or less and removing the 25 per cent import duty on mobile phones.

On pending bills, Ruto said the government had approved the settlement of 28,726 verified claims amounting to Sh27.8 billion, covering debts of Sh50 million and below dating back to 2005.

He added that Sh18 billion owed to public universities and another Sh16 billion owed to public and private hospitals under the former National Hospital Insurance Fund (NHIF) had been approved for payment and were undergoing Treasury processing.

“These are not isolated interventions, but parts of one comprehensive undertaking,” Ruto said.

He maintained that the government's economic strategy was anchored on reducing household expenditure, increasing incomes and expanding opportunities for Kenyans.

World.title: After 22 years of waiting, woman welcomes quadruplet boys
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Samuel Langat speaks to journalists outside St Clare's Kaplong Mission hospital in Sotik Subcounty, Bomet county after his wife Lily Langat gave to quadruplets at the hospital. [Kiprono Kurgat, Standard]

After 22 years of waiting to become a mother, a woman has welcomed quadruplet boys in a rare and joyful birth that has brought immense happiness to her family.

Lily Langat delivered the quadruplets through a Caesarean section at St Clare’s Kaplong Mission Hospital in Sotik Sub-County on November 14, 2026.

The four boys arrived after more than two decades of waiting for a child in what the family described as a double blessing.

The 43-year-old mother could not hide her joy, saying the arrival of the four babies was an answer to years of prayer.

“I am very grateful to God for giving me four babies at once. This is a great blessing to my family. I thank the hospital staff for ensuring I got to see these bundles of joy,” she said.

“I have been praying and waiting upon God to give me double for the trouble. I have been childless for a long time, and God could not have given me a better gift than this,” she added.

She said she had been looking forward to the moment after doctors informed her early in the pregnancy that she could be carrying quadruplets.

Hospital staff celebrated the successful delivery, describing it as a rare occurrence at the facility.

A nurse who spoke with The Standard said the mother and her four newborns were in stable condition.

“We were delighted to deliver the babies. The mother faced some difficulties because of the combined weight of the four babies, but both she and the newborns are now stable,” she said.

The nurse said the babies had been placed in the nursery for observation and were doing well.

“This is a rare case in this hospital. We have had twins before, but this is different. None of the babies has developed complications so far, and we expect them to be discharged once they are fully stable,” she said.

She added that the mother was also recovering well and was expected to be discharged once doctors were satisfied with the condition of the newborns.

Lily's husband, Samuel Langat, appealed to well-wishers to support the family as they prepare to raise the four children.

“Raising four babies at once is no easy task. I am calling on well-wishers to lend a helping hand as we begin this extraordinary journey,” he said.

“Our four precious miracles have arrived safely, and while our hearts are overflowing with gratitude, the reality of caring for four newborns at once has brought challenges,” he added.

Naturally conceived quadruplets are extremely rare, although the likelihood varies depending on several factors, including maternal age and fertility treatment.

The birth marks a remarkable new beginning for the Langat family after 22 years of waiting for a child.

World.title: Libyan Army denies withdrawal of Egyptian military experts from Benghazi
World.content:
The General Command of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces has denied reports about the withdrawal of Egyptian military experts from the city of Benghazi, affirming that cooperation between both sides continues as normal.

In a statement issued on Sunday, the General Command noted that it monitored reports circulating in certain media outlets and on social media platforms concerning an alleged rift with Egypt, dismissing such claims as entirely unfounded.

The command emphasized that Egyptian-Libyan relations remain firmer than ever, representing a deep-rooted and enduring partnership built upon strong historical ties, mutual trust, and shared interests.

This partnership is reflected in close cooperation across military and security sectors, as well as extensive collaboration on reconstruction, development, and infrastructure projects, it said.

The General Command affirmed that this partnership reflects the depth and significance of the relationship between both nations, as well as its role in safeguarding their shared national security and enhancing regional security and stability.

It reiterated its pride in the ties with Egypt and its commitment to further strengthening them across various fields.

Furthermore, it urged media outlets to ensure accuracy, rely on official sources, and refrain from circulating unverified reports concerning the relationship between the two countries.

Egypt remains committed to Libya’s stability

Egyptian Minister of State for Information Diaa Rashwan previously denied claims circulated by certain media outlets and social media platforms suggesting that Egypt had withdrawn its military experts from Benghazi, allegedly due to disagreements with the General Command of the Libyan National Army (LNA).

In a statement issued by the Ministry of State for Information, Rashwan affirmed that Egypt remains committed to supporting Libya’s stability, territorial integrity, and the preservation of its national institutions.

He emphasized that communication and coordination with the LNA’s General Command continue as usual, showing a shared commitment to upholding security and stability in both Libya and the broader region.

The minister urged media outlets to exercise accuracy and avoid being swayed by unsubstantiated claims—allegations intended to sow doubt in the deep-rooted and multifaceted relationship Egypt and Libya share.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Prime Minister issues new decision regarding private sector participation in Egyptian government projects
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly has issued a new decision concerning the disclosure and regulation of investor access to data on infrastructure, service, and public utility projects intended for implementation through public-private partnerships (PPP).

The decision was published in the Official Gazette on Sunday and enters into force on Monday.

What does the decision entail?

Its first article mandates that administrative entities must submit a statement detailing any infrastructure, service, or public utility projects, for which they seek private sector participation, to both Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS) and the Central PPP Unit at the Finance Ministry, no later than January 1s following the date this decision takes effect

These administrative entities include ministries, government departments, local administration units, public service and economic authorities, as well as wholly state-owned companies (or those owned by public legal entities).

For each project, the statement must include its name, implementation location, sector, investment cost, duration, the scheduled date for its tender, the scheduled date for contracting, the applicable law, regulation, or rules, and the chosen contracting method along with the justifications for it.

The aforementioned entities and companies shall update this statement and submit it to the two bodies referred to in the first paragraph of this article on a quarterly basis—specifically, at the end of every three-month period, calculated from the aforementioned January 1st.

Projects intended to be tendered by any of the aforementioned entities or companies are exempt from the provisions of this article if national security considerations dictate that their details should not be disclosed or published.

Article Two

Article Two of the resolution stipulates that the Central PPP Unit shall categorize, classify, and enter the data submitted to it—pursuant to the provisions of Article One of this resolution—into its own database.

The unit shall update this data periodically, based on the quarterly information it receives, by incorporating new projects, recording any amendments to previously submitted data, and identifying projects for which contracts have been signed or which have been abandoned.

The Central PPP Unit shall publish this data on its website, including information regarding projects intended for contracting, and make this data accessible for review by investors and the entities concerned with such projects.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: French police officers convicted of racist assault on Black music producer
World.content:
Paris AP —

The lawyer for a Black man who was beaten up by three French police officers hailed a “historic ruling” on Saturday after a court acknowledged the racist nature of the violence and sentenced them to between one and two years in prison.

The assault on Michel Zecler, a music producer, took place six years ago during the coronavirus pandemic and was caught on camera. It showed the officers repeatedly punching him, using a truncheon and tear gas against him for no apparent reason.

Zecler told The Associated Press after the incident that the officers hurled repeated insults at him, including a very strong racist epithet.

“What is very important is that the racist nature of the violence he suffered has been recognized,” Zecler’s lawyer, Serge Money, told France Info. “As a legal professional, one can only be satisfied. This is a first.”

Money said that from the very beginning of the proceedings, Zecler maintained that he had been racially insulted, whereas the defendants’ accounts were somewhat inconsistent.

“Ultimately, they were convicted of lying, as the falsification of written records was established,” he said. The verdict was issued late Friday in Paris.

Music producer Michel Zecler (L) stands next to his lawyer Serge Money (R) addressing media during a lunch break at the Palais de Justice, the main law court of Paris on the Ile de la Cite, central Paris. Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images

Videos published showed the violent arrest of Zecler in the 17th arrondissement of the French capital. The three officers intended to stop him for not wearing a face mask during the restrictions imposed because of the pandemic.

The video images, obtained by the AP, both from a security camera inside the studio and filmed by neighbors outside, showed officers following Zecler inside his music studio, where they could be seen repeatedly punching him and beating him with a truncheon.

“I want to understand why I have been assaulted by people who were wearing a police uniform,” Zecler told AP at the time. “I want justice actually, because I believe in the justice of my country.”

Zecler suffered injuries to his head, forearms and legs.

French law enforcement agencies have long faced complaints of excessive force. After Zecler was taken into custody for violence against public authority, then-Justice Minister Eric Dupond-Moretti said in a television interview that he was scandalized by the images. He admitted that some officers were racists, but denied systemic racism within the force.

Money said that without the video, Zecler would have ended up in prison. He added that the officers apologized.

“This ruling should set a precedent for all those who have not been believed,” he said. “There has to be a first, a starting point. It is now up to the justice system to make use of this ruling. I have no doubt that everyone will recognize its significance. This is no small matter, particularly given that the investigating judges had initially dismissed the racist dimension of the case.”

Rap artist Stomy Bugsy said “this is a victory for all victims. If it can help curb, reduce and ultimately put an end to this kind of police misconduct and abuse, then it is a victory.”

World.title: Blacklisted Chinese universities procured Nvidia chips, records show
World.content:
At least six Chinese universities blacklisted by the US government have reported purchasing restricted Nvidia computer chips in recent years, a CNN review of business records found – highlighting US difficulties in controlling access to the in-demand technology.

Two of those universities known for their ties to the Chinese military establishment reported buying the high-powered chips just in the last few months.

The number of universities involved and full scope of their Nvidia purchases have not been previously reported.

The purchases, made through obscure sellers in China, were for relatively small amounts of older chips, not the industrial, cutting-edge computing technology that researchers fear could enable China to overtake the US in the artificial intelligence race.

Still, they show how widely available restricted Nvidia chips remain inside China, and how difficult it is for the US to block the sale of the chips even to some of the most high-risk entities – a particularly sensitive concern following allegations linking Nvidia’s CEO to a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

“Once these chips are in China, it’s very hard for anyone to be able to stop their sale,” said Kate Koren, a former US export control official who now serves as a research director at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “We know it happens, and it’s very difficult to stop.”

The issue is likely to be a major talking point in this week’s high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping as the White House moves to close loopholes that have allowed sensitive, AI-powering computer chips into China.

Concerns spiked over Chinese access to the technology as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week following the revelation he had a romantic relationship with a woman whose former company is suspected of helping smuggle chips into the country.

President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. Iori Sagisawa/China Pool/Getty Images Jensen Huang, pictured in London in October, resigned as CEO of Nvidia last week after admitting to a marital affair. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Speaking to reporters last week, Mao Ning, a spokeswoman for China’s Foreign Ministry, said Beijing rejects US claims that restrictions on high-powered chips are necessary for US national security.

“China firmly opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security and formulating various types of discriminatory lists to go after Chinese institutions,” she said.

CNN’s review was based on procurement documents from Chinese universities collected in a commercial database. Under Chinese regulations, universities and other public entities are required to publish notices on their websites when they make certain purchases.

Among the nearly 300 records CNN obtained and examined, most show purchases of Nvidia technology under US export control, such as A100, A800, H100, H200, and H800 chips. Among the 90 buyers CNN examined, nearly 80% are universities, and nearly 14% are research institutes, while government agencies also bought some Nvidia chips.

CNN’s review excluded purchases of computing power from overseas data centers – one of the loopholes that the Trump administration moved to close this week with new regulations.

Most notable, experts said, was a procurement notice from September that Harbin Institute of Technology had purchased an A100 chip for about $7,000, and two notices in September and October that Northwestern Polytechnical University had bought four H200 chips for a total of about $240,000.

An aerial view of Harbin Institute of Technology in Harbin, China, in May 2021. VCG/Getty Images The campus of Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi’an, China, in September 2022. CFOTO/Future Publishing/Getty Images

Both universities are part of a grouping known in China as the “Seven Sons of National Defense” because of their connections to China’s People’s Liberation Army.

“Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military,” said Gregory Allen, the CEO of Decision Tree Research, a firm focusing on tech and geopolitical issues. “If you’re talking about who’s going to be investing in military AI capabilities in China, a lot of that would start at these universities.”

The purchase notices had scant details about the supply chains that took the chips from Nvidia to the universities, or how the chips may be used there. Both universities reported buying the chips not from Nvidia itself or a major supplier, but from little-known firms in China. Reuters previously reported on one of the Northwestern purchases.

Under a new policy put in place last year after lobbying from Nvidia and Huang, the US government does allow the tech giant to sell the less powerful H200 chip to entities in China on a case-by-case basis – but those sales come with strict requirements related to reporting the end user of the chips. Experts said US officials were highly unlikely to approve sales that would go to a blacklisted university.

Sales of the A100 chip to China are still banned – but before the US government put restrictions in place in 2022, the hardware was widely sold there.

“It’s possible those were coming from stockpiles there before the controls were in place,” said Koren, because “there was a fairly large window of time” when the chips weren’t controlled under US export law.

A third university that’s part of the “Seven Sons” group, Beihang University in Beijing, also reported making more than a dozen purchases of Nvidia chips between 2022 and 2024, according to the records, mostly buying A100 and A800 chips. The university has been blacklisted by the US since 2001.

Signage for Beihang University, also known as Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, on a building at its Shenzhen campus in September 2026. Cheng Xin/Getty Images

In addition to the universities with tighter military ties, three other universities on the US government’s “Entity List,” a blacklist of organizations that are banned from receiving shipments of controlled items without approval from federal officials, also reported purchases of high-end Nvidia chips in recent years.

The records CNN obtained are likely incomplete because while public institutes in China are required to publicize procurement decisions, many only publish the notices locally or internally or take them down quickly. The commercial aggregator CNN used also doesn’t include all notices published by Chinese institutions.

CNN was not able to verify whether the Nvidia hardware was delivered in each case described in the notices.

US regulations require Nvidia and other chip suppliers to determine the end user for chips they sell abroad, and to take various measures to avoid the chips getting into China.

It’s unclear how the universities’ suppliers acquired the chips. But in general, smuggling operations for these chips can be based on “very sophisticated shell companies, with shipments going from other countries to China, multiple hops, multiple currency changes, and falsified documents that make it much harder to detect,” Koren said.

Government officials trying to disrupt this pipeline are facing a “constant” struggle to enforce bans, she said, “but rationally you have to know that despite your best efforts, some will get through.”

World.title: Republicans mulling deal that would fund military, but limit operations in Iran
World.content:
In the final days of the GOP’s complete power in Washington, there’s a real chance the Pentagon might not get another dollar this year – unless Republican lawmakers strike a deal with Democrats to rein in Trump’s ability to attack Iran.

Top Senate Democrats and Republicans are engaged in high-stakes talks about cutting off funding for future offensive operations in the Iran war in exchange for replenishing the tens of billions that the Department of Defense has said is urgently needed, according to multiple lawmakers and aides in both parties.

The push faces enormous obstacles in a bitterly divided Congress, with Republicans largely wary of crossing President Donald Trump on the war – even after their midterm losses – and emboldened Democrats seeking big restrictions on his power.

But if no deal is reached, the Pentagon has almost no other chance of getting the money this year. And that means they’d have to ask Democrats for the money next year — an even tougher task, when every House Democrat voted to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth earlier this month.

“I think there’s a way for Democrats to make their point without tying the hands of the commander in chief and the defense of our country,” Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker told CNN on Friday when asked about the emerging proposal.

Talks are in the early stages, and there are still major questions about exactly what any restrictions would look like, and what else could be included, such as funding for Ukraine’s war against Russia. Sources in both parties have said it’s not yet clear if there’s a way for Republicans to accept Democrats’ demands without hampering the US military’s ability to keep troops safe – and without infuriating Trump.

“I think there is a room for negotiation there, and it would have to be something that the administration would find acceptable, too,” said GOP Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota, who is in talks with both Democrats and the White House on the matter. “But again, we want to deal, we want to end the conflict from a position of strength, and we need to fund the military.”

Some Senate Democrats hope they can convince Trump and GOP leaders to put a proposal into next month’s stopgap funding bill. If that did not pass, it would mean a debilitating shutdown at a time when Republicans still control all of Washington.

US carriers Theodore Roosevelt and George Washington sailing at a location given as Arabian Sea, in this screen grab obtained from a video released on November 17. US Central Command/Handout/Reuters

But several Republicans said they fear the talks could shift yet again if and when Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wins a contested leadership election on December 1. They believe the looming contest has led him to strike such a firm posture on defunding the Iran war. (Several noted that House Democrats have privately struck a different tone, very eager to avoid a shutdown and suggesting they’re willing to punt the Iran issue to 2027, according to multiple sources in both parties.)

Still, many Republicans believe they have no real options, other than striking a deal with Democrats on next month’s funding bill, since they don’t have the votes to do it on a party-line basis.

At least one Republican, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, told CNN on Friday he is open to supporting a compromise.

More military funding has been a key priority for the White House. Top Pentagon officials have spent months lobbying Congress for more money in the middle of a war with Iran — including personal calls from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, countless closed-door briefings and treks to Camp David.

Privately, though, GOP lawmakers and aides say that Pentagon officials have hurt their own chances by repeatedly misleading lawmakers about the true need for the funds. Defense officials have sent over four separate funding requests — including one just this week — that have made it difficult to discern the most urgent priorities, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions.

“I can add up four numbers, so don’t think you’re tricking me by dividing it into different buckets, and so that is a frustration,” lamented Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, who is on the Armed Services Committee, about the various funding requests.

CNN has reached out to the Defense Department for comment.

The administration has been making a stronger case in recent days, according to sources. Senate Republicans heard a strong pitch from Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg at a closed-door meeting this week, and House Republicans are expected to hear from him in the coming days.

Kaine, who’s been a vocal advocate of ending the war while supporting US troops, has made clear that Democrats are not opposed to all of the Pentagon’s funding requests. But he also doesn’t consider most of them to be urgent.

“Most of what they’re seeking is important and needed, but not needed tomorrow. Because like munitions replacement, you put money in, you’re not going to get to munitions for some time. So this isn’t necessarily about tomorrow,” Kaine said. “Some of those priorities in the $350 [billion request] are needed, and you would find an openness to some of our other side.”

World.title: The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe and there are two reasons it will get worse
World.content:
Rather than peace, there is stark escalation.

That is the product of over six weeks of shuttling diplomacy, posturing, betrayal of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, Russian intransigence and the US’ failed reframing of the process as about European security and participation.

Put aside the near-zero public results from the Shenzhen trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US, and consider the violence of the past week alone.

Russia launched Friday what Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year – a six-hour crescendo of drones and missiles, after weeks of striking Kyiv’s bridges, and power infrastructure across the country. Dozens have died, and swaths of the country and capital are often in blackout.

Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea three times, in the days around the trilateral. And compounding that display of technical prowess, Kyiv’s drones apparently struck both a Russian-military linked ship this weekend off the coast of Kaliningrad, and then Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, on the Libyan coast.

Damage to the Kerch Bridge seen in a satellite image.

Where Moscow parades its brutal, relentless intensity, Kyiv strikes back with unexpected reach and precision.

Widening theater of conflict

The geography of Ukrainian strikes is important. Kaliningrad is a Russian enclave between Lithuania and Poland , hitherto considered safe – an odd legacy of the Soviet era, territory marooned in the heart of some of NATO’s most anti-Russian members.

The apparent strike against a Russian-linked military ship – the Sparta 2, one of their notorious military-cargo Sparta fleet – was likely by Ukraine, and either involved a drone launched from another ship, or one flying through Russian territory to the Baltic Sea. Inevitably Russia chose to blame a third option – that Lithuania permitted the drone to fly through its airspace – NATO territory. The accusation feeds the long-standing fiction that Russia is at war with all of NATO. It also raises further the possibility of more Russian malfeasance and sabotage around the Baltics , and the risks of escalation with NATO this carries.

The Libya strikes – hitting a Russian naval ship and cargo vessel off the coast of Benghazi, according to Zelensky – further showcases the ability of Kyiv’s drones to embarrass the Kremlin, which had over the last decade paraded its might in Africa, yet whose ships now bring great risk of damage in whichever Mediterranean ports they may dock.

The uptick in violence – and where it has spread – was unthinkable five years ago; from being contained inside Ukrainian territory, it spread to Russia in 2024, then to NATO’s eastern borders, with Russia-linked sabotage across the military alliance. The frog is truly boiling, as this war is slowly spreading across the continent, and the months ahead look perilous for two reasons.

What a Democratic Congress means for Ukraine

Firstly: the Kremlin has a small window before Capitol Hill is taken over by pro-Ukrainian Democrats, and everything from past conduct, to current funding – from Elon Musk to minor Pentagon officials – falls under their scrutiny, if not regulation. The peculiar sympathies with which Donald Trump acts in Russia’s favor will likely be reeled in, in sheer practical terms, and the focus of his inner coterie may turn more to survival under a looming Democratic White House, than their personal priorities when dealing with Putin’s war of choice.

Moscow has palpably tried to set the negotiation clock backward, through persuading the US to reframe the talks as about wider “European security infrastructure.” This is something Moscow has long sought, a chance to rewrite the Ukraine conflict as the symptom of NATO’s enlargement eastward.

Putin himself has fortified his demands, his most recent appearance in Shenzhen stating Russia had no interest in negotiating a ceasefire – the only real immediate deliverable for diplomacy now. Then he added if the Europeans wanted to join the talks on a technical level (as the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has said the Kremlin had consented to) they should travel to Moscow to make the case to him, and then he’ll think about it.

Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks at a press conference in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China on November 19. Maxim Shemetov/Reuters

Putin has clearly determined his best negotiating stance is to rip up what’s in front of him, step many paces back , and make any possibility of compromise seem remote.

There is a gruesome logic to this: reality is partially on Russia’s side on the battlefield. Capturing the remainder of the Donbas is openly Putin’s main war goal. And while Ukraine has kept Russia from occupying a Donbas town like Kostyantynivka for whole two years, neighboring Kramatorsk and Slavyansk are close to uninhabitable, as Russian drone and airstrikes force civilians out and streets into rubble, ready for the months of gruesome urban warfare ahead. Putin said in Shenzhen that Ukraine’s hold over this remaining 10% of Donbas may slowly become untenable. The horrific cost of Putin’s slow grind forwards, of at least 40,000 dead and injured a month, does come with some tiny results – almost absurd as they are, given the casualties.

Perhaps this is the short-term objective the Kremlin sees: make the remainder of Donbas rubble, and then accept a political settlement later, where you can claim victory over the ruins.

Disagreement over reality hinders diplomacy

But it is the longer term danger that poses the greatest risk to diplomacy. Currently, few of the words spoken by either side relate to each other’s reality. European participation in future multilateral peace summits? Kushner says it’ll happen, the Kremlin says it won’t yet. Territorially, Putin says he controls Kostyantynivka, when he palpably does not. He said Thursday Ukraine started the war, when it did not.

Both sides’ demands seem to be moving away from each other. The Kremlin appears to want NATO to fall back and westward, according to some reporting. In turn, some reports suggest Ukraine’s membership of the alliance has even been floated by the US. These are two incompatible red lines.

This photograph shows birds flying past a partially collapsed building in Dymer, Kyiv region, on Monday following an overnight Russian air strike. Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP/Getty Images

The two sides’ parallel realities are getting further apart, rather than converging on a possible path forward. That is entirely Russia’s intention, and a textbook example of how they use diplomacy to advance their military objectives. But the impact is to create a fictional universe for diplomacy, in which a future restraint of reality on the battlefield becomes elusive. In short: you can’t expect nonsense talks to ever stop the real business of killing.

This is where the last year’s mess of failed talks, cosying up to Putin, belittling and bullying Ukraine, European panic and Russian savagery has led the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s. A place where Ukrainian drones seem to hit anywhere there’s a Russian ship. Where Russian drones, missiles and helicopters stray monthly into NATO territory without fear of a military retaliation. And where the peace process seems merely a process to please Trump, devoid of actual peace. It is a bleak moment whose only end in sight is the unsettling and even more destabilising collapse of either side.

World.title: Foreign Minister inspects Swiss-funded water project in Upper Egypt
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty on Sunday, November 22, 2026, inspected the Drinking Water Management Programme in Upper Egypt in Aswan Governorate to review implementation progress and assess development projects funded by international partners.

The visit took place on the sidelines of Abdelatty’s participation in the sixth edition of the Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development.

The project is funded by the Swiss Confederation under the Egyptian-Swiss development cooperation framework and implemented by the Ministry of Housing, Utilities and Urban Communities.

World.title: Egypt, Iraq FMs discuss bilateral ties ahead of Iraqi PM’s Cairo visit
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty and his Iraqi counterpart Fuad Hussein discussed bilateral cooperation and regional developments, ahead of the Iraqi prime minister’s scheduled visit to Cairo on Monday.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of the sixth Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Nader Zaki said Abdelatty expressed Egypt’s keenness to bolster economic, trade and investment cooperation with Iraq.

The two ministers discussed preparations for the Iraqi prime minister’s visit to Cairo on November 23 and the fourth session of the Egyptian-Iraqi Joint Higher Committee.

The ministers also exchanged views on developments as well as challenges to security and stability in the region.

Both sides called for political and diplomatic solutions to regional crises and agreed to continue consultations on issues of mutual concern.

World.title: COP31 Ends Without Political Deal as Disputes Over Fossil Fuels and Finance Persist
World.content:
Countries adopted decisions on adaptation and just transition in Antalya, but failed to agree on the conference’s overarching political outcome. Photo: UNFCCC

Summary

COP31 ended without agreement on the proposed Antalya Pact after disagreements over fossil fuels, climate finance and the direction of global climate action.

Governments adopted decisions on adaptation and just transition, but failed to agree on the Mitigation Work Programme and several other proposals.

Developing countries left Antalya without a clear pathway for delivering adaptation finance, while attention turns to Ethiopia’s hosting of COP32 in 2027.

By Aria Deemie

The United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Sunday without agreement on its proposed overarching political deal, after nearly two extra days of negotiations exposed deep divisions over fossil fuels, climate finance and how governments should respond to rising global temperatures.



“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement following the conference.

“There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

The failure to adopt the proposed Antalya Pact left the conference without a common political statement addressing some of the most contested questions in climate action. But it did not mean all negotiations failed. Governments adopted separate decisions on issues including the Global Goal on Adaptation and the Just Transition Work Programme , while other proposals, including the Mitigation Work Programme , did not secure agreement.

The proposed Antalya Pact consisted of two Presidency-led decisions, one under the United Nations climate convention and another under the Paris Agreement. Together, they were intended to provide an overarching political response to the climate crisis and set direction for the next phase of international climate action.



But countries could not agree on the language. A central dispute was whether the decisions should explicitly address the transition away from fossil fuels, the main source of greenhouse gas emissions. Countries also disagreed over the strength of the language on climate action and whether the proposed text adequately addressed the financing needs of developing countries.

The breakdown is not without precedent. At COP6 in The Hague, Netherlands, in November 2000, negotiations also collapsed after countries failed to resolve disputes over emissions reductions, carbon sinks, compliance and financial support for developing nations. Conference president Jan Pronk suspended the talks without an agreement. Negotiations resumed in Bonn the following year, where countries eventually reached a compromise.

The disputes were different, but both conferences exposed the difficulty of reaching consensus when countries have competing priorities over climate action, financing and responsibility.

At COP31, the European Union found itself at the center of a dispute over the conference’s political outcome, this time insisting that any agreement must explicitly address fossil fuels. Speaking on behalf of the bloc, Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, said: “We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.”

The EU’s position, however, drew criticism from climate campaigners who accused the bloc of applying pressure on fossil-fuel language while resisting financing commitments needed by developing countries. Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, said the EU could not distance itself from the outcome of negotiations in which it had also played a role.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition,” Adow said in a response to the EU’s rejection of the final text.

Russia, meanwhile, opposed language on fossil fuels, warning that reducing supply faster than demand could cause price shocks and energy shortages. Saudi Arabia argued that all proposed solutions should remain available. The disagreement left governments unable to reach the consensus required to adopt the two decisions.

The dispute was not simply about whether fossil fuels should be mentioned. It was also about whether the conference would reaffirm commitments made at previous summits or weaken them through a new political text. More than 130 countries had called for stronger action on transitioning away from fossil fuels, following the commitment reached at COP28 in Dubai. The proposed Antalya Pact did not include that language, prompting objections from countries that said the text fell short of what science and previous agreements required.

Vanuatu’s delegation said the proposed decision was silent on “fossil fuels, the principal driver of the climate crisis.” It also warned: “Consensus must never come at the expense of our people’s survival, sovereignty and future generations.”

The conference nevertheless produced decisions in areas where governments were able to reach agreement. One of the most significant was the Global Goal on Adaptation, which seeks to measure whether countries are becoming better able to cope with the effects of climate change.

At COP30 in Brazil, countries agreed on 59 indicators intended to help track adaptation progress. But questions remained over how the indicators would be measured and whether countries had the technical capacity to use them. At COP31, governments agreed to establish a technical task force of national experts to refine the indicators and develop guidance for their use by October 2027.

The agreement is a step towards making adaptation progress more measurable, but it does not itself provide the money countries need to implement projects. That distinction is important for countries such as Liberia, where coastal erosion, flooding, extreme heat and pressure on agriculture require investments in infrastructure, public services and community protection.

An aerial view of flooding in Liberia after heavy rains left communities affected and families in need of food and other essential supplies. Photo:Mamadou Jallow/WFP.

Another decision was reached on the Just Transition Work Programme, which was extended for three years. The program provides a space for countries to discuss how the shift to lower-emission economies can protect workers, communities and people whose livelihoods depend on industries affected by climate policies.

However, governments did not settle the operational arrangements for the Just Transition Mechanism agreed at COP30. Disagreements over its governance and institutional arrangements meant those decisions were postponed until COP32 in 2027. The extension keeps discussions going, but countries have yet to agree on how the mechanism will provide practical support.

Other negotiations ended less successfully. Governments failed to reach agreement on the Mitigation Work Programme, which was due for renewal. The program provides a forum for countries to discuss ways to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Russia and Saudi Arabia objected to the draft decision, leaving the program without an agreed continuation at COP31.

Draft decisions on response measures and the Global Environment Facility also failed to secure adoption. The closing-day negotiations report documented the rejection of these draft decisions, leaving several issues unresolved as countries prepare for the next round of negotiations.

Climate finance remained one of the most difficult issues, particularly for developing countries that need funding to prepare for climate impacts they have contributed relatively little to causing.

At COP30, countries had agreed to efforts to triple adaptation finance by 2035. But developing countries came to Antalya seeking clarity on how that increase would be measured and delivered, including a baseline for calculating progress, predictable funding and stronger accountability from developed countries.

The African Group of Negotiators had also pressed for finance that is concessional and grant-based, rather than loans that add to the debt burdens of countries already struggling to fund basic services.

“Ambition needs to be supported by ambitious levels of finance,” Debra-Lee Swanepoel, the African Group’s finance thematic lead, said during a November 19 briefing on the group’s priorities.

The proposed Antalya Pact included language on accelerating adaptation finance and addressing barriers such as high borrowing costs, limited fiscal space and unsustainable debt. But because the overarching decisions were not adopted, those proposals did not become agreed outcomes. The conference did not resolve developing countries’ demand for a clear pathway to deliver the adaptation-finance commitment.

The Climate Action Network, a global coalition of climate organizations, criticized the outcome, accusing wealthy countries of blocking measures intended to strengthen support for vulnerable nations.

“Simply recalling the COP30 commitment to triple adaptation finance means nothing without a baseline or delivery plan. It remains an empty promise,” said Pooja Dave, the network’s adaptation lead.

The network cited annual adaptation needs of $305 billion by 2035, rising to $420 billion when adjusted for inflation, and said the Adaptation Fund had raised barely $50 million against a $300 million annual target. In its statement on COP31 , the network said wealthy countries had obstructed measures that could have strengthened finance and accountability for climate action in developing countries.

Mohammed Kamal of the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives, in an earlier interview , said the finance problem begins with the scale of the commitment itself. He argued that the $300 billion annual goal agreed at COP29 in Baku was far below the $1.3 trillion sought by African and other developing countries.

“Some African negotiators decided back then that it’s better to take something instead of nothing. And that’s quite problematic,” Kamal said.

He said the problem was not only the size of the target, but also how much of the money committed actually reaches projects and whether countries receive grants or loans. For countries such as Liberia, he argued, borrowing to protect forests, coastal communities and other resources can create repayment obligations for projects that do not generate income.

Kamal also questioned whether African countries were using their collective influence strongly enough in the negotiations. Although the continent has a common negotiating position through the African Group, he said governments needed stronger political coordination and should be more direct in challenging countries that fail to deliver promised support.

He offered a deliberately provocative example: African leaders could consider refusing to attend one future climate summit if their demands continued to be ignored.

“Imagine a COP where all 54 say we’re not joining the next COP. How would that be?” he said.

Kamal acknowledged that such a move would require political decisions beyond the conference itself, potentially through the African Union. His broader argument was that African governments should not continue attending the annual meetings without using their collective political weight to demand stronger outcomes.

The disappointment over the failed political deal was also expressed by Guterres, who called on developed countries to turn their adaptation-finance promises into concrete commitments.

“Put dates and dollars behind that pledge now. Lives depend on it,” he said, referring to the commitment to increase adaptation finance.

Simon Stiell, the United Nations climate change executive secretary, also acknowledged the failure to agree on the two Presidency-led decisions. But he cautioned against treating the entire conference as a failure.

“I share the deep disappointment of many: COP31 has been unable to agree on issues related to both Presidencies’ led decisions,” Stiell said in his closing remarks .

“At this COP, key negotiating decisions have been made including on a Just Transition. Fairness and inclusion in the climate fight is absolutely essential.”
