World.title: 19 Vubwi households left homeless
World.content:
-Nineteen households have been left homeless after a heavy downpour accompanied by strong winds destroyed houses in Sindemisale Ward of Vubwi district in Eastern Province.

The disaster also resulted in the destruction of household property, food supplies including mealie meal, maize, groundnuts and farming inputs including fertiliser.

Some houses had their roofs completely blown off, while others sustained partial damage to their walls, with no lives lost and no injuries recorded during the incident, despite leaving affected families facing difficulties in rebuilding their homes and restoring their livelihoods.

One of the affected residents, Damalesi Mwale said she was distressed by the loss of essential household items and the uncertainty of where she could find alternative shelter with her children.

Ms Mwale said the disaster has also affected her farming arrangements following the destroyed fertiliser and other farming inputs.

“I have nowhere to sleep with my children, and I do not know how I will manage my farming activities after losing my essential items,” she said.

Another victim, Alex Phiri said rebuilding his damaged house will be a major challenge because he was already experiencing financial difficulties.

Mr Phiri, however, expressed gratitude that his family escaped the disaster unharmed.

Acting District Commissioner Musinda Lunkuntwe who visited the affected families alongside the Council Chairperson, sympathised with the victims, acknowledging the difficulties caused by the disaster and its impact on family security and national development.

Mr Lunkuntwe said the government understood the challenges facing the affected households and would engage relevant higher offices to explore possible assistance.

He disclosed that an assessment of the affected areas had already been conducted, with only the compilation of the findings remaining before the report can be submitted to the relevant authorities.

“We understand the challenges these families are going through, and following the assessment, we will engage the higher offices to see how assistance can be provided,” he said.

And Vubwi Council Chairperson Debby Zulu has appealed to the government to urgently intervene by providing temporary shelter to the affected households.

Mr Zulu said the immediate provision of tents would help families find shelter as they begin recovering from the disaster.

He also appealed to well-wishers and other stakeholders to come on board and assist the affected families with essential supplies.

The Council Chairperson further urged residents to revisit and strengthen their rooftops to minimise similar destruction during heavy rains and strong winds.

He emphasised the importance of planting trees as windbreaks, to help protect communities against strong winds, particularly amid changing climatic conditions.

The disaster has left the affected households facing the difficult task of rebuilding their homes and restoring their livelihoods as they await possible government intervention.

World.title: Masvingo hospital among Treasury’s priority projects
World.content:
FINANCE minister Mthuli Ncube has listed the rehabilitation of Masvingo Provincial Hospital among its priority projects as government expands access to healthcare and improves medical services in underserved communities.

Presenting the 2027 National Budget last week, Ncube said the hospital was among the health infrastructure projects targeted for completion next year.

He said focus would be on construction of 26 primary and secondary care health facilities in underserved communities, in addition to the completion of Lupane and Masvingo provincial hospitals, and two urban district hospitals in Harare and Bulawayo.

World.title: Ancient Chinese healing finds new following in Zimbabwe
World.content:
An ancient system of medicine developed thousands of years ago in China is gradually finding a place in Zimbabwe’s healthcare landscape, as more patients explore acupuncture and other traditional therapies for pain management, rehabilitation and general wellbeing.

Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), which incorporates acupuncture, herbal medicine, nutritional therapy and therapeutic massage, is based on a holistic understanding of health that considers the relationship between the body, mind and an individual’s overall wellbeing.

In Harare, one Zimbabwean practitioner, Richard Mutingwende is seeking to expand access to the system after undergoing specialised training through a partnership between the Zimbabwean and Chinese governments.

World.title: Forest Commission wins Movember football contest as men’s health takes centre stage
World.content:
FOREST Commission emerged as winners of the Generation Health Movember Soccer Tournament at Vainona High School in Harare on Saturday, as more than 200 people gathered for a football competition that doubled as a platform for men’s health awareness and medical education.

The tournament, organised by Generation Health in partnership with Men’s Clinic International, brought together teams from various organisations, using football to encourage men to engage with health issues they often shy away from discussing.

Forest Commission secured the title after a penalty shootout, with the final ending 0-0 against Renovation Construction in regulation time before the teams were separated by spot-kicks.

World.content:

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 24, 2026
World.content:
Amnesty Seeks War Crimes Probe Into Deadly Ethiopia Attacks

Amnesty International is calling for an investigation into possible war crimes following artillery attacks by Ethiopian government forces and their Tigray Peace Forces allies that killed at least 14 civilians in Alamata, northern Tigray, between 26 and 28 September. The organisation said the shelling struck densely populated neighbourhoods, including residential homes and commercial areas, and injured numerous others. Amnesty also found that Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters had established military bases in residential areas and schools, putting civilians at risk. However, it stressed that this did not justify indiscriminate attacks and called for an independent international investigation and accountability for those responsible. The Ethiopian military and its allies had not responded to Amnesty's allegations at the time of publication, while the TPLF rejected the claims against its forces.

Sudan Famine Driven by War, Not Natural Disaster – Report



Nearly 19.5 million people in Sudan are facing crisis levels of hunger or worse, with the risk of famine remaining high in several parts of the country, according to the World Food Programme and a report by the Somoud Alliance. The ongoing war, displacement, restrictions on humanitarian aid, destruction of farmland and markets, and rising food prices have worsened food insecurity, with around five million people facing emergency levels of hunger and 135,000 in catastrophic conditions. An estimated 825,000 children under five are also expected to suffer acute malnutrition in 2026. The alliance has called for an immediate ceasefire, safe humanitarian access and increased international funding to prevent further loss of life. It warned that funding shortages are leaving many households with only half their food rations, while attacks on aid workers and convoys continue to obstruct relief efforts.

DR Congo Fighting Traps Ebola Responders in Hospital

Heavy fighting near a hospital in the Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ituri province has forced Ebola responders and World Health Organization staff to shelter in a maternity ward for more than 24 hours. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said teams were working to evacuate trapped staff safely and called for protection for healthcare workers, patients, and medical facilities. The violence has disrupted efforts to contain the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, with Ituri accounting for more than two-thirds of confirmed cases. The outbreak has recorded 11,762 confirmed cases and 5,775 deaths across eight provinces, according to figures released on 20 November. The WHO has also verified more than 87 attacks on healthcare facilities and workers in the DR Congo since the beginning of the year.

Borno School Enrolment Nearly Doubles After Years of Boko Haram Violence

Education is gradually recovering in Nigeria's northeastern Borno State after more than a decade of Boko Haram violence forced schools to close and displaced thousands of families. Government figures show enrolment in public and private schools increased to 1.4 million learners in 2025, up from about 766,000 during the 2017-2018 academic year. Authorities said that they have built 104 new schools and renovated nearly 3,000 classrooms. The number of out-of-school children has reportedly fallen from 2.2 million to fewer than 800,000. However, insecurity, poverty, teacher shortages and limited access to schools in rural communities continue to threaten efforts to restore education. Officials said that rebuilding confidence among parents and ensuring children receive adequate learning support remain key to sustaining the progress.

Zimbabwean Preacher Uebert Angel Arrested on Sexual Assault Allegations

Prominent Zimbabwean preacher Uebert Angel has been arrested in Harare on allegations of indecent assault and sodomy. The founder of Spirit Embassy was reportedly detained during a church service. The police are yet to provide details about the allegations or confirm when he will appear in court. Angel, who was appointed Zimbabwe's special presidential envoy and ambassador-at-large in 2021. He previously faced controversy following a 2023 Al Jazeera undercover investigation that alleged he offered to use his diplomatic status to facilitate money laundering through a gold-smuggling scheme. He has also previously faced allegations of sexual impropriety, which he denied. A member of his team confirmed that he remained in police custody. The timing of his court appearance was still unclear.

Close 

Final Verdict Due in Senegal-Morocco AFCON Title Dispute

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) is set to deliver its ruling on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip the country of its 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title and award it to Morocco. Senegal initially won the January final 1-0 after extra time, but the Confederation of African Football's appeals board overturned the result in March, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match after players walked off the pitch in protest over a controversial penalty decision. Morocco was subsequently awarded a 3-0 victory. Senegal's football federation challenged the decision, describing it as unfair, and is seeking to have the original result reinstated. The ruling could have wider implications for CAF's credibility and the application of tournament regulations. CAS's decision will be final, barring limited grounds for a further appeal before Switzerland's highest court, potentially bringing an end to the months-long dispute.

Johannesburg residents have been warned to prepare for more severe thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail and strong winds, reports EWN. World.title: Zimbabwe: 2027 Budget Tax Relief Still Leaves Poor Households Below Poverty Line - MPs Told
World.content:
A vendor who requested that his face not be shown holds bills of Zimbabwe's outgoing currency, in Harare, April 15, 2024.

THE 2027 National Budget offers some tax relief to low-income earners but falls short of lifting vulnerable households out of poverty, Public Finance Specialist Pepukai Chivore has told MPs.

Presenting his analysis during a Post-Budget Seminar on Monday, Chivore said the budget's ZiG349.5 billion revenue target, equivalent to 18.1% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), offered some relief to low-income workers but left marginalised groups exposed to persistent economic hardship.

He argued that the biggest burden could fall on small informal traders, while tax concessions for low-income earners remained too small to improve their living standards significantly.

Under the proposals, the tax-free threshold rises from US$100 to US$150, at an estimated cost of US$81 million to Treasury.



For a worker earning the US$270 minimum wage, Pay As You Earn (PAYE) would fall to US$24.72, leaving take-home pay of US$245.28.

However, this remains below the estimated US$253 poverty line for a five-person household.

"Adequate relief for single earners at the bottom; not enough to lift a one-wage household clear of the poverty line," Chivore said.

He noted that the revised tax-free threshold represented only 56% of the minimum wage and failed to account for workers supporting dependants.

Chivore proposed indexing the tax-free threshold to the poverty line and introducing a tax credit for dependants to provide more meaningful relief to low-income households.

Domestic workers earning between US$90 and US$117 a month are exempt from PAYE under the proposed threshold.

However, Chivore said the exemption did not necessarily translate into improved living standards, as their earnings remained less than half the poverty line.

"That is protection, but not prosperity. Their earnings are still less than half the poverty line. With VAT at 15.5%, every purchase still carries tax," he said.

He identified informal traders as facing the greatest risk under the proposed tax measures.

The budget introduces a US$500,000 VAT compliance surcharge per tax period for unregistered traders, a provision Chivore warned was disproportionate because it was not linked to business turnover.

He said the measure could wipe out a small trader's business over a compliance failure, regardless of the scale of their operations.

Chivore also questioned the contribution of the mining sector, which accounts for 14.5% of GDP and 75% of exports but reportedly paid an effective tax rate of just 14% in 2024.

He called for proper costing of every budget measure, a comprehensive tax gap study and stronger efforts to close revenue leakages in the mining sector.

Close 

"The relief is real but narrow, and the structural gap is the tax base, not the poor. Treasury must tax wealth and large leakages, not the vendor and domestic worker already at the poverty line," he said.

World.title: Ethiopia: Lethal Artillery Strikes On Civilian Neighbourhoods in Tigray's Alamata City Must Be Investigated As War Crimes
World.content:
Artillery attacks by Ethiopia's military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) that killed dozens of civilians and injured many more in the city of Alamata in the northern region of Tigray, between 26 and 28 September, must be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization also found that forces affiliated to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), put civilians in harm's way by establishing military bases in populated residential areas, including in several schools in Alamata, prior to the outbreak of renewed fighting in the region.

The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and its TPF allies seized control of the strategic city of Alamata, a key supply hub for troops, food, and fuel, from the TPLF on 28 September.



"For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants. The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes," said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director, Regional Human Rights Impact.

"For three consecutive days, the ENDF and TPF repeatedly shelled Alamata in total disregard of the lives of its 80,000 inhabitants.Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Regional Director for Human Rights Impact

Amnesty International investigated four incidents of artillery shelling on Alamata by the ENDF and TPF between 26 and 28 September and independently verified the deaths of 14 civilians in these attacks. Researchers interviewed 28 individuals, including survivors, witnesses, relatives of victims, humanitarian and medical personnel. Amnesty International's Evidence Lab analysed eight videos and 17 photographs, as well as satellite imagery of the site and other open-source information.

All names and identifying details have been withheld or changed to protect interviewees who requested anonymity.

Amnesty International wrote to the ENDF, TPF, and TPLF on 27 October, requesting information about these incidents. On 17 November, the organization shared its investigation findings with the ENDF and TPF and invited their comments. ENDF and TPF had not provided a response as at the time of publication.

The use of artillery, a weapon with wide-area effects, in densely populated neighbourhoods has a terrible impact on civilians. Indiscriminate attacks violate the rules of international humanitarian law, and these strikes must be investigated as war crimes.Yasmine Ahmed

In a four-page letter sent to Amnesty International on 18 November, the TPLF "categorically reject[ed]" the allegations made against it.

"While the preliminary findings acknowledge certain atrocities committed by the Ethiopian Federal Government and its forces we are deeply concerned by the allegations directed against the Tigray Security Forces [TPLF]. We categorically reject these allegations as unfounded and believe that they require further independent, impartial, and comprehensive investigation before any conclusions are drawn regarding responsibility" stated the letter sent by the TPLF.

Residential neighbourhoods at the mercy of ENDF and TPF Artillery shelling

Based on interviews with residents and two sources with direct knowledge of military movements during the offensive, Amnesty International identified Waja Ena Tumuga area as the main location from which ENDF and TPF forces shelled Alamata, approximately 13 kilometers south of the city. Two individuals with close knowledge of the TPF's military capabilities told the organization that the TPF possessed artillery weaponry and participated alongside the ENDF in the operation to capture Alamata. One eyewitness saw ENDF forces moving their artillery into Waja, particularly the area that is called Ayer Marefiya.

Witnesses also told Amnesty International that the TPLF based themselves in and, in some instances, launched attacks from densely populated civilian areas in the city.

International humanitarian law requires all parties to a conflict to avoid, to the maximum extent feasible, placing military objectives within or near densely populated areas. They are also obliged to protect civilians from the effects of attacks by facilitating the evacuation of civilians from the vicinity of military objectives and giving effective warning of attacks that may affect the civilian population.

Any possible violation of international humanitarian law by TPLF through placing their forces and military objects inside densely populated neighbourhoods, does not absolve the ENDF and its allies of their obligations and can never justify the indiscriminate use of explosive weapons, such as artillery, in a densely populated area.Yasmine Ahmed

Even though TPLF fighters possessed artillery capabilities and were actively launching artillery, it is highly unlikely that the shelling of Alamata was caused by direct shelling from their own forces within the city. While the possibility of technical failures cannot be fully dismissed, the likelihood of such a scenario is extremely low.

"Any possible violation of international humanitarian law by TPLF through placing their forces and military objects inside densely populated neighbourhoods, does not absolve the ENDF and its allies of their obligations and can never justify the indiscriminate use of explosive weapons, such as artillery, in a densely populated area," said Yasmine Ahmed.

A medical worker, who was on duty in Alamata hospital between 26 and 28 September, told Amnesty International that almost all casualties recorded during those three days were civilians and that most of the injuries appeared to have been caused by shrapnel from explosive munitions.

Indiscriminate attacks on populated areas

One of the neighbourhoods most heavily hit by shelling was an area commonly known as the condominium area in Kebele 04, a densely populated area comprised mostly of houses and two multi-story buildings, which house hundreds of civilians and are adjacent to the single-family homes that were struck. Three eyewitnesses told Amnesty International that artillery struck five houses on 27 September at dawn, killing seven people and injuring four others.

Among those killed was Meron Sewasew, a 26-year-old mother of two, who died inside her home alongside her eight-year-old son, Markon Girmahiwot, and her older brother, Tewekel Sewasew, 33. Meron's husband, Girmahiwot Negash [real name], said their two-year-old son was also in the house at the time of the attack but survived with minor injuries.

"I was away from the city for work. They were staying in the house because it was supposed to be safe from the war. She was my high school love, and our story ended too soon," Girmahiwot said.

The same artillery attack also killed four members of a family living next door: Kumhis Kahsay, 40, and her 14-year-old child Helina Hailay, alongside Lezeu Yirga, 38, and her three-year old child.

I was away from the city for work. They were staying in the house because it was supposed to be safe from the war. She was my high school love, and our story ended too soon.Girmahiwot

"Kumhis came from church that morning. All of the victims were outside the house doing chores. Kumhis, the older sister, was baking injera in the compound. I was inside the house. The remnants of the strike landed in the compound and struck them," said a family member who survived the attack.

Amnesty International's Evidence Lab verified four videos that showed damage to the two houses and one external structure within a compound located some 150 meters from Werknesh Hotel, a hotel which residents said had housed TPLF fighters.

"I saw TDF [TPLF] fighters on top of tall buildings with their weapons. They were telling us not to come closer. Some were staying at the Werknesh Hotel.... they were telling people to use a different route," said an eyewitness who was in the area on 26 September.

Another individual who was near the hotel on the day of the attack told Amnesty International that TPLF fighters were not present near the hotel on the day of the strike. Amnesty International could not independently verify whether TPLF fighters were inside or near the hotel at the time. Three eyewitnesses said that minutes before artillery shells struck nearby residential homes, a separate strike fell just outside the hotel, causing significant damage to its exterior.

The ENDF and TPF also shelled areas where residents said there was no military presence.

On 26 September, artillery hit a local bar called Nigus Shimoy at around 11am, killing at least three people, according to a survivor who was injured in the attack and one witness. The bar is located at the entrance of a bustling market in a predominantly commercial area, bordering residential neighbourhoods. The attack took place as people came out en masse to celebrate Demera, the eve celebration of Meskel (Finding of the True Cross) holiday of the Ethiopian Orthodox Christians.

I saw TDF [TPLF] fighters on top of tall buildings with their weapons. They were telling us not to come closer. Some were staying at the Werknesh Hotel.... they were telling people to use a different route.Eyewitness

On 27 September, shelling hit a family home in another residential area, Kebele 02. Deyima Rebso, 55, was killed immediately in the attack in her home, while her husband, Ararse Yasin, 62, survived with severe injuries, according to an eyewitness. Their children, Saliha and Kedir, and grandchild, 10-year-old Sufiyan Abdulatif, also sustained serious injuries. Amnesty International's weapons investigator identified munitions fragments recovered at the scene as consistent with an artillery round of the type fired by the ENDF and their allies.

One witness told Amnesty International that the house was the only structure to be struck in the area and that no military activity had been observed in the vicinity prior to the attack.

TPLF set up military bases in schools

Six people interviewed by Amnesty International said almost all schools in Alamata were used by TPLF fighters as military bases in the months before the outbreak of renewed hostilities. Witnesses said several schools, most of which were located close to civilian neighbourhoods, had been the site of military operations, including the launching of artillery shells after the renewed conflict began. All residents interviewed for this research said the TPLF didn't issue any warnings or evacuation orders for residents near these locations.

On 26 September, an artillery shell struck a house in a highly populated neighbourhood known as Missionary Camp, near to Biruh Tesfa School, which had been used by the TPLF as a base. The attack, which occurred at around 6:45 pm, killed three civilians and injured four others. One witness said most of the fighters had left a week before the fighting broke out. Another saw a few fighters guarding the school in the days leading up to the strike.

Amnesty International could not independently confirm whether the school was ever attacked and whether or not the school was still harbouring fighters by the time of the strike. No damage or destruction was clearly visible in satellite imagery at the Biruh Tesfa school north of the charity compound.

A resident living near Alamata Preparatory School, another school, said that the school was targeted by an ENDF drone strike on 22 September. He said the school had been the main site from which TPLF launched artillery strikes to defend Alamata, until they began withdrawing from the city on 28 September.

Close 

"The explosion of weapons after it was hit by drone strikes affected the city, and we also saw some remnants fly by my house. There was artillery inside the school compound. We saw the weapons burning in the school that day," said the resident.

Satellite imagery confirms a new burn scar became visible adjacent to the school on 22 September, aligning with the reports of a drone strike. Changes in vegetation were also detected around the school between 24 September and 1 October, though high-resolution imagery is not available to confirm the reason for the changes. Higher-resolution imagery from 21 October shows the clearing in more detail, along with a burned area within the trees.

"Civilians are paying the ultimate price for the failure to hold perpetrators accountable in past and ongoing conflicts in Ethiopia. Impunity has emboldened perpetrators to carry on committing serious violations with no fear of the consequences. This must end. The UN Human Rights Council must act fast to establish an independent mechanism to investigate, identify those responsible for crimes under international law, and ensure they are held accountable," said Yasmine Ahmed.

"Amnesty International also calls on the Ethiopian authorities to cooperate with independent international monitors, journalists, and humanitarian organizations to gain unhindered access to all conflict-impacted areas in the country.

Impunity has emboldened perpetrators to carry on committing serious violations with no fear of the consequences. This must end. The UN Human Rights Council must act fast to establish an independent mechanism to investigate, identify those responsible for crimes under international law, and ensure they are held accountable.Yasmine Ahmed

"Considering the Ethiopian authorities' persistent failure to ensure justice and accountability for crimes under international law, particularly where state forces themselves are alleged to have committed serious violations, urgent international scrutiny is needed. This is especially critical given the authorities' record of suppressing independent human rights monitoring and the fact that Ethiopia is currently facing three ongoing armed conflicts, with growing risks of wider regional escalation" said Yasmine Ahmed.

Background

The armed conflict between the ENDF and its allies, including the TPF and other allied security and informal militia forces, and the TPLF and allies, including Amhara Fano forces and six other organized political and armed groups, erupted on 21 September 2026.

Fighting spread across three principal fronts initially: in southern Tigray, particularly the Raya Kobo Zone; western Afar (Zone 2); and the Wag Hemra Zone of the Amhara Region.

Since 21 September, the ENDF has carried out multiple aerial strikes in the southern Tigray, including in and around Alamata city.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Heavy Fighting in Ituri Traps DR Congo Ebola Responders - WHO
World.content:
Heavy fighting near a hospital in Ituri province in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has disrupted the vital work of Ebola responders and forced emergency teams to take cover for more than 24 hours.

In a post on X on Sunday, World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said that agency staff and Ebola responders had been forced to shelter "for their lives" in a maternity ward of the hospital.

The WHO chief added that the agency was working with partners to evacuate trapped staff safely, before calling for their "immediate safe passage and for the hospital facilities, staff and patients to be protected".

Since 1 January, WHO has verified more than 87 attacks on healthcare in DRC.



The development follows a warning earlier this month by the UN's Senior Ebola Response Coordinator, Julien Harneis, that more people have been killed by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters than by the Ebola vitus in recent days. "The violence in tens of villages all across the south of Ituri and North Kivu (provinces) goes unnoticed", Mr. Harneis insisted. "People are scared; people are furious at the lack of action on this."

Repeated ADF attacks and human rights abuses against civilians have been happening for more than two decades in eastern DRC. "Following up contact tracing in areas where ADF is operating is a very hazardous idea," Mr. Harneis told journalists in Geneva on 13 November.

Ituri province remains the epicentre of the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus and accounts for more than two-thirds of confirmed cases.

A total of eight provinces have been impacted and the latest incident near the hospital in Ituri happened in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak was first detected.

Increasing violence

WHO has warned repeatedly that rising insecurity in eastern DRC is one of the main obstacles to containing the virus, with attacks on civilians and health workers hampering response efforts.

More than six months after it was first declared, the Ebola outbreak in eastern DRC continues to spread. A high proportion of deaths continue to occur in communities and outside dedicated treatment centres, especially among young children, highlighting challenges in early case detection and access to care.

According to figures released on 20 November, the outbreak has resulted in 11,762 confirmed cases, including 5,775 deaths, across 68 health zones in eight provinces.

Danger zone

Ituri remains the hardest-hit province, with a cumulative total of more than 8,000 confirmed cases and 3,791 deaths, representing a case fatality rate of 47 per cent. The province accounts for more than two-thirds of all confirmed cases and nearly 60 per cent of newly reported infections.

Close 

Of the 39 new confirmed cases reported in the latest epidemiological update, 23 were recorded in Ituri.

World.title: Sudan: 'Famine in Sudan Is a Product of War, Not a Natural Disaster' - Reports
World.content:
In November, trucks finally arrived at the famine-stricken Zamzam camp in North Darfur.

Amsterdam — The World Food Programme (WFP) says the risk of famine remains a major concern in parts of Sudan, with around 19.5 million people facing crisis levels of hunger or worse. A report by the humanitarian working group of the Somoud Alliance attributes the famine to the continuing war, restrictions on aid, displacement, and the destruction of livelihoods, rather than natural causes.

The World Food Programme (WFP) says the risk of famine remains a major concern in parts of Sudan. According to a report seen by Radio Dabanga, an Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) analysis found that approximately 19.5 million people faced crisis levels of hunger or worse between February and May 2026. This means that households are experiencing severe food shortages or being forced to sell essential possessions and other assets to obtain food.

The European Union has separately highlighted Sudan's enormous humanitarian needs, reporting that 33.7 million people require humanitarian assistance, 19.1 million face acute food insecurity, more than nine million are internally displaced, and 4.4 million are living outside the country.

Meanwhile, the humanitarian working group of the Somoud Alliance has stressed in a report that famine in Sudan is linked to the continuation of the war rather than natural conditions. Other contributing factors include the obstruction and politicisation of aid, looting, displacement and loss of income, the destruction of farmland, markets, and transport networks, rising food and fuel prices, shortages of agricultural inputs, extreme weather conditions, inadequate international funding, and the spread of disease. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 37 per cent of health facilities have ceased operating.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The report identifies children under five, pregnant and breastfeeding women, people with disabilities, displaced people, refugees and returnees, older people, those without an income, farmers and pastoralists, and residents of besieged areas as the groups most severely affected.

Food insecurity indicators and the response funding gap

The Somoud Alliance humanitarian working group's report estimates that approximately 19.5 million people - around 41 per cent of the population - are facing high levels of food insecurity. This includes around five million people in the Emergency phase and 135,000 in the Catastrophe phase of food insecurity. An estimated 825,000 children under five are expected to suffer from acute malnutrition during 2026.

The report points to WHO warnings in October 2026 of an escalating risk of famine in parts of Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Many households are receiving only half their food rations because of funding shortages, while aid convoys and humanitarian workers are facing attacks and looting.

The report also highlights funding shortages and administrative obstacles. In February 2026, the United Nations launched a Humanitarian Response Plan worth USD 2.87 billion, but funding remains severely inadequate.

By 31 July 2026, UNICEF had secured only USD 352.2 million of its USD 962.9 million funding requirement, leaving a 63 per cent shortfall. Funding for the health sector had reached just 36 per cent of its USD 325 million requirement.

Visa and work-permit restrictions, harassment of emergency response rooms, and the bombing of aid supplies are also hampering relief efforts.

Impact of famine across Sudan and areas at risk

The report says Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan are experiencing fighting, sieges, displacement, the closure of markets, and the destruction of crops and livestock. Malnutrition and disease are spreading, while shortages of water and medical treatment, together with the isolation of communities, are worsening conditions.

In Khartoum and El Gezira, infrastructure, services, and markets have been damaged, while sources of income have been lost. Returning families face the risk of hunger and unemployment, a shortage of housing, and disruption to the winter agricultural season.

Eastern and central states, particularly Red Sea, Kassala, and Gedaref, are under considerable pressure from displacement. This is driving up prices, placing additional strain on services, and threatening agricultural production because of the rising costs of agricultural inputs and fuel.

Meanwhile, White Nile, Blue Nile, and Sennar are experiencing displacement, declining agricultural production, and increasing pressure on host communities.

According to the reports, famine hotspots include 14 locations and displacement settlements in North Darfur and South Kordofan.

In North Darfur, these include El Tina and its surrounding settlements, Karnoi, Um Baru and its surrounding settlements, El Fasher, and the Tawila displacement settlement.

In South Kordofan, they include El Buram and its surrounding settlements, Delling, Kadugli and its surrounding settlements, and the Um Doreen settlement.

Close 

However, Beleil locality in South Darfur has been removed from the list of areas projected to face famine risk between October and January, owing to expected improvements following the harvest.

Calls for action

The Somoud Alliance has called for an immediate and sustained ceasefire, protection for civilians and humanitarian workers, and the opening of safe humanitarian corridors and border crossings under neutral supervision. It has also called for an independent national system to manage humanitarian assistance, with the participation of Sudanese civil society.

The alliance has urged increased funding and support for local initiatives, as well as the provision of food, therapeutic nutrition, water, healthcare, shelter, and agricultural inputs.

It has also called for transparency in data reporting, an end to the use of starvation as a weapon and the weaponisation of humanitarian assistance, and accountability for those responsible for violations.

The report concludes that saving lives depends on urgent international action to end the war, open access routes, and fund the humanitarian response before famine claims more Sudanese lives.

World.title: South Sudan: MSF Suspends All Activities in Yei River County Following Abduction
World.content:
press release

Juba — Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders (MSF) suspended all its activities for a minimum of three months starting Tuesday 17 November, in South Sudan’s Yei River County, Central Equatoria State, after armed assailants abducted an MSF staff member and a Ministry of Health midwife on Thursday 12 November. Although both staff members were released unharmed on Saturday 14 November, this incident highlights the continuation of violence against healthcare workers in South Sudan.

MSF denounces in the strongest terms the abduction of humanitarian and medical workers as utterly unacceptable. MSF calls upon authorities and other actors to take responsibility and act decisively to put an end to these incidents.

"The suspension of services was a painful and uneasy decision, given the people's needs in the area, particularly among vulnerable groups, such as pregnant and lactating women, children and the elderly," says Dr Ferdinand Atte, MSF's Head of Mission in South Sudan. "In addition, we had to suspend MSF’s support to the Ebola preparedness, in particular for the management of the isolation facility, which could have dramatic consequences in case of the outbreak in the area."

Only a substantial, sustained and verifiable improvement in the security environment, together with concrete measures to prevent and actively combat abduction crimes would allow MSF to restart activities. At present, no such conditions are in place. "MSF cannot continue operating in Yei area while abductions are now taking place even within the town. The safety and security of our staff comes first," adds Dr Atte.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In August 2025, MSF was forced to temporarily suspend all activities in the same county following two abductions in just over a week. "Following last year's abductions, we received verbal assurances from authorities that medical staff and patients would be safe and protected within the 5-mile radius around Yei," adds Dr Atte. However, on 17 November, armed assailants stopped the MSF ambulance approximately 3 miles from the town.

The MSF driver and Ministry of Health midwife were abducted after an MSF ambulance was stopped at gunpoint by unknown armed assailants while heading back to Jansuk from the Yei Civil Hospital, after referring patients. The incident took place 500 metres from the Jansuk primary healthcare facility.

This was the fifth abduction affecting MSF in Yei River County since 2024, following a period of bombardments, attacks, looting and vandalism of MSF facilities throughout South Sudan. All actors must fulfil their obligations to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, including healthcare workers, patients, and medical facilities. Healthcare workers must never be targeted.

MSF was supporting Yei Civil Hospital and Jansuk clinic, performing community-based care for gender-based violence, as well as establishing the Ebola Isolation Unit with 10-beds capacity, the only such facility in the County.

Close 

MSF provides medical care to people affected by conflict, displacement and disease outbreaks across six states and two administrative areas in South Sudan, including in areas where hospitals are difficult to reach. MSF has been present in what is today South Sudan since 1983 and remains one of the largest medical humanitarian agencies in the country. From January to October 2026, MSF provided more than 719,349 outpatient consultations (including for children under 5), inpatient care for over 99,658 patients (including 8,771 surgeries), and screened 303,063 children for malnutrition.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Have Drones Given M23 a Regular Army's Reach in Eastern DR Congo?
World.content:
analysis

As government forces also expand their aerial arsenal, the strategic value of these systems complicates prospects for de-escalation.

The eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is rapidly emerging as a key theatre of drone warfare. State militaries and non-state actors alike are exploiting technological advances, a thriving military drone market and cheaper access to commercial aerial vehicles that can be adapted for conflict.

Since 2022 both the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) and rebel groups like M23 have been ramping up drone acquisition and use. The Rwanda-backed rebels captured Goma in North Kivu in January 2025 and Bukavu in South Kivu a month later. Many experts believe these gains would have been impossible without an extensive arsenal of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

UAVs are used for intelligence, reconnaissance, surveillance and, increasingly, attack missions. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data's John Ngono notes that 'since July we have seen [increased drone use] by M23 during its counter-offensive to prevent the FARDC from gaining control of Minembwe, a strategic headquarters for M23 in South Kivu.'

Recent shifts in the DRC's political landscape may have contributed to this growing trend. In early October former president Joseph Kabila declared himself leader of the M23-aligned Front for the Refoundation of the Nation.

Fierce fighting followed between M23 and the FARDC and its allied Wazalendo militias. The key focus was an aerial bombing campaign around Uvira - a strategic stronghold near the Burundi border. M23 briefly took the city in December 2025 before the FARDC regained control.

Multiple sources, including the United States (US) Representative to the United Nations (UN), Ambassador Mike Waltz, said M23 used attack drones and Rwanda-supplied artillery during that initial seizure. Several reports suggest the drones were Turkish-made YIHA-IIIs - long-range precision-strike loitering drones.

DRC government-aligned media claim the FARDC shot down three powerful M23 drones during the October offensive, which they claim are Rwanda-supplied long-endurance kamikaze YIHA-III OWA (one-way attack) drones. Rwanda is accused of violating the December 2025 Washington Accords, and numerous senior Rwandan officials face US sanctions.

'We have also seen M23 using civilian or commercial drones and modifying them for their use,' says Ngono. Such drones often require less on-the-ground support and are easier to adapt.

The FARDC's accelerated drone use is also extensively documented. The UN Group of Experts' final report, released in June 2026, says the army has used Turkish long-endurance drones (with 'external technical or operational assistance') and Chinese CH-4 and CH-5 drones. And Burundi has reportedly purchased drones for use in the DRC.

Media reports also suggest the FARDC's capabilities have been enhanced with support from Blackwater founder Erik Prince, a private US military contractor who is part of a DRC military support mission.

All this points to growing drone use, which the International Committee of the Red Cross warns 'drastically' increases the risk of civilian harm. '[More] drones have been used in this past year than in all the previous years' since the military started using drones in the DRC in 2022, says Ngono.

Two main drivers are the terrain and availability. The DRC is vast, and UAVs have given both sides a commanding presence in the skies.

M23's capture of airports and an airstrip has given it the infrastructure to launch larger military-grade drones. It has also enabled the M23 rebels to project power beyond the conflict zone and level the playing field between armed groups and the state.

The UN report says M23 used kamikaze drones in its February 2026 attack on Kisangani airport, some 400 km from the frontline. The rebels claimed the FARDC was using the airport as a military drone command centre.

The attack significantly damaged the control tower and runway. Peter Sereko, a former South African Army brigadier general who commanded an infantry unit in the DRC as part of a stabilisation force, told ISS Today that 'it was just small calibre weapons' a decade ago, 'but ... when I returned to DRC in 2024 ... the M23 had the capability of a regular army.'

UAV advances have also enabled each side to target economic assets. According to FARDC sources, the army has mounted drone strikes on key rebel-held mining sites such as Rubaya, which Ngono says 'produces around 15% of the global coltan supply.' UN experts estimate the site earns M23 US$800 000 a month - revenue that helps the rebels stockpile weapons.

Both sides have relied on external help to restock their drone arsenals, but Ngono believes M23 is depending less on Rwandan trainers and on-the-ground support. Although the rebels may still receive intelligence support and access to mobile air defence systems from Rwanda, technical operations are largely driven by M23 coalition fighters themselves, he says.

Rwanda justifies its military presence in the DRC as protection against the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) militia. As recently as December 2025, UN estimates put the number of Rwanda Defence Force troops at up to 10 000 in South Kivu and 8 000 in North Kivu.

Given drones' strategic, tactical and psychological value, their rapid proliferation in the DRC could complicate military de-escalation and lasting peace. There is mounting evidence that simply possessing UAV capability has significant strategic value, including as a propaganda tool.

Close 

A recent Africa Center for Strategic Studies (ACSS) report notes that 80% of Africa's major armed non-state actors 'have now used small unmanned systems to drop mortars or conduct Kamikaze attacks.' Drones are also growing more sophisticated, with 'capabilities such as fibre-optic controls and AI enabled targeting' that make them harder to detect and neutralise.

The ACSS echoes earlier calls by the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) and others for African governments to consider a more risk-based approach to importing drones and drone parts, and to invest more in anti-drone technologies.

However, an African drone arms race is already underway, with unconfirmed reports that Ukraine is becoming a player in this space - including in the DRC. If so, it would join global and regional powers such as China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates - all with a stake in the DRC conflict.

Karen Allen, ISS Consultant, independent researcher and former BBC foreign correspondent

World.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

World.title: Massachusetts sues Trump admin to stop ICE's courthouse arrests: 'Unnecessary fear'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law.

The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3.

Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion.

"The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement.

DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS

"ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued.

The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026.

Campbell said ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect.

"I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell said.

FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS

Campbell said that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit.

In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests.

The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems.

"The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

In a statement to Reuters, a DHS spokesperson argued that making immigration arrests at courthouses "conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already ​know where a target will ​be," adding that "the ability of law enforcement ⁠to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense."

A similar lawsuit against ICE arrests at state courthouses was filed in October by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

World.title: Trump's Nixon-to-China moment: There's an immigration move only he can make
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"Maybe we could touch the subject of immigration." That was President Trump’s suggestion to host Kayleigh McEnany during his Nov. 21 appearance on Fox News’ "Saturday in America."

If the president deploys his power of pardon for a defined class of illegal immigrants, it will be a "golden touch" for them that will enshrine his memory among their communities and add another achievement of enormous significance to his already lengthy column of them.

Such an act of presidential mercy would be unprecedented—without a parallel mass grant of grace in American history—and it would be approved of by supermajorities of Americans and certain to be counted among his greatest achievements as president by citizens of all political persuasions who have long desired an actual breakthrough on this stalemated front.

TRUMP AND IMMIGRATION REFORM: WILL DEMOCRATS MAKE HIM AN OFFER HE CAN'T REFUSE?

The president’s carefully phrased suggestion to McEnany is a good topic for a Thanksgiving dinner conversation: "What should we as a country do about or to the country’s illegal immigrant population?"

Frame the question this way:

"What do we think about a presidential pardon for, say, the 10% of the illegal immigrant population, people whom everyone here could agree ought to be left alone and free of the fear of deportation?"

The best studies estimate the population of illegal immigrants in the country at between 15 and 20 million. Some crossed the border right up to the day President Trump returned to office, but very few have arrived in the country since the spring of 2025. Trump sealed the southern border, and it remains, for all practical purposes, shuttered. "The Wall" has now been built over more than 750 miles. Another 600 miles of wall are planned between now and the end of Trump’s second term. The Border Patrol is funded through the end of Sept. 2029.

President Trump delivered on his promise to close the border.

On Nov. 8, after being asked by Ross Douthat of "60 Minutes" about deportation policy in the past two years, the president said, "I think it was too tough." President Trump then added, "I think it might be too tough, yeah."

TRUMP CAN FINALLY DELIVER THE IMMIGRATION BARGAIN REAGAN WAS PROMISED

His explanation was straightforward.

Some of the election results on Nov. 3 were "because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

"Now, there is a large part of the country that thinks that they should be put out," he added. "And there's a large part of the country that thinks that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

So, what should be done? What should President Trump do?

FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE

Democratic leaders in Congress have a wide-open door to the Oval Office to negotiate a reasonable set of statutory reforms that are not "amnesty" and don’t involve a "path to citizenship."

But as President Trump has noted on a few occasions, he doesn’t have to wait on them, as he has the "very powerful power of the pardon," which is indeed complete and within his sole control.

He could use the power of pardon on any segment of the illegal immigrant population before COB today or on Thanksgiving if he wanted to.

What might a presidential pardon look like that would (1) reflect the views of a supermajority of Americans and (2) not create an incentive for immigrants to think they should come toward our country or overstay visas?

A number of violations of federal statutes could be the subject of a presidential pardon. Illegal entry into the country is a crime, as is an illegal return after deportation. It is also a civil offense—still within the pardon power—to have entered legally but to have overstayed the permitted time of presence in the country.

TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION OLIVE BRANCH THREATENS TO OPEN PANDORA'S BOX AS EXPERTS WARN OF FAR-REACHING FALLOUT

So ask the people around the table: What would you think of any sort of presidential pardon for those who have broken these laws? Is there a version of one you could endorse and even applaud?

President Jimmy Carter’s pardon of draft dodgers who had broken the Selective Service laws of the Vietnam era is a model and included this language:

"I, Jimmy Carter, President of the United States, do hereby grant a full, complete and unconditional pardon to: (1) all persons who may have committed any offense between August 4, 1964, and March 28, 1973, in violation of the Military Selective Service Act or any rule or regulation promulgated thereunder; and (2) all persons heretofore convicted, irrespective of the date of conviction, of any offense committed between August 4, 1964, and March 28, 1973, in violation of the Military Selective Service Act, or any rule or regulation promulgated thereunder, restoring to them full political, civil and other rights."

On its face, the pardon of 50 years ago was narrowly tailored, and its accompanying language specifically excluded those whose Selective Service violation involved force or violence and those who committed violations in connection with employment as an agent, officer, or employee of the Selective Service System.

It also did not cover military deserters or people who had gone AWOL from the armed forces.

TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

President Trump thus has it within his power to immediately and carefully address the excesses of deportation policy that he knows were "too tough."

Thus, President Trump is in a position to do a Nixon-to-China on illegal immigrants. There might be a "Trump-Schumer-Jeffries Regularization Act" a year down the road, a statute that should not include a general "amnesty" and cannot provide a "pathway to citizenship." Such a statute could provide a detailed legislative change to grant a right of continued residence to a defined subset of illegal immigrants upon a showing of certain conditions, such as no felony arrests, past or future, for people in the country for a decade or more.

But President Trump does not have to wait on Democrats, and indeed he shouldn’t, to make clear it was his decision. Pardon seekers would have to present proof of near-continuous employment and such other evidence of character and commitment as President Trump details in the language of the pardon. A pardon could be very focused and also include such conditions and exclusions as the president deems fit.

President Trump could issue such a pardon today. He can act tomorrow. He can act on Thanksgiving or Christmas. The pardon power is unlimited. If President Trump deploys it carefully, the public would first be thunderstruck and then almost wholly united in praising his act of mercy.

There is a very deep and broad sense of justice and fairness in the American public. The deportation of long-time residents who have worked hard and are raising families—especially those with children born in the country—deeply disturbs most Americans of all political persuasions. Continued deportation of individuals whose life circumstances jar ordinary voters especially upsets legal residents, family members, and friends of illegal immigrants.

Hardly a week goes by without a story of a deportation that elicits the pity of most Americans while triggering anger at government officials who are just applying the law. President Trump can unilaterally defuse the worst assaults on the collective American sense of justice. There will be critics, and they will be loud, but they would actually represent only a tiny portion of the country.

TRUMP BORDER CRACKDOWN DRIVES ENCOUNTERS TO RECORD OCTOBER LOW AS ZERO-RELEASE STREAK HITS 18 MONTHS, DHS SAYS

The deportation excesses of the past two years are also going to be a barrier to the return of Republican majorities in either the House or the Senate if they do not end. Reasonable people will disagree on the specifics of a presidential pardon (or of a statutory "regularization" bill down the road), but—assuming the Bell Curve applies to illegal immigrants—there are more than a million illegal immigrants who ought obviously to be deported as soon as possible and at least a million who are just as obviously good people and community members who should not be rousted out of their lives and deported.

The online world separates quickly from the reality of the American center on this issue, but President Trump intuits he has to course-correct on deportation policy. Thus, there is a great opportunity right now for a legacy achievement via his pardon power and down the road via statutory compromise, if Democrats do not overreach and seek political advantage from a "regularization" bill.

Presidents Obama and Biden could not bring themselves to do the necessary thing prior to such a statute, which was to have built the border wall.

President Trump has provided the necessary precondition to a wide-ranging pardon: He has shown that the border is secure. Now he can accomplish an immediate and vast good via the pardon power and begin negotiations on a breakthrough, provided the Democrats do not allow their extremists to poison the political well, even as center-right to conservative Republicans reject the instant denunciation of a pardon and every bill as "amnesty," which regularization efforts would not be.

The question for the adults at the Thanksgiving table on Thursday: If President Trump were to issue a pardon, to whom should it apply and what limits on that pardon should there be?

If I were White House Counsel Will Scharf, I would urge President Trump to begin with a fairly narrow pardon and one with explicit parameters that excluded felons and people who have been arrested for violent crimes. It should—at least in the first round—require those seeking its benefit to be able to show unbroken residence in the country prior to, say, January 21, 2020. It might also require proof of having worked and paid taxes and perhaps be limited to adults with children who are American citizens. There are a lot of fine points and exclusions to be debated here. The White House Counsel and his team could prepare many pardon options, and President Trump could decide among them.

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

The debate in the comments below or on a related Reddit forum will be angry but unrepresentative of the whole of the public, and President Trump already knows he must course-correct. If a pardon from President Trump does issue, it ought then to be the subject of careful consideration by serious people of goodwill, and their reactions should be guided by reason.

A carefully crafted pardon would be life-changing for more than a million people who would thereafter brook no criticism of Trump. It would lift an enormous burden from intact families of law-abiding people who work hard and have no inclination to break the law and who have had children in this country who are citizens. It should be easy to understand and to apply in practice. Its successful implementation could yield permission to remain in the country contingent on not committing a serious offense.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Such a pardon would immediately refocus the debate around deportation away from the deportation cases that trouble three-quarters or more of Americans. If you pay attention to these stories, you know there are many, many cases that jar ordinary Americans.

"Maybe we could touch the subject of immigration," said President Trump.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

He is right to make that touch. If he did so with a pardon that was satisfactory to the vast majority of Americans, that touch would indeed be a golden one.

World.title: Commanders' Jayden Daniels spoils Joe Burrow's night, leads team to game-winning drive vs Bengals
World.content:
Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow, the MVP frontrunner, was heading into another Primetime slate on "Monday Night Football" with NFL history on the line, as he could’ve been the first player ever to tally four or more touchdown passes in six straight games.

Well, he didn’t accomplish that, but against the 31st-ranked pass defense in the NFL, surely he was able to lead the Bengals past the Commanders, right?

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Well, he seemed to do so with a strong, "Thank you!" to kicker Evan McPherson for drilling a 56-yard field goal with 46 seconds left through the wind.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

That is until Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels spoiled an 8-2 start for the Bengals through 10 games with a gutsy game-winning drive of his own to upset Cincinnati, 20-19, at Northwest Stadium on Monday night.

Daniels led the Commanders on five straight scoring drives before the Bengals retook their lead late in the fourth quarter, but they weren’t for six points. Rookie kicker Drew Stevens was called upon for all of them, but he kept the Commanders in the game by doing his job and knocking through three points each time.

On the final drive, Daniels needed to get Stevens into range to make it a perfect five for five, which would win Washington the game. The problem is Daniels had no timeouts left, making things a bit tricky.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

However, Antonio Williams, the third-round pick out of Clemson who had a fantastic night, came through in the most clutch way for Daniels when he hauled in a 22-yard strike to quickly get the ball to midfield. Then, after spiking the rock, Daniels linked up with Williams again, this time for 42 yards, giving Stevens a 26-yard field goal for the win.

He drilled it, and the Commanders and their fan base at home went ballistic as, for the second straight week, they came away with a miraculous victory to keep their NFC East division title hopes alive at 4-5-1. The New York Giants, whom the Commanders shocked on the road in a "Thursday Night Football" thriller last week, sit in first place at 6-3-1, but the Commanders have the tiebreaker over them now due to the win in Week 10.

Burrow and the Bengals couldn’t believe it, but this game certainly wasn’t what their offense has been doing of late.

The first half pouring rain didn’t help matters, but both defenses were suffocating the quarterbacks on the gridiron. Burrow and Daniels couldn’t get anything going, that is until the rain started to lighten up before the first half came to a close.

Burrow finally found the end zone when he dropped in another perfect ball this season to Tee Higgins. How in the world Higgins came down with the touchdown grab, as the ball wasn’t fully secured in one of his hands, was a feat.

However, Jacksonville Jaguars fans won’t be happy as it was eerily similar to Parker Washington’s no-touchdown call on Sunday against the New York Giants. This time, referees confirmed Higgins was in bounds and had control for the first touchdown of the game.

Daniels, though, made things very interesting for the second half when he ripped off a 47-yard run to get into the red zone for the first time. A few plays later, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, playing his first game since suffering a groin injury against the Giants in Week 5’s tie at home, scored to make it a 10-7 game.

Burrow was able to find Colbie Young in the third quarter for his first career touchdown, giving the Bengals a 17-10 lead. But back-to-back punts, while the Commanders continued to tack on points, made things tight down the stretch.

Cincinnati looked like they escaped with a win, but Washington continues to show the NFL that, until the clock hits zero, it’s simply not over.

Just like their playoff hopes.

World.content:

The U.S. Coast Guard deployed specialized cyber teams to board two foreign-flagged commercial ships bound for U.S. ports in August after indications that their networks had been compromised by "foreign cyber actors," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Monday.

The offshore operations took place Aug. 21 and 24 in the Gulf of America, with teams mitigating the threats before the vessels reached U.S. ports.

The confirmation came as The Wall Street Journal also reported Monday that U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was involved in dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers.

FEARS OF CHINA SPYING ON US MILITARY PROMPT GOP HAWKS TO DEMAND RETALIATION AGAINST THE SHIPPING GIANT

"The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), in close coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and federal cybersecurity experts, recently conducted joint offshore security boardings of two inbound foreign-flagged commercial vessels in the Gulf of America," a Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"The measures were designed to ensure the integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised by foreign cyber actors."

The Coast Guard said a specialized team of law enforcement personnel, Coast Guard Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the first vessel Aug. 21 to investigate the suspected cybersecurity breach.

"The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," the spokesperson added.

A similar multiagency boarding and safety verification operation was conducted Aug. 24 aboard the second vessel, also in the Gulf of America, the Coast Guard said.

FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE

No operational disruptions, vessel instability, threats to crew safety or environmental impacts have been reported.

The Coast Guard said it is coordinating with port operators, vessel owners and local maritime stakeholders to ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption.

According to The Wall Street Journal, attackers exploited vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking equipment, prompting Coast Guard boardings after crews received bomb threats warning that "traitor ships will burn in hell."

STRAIT OF HORMUZ CRISIS TRAPS 6,000 SAILORS AS ATTACKS ON SHIPS MOUNT, UN MARITIME CHIEF SAYS

As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially explosive cargo are believed to have been targeted, the outlet reported, citing U.S. officials.

A European shipping executive also said officers received threats on their cellphones.

A ransom letter addressed to the captain of the Liberian-flagged supertanker Prosperity, which was carrying about 2.3 million barrels of oil, described the operation as a "planned execution."

Hackers reportedly breached one vessel's propulsion and navigation systems, disrupting communications for about 30 hours and forcing the crew to switch to manual procedures, potentially delaying energy shipments to Asia and Europe.

AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR

"The Marine Transportation System is vital to America's economic prosperity and national security, and safeguarding it against potential cyber risks is a standard part of the United States Coast Guard's safety and security mission," the Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterways.

"While confirmed cyber disruptions in the maritime domain remain uncommon, even isolated technical issues can cause avoidable commercial delays.
