World.title: 'I'm not a hero,' says Arizona man who found lost toddler alone in the desert
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jay Stewart has a lot of precious memories, but he says nothing compares to the moment he found two-year-old Vella Campillo alone in the cold, dark Arizona desert, wearing nothing but a diaper.

Police are hailing Stewart as a hero after he found the missing toddler who wandered away from her backyard last week, sparking a massive search-and-rescue operation in the rural community of Eloy, Ariz.



"I am so grateful to have experienced that life event, because there's no other feeling like it in the world," Stewart told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.

"That's No. 1 in my life, the most emotional moment I've ever had."

Vella was unharmed and has been safely reunited with her parents, police said.

LISTEN | Interview with Jay Stewart about finding Vella: As It Happens 6:16 Arizona man describes the emotional moment he found a lost toddler alone in the desert

Vella was reported missing around 6 p.m., local time, on Nov. 17, according to the Pinal County Sheriff's Office.

Her parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, told Fox News affiliate KSAZ that she'd been playing in the backyard with her siblings under the care of another family member when she wandered off.

Officials from several police and fire departments spent hours scouring the area along with dozens of volunteers, two helicopters, K-9 units and heat-detecting drones, all to no avail.

Then, just after midnight, Stewart called Vella's name and saw her pop out of a tiny patch of plants in the desert.

"I spun around, and she jumped back down into this little bush … the size of, like, four dinner plates put together," he said. "She almost looked like she was swimming. Her little arms were moving around like she was treading water."

Pitch black and freezing cold

Stewart and his wife had been looking for Vella ever since the emergency alert hit their phones notifying people of a missing child in their area.

They spent two hours searching along the side of the road, he says, before heading home to check the news and bundle up in warmer clothes as the sun went down and the cold set in.

"The desert is kind of like being in a mine. It could be pitch black where you can't see anything. And that's what it was like," he said.

On their second try, they drove into the desert behind Vella's home on their ATV.

"I've lived out there 20 years and I fly over it all the time in our helicopter. So I know it like the back of my hand," he said. "It's my backyard."

Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple, right, awarded Stewart a plaque and a badge the day after he found a missing toddler near Eloy, Ariz. (Pinal County Sheriff’s Office)

Stewart says he'd separated from his wife as he wandered about a mile down a ditch calling Vella's name. He heard a yell, then saw her pop up and back down again.

He reached down, plucked her into his arms, unzipped his jacket and tucked her inside.

"She whimpered for about 15 seconds when I picked her up, and then once I snuggled her to me and got her, she seemed pretty happy," he said. "She warmed up pretty quick."

Stewart says she didn't make a peep until he dropped his phone while talking to a 911 dispatcher.

"And she went, 'Phone!' I started laughing. And I'm like, 'Yeah, baby, phone!' " he said. "It chokes me up. I can hear that little voice."

Within 10 minutes, he says, police and other searchers were on the scene.

Body cam footage released by the Pinal County Sheriff's Office shows Stewart holding the toddler on his hip. By that point, she was wrapped in a blanket provided by another searcher and chattering away happily in baby talk.

When the officer took Vella to check her over, the little girl clutched onto Stewart.

"She wouldn't let go of me," he said.

'The very best of our community'

At a news conference on Nov. 18, Sheriff Ross Teeple awarded Stewart a plaque and a badge for his community service.

"Your selflessness and willingness to get involved amplify the very best of our community," Teeple said. "Your actions remind us that every citizen has the power to make a meaningful difference and that sometimes, the greatest acts of service come from simply choosing to help."

But Stewart says he was just one of dozens of volunteers who showed up for Vella, and he happened to get lucky.

"I'm not a hero. I'm a searcher, just like everyone else was," he said.

He called the rescue the most emotional moment of his life, followed by the birth of his children and the day he married his wife.

"The reason I put it ahead of my kids is because I knew where my kids were. They weren't lost. I was holding them," he said. "But to find something that's lost like that, helpless and lost? I can only imagine what the parents were going through."

World.title: Dentist pleads guilty to professional misconduct in 23-year-old's death
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Manitoba dentist was found guilty of professional misconduct Monday in connection with a woman's 2024 death, admitting he gave Virginia Blatz much more local anesthetic than the recommended dose.

Dr. Ronald Janz pleaded guilty to charges under the provincial Dental Association Act inside a brightly lit room flanked by windows at a downtown Winnipeg law firm during a morning hearing.

By that afternoon, a Manitoba Dental Association inquiry panel had found him guilty of several breaches of the association's code of ethics, including going against the principles to do no harm, to improve the patient's condition and to provide competent care.

The panel found him guilty of professional misconduct, and of displaying a lack of knowledge, skill or judgment in his dental practice with respect to the care he provided to Blatz.

Blatz, 23, was pronounced dead after she went to the Boundary Trails Dental Centre in Morden, Man., to get her wisdom teeth removed on Nov. 27, 2024.

According to an agreed statement of facts, Janz far exceeded the recommended dose of Articane — a local anesthetic drug typically given to manage pain — when providing care to Blatz.

At the time of her death, Blatz weighed about 100 pounds, and the dose given to her exceeded the maximum dosage she should have been given by up to about 200 per cent, an expert report included in the agreed statement of facts said.

Blatz's family is suing the dentist. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

A final report by the regulator's complaints committee referenced in the statement of facts concluded that Blatz was given 10 carpules of the local anesthetic.

Janz told an investigator with the dental regulator he might have given Blatz seven carpules. Still, he said his intention was to give 10, as that's the amount he said he usually uses for wisdom teeth procedures.

Lawyers for the dental association's complaints committee said that regardless of whether she was given seven or 10 carpules, the dose given to Blatz "well exceeded" what would be considered safe for a person of her size. The expert report suggested she should have been given about four carpules instead.

Janz told the investigator he did not know what the maximum dosage was for articaine, and that he did not know he had given Blatz too much based on her weight, according to the facts read out in the hearing room.

As a result of the articaine overdose, Blatz experienced local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), in which levels of the pain-blocking medication become too high in a person's blood.

Janz didn't recognize Blatz was experiencing LAST and failed to appropriately treat it, said the agreed statement of facts.

Blatz's mother, Victoria Blatz, said in a victim impact statement read before Monday's inquiry panel that her daughter was a friendly and smart young woman who was considered an anchor within the family.

For two years, Victoria has been replaying what she saw in the clinic over and over in her mind, thinking about the ways she could have possibly saved her daughter. She said she's struggled with nightmares and brain fog since her daughter's death.

Her father, Dulaney Blatz, said he was so proud of his daughter, who had planned to follow in his footsteps and build her own farm one day. Now he's trapped under an "overwhelming fog of grief" that makes it hard to concentrate on life both on and off the farm, he said.

Blatz's sister says she was her best friend and 'safe space.' (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

Miranda Blatz said her sister Virginia was her best friend and "safe space," who always fostered a sense of calm and peace. Without her best friend, it has been hard to dream of the future, she said with a wavering voice.

The inquiry panel hearing has yet to make a decision about the penalty Janz will face.

Lawyers for the dental association's complaints committee argued his licence should be suspended. However, the counsel didn't specific how long the suspension should be for, saying that's up to the inquiry panel to decide.

They also argued Janz should have to repay about $135,000 related to the costs of the investigation.

Janz's lawyer argued the dentist shouldn't be suspended and that he should instead repay a portion of the costs, suggesting a payment of $30,000 instead.

Both sides agreed the penalties should include a $10,000 fine, a reprimand and the publication of the decision.

Janz had previously agreed to be restricted in his ability to administer local anesthesia after the incident. The hearing was told Janz was not allowed to administer local anesthetic until January and the dental association's registry currently shows he can now only provide it under supervision.

In a prepared statement read by his lawyer, Janz shared his sympathies with Blatz's family, saying he has thought about her every day since she died. He said his dental practice has been affected and that he has done training in the wake of Blatz's death.

Janz has taken several courses since the incident, including one about local anesthesia and one on medical emergencies, his lawyer said.

Blatz's family is suing Janz, his dental practice and the corporation that owns and operates the Boundary Trails Dental Centre, alleging the care provided to Blatz was negligent.

CBC News did not initially name Janz or the clinic involved in this article because the Manitoba Dental Association Act prohibits reporting the identity of a dentist until the inquiry panel makes its findings.

World.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator asks court to revoke detention order
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An American accused of helping Jesse Van Rootselaar plan the Tumbler Ridge massacre has filed an application to get out of jail, asking a Seattle court judge to review and revoke a previous detention order.

A magistrate judge ordered the detention of Melody Bryant, who was charged under the name James Cody Bryant in October, after the government argued the accused would be a danger to the public if released.

Bryant, 30, is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, an offence that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison and a $250,000 US fine. She has pleaded not guilty.

The trial was originally scheduled to begin next month, but has been moved to December 2027.

Her lawyers say in court filings that their client is not a danger to the public and should be released with conditions. They say at the time of the Oct. 13 detention hearing, they had not yet received discovery documents and could not properly respond to the government's argument.

WATCH | Bryant allegedly gave money and advice to Van Rootselaar: U.S. resident allegedly gave advice, money to Tumbler Ridge shooter | Duration closed caption 8:26

On Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother Jennifer Strang, 39, and half-brother Emmett Jacobs, 11, in their home.

She then drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she gunned down Abel Mwansa, 12, Zoey Benoit, 12, Ezekiel Schofield, 13, Kylie Smith, 12, Ticaria Lampert, 12, and educational assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39.

Two other students were shot but survived.

In their 33-page motion for revocation of detention order filed last week, Bryant's lawyers say the case is based mainly on nearly 74,000 individual texts between Van Rootselaar and Bryant on messaging platform Discord, sent between Aug. 1 and Feb. 10, 2025.

Approximately two-thirds of those messages, numbering 47,750, are from Van Rootselaar to Bryant.

Bryant's lawyers say while some of their clients messages "may be tasteless and, in retrospect, were ill considered" they are protected by the First Amendment.

"For better or worse, the First Amendment also protects their debate about whether a school shooting or attack on a crowd would be more likely to make someone infamous, even if the government tries to recast that conversation as 'tactical advice,'" said the Nov. 18 motion filed by Bryant's lawyers.

WATCH | Discord messages reveal interactions between Bryant and Van Rootselaar: Discord messages reveal Tumbler Ridge shooter, U.S. resident planning attack | Duration closed caption 3:00

The motion includes excerpts of chats between Bryant and Van Rootselaar, including one on Christmas Day 2025 used to show instances where Bryant refused to engage in violent rants.

"I hope I ruin everyone's life when I do my plan. I want nobody to recover … whenever I say some mentally ill ahh stuff I feel like u stop messaging me lol…," wrote Van Rootselaar.

Bryant wrote back, "Harder to reply to."

The court filings say, for part of the six-month period where Bryant spoke daily to Van Rootselaar, the shooter's "plan" was clearly a fantasy because Van Rootselaar did not have access to guns.

"Eventually, however, the RCMP returned her seized weapons."

Seized guns used in shooting: documents

According to the court filings, Bryant was not the only one who initially failed to recognize Van Rootselaar was "genuinely dangerous." The motion says records show the shooter shared her plans widely and had even "received encouragement from other online contacts."

She got tactical advice from ChatGPT, family and friends bought her ammunition, even after she was released from psychiatric hospitalization and the RCMP, according to the motion.

Bryant's lawyers add that the RCMP had removed, and then later returned, Van Rootselaar's guns, "one of which had been altered to enable more rapid firing."

"In fact, the RCMP apparently returned the gun with the alteration intact. Van Rootselaar then used the altered firearm in the shooting," said the Nov. 18 motion.

Days after the Tumbler Ridge shooting, RCMP said a long gun and modified rifle were seized from the school, and two firearms including a shotgun were seized among a number of other firearms at the residence.

The shotgun is believed to have been used in the homicides at the home and had not been previously seized by police. Mounties also said they had not previously seized the main firearm used in the school shooting and its origins are unknown.

WATCH | Report details interactions between shooter and ChatGPT: Report details Tumbler Ridge shooter’s alleged ChatGPT interactions | Duration closed caption 2:58

Bryant's lawyers say their client promised not to snitch on the shooter because Bryant believed it would result in violence, and accelerate the shooter's homicidal plans.

"While it is horrifying in retrospect to imagine that Ms. Bryant might have stopped Van Rootselaar from committing a terrible crime if she had contacted the police, it is undisputed that the law provided no affirmative duty to do so," said the motion.

The court filings said in the past Bryant was able to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing a crime, and did not understand violence was imminent.

A memorial for the victims of a school shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School is pictured on Feb. 11, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Bryant's lawyers say the shooter viewed Bryant as "a nonjudgemental sounding board for ruminating about her mental illness," and that Bryant helped her resist her urges.

The defence included chats to illustrate that.

In an undated message, Van Rootselaar writes "I **really** wanna shoot ppl, idk what to do with that feeling lmao. Like how do I relieve that? I can't talk about it much even."

"Yeah I think most would snitch," replies Bryant.

"Except for you who silently discourage it and a few others who openly encourage it," responds Van Rootselaar.

Government distorted evidence: defence

Bryant's lawyers say the U.S. government's 41-page complaint against their client is "replete with distortions" and includes rearranged text messages made to appear that Bryant was agreeing to help the shooter build a bomb.

The motion for revocation of detention order says the conversation included in the complaint showing Bryant agreeing to pay for a lighter needed to make a bomb occurred over two days and in between 225 messages.

"In fact, nowhere in the complete chats does Van Rootselaar say that she needs a lighter for the bomb. Nowhere does Bryant offer to provide Van Rootselaar a lighter for that purpose," said the court filing.

WATCH | Omegle allegedly where Bryant and Van Rootselaar met: U.S. resident met Tumbler Ridge shooter on Omegle: FBI | Duration 1:27

Bryant's lawyers say the decision to piece the texts together "seems designed to lead the magistrate judge to make a false inference."

They say while Bryant agreed to watch a livestream and if possible distribute it, she did not agree with Van Rootselaar's plans to kill people.

The motion says the fact that law enforcement left Bryant in the community for seven months after reviewing her Discord chats shows she does not pose a danger.

The magistrate judge concluded Bryant suffers from a "deeply rooted" mental illness and substance abuse history.

Bryant's lawyers say that is not true. Bryant is currently being treated for gender dysphoria and had previously been prescribed medication for anxiety but no longer takes that drug, according to the motion.

The U.S. state's attorney's response is due Wednesday, then a judge will decide if Bryant should be released.

World.title: Steven Galloway asks judge to declare rape allegations false as defamation trial enters final submissions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway is asking the presiding justice in his defamation trial to vindicate his reputation by making an explicit finding of "falsehood."

"There's been a horrific stain on his name for over a decade," said Galloway's lead counsel Daniel Burnett during closing submissions on Monday. "It's in the public interest to have a final resolution of these allegations that have floated around for so long."

Galloway alleges defamation against a former student with whom he had an extramarital affair, and three other defendants who repeated rape allegations online and elsewhere.

Galloway's main accuser, identified only as A.B. because of a publication ban, earlier withdrew her defence of justification, choosing not to argue that claims Galloway raped or sexually assaulted her on three occasions in 2011 were true. Justice Neena Sharma had said the woman had not admitted that her accusations are false and the court couldn't make assumptions until it hears all evidence.

A.B. is a former UBC graduate student who is five years older than Galloway. She did not appear or testify at trial because of mental health concerns. Three other defendants — Mandi Gray, Glynnis Kirchmeier and Dana Kagis — are alleged to have repeated A.B.'s claims on social media and elsewhere.

"It's an unfortunate reality in this day and age that truth can often end up being in the hands of those who shout the loudest, those who tweet the most and those who recruit the most allies. And the court trial process is the last stop," Burnett told Sharma.

Steven Galloway is pictured in his office at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver on March 31, 2014. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

A.B. brought her allegations to UBC in November 2015. Soon after, Galloway was suspended, a move the university announced publicly by citing "serious allegations" against him.

A retired judge hired by UBC to conduct an investigation found that on a balance of probabilities he had not committed sexual assault.

Galloway was fired for misconduct. He was never criminally investigated.

Burnett told the court there was "overwhelming evidence of deliberate and calculated falsehoods built upon falsehoods." He said A.B. ran a strategic campaign to leverage criminal accusations against Galloway through other people.

That included, Burnett said, A.B. lying to friends and UBC officials that her story would be featured on an episode of the CBC's fifth estate if UBC didn't act against Galloway, and that CBC lawyers had found her evidence of the rape to be damning.

Burnett said A.B.'s "fabrications" cast serious doubt on everything she said, citing a disturbing claim A.B. made about being possibly drugged into unconsciousness and violently raped by Galloway in his UBC office.

Burnett said text messages between A.B. and her ex-husband on the night in question, along with other inconsistencies in her account, demonstrated that the allegation was not simply false but a "knowing lie."

The author of The Cellist of Sarajevo admitted during testimony that he and A.B. had an affair between 2011 and 2013 while both were married.

His defamation lawsuit filed in 2018 originally named more than 20 defendants, the majority of whom settled before the trial began. A number of the defendants have also issued public apologies.

Burnett said Galloway has endured loss and suffering since 2015 that no person should wish on another.

"Hopefully, the outcome of this case will — as far as any court decision can — enable him to recover something back and have a better future," said Burnett.

Defence's closing submissions are expected to begin Tuesday in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-year-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: The deteriorating press freedom in Colombia and the Americas
World.content:
I sat down with Joshua Collins of Pirate Wire Services to discuss the deteriorating press freedom situation in Colombia and the rest of Latin America.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.

World.title: Colombia rejects US proposal to conduct joint strikes against drug trafficking: NYT
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rejected a US plan to conduct joint military operations, anonymous US officials told the New York Times (NYT).

According to the NYT, De la Espriella told the US government he supported working with the US military, but lacked congressional support invite US soldiers on Colombian soil.

The conversation would have taken place in the week ahead of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Colombia on Wednesday.

In a response, the president and the defense secretary said that the alleged US plan was “fake news.”

“I have not rejected any proposal of the Government of President Donald Trump,” De la Espriella said on social media platform X.

Colombia and the United States maintain strong and increasingly close cooperation in the areas of security, intelligence, and the fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president confirmed that congressional approval would be required for him to invite foreign troops into Colombia.

Between visits to Venezuela and Ecuador, Hegseth briefly stopped in Colombia, and met with Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora and Foreign Minister Omar Bulla.

The defense secretary expressed his support for the government’s plans to combat drug trafficking.

“You, sir, are never going to have a stronger partner than President Trump, Secretary Hegseth an the War Department,” Hegseth told Bula.

Both the US and the Colombian governments have assumed a militaristic approach to drug trafficking, contrary to their predecessors.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: A Christmas of Fake Snow and Empty Pockets is Coming to Havana
World.content:
“Un turrón, 9.000 pesos. Yo no gano eso de salario al mes”, se queja una joven vestida de enfermera ante un anaquel con vinos, dulces y un reno de peluche / 14ymedio

Dressed as the Virgin of Charity of El Cobre, a woman begs for food at a traffic light: Cuba’s patron saint transformed into a beggar reflects the country’s sad reality.

By Yoani Sanchez (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – The early morning brought rain to Havana, and Monday dawned in a mess of blackouts and mud, paralysis and hustle. Before I got out of bed I could already smell the odor of the coffee factory near my house. For days now a burnt small has invaded the neighborhood, accompanies by smoke that seeps in through the windows. A good part of that coffee will end up being sold for dollars, a currency that this Monday reached 965 pesos in the informal market.

I go out seeking provisions. The forecast predicts strong storms for the coming days, but another whirlwind has already hit the markets. What cost 2,000 pesos Sunday, yesterday, today costs 2,100 or more. In the window of a private bakery, a sign tries to justify the 690 pesos price for a bag of bread. “The cost of raw materials has gone up,” it explains. In front of the counter, where before you had to push your way through the customers, I find no one. Inflation has managed to eliminate the lines.

In my building’s WhatsApp group, at last, some good news appears: Today there is bread. However, the lack of electricty converts this small victory into a, obstacle course for the elderly residence on the upper floors. Going down more than a dozen floors and climbing back up is not a small thing, especially when the reward is that ever small and tasteless ration and sold in the ration market.

Christmas is beginning to timidly appear in some private businesses and dollar stores. The red hats worn by the clerks seem to have come from a distant planet, in stark contrast to the dull reality. “A nougat bar, 9,000 pesos. I don’t earn that much a month,” complains a young woman dressed as a nurse in front of a shelf laden with wines, sweets, and a stuffed reindeer.

In Carlos III Plaza, the stores that sell in hard currency remain empty of customers, but the employees are putting up little trees, garlands and fake snow made of cotton. The winter decorations contrast with the market’s sticky heat, where the air conditioning barely works.

At the corner of Ayestarán and 20 de Mayo, a woman dressed as the Virgen de la Caridad del Cobre approaches the cars stopped at the traffic light. She carries a basket with a doll also adorned in gold and asks for something to eat. The Patron Saint of Cuba, transformed into a beggar, encapsulates the country we live in better than any speech.

In a city where almost nothing gets repaired, the gas station business seems to be the only one with any vitality. / 14ymedio

Further along, I come across the only construction site I’ve seen on my entire journey: a gas station. Several construction workers are working inside a enormous hole where fuel will be stored. They’re building walls and sealing cracks while, all around, the sidewalks remain in ruins. In a city where almost nothing gets repaired, the gas station business seems to be the only one with any semblance of life.

In a private market, I stumble across a ten-pound bag of chicken quarters for 9,550 pesos. The price takes me back to my childhood and that television program, 9,550, whose title alluded to the kilometers between Havana and Moscow, while the pipeline of subsidies fueled the political deliriums of Castroism. Today, the Russian bear offers only declarations of friendship and economic agreements that rarely materialize, even though they fill the headlines of the official press.

Before leaving the store, I see a little girl who insists on buying a jar of American peanut butter. It costs 4,500 pesos. Her mother promises to buy it for her for Christmas. “I won’t forget,” she assures her. The clerk is wearing a red hat. I look at the little girl and wonder how many promises that woman will have to make before December, and how many she’ll be able to keep. Outside, the sky is clouding over again.

The storm hasn’t arrived yet, but in Havana we’re already living under a downpour.

Translated by Translating Cuba.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: The Daily Struggle to Find Food
World.content:
Photo: Nike

By Nike

HAVANA TIMES – No matter how hard I try to make each day different, it always turns into the same routine when it comes to finding food.

I get up early and go to the kitchen to make coffee over charcoal. That means spending half an hour getting the precious fuel lit. Even though they tell you it’s made from marabu wood and is the best charcoal in the world, lighting it takes blood, sweat, and tears. And I mean that literally, because on more than one occasion I’ve burst into tears. It’s expensive on the market, and the price keeps rising every day. A sack now costs around 3,000 Cuban pesos. Three thousand pesos is the basic monthly salary of a Cuban worker, while a retiree’s pension ranges between 1,200 and 1,500 pesos. In other words, an entire month’s work for a sack of charcoal that, even when used sparingly, won’t last the whole month.

The coffee I have right now was a gift from a friend. His grandmother has several coffee plants at her home in Camagüey, and she roasts and grinds the beans herself. It’s good Cuban coffee. Imported coffee costs between 3,500 and 4,000 pesos, while locally grown coffee—like the kind my friend’s grandmother produces—costs 1,500 pesos for 250 grams. Despite the high prices, Cubans make sacrifices to buy it.

After coffee, I head out into the streets in search of the day’s food, like any ordinary Cuban. I bring my own shopping bags because otherwise I have to pay 15 or 20 pesos for each plastic bag. The days when merchants gave you bags or paper sacks at no additional cost are long gone.

The first thing I buy is rice. It isn’t particularly nutritious, but it fills your stomach. It costs 450 pesos a pound. I prefer root vegetables and other starchy staples, which are more nutritious, but buying them is like opening a box of surprises. They may look perfectly good on the outside, but when you peel them, they can be black or green, like sweet potatoes affected by the sweet potato weevil. It’s a pest with a French-sounding name that givers sweet potatoes a bitter taste that not even animals can eat them. That’s like throwing your money away, so I stick with rice. I call this survival.

They also sell plantains, the kind known as plátano macho, but they’re not the same ones I remember from childhood. They’re a hybrid developed to make the plants produce more frequently. Their flesh is firmer, and they’re smaller than the original plantains. I’ll take the plátano macho of the 1980s any day. Today’s plantains cost between 150 and 200 pesos apiece.

There are also plátanos burros, another variety of banana. A bunch of eight small bananas sells for 300 or 400 pesos. They go further because what matters to us is quantity—having enough to fill a stomach that roars like a lion in heat and needs to be silenced.

There’s no fruit. The onions aren’t good, and at 600 pesos a pound they’re unaffordable anyway. I can’t buy them with the money I have. At home, I season our meals with Cuban oregano, basil, ají cachucha peppers, and some green onions I’ve planted myself.

As I continue my search, I settle on rice and, like “Martina the Little Cockroach” from the children’s story, I count my money and figure out that I have enough for some black beans, whose price has risen to 700 pesos. They’ll last for two meals, provide nourishment, and fill our stomachs.

I look for some protein, but chicken costs 850 pesos a pound, and eggs are 130 pesos each. I pass a house and notice a sign advertising “dehydrated eggs.” The man there very kindly explains how to prepare them. I buy a pound for 600 pesos.

I’ve almost completed the food shopping for my family, but I still need some vegetables. At the produce market, the only thing for sale is some very ugly cucumbers, and I can’t afford them on my budget either. So I head to the coast and gather salicornia—a type of sea vegetable—and purslane, which contains omega-3 fatty acids. They’re free and nutritious.

I’m worried because my children get hungry at night. So I stop by a recently opened bakery called Riki Pan. The owner is a doctor who gave up his medical career to make bread. He bought a house, installed an electric generator, set up ovens, and has been baking bread nonstop ever since, with help from relatives abroad.

People welcomed the bakery enthusiastically, and it has become a favorite here in my town. Lately, however, customers have been upset because he raised bread prices, and he has even faced criticism on Facebook.

I stop at the bakery and buy a bag of the least expensive bread rolls for 400 pesos. It’s for snacks between meals, which are yet another food-related problem in this country.

Add up my expenses yourselves and tell me whether, with today’s salaries, a Cuban can afford breakfast, lunch, and dinner every single day.

This is how families in my country live, day after day.

Read more from Nike’s diary here on Havana Times.

World.title: Smoking in Cuba and Our New Poverty
World.content:
Popular is a low end brand of cigarettes made in Cuba.

By Angry GenXer

HAVANA TIMES – A street vendor passes in front of my building hawking homemade sweets, announcing that he accepts cigarettes as payment.

A healthcare technician, whenever he is on duty at his hospital, makes the rounds along the ramp used to transport stretchers, looking for cigarette butts.

A friend of mine makes four pencil marks on every cigarette she smokes, so she can smoke it “in stages” and avoid having to buy more too often.

Smoking is an addiction that harms your health (in Cuba we call it “a vice”), but it is also a quick way to relieve stress for those living under constant pressure. That is why societies in crisis or at war suffer chronic shortages of “smokable material.” When a critical period begins and the “new poor” emerge, the scarcity of anything containing tobacco quickly becomes visible and painfully apparent, as we have learned from so many novels and movies.

Smoking and Inflation

Since the pandemic, the price of cigars (the inexpensive ones smoked by ordinary Cubans, not the famous Havana cigars exported and sold to tourists) has skyrocketed from 3 to 150 pesos, the latter representing 5% of the official monthly minimum wage (currently 3,210 pesos; pensions and social assistance payments can be even lower). Packs of cigarettes are now sold at private kiosks for prices ranging from three to four digits in Cuban pesos, roughly equivalent to between 15% and 40% of the minimum wage, depending on the brand. Most of these businesses, as well as individual informal vendors, also offer the option of buying cigarettes individually.

Smokers must devote considerable portions of their budgets to satisfying their tobacco addiction, reduce their consumption, or quit smoking altogether.

In Cuba, there are few places where smoking is prohibited. Furthermore, our people are not particularly careful about keeping public spaces clean, so cigarette and cigar butts can be found everywhere. And it has become common to see all kinds of people collecting them. Some use improvised pipes (“cachimbos”) into which they insert the butts to smoke whatever tobacco remains inside; others resort to more sophisticated homemade contraptions.

Finding Our Own Ways to Smoke

This is not the first time that the Cuban people, living in a world tobacco powerhouse and the historic homeland of tobacco cultivation and consumption, have experienced difficulties obtaining it.

In the 1970s, there was a cigarette shortage, and people said it was due to the massive export of tobacco products to other countries belonging to the Soviet-led Eastern European bloc economic alliance that, in turn, supplied the Caribbean nation with all kinds of goods.

People found a solution: they rolled homemade cigarettes using tobacco recovered from previously smoked butts or from cigars distributed by the state through the family rationing system (not everyone in Cuba smokes cigars). These homemade cigarettes were jokingly called “Tupamaros” (after the Uruguayan guerrilla organization whose bank robberies were famous at the time).

The “Tupamaros” returned in the 1990s, along with cigarette shortages during the crisis of the so-called Special Period. I remember that my late father built a rudimentary wooden machine to make them. Some people turned the sale of “Tupamaros” into a business to survive.

Cigarette Butts in Today’s Cuba and Measuring Poverty

“Every time I make my rounds, I find more Tupamaro butts around here…” a cigarette-butt collector tells me. I frequently run into him on the streets of my neighborhood. This means that more and more smokers are rolling their own cigarettes using tobacco left over from other people’s smoking.

It occurs to me that the number of “Tupamaro” butts found on Cuban streets could serve as a measure of emerging poverty: an indication of how many people can no longer afford commercially sold cigarettes.

The length of the butts left from commercially manufactured cigarettes is also an indicator of scarcity: the shorter the butts, the more precious every second of smoking becomes.

Perhaps some sociologist could devise a field study using these indicators to measure emerging poverty in Cuba.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Monday, November 23, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Monday, November 23, 2026.

U.N. Climate Summit Collapses After Countries Fail to Agree to Phase Out Coal, Oil and Gas

Nov 23, 2026

In Turkey, the United Nations climate summit collapsed on Sunday as nations failed to produce an agreement phasing out the use of fossil fuels, with a draft text that did not even mention coal, oil or gas. Many poorer countries also objected to the lack of financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to a warming world. This is youth climate activist Xiye Bastida.

Xiye Bastida: “I saw my first climate disaster when I was 13 years old, when my hometown flooded. I have friends whose glaciers in Peru are melting, in Nepal. Those are my friends. People, the politicians are not understanding. They came here to backtrack instead of giving us what we need. This is the first COP that we have where we know we’re reaching 1.5 degrees. Where is the ambition?”

The effort to strip the text of references to coal, oil and gas was led by Saudi Arabia and joined by Russia. The United States did not participate in the COP31 talks, after President Trump once again withdrew from the Paris Agreement last year. After headlines, we’ll have more on the failure of COP31 to reach a major new deal.

Three More Ships Are Struck Amid Record Pace of Attacks in Strait of Hormuz

Nov 23, 2026

At least three more ships have been struck by projectiles while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz. The weekend attacks came as CNN reported the pace of strikes on ships in and around the strait has reached its highest levels since the U.S. attacked Iran in February.

Student-Led Protests Sweep Europe, Demanding Higher Wages, Lower Rents and Better Schools

Nov 23, 2026

In Italy, thousands of protesters marched through the streets of Rome and more than 100 other cities on Friday as a nationwide strike disrupted transport and school services. The protests were led by workers and students and were part of a wave of actions across Europe over the weekend.

Laura Peritore: “Young people and students across Europe are mobilizing today for this strike against rearmament, against military conscription and against the cuts being made to healthcare and public spending, while billions are being invested in weapons.”

Tens of thousands marched in Paris over the cost of living, disinvestment in public services and political gridlock ahead of next year’s presidential election. Protesters also marched in cities across Spain, Portugal, Germany, Austria, Croatia and the U.K. to demand better housing and public education, and higher wages. In Albania, Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joined students in the capital Tirana, which has witnessed months of protests against a luxury coastal resort backed by President Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Greta Thunberg: “Students from all over the world are walking out of school and university under the the slogan ‘Fight for Our Future, Not Their Wars,’ where young people are saying no to the continuous robbing of our future, where we live in destructive systems that prioritize wars, militarization and privatization over actually funding welfare systems, education.”

Israeli Attacks on Gaza Kill Palestinians Delivering Aid and Worker with U.N. Agency

Nov 23, 2026

In Gaza, an Israeli airstrike killed three Palestinians on Saturday as they drove in a vehicle carrying packaged food for forcibly displaced people in Gaza City. Papers for the World Central Kitchen charity were found inside their bombed-out car, along with meals of cooked rice and the blood of the victims of the attack. This is an eyewitness to the strike.

Abu Zein al-Daya: “It’s a bus, as you see, that distributes food and drink to the poor, to the needy, to the people in tents, to the displaced. It was just about to stop to distribute the food and drink to children. It was hit by a missile. The young man who was leaving the bus fell here, and the bus went on and stopped here. And the target is anyone who is giving the people food.”

The Palestinian Health Ministry reported six Palestinians killed and 33 wounded on Saturday. Six more were killed on Sunday, including an 11-year-old boy shot in the back by Israeli soldiers. At least four more Palestinians have been killed today. One of them was Adel Al-Helo, an employee of UNRWA, the U.N. agency for Palestinian refugees. Al-Helo was working near a water well in northern Gaza when he was killed in an Israeli airstrike.

Israeli Settlers Attack Palestinian Villages, Setting Fires and Spray-Painting Racist Graffiti

Nov 23, 2026

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers attacked several Palestinian towns and villages over the weekend, setting fire to vehicles and spray-painting homes and businesses with racist slogans. The attacks drew criticism from Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been attempting to form a government after last month’s inconclusive elections. Eisenkot wrote that the arson attacks were “Jewish terrorism in every sense.” He added, “Sabotage acts by extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers human life, and seriously harms the national security of the State of Israel and its foreign relations.”

Outcry Erupts as Video Shows ICE Agents Arresting Father and Daughter at Seattle Airport

Nov 23, 2026

Image Credit: X/@KimKatieUSA

In Washington state, Democratic officials have denounced federal immigration agents after they were filmed violently arresting two people boarding a flight at the Seattle-area airport Sea-Tac on Saturday. Video of the arrest shows ICE officers holding down a passenger and dragging her out the door of an Alaska Airlines jetway while she screams loudly. Another passenger who tried to intervene is shoved by a masked officer.

Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia: “No! No!”

ICE agent 1: “Hey! Hey! You’re coming with us!”

ICE agent 2: “Get back.”

Passenger 1: “What’s your name?”

Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia: “Sofia Larrondo. I’m getting arrested by ICE.”

ICE agent 2: “Come on. Get back.”

Passenger 2: “What is your name?”

Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia: “We are Americans.”

Passenger 1: “Identify yourselves!

Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia: “We have a work permit.”

ICE agent 2: ”ICE.”

Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia: “We have a work permit.”

At least two people were arrested: Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia. Both Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle said ICE agents carried out the operation without their participation or knowledge. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said in a statement, ”ICE is completely and totally out of control. Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities.”

Internal Report Concludes ICE Went Too Far in Loosening Training Standards for New Recruits

Nov 23, 2026

An internal investigation at the Department of Homeland Security concluded that ICE went too far last year in loosening training standards for thousands of new officers as it sought to rapidly hire and deploy 10,000 new recruits. One instructor quoted in the draft report by DHS’s inspector general called the rollbacks in training standards a “catastrophic failure.” Among other things, the report cited a decision to allow nearly 6,000 officers with prior experience to speed through training, with most of them completing an online course in 10 days or less.

Ukraine Sinks Russian Warship Docked in Libya as Russian Strikes Kill Civilians

Nov 23, 2026

Image Credit: Volodymyr Zelensky via Telegram

In Libya, a Russian warship has sunk after it was struck while docked in the port city of Benghazi early Sunday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky later claimed responsibility for the attack on the Russian Navy corvette, saying a Ukrainian sea drone sank the vessel and also destroyed a military helicopter. A Russian cargo ship was also damaged off Libya’s coast on Sunday. Meanwhile, in Ukraine, the death toll from a Russian strike on the town of Dymer rose to 11, after rescuers pulled another body from the rubble earlier today. Two survivors had been ​trapped under the rubble for nearly a day, including a 79-year-old woman and a 7-year-old boy.

Spain Frees Pro-Palestinan Activist James “Fergie” Chambers on Bail After U.S.-Backed Arrest

Nov 23, 2026

The Pro-Palestinian activist and philanthropist James “Fergie” Chambers was released on bail by a court in Spain on Friday. Chambers had been detained in Spain since July, when he was arrested at the request of the U.S. The Trump administration is seeking Chambers’s extradition, accusing him of supporting Hamas in connection with his donations to Palestinians in Gaza and pro-Palestine advocacy. Chambers, who is an heir to the Cox Communications fortune, spoke after his release on Friday.

James “Fergie” Chambers: “In the end of the day, I understand that the sacrifice I’ve had to make is very, very small in relation to the struggle that we are all a part of for the Palestinian people, for their liberation, for their sovereignty, for their respect, for their right to live. But in the context of just being alone in a cell all the time, it feels like a long time. I just missed my family. I really missed my family and my friends.”

Delta Delays 1,300 Flights Due to Tech Failure

Nov 23, 2026

Delta Air Lines says it has resolved a technical problem that caused it to delay more than half of its flights on Sunday. Delta blamed an outage in the system that records weight and balance on aircraft. The 1,300 flight delays came a week after a nationwide ground stop that resulted in the cancellation of more than 18,000 flights — and after a recent series of massive tech failures plaguing banks, email systems and even the NSA. On Friday, the Trump administration fired White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross — a former executive at the Republican National Committee with no experience in cybersecurity.

FBI Probes Apparent Breach of Criminal Information Database

Nov 23, 2026

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database. It’s believed to be the second breach in recent months of the National Crime Information Center, which is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

Democrats’ House Majority Swells to 259 as Chuck Hubbard Defeats 11-Term GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx

Nov 23, 2026

In North Carolina, Democrat Chuck Hubbard has narrowly defeated 11-term Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx. Hubbard’s win gives Democrats at least 259 seats in the next Congress — its largest total since after the 1992 elections. Three U.S. House races remain uncalled.

Army Plans “Controlled Detonation” of Toxic Material at Iowa Ammunition Plant, Despite Court Order

Nov 23, 2026

The U.S. Army is planning to blow up nearly five tons of a toxic lead-containing compound at an ammunition plant in Iowa — despite a court order that put the initial detonation on hold. The Army had been planning to carry out what it called a “controlled” detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, today. It now says it will execute the plan on Wednesday, under what the Pentagon claimed were emergency legal powers allowing it to bypass a court order. Environmental groups have sued to halt the detonations, arguing they would release a toxic plume of lead dust ​into the air that could travel up to 100 miles.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani Unveils Plan to Close Rikers Island Jail by 2032

Nov 23, 2026

Here in New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan Friday that would see the notorious Rikers Island jail complex closed by the end of 2032. Under the plan, Rikers will be replaced by four smaller new jails in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Manhattan. The plan also seeks to reduce recidivism, while ending case delays that can keep people jailed for years as they await trial. Hundreds of prisoners have died at Rikers, which is notorious for medical neglect, physical and sexual violence, and brutality by guards. This is New York City Public Advocate Jumaane Williams.

Jumaane Williams: “This plan is about public safety for the people of the city. Rikers is ineffective, and it is dangerous. And the best way to protect people on both sides of those bars, who very often come from the same community, is to finally shut it down.”

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: Even Two Jobs in Cuba Aren’t Enough to Put Food on the Table
World.content:
What was announced as an opportunity to earn more has become, for many, the only way to keep from sinking. / 14ymedio

A woman engineer who sells cold cuts and a former tourism employee portray the exhaustion of those in Matanzas who sacrifice their rest just to survive.

By Julio Cesar Contreras (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – Roxana opens the freezer to look for a tube of chorizo. She rummages through several packages, sets others aside, and for a few seconds seems confused. Then she remembers that she is looking for the merchandise as if she were at the other kiosk where she also works. After spending all seven days of the week behind a counter, the two establishments end up becoming confused in her mind.

“It’s happened to me that I enter a number in the inventory that belongs to the other place. It’s not carelessness, but exhaustion,” she explains.

The young woman is a single mother of two small children, and every day she pedals the kilometers separating the neighborhoods of La Playa and Versalles. Her bicycle is the means of transportation that allows her to juggle her family responsibilities with two jobs that leave her barely any time to rest. “My workday, from Monday to Sunday, starts at 6:00 in the morning,” she tells 14ymedio.

A little over three years ago, she graduated with a degree in agricultural engineering. She completed her mandatory social service and ended up trading the furrows of farmland for shelves stocked with beverages and sweets. “You can’t work for the State,” she declares. The 30,000 pesos ($31 USD) a month she earns by combining both salaries are barely enough to feed her children. Her parents look after the little ones and, when money is scarce, they also lend her a few pesos.

The young woman who serves customers buying food in the morning can sell clothes in the afternoon. / 14ymedio

“To make sure my children have food, I’m willing to do whatever is necessary,” she says. Her university degree has been relegated to a memory, while she learns to distinguish brands of cold cuts, organize inventories, and verify bank transfers.

In Matanzas, finding the same employee working at two different establishments is no longer surprising. The young woman who serves customers buying food in the morning may sell clothes in the afternoon, while a shop assistant supplements his salary with errands, repairs, or any activity that brings in a few extra pesos. Holding multiple jobs, once an exception, has become a survival strategy.

For decades, holding several jobs simultaneously was subject to strict restrictions. In June 2009, Raul Castro’s Government approved a law which explicitly regulated multiple employment and allowed workers to enter into additional contracts. The measure was presented as an opportunity to increase incomes and stimulate productivity. Another law maintained this possibility, subject to different working conditions and schedules.

Inflation is devouring salaries, and even the private sector does not guarantee sufficient income. / 14ymedio

Seventeen years later, what was announced as an option for earning more has become, for many, the only way to keep from sinking. Inflation is devouring salaries, and even the private sector does not guarantee sufficient income. In many small businesses in Matanzas, workers are paid around 1,000 pesos (just over $1 USD) per shift, with no sales commissions.

Kenia, 51, knows this reality well. Until the beginning of the year, she cleaned rooms at a hotel in Varadero, but the establishment’s closure forced her to reinvent herself. Now she sells food at a kiosk and, when she finishes, runs a garage sale at her home, where she offers secondhand clothing and other items.

“Ever since the hotel closed at the beginning of this year, I’ve had to become a jack-of-all-trades just to keep going,” she says, while waiting for a transfer confirmation to appear on her phone.

She and another saleswoman divide the work at the establishment. Each receives around 15,000 pesos ($16 USD) a month. “It sounds like quite a lot, but with how expensive everything is, that money is gone in less than a week.

”There are goods available, but buyers lack sufficient money. / 14ymedio

Behind the bars of some shops, cartons of eggs, bottles of cooking oil, and packages of imported rice create a misleading impression of abundance. There are goods, but buyers lack sufficient money. During slow periods, Kenia updates her WhatsApp group with the offers from her home-based business.

Necessity does not even respect retirement age. Many elderly Cubans return to the labor market because their pensions do not cover basic expenses. Seeing an elderly person working is an increasingly common sight, but in their case they almost always return to the state sector because they cannot find work in the private sector. “Here you have to stand all day, and the job requires a lot of moving around from one place to another, as well as carrying merchandise,” Kenia says.

“I’m still strong, and fortunately, my daughter brings me lunch,” the woman says gratefully. Other workers eat at irregular hours or simply skip a meal. She still needs to finish building her house, but all the work is beginning to take its toll on her body.

“I need these two jobs, but I just can’t keep going anymore,” she admits. If in the past having two jobs was a sign of prosperity, now, in Matanzas, it is merely a way to postpone poverty until the following week.

Translated by Regina Anavy for Translating Cuba.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.
