Key Facts Who. Mexico’s national election authority and the state election bodies of Colima and Yucatán.

What. Both state bodies are at a high INE monitoring level over missing money.

Where. Colima and Yucatán; 31 of 32 state bodies have approved 2027 budgets.

When. Announced Monday 23 November 2026; election day is Sunday 6 June 2027.

As of. 24 November 2026, 07:30 GMT.

Two state election bodies are short of money for the 2027 vote, and Mexico’s national authority has put both at a high monitoring level.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

INE’s committee for coordinating with the 32 state electoral bodies, known as OPL (Organismos Públicos Locales), heard budget reports at its 21st extraordinary session, INE said. These bodies run state and municipal votes while INE runs the federal one, which formally opened on 10 September 2026.

INE said the Colima state electoral institute stays at a high monitoring level because 53 percent of the resources first projected were cut. Of about 24 million pesos requested in a budget extension, only 7.5 million pesos were authorised (about US$1.25 million and US$0.39 million at 19.15 pesos per dollar, the 24 November rate used throughout).

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 70.8 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Yucatán’s institute moved from a medium to a high level “debido a la falta de ingresos adicionales para garantizar la operatividad del proceso electoral”, INE said, meaning for lack of extra income to guarantee that the electoral process can operate. INE describes the lost resources as relevant for the continuity of Colima’s institutional activities.

The strain is not new. INE’s third budget report, with data to 10 July 2026 and reported by La Razón, a Mexico City daily, on 30 July, found that state congresses approved 13,714.4 million pesos (about US$716 million) of the 17,002 million pesos (about US$888 million) the state election bodies had asked for in 2026.

That left a gap of almost 3,300 million pesos (about US$172 million), and Colima was then in red, with no money received for the start of its electoral process. Guerrero, Nuevo León and San Luis Potosí were in yellow in July, and INE now lists them with Hidalgo and Puebla at medium level after budget adjustments and extensions that were not approved.

Yucatán’s Budget Is Still Open to Change

Yucatán’s institute, IEPAC (Instituto Electoral y de Participación Ciudadana), unanimously approved a 2027 budget project of 631.5 million pesos (about US$33 million), Por Esto, a Yucatán newspaper, reported on 16 October. Of that, 212.8 million pesos (about US$11.1 million) is for parties and independent candidates and 161 million pesos (about US$8.4 million) for running the vote.

The project goes to the state executive and then to the state Congress, which can change it. In 2024 the legislature first authorised 436.6 million pesos (about US$22.8 million) of the 523.6 million pesos (about US$27.3 million) requested.

File photo. Paseo de la Reforma, Mexico City’s main avenue.

Yucatán’s local process opened on 6 November 2026, with precampaigns from 15 January to 12 February 2027 and campaigns from 20 April to 2 June 2027, Por Esto reported. The state elects its Congress and municipal councils in 2027.

Carla Humphrey, an INE councillor, said, as quoted by La Razón on 30 July, “the only authorities that can determine whether acts are pre-campaign or early campaign acts are the local authorities” (translated from Spanish). The same report noted that the local bodies with the least money are the ones that police early campaigning by aspirants.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mexico politics Email address Follow

INE Points to Progress Elsewhere

INE stresses progress. Thirty-one of the 32 bodies have approved their 2027 draft budgets, and only Michoacán’s is pending.

INE’s coordination calendars list 11,997 activities, of which 7,017 belong to INE, 4,150 to the state bodies and 830 are shared. So far 4,053 (33.8 percent) have started and 2,908 (24.2 percent) are finished, 87 percent of them on time, and 21 state bodies have already held their opening sessions.

INE says it keeps permanent monitoring of these cases to spot problems early and to support the local bodies, which also carry the checks on early campaigning that Humphrey described. INE’s statement does not suggest any change to election day on Sunday 6 June 2027.

INE has not said whether the state governments of Colima and Yucatán will grant the pending extensions, and no decision date has been published. We have not read INE’s full budget report, so the figures on Colima and Yucatán come from its press statement of 23 November.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did INE flag Colima and Yucatán?

INE says both state election bodies lack the extra money needed to run the 2027 process. Colima’s shortfall is the sharper, while Yucatán’s is newer.

Does the shortfall threaten the June 2027 vote?

INE’s statement does not say so, and it does not suggest any change to the election date. The federal vote is run by INE itself, not by the state bodies.

Will the missing money arrive?

INE has not said whether the state governments will grant the pending extensions. No decision date has been published.

World.title: Guyana Gas Plant Cost Climbs to US$956M
World.content:
Guyana’s gas-fired power plant at Wales now costs far more than first planned, and the government says it must pay to avoid stopping work.

The Demerara Harbour Bridge links the East Bank of the Demerara River, south of Georgetown, with the West Bank, where the Wales gas-to-energy plant is being built; file photo from November 2019 (Photo: Dan Lundberg, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Energy: Guyana

Guyana’s National Assembly, the country’s parliament, approved G$24.7 billion (about US$118 million at G$208.5 per US$, the Bank of Guyana transaction rate) on Monday 23 November 2026 for the gas-to-energy plant at Wales, on the West Bank of the Demerara River in Region Three. The Department of Public Information (DPI, the government’s information agency) said the project’s revised cost is now US$956 million.

Prime Minister Mark Phillips, a retired brigadier, told the Assembly’s Committee of Supply, its spending committee, that the money for the plant’s first and second stages will “complete Phase 1 and secure turbines for Phase 2, among other things,” DPI said on 23 November. The government says it must pay to avoid pausing the project or going to litigation.

Key Facts Who. Guyana’s government and the builder of its Wales gas-fired power plant.

What. Parliament approved G$24.7 billion more, lifting the revised project cost to US$956 million.

Where. Wales, Region Three (West Bank Demerara), Guyana.

When. Approved Monday 23 November 2026; all four first-stage turbines due by end of 2027.

As of. As of 24 November 2026, 06:30 GMT.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Energy story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Guyana’s gas-fired power plant at Wales now costs far more than first planned, and the government says it must pay to avoid stopping work.

The plant is meant to burn natural gas from offshore wells to make electricity, and the government has tied its promise of cheaper power to it. Phillips told the committee on 23 November, as DPI reported: “We want this project to continue to its end and deliver on the promise to the people.”

Finance Minister Ashni Singh said the money should finish the project as quickly as possible, News Room Guyana, a Guyanese news site, reported on 23 November. The Assembly approved G$89.8 billion (about US$431 million) in extra spending that day, and the plant’s money was part of it.

A jetty on the Demerara River, Guyana, in March 2010; file photo. Photo: Nils Ally, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Demerara Waves, a Guyanese news site, reported on 23 November that the original contract was worth US$759 million, and that the new financing is 12.8 per cent above it plus a further US$100 million. That puts the revised cost about 26% above the original, a rise of US$197 million.

Kaieteur News, a Guyanese daily, wrote in an editorial on 21 November that completion was first scheduled for the end of 2024, and it said the project is “fast becoming a monument to mismanagement, mounting costs.” It noted that G$19 billion (about US$91 million) was approved in July, and added: “Every additional dollar requested should be subjected to rigorous scrutiny.”

The builder is LINDSAYCA, a US-headquartered firm that Demerara Waves identifies as the builder, and DPI says it asked for US$200 million more, which the government agreed to pay. DPI says US$130 million has been paid so far, while Demerara Waves puts the amount already paid at US$170 million.

DPI’s release does not name LINDSAYCA, Siemens Energy, the German turbine maker, or sole-sourcing, so the two accounts cannot be reconciled from official papers. Kaieteur News said the 57 megawatts promised for December are now uncertain.

The sharper question is Phase 2, the planned second stage, which needs more turbines. Demerara Waves reported that about US$20.3 million was approved on Monday for a second 10 per cent payment to Siemens Energy, with the first 10 per cent already paid.

Phillips said, as that outlet reported, that the government chose to sole-source, meaning to buy without a tender, because Siemens Energy was “the only company that was manufacturing them.” He added that the government was “forced to do long-lead procurement, which is pay up some money up front” to secure the supplier’s commitment.

Opposition legislator Dr Terrence Campbell asked the committee about spending caps and penalties, Demerara Waves reported. Phillips replied that he “could not look into the future,” and said he “did not envisage any slippage.”

Deodat Indar, the Minister of Public Utilities and Aviation, gave the practical case for speed to the committee on 23 November, as DPI reported. He said the grid sees “a demand between 250 and 260 MW” (megawatts, a measure of generating power) every night, more than the country can generate.

Demerara Waves reported that the gas comes from offshore fields run by a consortium led by ExxonMobil, the US oil company, through a US$1 billion pipeline that ExxonMobil financed and Guyana must repay. The pipeline is not counted in the plant’s cost, and the gas itself is to arrive “free of cost.”

The project also has a loan under a credit agreement with US EXIM, the US Export-Import Bank, the American government’s export-credit agency. Singh tabled two amendments on 18 November, DPI said, to simplify reimbursement requests and extend the final disbursement date.

Demerara Waves reported that the government targets the first quarter of 2027 for start-up of the electricity plant, and DPI said all four Phase 1 turbines should be running by the end of the fourth quarter of 2027. No tender record for the Phase 2 turbines was seen in the documents available, and the sources differ on how much the builder has been paid.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is the gas plant costing more?

The government says the builder asked for extra money and that paying it avoids a pause or a court fight. Kaieteur News argues that every extra request deserves close scrutiny.

Who pays for the pipeline that feeds the plant?

Guyana must repay ExxonMobil, which financed the pipeline, according to Demerara Waves. The gas itself is to arrive free of cost.

When will the plant start producing power?

Demerara Waves reported a government target of the first quarter of 2027 for start-up, and DPI said all four first-stage turbines should run by the end of 2027. Phillips said he did not envisage delays.

World.title: Flying Through the US for Christmas? A Dec. 12 Deadline Could Slow Your Trip
World.content:
If your trip to or from Costa Rica passes through a US airport after Dec. 12, a budget fight in Washington could make it longer. Money for the Transportation Security Administration and the Federal Aviation Administration runs out after Dec. 11. If Congress has not passed new funding by then, a government shutdown starts the next day.

The airports would stay open. The people who screen your bags and guide your plane would be told to keep working without a paycheck, and that is where the trouble begins. In earlier shutdowns, unpaid staff called out, security lines stretched for hours and the FAA cut traffic at busy airports when it ran short of controllers, which meant canceled flights.

The timing is the problem. The deadline falls two weeks before Christmas, when planes are full. A canceled flight in late December leaves airlines with few empty seats to move you to. Airline newsletter writer Zach Griff told CNN that December already combines snow with schedules flown at maximum capacity, and that a staffing shortage on top of that could be “a disaster.”

None of this is certain. Dec. 12 is the deadline for a deal, not the day delays begin, and past shutdowns took days or weeks to bite as missed paychecks piled up. Congress could also settle it at the last minute. You do not need to cancel anything. A few steps now cost little and help if it happens.

Check how long your US connection is. Under two hours is tight when security or customs lines grow, so ask your airline about a longer layover while seats remain. Pick a morning flight if you are still booking. Delays build through the day, and an early departure gives you more later flights to fall back on.

Install your airline’s app and turn on alerts. Check your flight’s status before leaving for the airport. Rebooking in the app is usually faster than the counter line. Connecting through the United States to a third country carries the same risk, so apply the same checks even if the US is not your destination.

Read your travel insurance or credit card coverage. Many policies cover delays and missed connections, but some exclude government action, and it is better to know before you need it. Juan Santamaría and Liberia airports are not affected directly. The delays would start at the other end of the route and travel with the plane.

World.title: Refugees in Costa Rica Lose UN-Funded Health Coverage on Jan. 1
World.content:
A program that gave public health coverage to more than 14,000 refugees, asylum seekers and stateless people in Costa Rica over seven years will end on Dec. 31. Those still enrolled will have to find another way into the public health system from Jan. 1, 2027. The Costa Rican Social Security Fund, known as the Caja or CCSS and the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, said the collective insurance agreement is closing for lack of funding. UNHCR attributed the decision to budget limits it faces worldwide.

The agreement began in 2019 as a pilot for people in economic hardship with serious medical needs, four years before Costa Rica expanded the coverage to more asylum seekers and refugees. It paid for consultations, medicines, specialized treatment and follow-up for chronic illness. UNHCR put more than $11.5 million into it between 2020 and 2026.

About two-thirds of the beneficiaries were women and roughly 60% were between 18 and 50 years old with chronic or serious illnesses, according to figures released with the announcement. The two institutions have not said how many people are covered today. For 2025, UNHCR committed 1,048.2 million colones (about $2.3 million) to insure an estimated 4,330 people and the agency has said the program was running at reduced capacity this year.

Eithel Corea Baltodano, the Caja’s interim financial manager, said the agreement had a positive effect on more than 14,000 people in extreme vulnerability, many of whom needed continuous treatment for chronic disease. People whose coverage runs out on Dec. 31, along with those on waiting lists, must apply to the Caja directly for another form of insurance.

Enrollment is not automatic and each option has its own requirements and the Caja will assess applications case by case at the rights-validation desk, or Validación de Derechos, of each person’s assigned health center. The options include insurance paid by the state for those who qualify and an assessment by the Joint Social Welfare Institute (IMAS) for people living in poverty, which does not guarantee coverage. Workers in formal jobs are insured through their employers.

Voluntary insurance is also available but the migrant women’s organization Mujeres Raíz said its lowest monthly payment, about 32,000 colones (about $72), is out of reach for many refugees and it asked UNHCR and the government for an option matched to their incomes. Some groups keep their access.

Children, adolescents and pregnant women are entitled to state-covered care whatever their nationality or migration status, once they are enrolled through the Caja. People living with HIV can continue antiretroviral treatment without interruption. No special transition has been announced for other patients who need permanent treatment. UNHCR said it will keep working with the government to inform refugees and asylum seekers about their rights and the options open to them.

The change comes three months after Costa Rica reopened an immigration category for 10,000 rejected asylum seekers. Requirements for each type of insurance are published by the Caja, and applications are handled in person at local health centers.

World.title: Who Would Pay Costa Rica’s Proposed 10% Tax on Airbnb Platforms
World.content:
A proposal to tax short-term rental platforms in Costa Rica has opened a dispute over who would end up paying, the companies or the people who book through them. The bill carries the signatures of Frente Amplio’s José María Villalta Flórez-Estrada and six party colleagues, and targets what short-stay platforms collect in commissions and service fees with a special 10% charge. Where a company is domiciled makes no difference, as long as the property is in Costa Rica.

The charge is aimed at the intermediary’s earnings, not at the full price of a stay. On a booking where the platform keeps 15%, the tax would equal 1.5% of the total, if the company passed all of it on. The Asociación de Consumidores Libres expects exactly that. Its president, Juan Ricardo Fernández, argued that guests would absorb the cost directly, and noted that it would sit on top of the 13% value-added tax while leaving other kinds of lodging untouched.

The group called the plan protectionism in favor of competing lodging sectors and warned of fewer listings and higher rates. Among those it says would be hurt are Costa Rican families on vacation and patients or students who travel to San José from outside the metropolitan area. Villalta has said the aim is to bring order to the business, not to prohibit it. His explanatory statement cites a 2025 OECD report in arguing that short-term rentals have pushed up rents and squeezed housing access, above all on the coasts.

Half of the revenue would go to municipalities, 30% to the national housing bank Banhvi and 20% to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute. Banhvi’s share is earmarked for housing and affordable rental programs in cantons under heavy tourist pressure. The tax is only one part of the text. Local governments could limit how many short-term rentals operate in a district, neighborhood or building, provided technical studies support the limit.

An owner renting out a single apartment would have to meet seven requirements to register with the tourism institute, and operators could be fined up to 20 base salaries, about 9.2 million colones ($20,600). Platforms would also have to hand host and guest information to state institutions, a clause the consumer group says lacks explicit data protection safeguards.

The debate has not started and the Legislative Assembly has been in extraordinary sessions since Nov. 1, and the Executive Branch, which sets the agenda in that period, has not included the bill. Until it does, the proposal cannot advance, and any change to what a rental costs or how many can operate remains months away at the earliest.

World.title: Route 1 Traffic Costs Commuters 38 Days a Year as Costa Rica Pledges a Fix
World.content:
A driver who commutes on Route 1 between La Uruca and La Garita loses about 907 hours a year to congestion, the equivalent of 38 days, according to the State of the Nation 2026 report. On Sunday the government answered Costa Rica traffic complaints with the largest budget in the history of the public works ministry and a rebuilt highway that it says will take more than 40 minutes off the trip.

The report puts the added travel time on that stretch at about 216 minutes a day. That is 57 minutes in the morning and 112 in the afternoon, plus a buffer of roughly 23 minutes each way that drivers allow for the unexpected. It prices the lost time and the extra cost of running a vehicle at 1,687,233 colones a year (about $3,780) for a person who works a standard weekday schedule.

That equals 2.8 times the monthly gross salary of about 600,000 colones used as a reference, or 21.7% of annual gross income. In 2019 the cost was about 1.1 million colones, or 15.9%. On the Circunvalación beltway, Route 39, the added time between Zapote and Calle Blancos is about 26 minutes a day. The report estimates the annual cost there at 220,000 colones (about $490).

Both roads were widened in recent years and the report concludes that the relief was temporary. Luis Vargas, an economist and researcher with the State of the Nation Program, said congestion eased after the works and during the pandemic, began rising again in 2023 and by 2025 was above its 2019 level.

Vargas said no road can keep pace on its own. He said infrastructure investment has to come together with public transport, urban planning and a smaller vehicle fleet. The report notes that only 52% of the national territory has a current zoning plan and that about 110,000 vehicles use the Route 1 corridor, a number that could grow by as much as 7% by 2032.

In a pre-recorded national broadcast yesterday, President Laura Fernández said the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) will have 550,000 million colones (about $1.23 billion) in 2027. She attributed the congestion to decisions postponed by previous administrations. The broadcast did not explain how the money will be divided among projects.

Public Works Minister Efraím Zeledón said work on the central section of the San José–San Ramón highway expansion will begin in 2027 with earthworks, drainage and a bridge over the Cañuela River. He said the Coyola interchange will start in February. Zeledón said the finished project will cut travel times by more than 40 minutes for people who live in the west of the Central Valley. He did not present data to support the estimate. The expanded highway is also expected to carry four tolls.

The government also said the widening of the Barranca–Limonal highway will be finished in 2027 and that 10 overpasses will replace roundabouts on the route between Guápiles and Limón. It gave no cost or start date for the overpasses. The tender to design and build a metropolitan train is to be published in the first quarter of 2027, according to the broadcast. No route, cost or financing model was given.

The San José–San Ramón contract went out in October Fand the start dates announced on Sunday are the government’s own projections. The report’s figures describe the corridor as it is today.

World.title: Thousands of Costa Rica Teachers Could Lose Pay After Court Rules Strike Illegal
World.content:
A San José labor court has declared illegal the Nov. 11 strike called by five education unions, a ruling that allows the Ministry of Public Education (MEP) to deduct pay for the time workers missed. The ministry counted 36,994 staff members absent that day. Judge Carolina Muñoz González of the Labor Court of the First Judicial Circuit of San José issued the sentence on Friday and the decision became public last night. The case was brought by the State through the Attorney General’s Office.

The ruling covers the Secondary School Teachers Association (APSE), the National Association of Educators (ANDE), the Costa Rican Educators Union (SEC), the National Union of Guidance Professionals (Sinapro) and the Patriotic Education Union 7 de Agosto (Sinpae). The court found that the unions did not meet the legal requirements for a lawful strike. According to the ruling, the stoppage went ahead without the plan the Labor Code requires to keep basic school services running, including cleaning, security and care for students with disabilities.

The judge also found that staff from MEP school cafeterias took part in the strike. The court treated school meals as an essential public service, in which strikes are prohibited. The ruling further cited defects in the strike notices and in the proof of the minimum level of worker support.

Under the Labor Code, a declaration of illegality allows employers to deduct wages for time not worked. Workers who prove a justified absence through the ministry’s administrative process are exempt. The ruling also leaves the ministry the option of ordering that lost time be made up instead, through a reasoned resolution copied to the Comptroller General’s Office and the Ombudsman’s Office.

The decision is a first-instance ruling. The parties have three days to appeal before the same court and it comes after the government moved to dock pay for education workers who joined the strike earlier this month. Education Minister Leonardo Sánchez Hernández said at the time that the 36,994 absences represented about 35% of the ministry’s staff. The ministry also reported that 175 school cafeterias did not open and that about 800 schools had problems with cleaning or security.

An earlier ministry count, taken on the day of the strike, showed 13,074 officials absent and 58 cafeterias closed. A certified court record cited in the case put the number of closed cafeterias at 50. During the proceedings, ANDE, APSE and Sinapro argued that school closures could not be attributed to the protest without proof for each individual worker. The judge found that the timing of the absences and closures established an objective link between them.

The unions did win on one point. The government had argued that the stoppage was a dispute over employer obligations. The judge instead classified it as a protest against public policy, covering the education budget, salaries and pensions, a type of strike the Labor Code allows without prior conciliation.

The court also noted that neither the ministry nor the unions sought dialogue to agree on a basic-services plan before the strike, and it exempted both sides from paying legal costs. The one-day strike, which included a march from Parque La Merced to the Legislative Assembly, was called to protest cuts to public education in the 2027 national budget. Those cuts had already drawn warnings that the National University could stop round-the-clock tsunami monitoring on Jan. 1.

The budget fight has since moved to the courts on several fronts. The Constitutional Chamber has ordered lawmakers to strip conditions from the 2027 budget bill, including restrictions on funds for the Judiciary. Whether the unions appeal will determine how soon the ministry can act on the deductions. The broader dispute over education funding will continue as lawmakers finish work on the 2027 budget, which the Constitution requires them to approve by the end of November.

World.title: Costa Rica Will Co-Host the 2031 Women’s World Cup After FIFA Approval
World.content:
Costa Rica will co-host the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup after FIFA’s member associations approved on Monday the joint bid it shares with the United States, Mexico and Jamaica. It will be the first time matches of a senior World Cup, men’s or women’s, are played in Costa Rica.

The decision came at an extraordinary FIFA Congress held by videoconference. The four-nation proposal was the only bid for 2031, and FIFA said the hosts were appointed by acclamation. The same Congress awarded the 2035 tournament to England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

Osael Maroto, president of the Costa Rican Football Federation (Fedefútbol), said the tournament is a chance to put Costa Rica’s name before the whole world and thanked FIFA’s members for backing the bid. He said a long road of preparation lies ahead and that the event should leave a legacy for future generations.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino said the 2031 and 2035 tournaments should reach beyond the pitch, with more women and girls playing, coaching, refereeing and leading in the sport.

The 2031 edition will be the first with 48 teams and the first played across four countries. The bid calls for 104 matches from mid-June to late July in 20 stadiums: 14 in the United States, four in Mexico, one in Costa Rica and one in Jamaica.

Costa Rica’s venue is the Estadio Nacional in La Sabana, San José, which opened in 2011 and holds about 35,000 people. FIFA’s evaluation report gave the stadium 3.8 out of 5 and said it appears to meet most requirements. The bid as a whole scored 4.4 out of 5 in the technical evaluation.

Fedefútbol also put forward the Ricardo Saprissa stadium in Tibás, which is not among the 20 recommended venues. With a single stadium, Costa Rica may host the matches of only one group. How many games come to San José has not been decided.

The same report identifies transport as the weak point. FIFA wants better ways to move fans from Juan Santamaría International Airport to San José and to the stadium. It noted a heavy dependence on cars and, so far, no formal commitment to free public transport on match days.

Hotels, telecommunications and government support met FIFA’s requirements, according to the report. The airport recently opened a single pickup hub for taxis, shuttles and rental cars, but the road into the capital remains one of the most congested in the country.

Costa Rica has staged two FIFA youth tournaments, the U-17 Women’s World Cup in 2014 and the U-20 Women’s World Cup in 2022. The United States hosted the senior women’s tournament in 1999 and 2003, while 2031 will be a first for Mexico, Jamaica and Costa Rica.

Monday’s decision was the last formal step in a process that saw FIFA inspectors visit Costa Rica in February and the bid clear FIFA’s technical evaluation on Nov. 11. The match schedule, the final list of stadiums and ticket details will be announced later.

World.title: Nicoya Towns Got 10 Minutes of Tap Water a Day as El Niño Dried Their Wells
World.content:
Residents of Iguanita, a rural community in Nicoya, received piped water for about 10 minutes a day through most of October, after the springs that feed the local aqueduct came close to running dry. It is one of several cases of water rationing in Guanacaste, where community-run systems are cutting service or relying on tanker trucks as El Niño reduces their supplies.

Luz Marina Villegas, vice president of Iguanita’s community water association (ASADA), said recent rain has partly restored the springs. The association still fears the shortage will return. It has begun the process of asking the national water utility, AyA, to take over the system because there are no nearby sources to fall back on.

In Moracia, also in Nicoya, the association’s main well dried up on Oct. 31 after its flow had been falling since May 20. Homes there now get piped water every second day, from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m. A tanker truck arrives from Santa Cruz on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. Gabriela Fonseca, the Moracia association’s administrator, said anger over the rationing has led to confrontations with residents.

The association is working with the Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE) to drill a new well. It has also asked AyA for a hydrogeological study to determine whether the existing wells can be deepened. Elsewhere in Guanacaste, the Pilangosta association, which also serves Marbella and Pita Rayada, has been supplying water for about 12 hours a day for the past two months.

Pita Rayada is the worst affected. Its springs are low and its well cannot meet demand, so the association is drawing water from a stream, chlorinating it by hand and building a new well. Association president Emel Rodríguez said rain raised the levels for a time. He expects the shortage to deepen as the rains stop. The dry season began in Guanacaste earlier this month.

AyA executive president Lourdes Sáurez said several associations have reported that their sources have dried up. Systems run directly by AyA have lost flow, she said, but none has run dry. Guanacaste has 304 community water associations, and the effects of El Niño vary from one community to the next.

The utility has assigned two tanker trucks to community aqueducts and announced two more. It has also bought 16 tankers, with deliveries scheduled for November and December. From about Dec. 15, AyA plans to place storage tanks of up to 22,000 liters (about 5,800 gallons) at fixed points, so residents can collect water without trucks stopping at every home. It will also distribute pipe to replace damaged and leaking sections.

The pressure is not limited to rural systems. AyA has already asked households to cut their water use, and the World Meteorological Organization expects El Niño to peak in December. Rationing schedules on community systems are set by each local association, which is the first place to check for changes.

World.title: Costa Rica Starts the Week at 35°C With a Cold Push Due by Thursday
World.content:
Pack for heat if you are heading to the Pacific coast. Costa Rica weather this week starts hot and dry, with Monday’s high reaching 35.4°C (96°F) in Liberia and clear skies over most of the country, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). Nicoya and Puntarenas are close behind at about 35°C (95°F). There is very little moisture in the air, so few clouds form, and that is why temperatures are climbing on both coasts and in the center of the country.

In the Central Valley, expect a clear, warm morning and a few clouds in the afternoon. San José tops out at 27.5°C (82°F) and drops to 19°C (66°F) overnight. Alajuela reaches 30.7°C (87°F). You will feel the trade winds in the morning over the valley and Guanacaste, where they blow at moderate strength. They ease after midday, which is when the heat is hardest to escape.

You only need a rain jacket in two areas. The mountains of the Central Pacific get scattered showers in the afternoon, and the South Pacific sees brief, isolated ones. Golfito still reaches 33°C (91°F). The Caribbean and the Northern Zone stay mostly clear all day. Limón reaches 31.6°C (89°F), Sarapiquí 33°C (91°F) and Upala 34°C (93°F).

This follows a hot, nearly rainless weekend, and it marks a turning point in the calendar. The Central Valley finishes its shift from rainy season to dry season on Monday, the IMN says. The Central Pacific follows by Nov. 30, when the change begins in the South Pacific, and the western Northern Zone starts around Dec. 3.

Conditions change later in the week and the IMN expects a weak cold push to influence the weather between Thursday and Friday. Cold pushes usually strengthen the wind and bring rain to the Caribbean side, but the institute has not yet given details for this one, so check the forecast again midweek if you have weekend plans.

One thing you can stop watching for is a tropical storm. The Atlantic hurricane season ends on Nov. 30, and the IMN does not expect any more systems in its final week. Until the cold push arrives, the sun is the main thing to plan around. With almost no cloud cover, midday exposure is intense at any elevation, so carry water, use sunscreen and take your breaks in the shade.

World.title: Killer strikes again!
World.content:
A 70-year-old Portland man who was out on parole after serving 24 years for killing, dismembering ,and burning a woman with whom he had a relationship in 1989, has been sent back to prison after he again chopped and killed another woman with whom he claimed to be in a relationship in 2021.

The man, Jasper Jemison, otherwise called Sojie, a farmer of Hopefield District in the parish, had been sentenced to life in prison for the first murder.

On November 17 this year Jemison, who has been before the courts since 2022, pleaded guilty to the July 2021 murder of Cynthia Hinds, also called Tiney, in St Margaret’s Bay.

Supreme Court judge Justice Judith Pusey, who presided over the trial, slapped Jemison with a 25-year sentence at hard labour. He will be eligible for parole after serving 20 years.

The case was prosecuted by Acting Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Malike Kellier and Crown Counsel Nyron Wright.

The court heard that Hinds left her home on the morning of July 22, 2021 for her farm, which was neighbouring Jemison’s, on lands located across from Ken Jones Aerodrome in St Margaret’s Bay. Her partner, after calling her several times on her cellular phone with no success, later that morning went to her farm and found her hut ablaze, but saw no sign of her.

After summoning help, the partner, along with Hinds’ daughter and a police corporal, who was seen along the way, returned to the farm and attempted to put out the blaze. Hinds’ charred body was then found face down with the lower part of the right leg missing.

Investigations led to Jemison being taken into custody after it was discovered that he was the last person to see her alive. Three days later he told cops in a caution statement that he and Hinds were in a quarrel when he chopped her, using her own machete, after she attacked him. He claimed she then fell into a fire in her hut where she had been cooking and was burnt.

Jemison later led the lawmen to his farm where he dug up the machete that he had buried. A day later, in the presence of his attorney, Jemison was charged with murder and arson. When cautioned he said, “Officer, mi neva mean fi kill Tiney, and when mi tell yuh seh mi slap her wid mi cutlass, mi mean fi seh chop.”

When cautioned for the offence of arson, Jemison made no comment.

He later claimed during an interview before sentencing that he had been “experiencing remorse since the incident”, claiming he had shared an intimate relationship with Hinds and described her as a good person who was well regarded by himself and the community.

Vaginal swabs of Hinds’ body revealed semen which matched buccal swabs taken from Jemison, according to the evidence unveiled in the matter.

An assessment of the farmer, who claims to be a Muslim, by the Portland Probation Office said Jemison’s behaviour was of “significant concern, particularly given that he was previously convicted of murder and was afforded the opportunity of clemency through parole”.

In noting concern that the crime was committed while he was on parole for another crime, the parole office said it suggested that his previous experience with the justice system did not “sufficiently deter him from further offending”.

Additional concern was voiced over the fact that Jemison appeared to have withheld information from investigators about his behaviour, as community and family members said before the murder Jemison began “consuming alcohol and displaying behaviours they considered uncharacteristic of him”.

Probation officers further lamented the fact that his age had not acted as a deterrent noting, “Research on recidivism identifies age as an important consideration in understanding patterns of offending… studies have generally establish that offending tends to peak during adolescence and early adulthood before declining as individuals advance in age. However, at the age of 70, Mr Jemison has found himself once again before the court.”

The probation officers also said, “The offender’s actions suggest not only a lack of appreciation for the value of the lives of others but also a resistance to societal norms and values. In addition, his violation of the conditions of his parole order further indicates that community supervision has been ineffective and a custodial sentence is therefore the most appropriate disposition of this matter before this Honourable Court.”

In the murder of then 19-year-old Dorothy Williams for which Jemison was first tried and convicted, he had, for days, told individuals, including the man he accused her of cheating on him with, that she had gone to Kingston and would return shortly.

Ironically, that man was among the people who discovered the body of Jemison’s second victim.

When Jemison confessed to the first murder in February 1989, he told police who had taken him into custody as a person of interest that on January 31 he was going down a steep hill with his cutlass in hand and Williams was behind him. He said she held onto his shoulders and both of them slid down the gully bank at which point she fell onto the cutlass and started to bleed from her neck.

He claimed that he covered her up with a bag and decided not to tell anyone. He told the court at the time that when he returned another day “something had eaten her hands and feet and so he put trash on the body and burnt it”.

He was found guilty in the Port Antonio Circuit Court and sentenced to life. Jemison lost a subsequent appeal in which the court ruled that the burnt body was enough for the jury to infer that he was responsible for Williams’ death and that there was sufficient evidence to rebut the defence of an accident.

World.title: ‘Go back to the JDF’
World.content:
Opposition Leader Mark Golding speaking at a news conference at the Office of the Opposition Leader in St Andrew on Monday. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

INSISTING that someone must be held accountable for the less than desirable state of affairs at the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), Opposition Leader Mark Golding has called for the resignation of the agency’s head, Commander Alvin Gayle.

The call comes following last Tuesday’s release of an Auditor General’s report that uncovered a litany of problems at the disaster management agency in relation to its handling of relief supplies meant for victims of Hurricane Melissa which devastated south- and north-western parishes in October 2025.

According to Auditor General Pamela Monroe-Ellis, only 31 of 200 container houses donated by the Chinese Government have been accounted for and hundreds of bags of rice, crackers, and other food items meant for victims of the hurricane were spoiled after they became infested with insects.

Questions have also been asked about how hurricane relief money was spent.

Gayle was seconded from the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) in November 2025 to serve as director general of ODPEM, but Golding is unimpressed with his performance to date, in light of the unflattering auditor general report.

Golding made the call for his head on Monday during a press conference at the Office of the Opposition Leader in St Andrew.

“In terms of what Commander Gayle has said, as far as I’m concerned, Commander Gayle should really step down as the head of ODPEM and return to the JDF,” said Golding.

“What has happened under his watch is totally unacceptable, and if the prime minister is going to deny accountability for it, Commander Gayle, as the de facto CEO of the agency over this period, cannot,” he added.

Golding noted that after Melissa struck on October 28 last year, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness took a decision to relocate ODPEM to the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) in November 2025, “promising in doing so, that it would manage the situation to the highest standards of transparency and accountability”.

“The various Auditor General’s reports to come out in 2026, including this most recent one, show the abject failure of the prime minister as the accountable minister for the Office of the Prime Minister, in executing on that commitment,” Golding said.

He argued that Jamaica must hold Holness and the Government fully accountable for what has happened on his watch.

Asserting that the prime minister has failed to deliver on his promise, Golding spoke to what he said was delivered instead.

“Money that was donated for the benefit of victims of the hurricane, trust funds, diverted and paid to clear goods for third parties,” said Golding. He suggested that it was obvious that Jamaica Customs “received a lot of those funds so no doubt the Government was paying itself with money that was entrusted for the benefit of the people who needed it”.

Golding charged that there has also been a total failure to account for the supply of goods that has come into the country through ODPEM, with only 15 per cent of donated container homes accounted for. He also emphasised that 15 donated containers remained unopened.

“It is a litany of woes for which the Government must be fully accountable,” Golding insisted. He also took a swipe at the prime minister, remarking that “good leaders take the blame for their failures and give their teams credit for their successes. Weak leaders take the credit for successes and publicly blame the team when things go wrong”.

Golding asserted that the prime minister cannot take control of ODPEM and then disown the results of ODPEM’s work under his watch.

“Prime Minister, you cannot promise the highest standards and then try to wash your hands of those standards when you fail to execute and maintain the very standards that you’ve promised to keep; accountability is not a convenience,” the Opposition leader said.

He demanded that the prime minister make a full statement to Parliament accepting responsibility for ODPEM’s non-performance under his office. He also demanded that the report of the Disaster Risk Management Review Committee be published with an indication of which recommendations have already been implemented. Additionally, he called for the publication of every cash and in-kind donation received showing where it went and who received it.

“And the Government needs to urgently put in place an appropriate legal mechanism for receiving donations from outside of Government that are intended for disaster victims and for distributing those donations in a timely, transparent and accountable manner,” Golding said.

He also called for the $45.1-million that was wrongly diverted from the donations account to be clawed back and instead be spent for roof repairs or other direct support for Melissa victims.

“And we would like to see a list of who received the 200 prefabricated houses that were donated,” he added.

According to Golding, “Jamaica deserves a Government that treats every dollar, and every item of every donation as if it belongs to the people for whom it was given.”

He said a future PNP Government would remove ODPEM from under the OPM and pushed back on claims that the decline of ODPEM started under the previous PNP Administration.

“That’s more than 10 years ago. If that were so, and it isn’t, the Government has had over 10 years to address the issue and has deep responsibility to do so in the context of what’s happening globally with climate change,” Golding argued.

World.title: MECA isn’t closed!
World.content:
International rapper Offset enjoying himself at MECA during a past visit to Jamaica.

Michael Dawson, owner of MECA nightclub, is dispelling rumours that the Kingston hot spot is shutting its doors.

Adamant that the entertainment establishment isn’t going anywhere, Dawson said plans are underway to catapult the club into a new era.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer, Dawson said the club’s parent company, MECA-Whirlwind Group, is preparing for a busy period, centred on international theatre productions and an even bigger announcement still to come.

“We have been legally handling some social media posts about us being closed and out of business, so we want to take care of that before dropping the biggest news in our nightclub’s history,” he said, highlighting that expansions are underway at MECA.

“There is so much happening right now that I am not at liberty to say just yet. I just want persons to know that the club that reignited Kingston’s nightlife and reimagined nightly entertainment will raise the bar even higher,” he said. “We remain the celebrity hot spot of choice. I know people’s memory can be short, but I don’t want you to forget where the likes of Cardi B, Offset, Chris Brown, and Kartel chose to party when they craved an unforgettable experience.”

“We are still very much in business and when you see what we have in store, there will be no doubt about which entertainment spot continues to give quality experiences,” he added.

In the meantime, Dawson shared that the group’s Whirlwind Live Performances division, continues to carry the entertainment baton through its US theatre tour over the weekend.

The tour will take Jamaican theatre to nine American cities for 10 performances over 14 days.

Billed under the banner ‘Jamaican Theatre Is Back’, the tour features two productions led by veteran comedians Oliver Samuels and Glen “Titus” Campbell.

Samuels will headline Where Dere’s A Will, Dere’s A Criminal, while Campbell takes centre stage in Patrick Brown’s Boopsie’s Homecoming.

The productions will travel through Florida, Connecticut, New York, and Georgia, bringing Jamaican theatrical comedy to audiences across the Caribbean Diaspora. The schedule includes stops in Tampa, Orlando, Hartford, Brooklyn, Atlanta, Queens, Coral Springs, Bridgeport, and the Bronx, with the two productions running concurrently in different markets.

World.title: Lack of preparation letting down U-17 W-Cup Boyz, say coaches
World.content:
HALLIMAN... this is the World Cup, the highest level we can get to, and yet the team was not properly prepared — and this is unfair to the players (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

VETERAN football coaches Lebert Halliman and Patrick “Jackie” Walters have blamed a lack of international practice games for the below-par performance of Jamaica’s young Reggae Boyz footballers at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Doha, Qatar.

The Jamaicans have given up 12 goals in two games in losses to Italy and Uzbekistan in Group E, and the odds of them advancing to the knockout round is all but over.

After going down 0-6 to Italy in their opening game on Friday, Jamaica led Uzbekistan twice on Monday, with goals from Kelvin D Brown, before collapsing to a 2-6 defeat.

Italy, who beat Ivory Coast 2-1 on Monday, lead the group with six points, followed by Uzbekistan and Ivory Coast with three each. The Jamaicans are without a point.

Only two teams have conceded more goals than Jamaica so far, Fiji with 21 and Concacaf neighbours Cuba with 14.

Both Walters and Halliman, who have coached at the national junior team level, said not having friendly games against international teams left the young Boyz short on preparation.

“Look how long the team qualified for the World Cup and the team got no exposure after the Concacaf qualification [ended in March],” Halliman noted.

“This is the World Cup, the highest level we can get to, and yet the team was not properly prepared — and this is unfair to the players,” added Halliman, who won Manning Cup schoolboy football titles as coach of Excelsior High and St Andrew Technical.

Walters, one of the most respected youth coaches in the country, said while Brown caught his eye with two “excellent goals” overall, he was less than impressed with what he saw.

“What can we really expect?” Walters asked. “The team did not get the right kind of preparation, they did not get proper exposure,” he said, pointing out that Uzbekistan played 21 games, and Italy almost the same number, leading up to the World Cup.

He noted that the team appeared to lack pace in both games.

“The players were slow to react, and this could be a mental thing. They had little spatial awareness, in that they did not seem to be scanning wide areas of the field and were only focused on small areas.”

Additionally, Walters slammed the selection of the team, saying more scouting should have been done.

“There seemed to be a focus on players in Kingston, and that is disgraceful,” he said.

Dwight Jeremiah, head coach at Trelawny-based William Knibb Memorial High and broadcast analyst, agreed with Walters. He the federation’s technical development plan had not spread far enough across the island.

“It appears the programme is only in Kingston, and as such, players outside that geographical area are not fully included and so we don’t always have the best players for representation.”

On Monday, Uzbekistan scored five unanswered goals after Jamaica took a 2-1 lead. The Uzbekistan team dominated the game, earning 18 corners and accruing 40 attempts at goal, with 14 on target.

Sukhrob Sadirdjanov scored a hat-trick to lead Uzbekistan, who had lost 1-2 in their opening game to Ivory Coast.

Brown gave Jamaica the lead with a fine finish in the eighth minute, beating goalkeeper Olimjon Shamuratov to his right.

But Uzbekistan responded almost immediately, with Laziz Abduraimov pouncing on a ball that was only partially blocked by goalkeeper Omario White, firing into the unprotected goal.

Brown restored Jamaica’s lead in the 25th minute when he received a pass from the left wing and muscled his way past two defenders to fire into the corner of the goal.

Sadirdjanov got his first in the 31st minute when he brought Uzbekistan level at 2-2, and then scored in the 47th and 58th minutes to kill off the game as a contest.

Amikhon Erkinov scored Uzbekistan’s fifth in the 79th minute before substitute Akhrorbek Ravshanbekov added a sixth in second-half stoppage time.

World.title: SMALL ISLAND, BIG DREAMS
World.content:
Jamaica’s Allyson Swaby (right) and teammates (from left) Drew Spence, Deneisha Blackwood, and Atlanta Primus celebrate scoring the team’s first goal during the Women’s World Cup Group F football match versus Panama at Perth Rectangular Stadium in Australia on July 29, 2023. (Photo: AFP)

WHEN Michael Ricketts became Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) president in 2017, hosting a FIFA World Cup was far from being a reality. Now nearly a decade late, the island’s confirmation as a co-host of the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup has given him reason to celebrate a milestone he believes will transform the country’s sporting landscape.



Following the Jamaica Observer’s report last Friday, FIFA President Gianni Infantino officially announced Jamaica as a co-host alongside the USA, Mexico, and Costa Rica at Monday’s FIFA Extraordinary Congress in Zurich, Switzerland.

It’s a significant moment for the island which will not only become the first Caribbean country to host a senior World Cup but also secure automatic qualification for the Reggae Girlz, who could make their fourth-consecutive appearance at the tournament.

Although joining the bid in October 2025, Jamaica wasn’t initially part of the plan. However, that changed following a game-changing conversation between Ricketts and Montagliani during the Reggae Girlz’s second World Cup appearance in Australia and New Zealand in 2023.

“The thought came up about how Jamaica could be rewarded for being so consistent with our women’s programmes and the suggestion came up that maybe we should try and bid for a World Cup tournament,” Ricketts told the Observer. “The truth is that we were focused initially on a youth world cup tournament but as it turned out Victor and myself had some discussions and then he introduced me to Cindy Cone [US Soccer president] and then Cindy and myself started having some intense discussions and then it became real.

“We then invited Victor to Jamaica maybe two or three years ago and we sat with Minister Grange and we posed the questions — how would Jamaica handle this? Would the stadium be ready? Would you really be interested? And she was super-excited and then we got further word from her that the Prime Minister [Andrew Holness] was as excited as she was so the preparations really got into high gear and, like I said, the rest is history.”

Ricketts admits turning discussions to tangible results wasn’t easy but believes divine intervention and the support of a strong team helped made it possible.

“It looked then an impossible task but you know, there’s the scripture that says, if Christ is in the vessel, you can smile at the storm,” he said. “We would have had some tumultuous times in my tenure, but we would have had some good times, some good moments, some great achievements, some historic achievements.”

“God has been good to me, he has given me some good people to work with, my directors have stood by my side and we have put a lot of work into this. Now we have crossed the line, and we must now bask in the glory of an achievement that seemed impossible some years ago.”

Ricketts was on hand in Zurich to witness Jamaica’s confirmation as co-host alongside former JFF Operations Manager Omar McFarlane, Concacaf President Victor Montagliani and the respective presidents of USA Soccer, Mexico Football Federation and Costa Rican Football Federation.

The JFF boss knew the announcement was coming days in advance, but nothing could prepare him for the moment it became official.

“It’s no longer a dream, it’s no longer a plan, it’s no longer a proposal. It is now real, it is now formal, it is now official,” said Ricketts. “[Monday’s] exercise was indeed one for the history books and we are just absolutely delighted, we are happy, we are excited. It is for real and the whole world will descend on Kingston in 2031 so we are just excited.”

All eyes will now be on Jamaica’s readiness for the tournament in less than five years’ time with the construction of the National Stadium central to the country’s plans.

However, Sports Minister Olivia Grange remains confident that all deadlines will be met.

“The Government of Jamaica, through the Ministry of Sport remains fully committed to fulfilling every obligation and to delivering an outstanding tournament experience,” she said. “Preparations are already underway [and] we will continue to work closely with the JFF, the Local Organising Committee, and all stakeholders to ensure Jamaica is ready to host the world in 2031.”

It’s being estimated that the expanded 48-team World Cup will see nearly five million fans in attendance and generate over US$4 billion ($633.8 billion) in revenue.

Ricketts says Brand Jamaica will be one of the tournament’s biggest selling points.

“People want to come to Jamaica not just to watch a game of football but to see what Jamaica is — to see our beaches, to participate in fun activities, to have Jamaican food, to listen to reggae music,” he said.

“We do not just want it to be a footballing event, but we want it to be an event that is going to socially impact the well-being of every single Jamaican from a commercial standpoint to a footballing standpoint, to providing a kind of catalyst so that people want to see what football brings and, of course, this will bring a number of tourists to our shores, which must have an impact from a commercial standpoint.”

World.title: A Good Cocktail-Hour Reception
World.content:
A good cocktail hour has a way of getting everyone into the party spirit.

The vows are sealed, the first tray of drinks appears, and someone spots a friend across the lawn. Within minutes, the laughter gets louder and the celebration finds its rhythm. A good cocktail hour has a way of getting everyone into the party spirit.

Guests love the freedom. They can move around, catch up with old friends and meet someone new without a seating plan deciding their company. One conversation leads to another, and suddenly two people who arrived as strangers are swapping stories.

Then there is the food. Little bites invite a little adventure and the pleasure of discovering what comes around next. Couples should keep portions small and trays circulating; nobody wants to chase a server or perform a balancing act with a plate, glass and handbag.

A chilled drink offered on arrival makes guests feel welcomed immediately. A signature cocktail with a unique name adds personality, while an equally appealing mocktail ensures everyone can join the toast. Attentive waitstaff keeps conversations flowing without repeated trips to the bar.

Music brings its own invitation to loosen up. An acoustic duo, a lively musical instrument, or a curated playlist can have guests tapping their feet before the dance floor officially opens. Keep the volume friendly enough for conversation, and that early energy can carry straight into the evening.

Guests also love a little discovery. An imaginative seating display, an audio guest book for leaving messages, or a striking cocktail presentation gives them something to explore and talk about. A few personal touches can turn a pleasant gathering into a celebration that feels unmistakably yours.

Comfort keeps the fun going. Lounge pockets invite longer chats, cocktail tables give drinks a landing place, and proper seating offers relief from those beautiful but ambitious heels. At an outdoor Jamaican wedding, shade and a welcome breeze can be among the most appreciated details.

Having the newlyweds there makes it even better. Planning some portraits before the ceremony, perhaps with a first look, can free the couple to join the fun. Enjoy the food you selected and the company you brought together.

There is room to linger, too. A slightly longer cocktail hour can be lovely when refreshments and service keep pace. For couples choosing a full cocktail reception, the same relaxed appeal can last all evening, with substantial food served throughout and enough seating to settle in comfortably.

With delicious things arriving and good conversations unfolding, guests will have every reason to linger.

World.title: He must stay
World.content:
Jamaica Labour Party Deputy Leader Desmond McKenzie (centre) speaking during a press conference at the party’s headquarters in St Andrew on Monday, as Senator Marlon Morgan (left) and chairman of the JLP Communication Taskforce Senator Abka Fitz-Henley listen. (Photos: Joseph Wellington)

Following Opposition Leader Mark Golding’s call for Commander Alvin Gayle to step down as director general of the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), the governing Jamaica Labour Party on Monday stood firmly behind the embattled agency chief.

The party argues that the failures exposed at ODPEM were not simply the result of decisions made under his leadership, but stemmed from long-standing weaknesses and resistance to reforms within the organisation.

The JLP has also accused the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP) of contributing to the long-standing problems at ODPEM, claiming that efforts by successive JLP Administrations to reform the agency faced resistance and criticism, leaving weaknesses that have persisted for years.

At a news conference at JLP headquarters in St Andrew following the Opposition’s mid-morning press briefing, JLP Deputy Leader Desmond McKenzie defended Gayle’s leadership, saying the director general had brought a level of direction to the agency that was previously lacking.

He argued that the findings contained in an October 2026 compliance audit of ODPEM by the Auditor General’s Department should not be viewed in isolation from the problems that existed before Gayle took office.

McKenzie said he had first-hand knowledge of the challenges involved in improving ODPEM’s operations, having overseen the agency when it fell under the Ministry of Local Government, which he heads, before it was transferred to the Office of the Prime Minister in November last year.

“Commander Gayle came and he did a fantastic job in pulling everyone around. What the PNP needs to do is to speak to the issues that the staff at ODPEM have been complaining about, why so many persons have left the ODPEM in frustration. Those are the questions that the PNP must ask themselves,” McKenzie said.

He also questioned why the Opposition had not raised similar concerns about the agency’s leadership before the latest audit findings became public.

He said ODPEM had failed to submit its annual reports for about seven years, while an earlier attempt to bring in a new head of the organisation had reportedly been undermined by a lack of support from some employees.

He said the problems went beyond the current leadership and described the agency as having a culture that had made it difficult for successive managers to implement changes.

“It is clear that the organisation has a culture that has been there since the early 2000s that really makes it impossible for people to want to follow the dictates of leadership, [and] the board, on many occasions, struggled to get things done,” he said.

McKenzie also recalled criticism directed at the Government when it sought to become more involved in ODPEM’s operations following Hurricane Matthew in 2016. He claimed that the Opposition and sections of the media had accused the Administration of interfering in the agency’s work.

He maintained that some of the weaknesses highlighted in the Auditor General’s report dated back to 2014 and 2015, before the JLP returned to office in 2016.

The JLP’s defence of Gayle centred on his efforts to strengthen accountability at ODPEM, with party officials detailing how he had instructed senior employees to improve the agency’s record-keeping and tracking of relief supplies, but said those instructions were not properly carried out.

Senator Abka Fitz-Henley, chairman of the party’s communication task force, said the Government had commissioned an assessment of ODPEM’s operations and appointed a new board and executive leadership as part of a wider effort to reform the agency.

He said the transfer of ODPEM to the Office of the Prime Minister in November 2025 was intended to improve coordination with other State agencies, including the Jamaica Defence Force, and address weaknesses that had been recognised before the audit report was released.

Fitz-Henley alleged that some senior employees had failed to carry out instructions from the agency’s leadership, including requests to complete inventory records needed to track relief supplies received and distributed after Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

“I’ve heard media outlets indicating, reading a trail of e-mail… where the commander had made certain demands and outlined certain actions which are to be taken by senior management at ODPEM. Several e-mail dating to as far back as March… and some of the actions have not been taken,” he said.

“I have no doubt that that would have frustrated Commander Gayle, who is a former army man. In the army, he perhaps could have pursued an immediate dismissal of the individuals who failed to execute his command, his demand for accountability mechanisms, in particular concerning inventory management. [But] the public service is a bit different, and therefore you would note, based on what has been put out in the public domain, that when the commander and ODPEM’s senior leadership transferred certain individuals, they resigned,” he added.

He also said the party welcomed an investigation by the Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency into the handling of some relief supplies and inventory under the responsibility of former ODPEM employees.

Fitz-Henley further claimed that at least one former senior employee involved in managing aid had links to the PNP. He said the Opposition had denied the allegation, but insisted that the party was not being truthful.

But despite defending Gayle, the JLP said it supported further changes at ODPEM andthat it did not believe the agency should remain in its present condition.

McKenzie said the transformation was not a response hastily introduced after the Auditor General’s report, noting that the Government had already begun reviewing the agency’s structure and disaster response arrangements.

The Government has said ODPEM is to undergo further restructuring, with the stated aim of improving its ability to prepare for disasters, coordinate relief and account for resources entrusted to it.

World.title: Fi Wi Land: The fight to save Jamaica’s dying lignum vitae
World.content:
A symbol of Jamaica’s natural beauty and national identity, the lignum vitae holds a special place in the island’s heritage. But despite its significance as Jamaica’s national flower, this treasured species is facing growing threats to its survival, raising concerns about the future of one of the country’s national symbols.

Renowned for its exceptionally hard and durable wood, the lignum vitae has faced years of overexploitation, habitat loss and land degradation, contributing to a decline in its population.

With the species subject to international trade restrictions under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), protecting and restoring its population is an important conservation priority.

In this week’s episode of Fi Wi Land, Environmental Officer for Flora at the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), Ashleigh Sanderson, sheds light on the threats facing Jamaica’s national flower and the efforts being made to safeguard its future.

From population surveys revealing concerns about its decline to conservation action plans and environmental protection measures, discover how NEPA is working to preserve the lignum vitae and other threatened plant species across the island.

Catch the latest episode on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse launches in UK
World.content:
The Meta logo is seen on a phone in Frankfurt, Germany on Jan. 8, 2025. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

Regulators will be watching the U.K. rollout of Muse carefully.

LONDON — Meta rolled out its personal AI agent Muse to the U.K. adults on Tuesday, promising users a tool they can trust to lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping.

It is the first AI agent product to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., and regulators will be watching closely.

The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF), comprising the Competition and Markets Authority, Financial Conduct Authority, Ofcom, and the Information Commission, published a statement last month warning that AI agent products “may amplify and accelerate risks” to consumers.

World.title: Can Europe stop Trump putting world leaders above the law?
World.content:
Donald Trump’s campaign against the International Criminal Court is ramping up — can Europe do anything to protect it?

Today on the show, Ian Wishart and Nick Vinocur unpack the U.S. president’s new push to overhaul the ICC’s rules following his meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen last week. The EU insists it wants to defend the top court, but what powers does the bloc have at its disposal?

Next, we head to Spain, where crucial elections are kicking off in just five days. The vote could shake up politics in the country — and across the continent — as Pedro Sánchez, one of Europe’s few remaining Socialist leaders, looks set to lose power to right-wing forces.

World.title: Budget de l’UE : c’est Noël avant l’heure pour Emmanuel Macron
World.content:
Le plus beau cadeau de Costa à Macron est d’avoir inclus, parmi ses propositions de nouvelles recettes fiscales européennes, l’instauration d’une taxe sur les géants du numérique — une ville idée française, écartée en 2018 par crainte de représailles américaines. Parmi les autres concessions faites à Paris, António Costa a préservé les aides aux agriculteurs de toute coupe, proposé de nouvelles taxes pour plafonner les contributions nationales au budget de l’UE, et reporté le remboursement de 10 milliards d’euros de l’emprunt commun post-Covid.

Preuve de la complexité du débat : la députée européenne Renaissance Fabienne Keller a, d’un côté, qualifié de “bonne nouvelle” la proposition de taxation des géants du numérique et, de l’autre, fustigé des coupes budgétaires qui “sapent les ambitions de l’Europe” et “lui coupent les ailes”.

Avec une enveloppe globale de 1 780 milliards d’euros sur sept ans, la dernière proposition budgétaire d’António Costa est inférieure de 44 milliards à la version présentée le mois dernier par l’Irlande, qui assure actuellement la présidence tournante du Conseil de l’UE. Les Etats membres se divisent entre ceux qui veulent un budget plus modeste, axé sur les priorités actuelles, telles que la défense et la compétitivité ; et ceux qui veulent que l’UE dépense davantage et se concentre sur les domaines habituels, comme l’agriculture et le soutien aux régions les plus défavorisées.

Malgré des divergences importantes, António Costa et la plupart des gouvernements nationaux sont déterminés à parvenir à un accord d’ici la fin de l’année.

“On dirait que le père Noël est passé plus tôt cette année pour les Français”, ironise un diplomate européen qui, comme d’autres personnes citées dans cet article, a souhaité garder l’anonymat afin de pouvoir s’exprimer librement sur ces négociations sensibles.

“Profondément décevant”

Le pas de Costa vers Macron représente une victoire rare en cette fin de mandat compliquée pour le président français. La perspective d’un second tour en 2027 entre une Marine Le Pen eurosceptique et un Jean-Luc Mélenchon qui veut “désobéir aux traités” — tous deux étant actuellement en tête des intentions de vote — est l’une des principales raisons qui motivent l’UE à parvenir à un accord sur le budget cette année.

World.title: Industrie vs. Gewerkschaften — Das Standort-Dilemma
World.content:

Deutschlands Industrie steht auf der Kippe. Während bei VW und Mercedes Zehntausende Jobs wackeln und Investitionen ins Ausland abzufließen drohen, wird mit harten Worten in die Tarifverhandlungen eingestiegen. Maximilian Stascheit ordnet zusammen mit Romanus Otte von PRO „Industrie & Handel am Morgen“ ein, ob der härteste Arbeitskampf in der Geschichte der Branche bevorsteht und welche drastischen Sparmaßnahmen die Autokonzerne jetzt durchdrücken wollen.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview stellt sich die IG-Metall-Vorsitzende Christiane Benner der Frage, ob die Gewerkschaft angesichts der Krise zu Kompromissen bereit ist. Sie erklärt, warum sie trotz drohender Werksschließungen an der Forderung nach fünf Prozent mehr Lohn festhält und warum die Geduld der Arbeitnehmer reißt.

In der Koalition braut sich derweil der nächste Streit zusammen. Der Kanzler will das geplante Rentenpaket noch vor Weihnachten durchs Kabinett bringen, doch aus der SPD droht ein Veto. Die Analyse mit Rasmus Buchsteiner zeigt, was hinter dem Machtkampf um die abschlagsfreie Rente steckt und wie fragil die Lage der Regierung wirklich ist.
