World.title: Türkei sieht Europas Wohlstand in Gefahr – wegen des IAA
World.content:
Er nutzte seinen Auftritt vor der Autobranche für Kritik an einer EU-Verordnung, die, so sagte er es im Interview mit POLITICO, Deutschland und der Türkei schaden könnte. „Die deutsche Wirtschaft hat sich als drittgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Welt dank internationaler Investitionen, des Außenhandels und einer offenen Außenwirtschaft erfolgreich entwickelt“, sagte Bolat. „Würde man sich dem internationalen Wettbewerb verschließen, würde der Wohlstand sofort sinken und die Preise für die Verbraucher steigen.“

Es geht ihm um den sogenannten Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA). Dessen Ziel ist es, die europäische Industrie zu stärken und Arbeitsplätze zu sichern – vor allem gegen den unfairen Wettbewerb aus China. Als Mittel sollen bei allen Förderungen innerhalb der Europäischen Union und in der öffentlichen Vergabe sogenannte „Made in EU“-Quoten eingeführt werden. Sie sollen dafür sorgen, dass ein bestimmter Anteil der Wertschöpfung in der EU erbracht werden muss.

Die Verhandlungen darüber laufen noch in Brüssel. Ein Abschluss wird Anfang kommenden Jahres erwartet. Die große Streitfrage ist: Zählt für die Erfüllung der Quote wirklich nur Produktion innerhalb der 27 EU-Staaten? Was ist mit Produktion in Partnerländern wie der Schweiz, Großbritannien und der Türkei? Und was mit den rund 80 Freihandelspartnern Brüssels?

Nach aktuellem Verhandlungsstand zwischen EU-Parlament und Rat wäre die Türkei raus. Das hätte massive Auswirkungen auf die europäische Autoindustrie, warnt Bolat.

250.000 Jobs in Europa seien in Gefahr, die Kosten für Autos könnten sich um bis zu neun Prozent verteuern, besagen Zahlen des türkischen Handelsministeriums. Da in Deutschland mehr als ein Drittel der europäischen Auto-Arbeitsplätze liegen, stünden 90.000 der noch 887.000 Jobs in der Autoindustrie infrage.

Auch für die Türkei könnte der IAA gefährlich werden. Um 68 Prozent könnten die Autoexporte in die EU bis 2035 einbrechen, so Bolats Zahlen. 330.000 türkische Jobs wären weg.

World.title: Back to 1936? Civil war ghosts haunt Spanish election campaign
World.content:
“The Popular Front that Pedro Sánchez has assembled will not relinquish power democratically,” Ayuso warned during an interview on the Cuatro television network last month, accusing the prime minister of leading Spain toward “revolution.”

Tensions over those historic fault lines of 1936-39 have only been heightened by the prospect of the far right entering national government for the first time since the restoration of democracy in the 1970s. Vox is expected to become the PP’s junior coalition partner, meaning old antifascist songs and slogans have become commonplace at left-wing rallies.

The resurgent guerracivilismo — rhetoric evoking the divisions and existential stakes of the civil war — underscores Spain’s increasingly divided society today.

A September survey tracking social cohesion and political polarization by More in Common found that 70% of Spaniards view their country as divided — the highest proportion since the polling organization began tracking the sentiment in 2021.

Pedro Riera, head of the social sciences department at Madrid’s Carlos III University, said he was not surprised to see politicians invoking the conflict. For Spanish society, he said, the war remains the most emblematic example of the country’s divisions and has become less taboo.

“Our transition to democracy was built on a pact of silence, but as time has passed, people — and political parties — have become less afraid of addressing the war, and politicians now invoke it to mobilize their supporters,” he said.

World.title: Estonian foreign minister: Why we’re closing our border with Russia
World.content:
These incidents form part of a broader Russian campaign targeting the whole of Europe, including countries far beyond its borders. The aim is to undermine the European security order, intimidate its neighbors and dictate the choices of sovereign nations. Civilian infrastructure, businesses and facilities connected to support for Ukraine have increasingly become targets.

Russian intelligence services exploit cross-border movement to gather intelligence, establish contacts and recruit individuals to carry out hostile activities. These operations are often deliberately designed to create fear, sow distrust, divide our societies and undermine confidence in our institutions from within.

Closing our border will not eliminate these threats, but it will limit opportunities for hostile intelligence activities. It will also help close channels for sanctions evasion, a crucial part of depriving Russia of the resources it uses to finance its war economy and sustain its aggression.

The same logic should guide Europe’s wider approach to forcing Russia to abandon the imperialist ambitions that continue to drive its actions. Let us recall the months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when Moscow issued ultimatums to NATO and the United States, demanding a fundamental revision of Europe’s security arrangements. Russia wanted NATO to roll back its military presence to the levels of 1997, effectively challenging the sovereignty and security choices of countries across Europe, including Estonia, Finland and Sweden.

Five years of war, death and destruction have done nothing to change the Kremlin’s ambitions. Following the talks in Abu Dhabi, Russian representatives have once again referred to the 2021 ultimatums and even suggested going further, adding new demands based on their experience during the war.

This should leave no room for illusions. Russia is not genuinely moving toward ending its war against Ukraine. Instead, it is trying to use negotiations to achieve what it has failed to accomplish on the battlefield, forcing sovereign nations to surrender their security choices and restoring Russian spheres of influence in Europe. Moscow made these demands five years ago and continues to make them today. Its latest invitation for European leaders to visit Moscow to hear Russia’s position changes nothing.

World.title: EU’s Socialists to hold formal discussion on Frederiksen’s migration stance
World.content:
Portuguese and German lawmakers objected to those comments at Monday’s meeting, then more members sought the floor. Group Chair Iratxe García proposed scheduling a formal discussion at a future meeting, according to four people who were in the room or were briefed on the exchange. They were granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations.

The discussion will put a renewed spotlight on divisions within the center-left group over how far the Socialists can support tougher migration policies. Frederiksen’s approach has drawn criticism from fellow party leaders before, including after she joined Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in condemning uncontrolled migration.

Following the Ceuta migration crisis, Frederiksen also co-signed a letter urging European Council President António Costa to take action to protect the EU’s borders. Frederiksen’s position does not represent that of the Socialist political family, Garcia told Spanish media at the time.

Christel Schaldemose, who leads the Danish delegation in the group, was caught off guard by the criticism, two of the people said. “I welcome the opportunity to discuss migration policy with my colleagues in the S&D Group,” she told POLITICO.

One Socialist staffer in the room said “this topic generates tensions in the group, and [Garcia] clearly stopped it from happening right there so things wouldn’t escalate.”

“There was a lot of clapping to the objections raised … clearly the debate needs to happen,” they added.

A spokesperson for García declined to comment on the group discussions. A spokesperson for Frederiksen did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

World.title: From Beaujolais wine to the midnight sun: Seven unusual European marathons and running events
World.content:
Who said that running a road race only means effort, sweat and a stopwatch? It can also be an opportunity to have fun, dance and, why not, taste a few good glasses of wine along the route.

 

I discovered this myself on Saturday 21 November, when I took part in the 13 kilometres of the Marathon International du Beaujolais, in the French wine-growing region north of Lyon, one of the most unusual and festive races on the European scene.

From the very first metres it is hard not to be swept up in the atmosphere: Most of the participants run in fancy dress, with outfits ranging from the highly imaginative to the frankly improbable.

On the roadside, residents of the villages on the route cheer on the runners with applause, music and plenty of smiles. Along the course, the traditional refreshment points become an opportunity to sample Beaujolais wines, while DJs, brass bands and entertainment groups turn the race into a huge travelling party (and in some cases a fully fledged nightclub).

Between one stretch of running and the next you find yourself dancing, laughing and joking with complete strangers, and forgetting about the stopwatch altogether.

Because taking more than three hours to cover 13 kilometres is a long way from a personal best...

The event offers several distances designed to involve both well-trained runners and those who simply want to enjoy the party: the full marathon of 42.195 kilometres, the half-marathon of 21.1 kilometres and the popular 13km du Rhône. The weekend programme also includes family runs, trail races and walks.

But how did this unusual mix of sport and conviviality come about? In 1995, on the flight home from the New York Marathon, three friends from Beaujolais, fresh from their NYC experience, decided to bring the same spirit of celebration and sharing to their region, with an extra twist: its flagship local product, Beaujolais wine.

The first experimental edition was held the following year, a sort of dress rehearsal with around 50 participants, before the official inauguration in 1997.

From that bet between friends an event was born that now attracts tens of thousands of people every year. In 2026 the Marathon International du Beaujolais celebrated its 22nd edition, with 35,000 participants from 92 countries.

But Beaujolais is not the only quirky running event in Europe. In fact there are several, with something to suit every taste.

Here are some of the most distinctive of their kind.

The Beer Lovers' Marathon in Liège, Belgium

Belgium means beer, as the saying goes. And in Liège beer has found a place of honour in a running event.

The Beer Lovers' Marathon, next scheduled for 16 May 2027, invites participants to cover 42.195 kilometres with a particular twist: along the route there are 16 refreshment points, each serving a different Belgian beer, accompanied of course by water, food and music so that nothing is missing.

Each stop is brought to life by DJs or bands, and at some of the refreshment points you can also taste local specialities such as classic chips and speculoos, the traditional spiced biscuits. And to get even more into the spirit of the event, as with the Marathon du Beaujolais, participants are encouraged to dress up, each year following a specific theme. The 2027 theme will be "Run wild - fauna e flora".

And the party in Liège does not end once you have crossed the finish line: the programme also includes an after-party and even a guided tour of the city the following day, with breakfast and a farewell beer. More than just a marathon, it is a weekend devoted to conviviality and to Belgian beer culture.

The Tiramisù Run in Treviso, Italy

Staying with the food theme, there is a race that made its debut this year in Italy and that offers finishers more than just a medal.

In Treviso, participants in the Tiramisù Run, a 10km held at the same time as the half-marathon, can earn themselves a much more tempting reward: a serving of the famous Italian dessert, which was created in the Veneto capital.

The event is designed above all as an opportunity for fun and not as a highly competitive race. Open to everyone aged 16 and over, it allows you to choose whether to run the entire route or simply enjoy it at a more leisurely pace, with no need for a medical certificate for competitive sport.

The reward at the Tiramisù Run 2026 Chiara Salvador/ La Mezza di Treviso - Tiramisù Run

The next mouth-watering edition is scheduled for 10 October 2027, and it remains to be seen whether it will top the number of participants in the inaugural race: 4,000 runners, 75% of them from abroad, proof that Italy's most iconic spoon dessert is hugely popular well beyond the Bel Paese.

The Oxenhope Straw Race in Oxenhope, England

In the small village of Oxenhope in Yorkshire, a true test of endurance takes place every year, involving beer, fancy dress and bales of straw. The Oxenhope Straw Race, scheduled for 4 July 2027, follows a route of around four kilometres linking six pubs in the English village.

Teams of at least two people have to tackle the race in costume, carrying between them a bale of straw weighing between 15 and 20 kilograms. There is a stop for a pint of beer at each pub, although drinking it is not compulsory to take part.

Oxenhope Straw Race © 2026 Woodentops

The origins of the competition are rather unusual: it is said to have started in the 1970s, when two local farmers made a bet after drinking a pint in a pub. The bet gradually turned into a race between locals, with the addition of the bale of straw to be carried.

Today the event has become a tradition in Oxenhope and an important charity occasion: over the years it has raised more than £500,000 (€597,875) for local organisations and initiatives. It is therefore a great way to combine sport, tradition and community spirit.

The Great Knaresborough Bed Race, Knaresborough, England

We stay in England, in Knaresborough in North Yorkshire, where competitors in this unusual race need not only a good pair of running shoes but also a bed on wheels.

The Great Knaresborough Bed Race, which next year will take place on 12 June, is one of the most unusual events in the British racing calendar.

Each team consists of six runners and one passenger, who lies comfortably on the bed, the coveted role if we are honest, while the other team members push it along a route of about four kilometres.

Before the race itself, the teams parade through the town streets with decorated beds and themed costumes, accompanied by bands and dance groups. But you should not be fooled by the carnival atmosphere, as the route is anything but easy: with steep climbs and cobbled streets, the challenge ends with a 20-metre crossing of the River Nidd, bed and passenger included.

The tradition dates back to 1966, when the local Knaresborough Round Table was looking for an original idea to raise funds for charity. Since then, what began as a small initiative for local people has become an international event, attracting up to 90 teams and hundreds of volunteers.

The Neujahrsmarathon in Schlieren, Switzerland

As the saying goes, well begun is half done, especially when it comes to the new year. While most people are toasting the arrival of the new year, in Schlieren, near Zürich, some prefer to celebrate by putting on their running shoes.

The Neujahrsmarathon Zürich is a particularly unusual race, because the start is set for exactly midnight on 1 January, just moments after the New Year celebrations.

The course follows a 10.55-kilometre loop along the River Limmat, which is repeated several times depending on the distance chosen. There are three distances for adults: 10.55 kilometres, a half-marathon of 21.1 kilometres and the full marathon of 42.195 kilometres, as well as a team option.

The first edition took place on 1 January 2005, giving rise to a tradition that combines sport with New Year celebrations. It is a very original way to ring in a new year.

At the finish line of the Neujahrsmarathon Zurich alphafoto/alphafoto.com

The Midnight Sun Marathon in Tromsø, Norway

And from a race where a head torch is essential, we move to another where it is pointless. Imagine running a marathon in the middle of the night but without needing artificial light: that is what happens at the Midnight Sun Marathon, held in Tromsø in northern Norway during the period of the midnight sun.

This natural phenomenon, typical of regions above the Arctic Circle in summer, means that the sun stays above the horizon even during the night, offering participants a truly unforgettable experience.

The next edition is scheduled for 19 June 2027 and offers several distances, from the full marathon and the half-marathon to a 10-kilometre race and a five-kilometre race. The event attracts runners from all over the world: in 2026 it set a new participation record, with around 9,000 runners from 97 countries.

Beyond the sporting challenge, the real star is the Arctic landscape. The route runs through Tromsø, with spectacular views of the sea, the surrounding mountains and some of its landmark sites, including the bridge linking the island of Tromsøya with the mainland and the famous Arctic Cathedral.

It is a race that lets you discover northern Norway through one of its most breathtaking natural phenomena.

NB: Some of the events described include tastings of alcoholic drinks. Alcohol consumption is reserved for adults and should be moderate. Alcohol abuse is dangerous for your health.

World.title: Is no deal better than a bad deal? Why some see hope in COP31’s collapse
World.content:
After 44 hours of overtime on top of two weeks of negotiations, COP31 ended on Sunday without a climate agreement.

 

The so-called Antalya Pact failed after several countries, including the EU, the UK and many small Pacific island states, rejected a final draft that made no mention of fossil fuels – the leading cause of climate change.

In fact, the pact proposed by co-hosts Türkiye and Australia did not even refer to the “transition away from fossil fuels”, or TAFF, the landmark agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai.

For a global population facing stronger, more unpredictable weather and ecosystem collapse, the failure to agree on a fossil fuel phaseout or provide climate finance to developing nations means another year without a collective action plan in a rapidly warming world.

More than a decade after nearly 200 countries agreed to limiting global warming to 1.5°C at COP21 in Paris – also known as the Paris Agreement – 2026 is on course to become the second calendar year to exceed that threshold. The UN warns that a long-term breach will happen soon, too, with every fraction of a degree increasing the risk of irreversible environmental damage.

“There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said after the summit.

But is there reason for hope anyway? While COP31’s failure marks a setback, some think the acrimonious ending in Antalya might come with a silver lining.

Why COP31 ended without a deal

The final hours of COP31 exposed some of the deep divisions that have long plagued the event.

While other COP summits have gone into overtime, most ended with deals. As last week progressed, it became clear that a COP31 compromise would be hard to reach.

Oil-producing nations, led by Saudi Arabia, began to dig in their heels in opposition to explicit references to coal, oil and gas. Climate finance was just as contentious a topic.

Despite setting a red line around the pact’s language on fossil fuels, the EU resisted calls for additional climate finance. The bloc’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, had even ruled out new funding commitments before the summit began.

In the end, although developing nations asked for more money to protect themselves against worsening floods, droughts and other disasters, a target of roughly €110 billion a year in climate adaptation finance by 2035 disappeared from the final draft.

The breakdown in talks means that Ethiopia, which will host COP32 next year, will face many of the same unresolved disputes all over again.

The climate campaign group 350.org said “the world deserves better”, with its East Africa team leader, Rukiya Khamis, accusing Türkiye and Australia of handing the incoming presidency “the wreckage of their failed leadership”.

“People across Africa and the world have spent this year struggling with rising energy prices and deadly droughts and floods. Yet rich polluting nations have chosen to side with the fossil fuel lobby and closed their wallets at a time when we urgently need a lifeline,” Khamis said in a statement.

“Countries on the frontline of this crisis should not have to beg for the resources they need to protect their people, rebuild after disasters and secure reliable and accessible renewable energy.”

Did COP31 achieve anything?

Despite ending ignominiously, COP31 still offered some reasons for optimism. For one, it avoided dressing up inaction as progress – or, in other words, greenwashing.

More than 130 countries had demanded that the final agreement reaffirm the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels made at COP28. Instead, the proposed pact promoted carbon capture, a technology championed by the fossil fuel industry that critics say is ineffective on the level it would be needed and allows oil and gas producers to continue polluting.

Former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres says the refusal to accept a weaker agreement shows that governments are prepared to defend their previous commitments, even if it means walking away from the negotiating table.

“Today nations stood up for what science and justice demand,” Figueres said after the summit.

COP31 had several, smaller climate wins throughout the week, too. Outside of formal talks, governments, civil society leaders and businesses announced several new commitments and investment plans that do not depend on global consensus.

For example, more than 90 nations backed Türkiye’s voluntary ‘35 by 35’ pledge to increase the amount of energy the world gets from electricity from about 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035.

“Despite this missed opportunity for progress within the COP process, the renewable energy transition is now unstoppable, delivering unprecedented volumes of renewable electricity across the globe,” says Ben Backwell, chair of the Global Renewables Alliance and CEO of the Global Wind Energy Council.

And COP is far from the end of climate talks, too. In April, 56 countries attended a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, dedicated to a fair transition away from fossil fuels. Afterward, several European nations committed to voluntary phaseout roadmaps. The next edition of the conference is planned in Tuvalu in 2027.

But the urgency of cutting emissions is now so great that the UN speaks of ‘limiting overshoot’ – clinical terms that describe a future in which the world breaches the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C limit, then attempts to bring warming back down.

Even if it succeeds, some of the damage may be irreversible, and climate change will continue to threaten lives and livelihoods in the meantime, the UNEP warns. Many are now questioning if the agreement-by-consensus model of COP summits no longer works and it is time for a different way of driving coordinated, global climate action.

“The climate crisis will not wait for governments to find common ground,” Guterres said. “Neither can we.”

World.title: All the major hotel loyalty programmes you need to know about in Europe
World.content:
Earlier this month, Euronews Travel took a dive into the complex world of airline loyalty programmes.

 

It stands to reason that if you’re a frequent flyer, you’re also likely to be staying in hotels regularly, too, so we thought this time around we’d look at their loyalty programmes instead.

Most schemes are free to join, and from the get-go may include discounted hotel rates for those booking directly, but that’s not the only reason to become a member.

Like airlines, those who reach a higher status tier through staying a certain number of nights, or spending a set amount of money, will enjoy perks like complimentary breakfast and late check-outs, while points can be used on free nights or upgrades.

As an added bonus, many hotel loyalty schemes offer the chance to earn miles instead, meaning you can gather enough for an on-board upgrade even faster.

Here, we’ve covered most of the major chains you might encounter in Europe, but it’s always worth checking if your hotel offers one, even if it’s a smaller group.

For example, on the luxury side of things, both Shangri-La and Mandarin Oriental have schemes. And if you travel domestically frequently, it’s worth looking into what is the biggest hotel group in your country, like Pestana in Portugal or Scandic Hotels in Sweden.

Marriott Bonvoy includes The Luxury Collection hotels, such as Amoh, a Luxury Collection Resort, Rhodes Marriott

Marriott Bonvoy

Hotel brands in the programme: EDITION, The Ritz-Carlton, The Luxury Collection, St. Regis, W Hotels, JW Marriott, Marriott Hotels, Sheraton, Westin, Le Meridien, Autograph Collection, Aloft, Moxy, citizenM, Renaissance Hotels, Tribute Portfolio, Design Hotels, Gaylord Hotels, and various other hotels by Marriott.

With more than 1.7 million rooms across the globe, Marriott International is the largest hotel chain in the world by number of rooms.

Initially launched in Arlington, Virginia in the US in 1957 with the Marriott Motor Hotel, the chain now owns brands including The Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis, and Moxy.

Through the Marriott Bonvoy loyalty programme, you can earn points on stays, food and beverage, and even rounds of golf.

There are several status levels through the programme which offer more bonus points on stays, but other perks include room upgrades and late check-out where available, and welcome gifts such as additional points or breakfast.

Points can be redeemed on stays, upgrades or car rentals, and you can also transfer your points at a 3:1 ratio on many European airlines including Air France, British Airways and TAP Air Portugal.

World.title: Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. What does it mean for Europe's AI stocks?
World.content:
Eleven days ago, the man who built the engine of the AI boom walked out of Nvidia. On Monday, he walked back in.

 

It took a scandal, a board that had ruled out his return, and the President of the United States to bring Jensen Huang back.

In between, some of Europe's most valuable tech companies, from ASML in the Netherlands to Nokia in Finland, lost as much as a sixth of their market value.

Nvidia's board voted unanimously on Monday to reinstate Huang as chief executive, president and board director, less than two weeks after he resigned over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer under US investigation.

The board said input from senior US government officials had left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

The market's verdict was instant.

Nvidia shares jumped nearly 32% on Monday, marking the company's best day since May 2003 and adding close to $1 trillion in market value in a single session.

Europe rallied with it. The Stoxx 600 closed 1.8% higher, Germany's DAX gained 2.2% and France's CAC 40 rose 1.5%, with chipmakers and suppliers of AI data centres leading the way.

Yet the rebound came with an uncomfortable reminder: some of the continent's biggest technology stocks now rise and fall with the fate of one man in California.

A president in the boardroom

In an unprecedented move by a US president, Donald Trump spent the past week publicly backing the return of a listed company's chief executive. On Monday, he celebrated the result.

"The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Trump wrote on Truth Social, calling Huang "a Great Patriot and National Treasure".

Not everyone in Washington agreed. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision "reckless" on X, and Huang faces a public Senate hearing on US export controls on 3 December.

Europe's chip stocks get their bounce

In Europe, the rebound was strongest among the companies that build the machines and materials behind AI chips.

German chip equipment maker SUSS MicroTec jumped 9.8%, Dutch peer BE Semiconductor Industries rose 9.3% and Franco-Italian chipmaker STMicroelectronics gained 9%.

ASML, the Dutch company whose lithography machines are needed to print the world's most advanced chips, including Nvidia's, climbed 8.9%.

So did Nokia and German equipment maker Aixtron.

The energy side of the AI build-out also rallied. Siemens Energy rose 6.9%, cable maker Prysmian 6.5% and Schneider Electric, which designs power and cooling systems for data centres with Nvidia, added 4.1%.

Germany's Infineon, which works with Nvidia on power systems for the next generation of AI data centres, rose 6.6%, after losing 12.8% during Huang's absence.

Yet Monday only repaired part of the damage.

Between the close on 11 November, the last session before Huang resigned, and Friday's close, ASML and Nokia both lost 16.8%. SUSS MicroTec fell 15.7%, Aixtron 14.2% and STMicroelectronics 13%.

Even after Monday's rally, ASML and Nokia remain 9.4% below where they stood before his resignation.

Why Nokia is so tied to Huang

Among European companies, few have ties as directly on Nvidia as Nokia.

In October 2025, Nvidia agreed to invest $1 billion in the Finnish telecoms equipment maker, taking a 2.9% stake at $6.01 per share.

The two companies agreed to build AI-powered mobile networks, known as AI-RAN, on Nvidia's computing platforms, with Nokia adding Nvidia-based products to its radio network range and T-Mobile US testing the technology.

The deal turned Nokia from a slow-growing network vendor into one of Europe's AI stocks. Its shares jumped more than 20% on the day of the announcement and kept climbing into this year, closing at a peak of €14.81 on 3 June.

They have since lost more than half of that value, closing at €7.02 on Monday, despite the 8.9% gain.

Soitec lags behind

Not every European AI name joined the party with the same conviction.

Soitec, the French company that makes the engineered silicon wafers used in the optical chips that move data with light inside AI data centres, rose 5.4% to €101.50, one of the smallest gains in the group.

The company dominates its niche. "We estimate that Soitec currently holds ~95% market share in supplying Photonics-SOI wafers," Bank of America analyst Oliver Wong said in a report.

But the stock fell 11.1% between Huang's resignation and Friday, and is still down 12.5% over the past month.

Analysts have also turned more cautious in recent weeks.

On 4 November, Morgan Stanley downgraded Soitec to equal-weight from overweight, cut its price target to €140 from €200 and removed the stock from its list of top picks.

The same day, UBS moved the other way, upgrading Soitec to neutral from sell and raising its target to €130 from €94. On 11 November, JPMorgan trimmed its target to €190 from €200, while keeping an overweight rating.

Relief, with caveats, analysts say

On Wall Street, the first reaction was relief.

Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse titled his Monday note "All is Right in the World Again", saying concerns over talent retention, the product roadmap, market share and margins "all go out the window" with Huang back in charge.

"At the end of the day despite this Jensen saga the Board knew it had no choice but to bring him back and for the US technology sector and global economy this was the move it had to make," Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives, wrote on X.

The comeback also prompted a round of rating changes on Wall Street.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon upgraded Nvidia to outperform from market perform, with a $200 price target, while Citi's Atif Malik raised his target to $240 from $225 and kept a buy rating.

Needham's Quinn Bolton and Baird's Tristan Gerra reiterated their buy and neutral ratings respectively, both with $200 targets.

Others were more cautious.

"Today's gains are a small dent in the month-long drawdown that preceded today," Daniel Newman, chief executive of research firm The Futurum Group, wrote on X.

"It is possible this is a bounce and not a full-blown sentiment shift."

Doug Kass, president of hedge fund Seabreeze Partners Management, went further.

"I don't for a minute believe any meaningful due diligence regarding the Huang affair has been done by the Trump administration," he wrote on X.

"It is not entirely clear to me whether President Trump's intrusion in making today's decision will hold up," Kass added.

Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, said the reversal raises its own questions about who oversees the risks at a company at the centre of the global AI ecosystem.

"The Board's decision to reappoint Mr. Huang, having only just accepted his resignation, leaves those questions unanswered," Stewart said in emailed comments.

Monday proved that Europe's AI champions still trade on what happens in Santa Clara.

What it could not settle is what happens in Washington, where Huang faces senators on 3 December and where, as Kass warned, the President's intervention may not hold up.

World.title: Signs of heart attack and stroke risk can appear decades earlier, study finds
World.content:
Warning signs that someone will have a heart attack or stroke may appear up to 30 years beforehand, new research has found.

 

Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, with an estimated 19.8 million people dying of a heart attack, stroke or another heart problem in 2022. Most cardiovascular diseases can be prevented by tackling lifestyle and environmental risk factors such as unhealthy diets, smoking and air pollution, and early detection can help funnel people into treatment and prevent deaths.

“For the vast majority of people, heart attacks and strokes are completely preventable. But many of us don’t realise we are at risk until it’s too late,” said Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, which funded the study.

Researchers from the University of Edinburgh tracked nearly 114,000 people’s health over three decades beginning in the 1980s. None of them had heart disease at that time, but nearly 17,000 people eventually had a heart attack, stroke or died of a heart problem.

Among those who developed heart problems, warning signs often emerged decades beforehand, according to the study, which was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

For example, systolic blood pressure — the pressure in the arteries when the heart pumps blood — was consistently higher in people who later developed heart problems compared with those who did not.

Blood biomarkers were another early signal. Changes in NT-proBNP — a protein fragment used to assess heart failure — were apparent 10 years beforehand.

Other early warning signs included kidney function, physical activity, diabetes and a higher body mass index (BMI), which is a measure of obesity. Several are already known risk factors for heart disease, along with high blood pressure and elevated cholesterol, but the study shows how these risk factors progress over time.

“This study adds to growing evidence that red flags for cardiovascular disease appear decades before it arrives,” Williams said.

Notably, the study did not analyse risk factors by ethnicity, and more research would be needed to determine any differences across groups.

Even so, Williams said the findings could help doctors identify patients at risk of a heart attack or stroke later in life, using simple tools like a blood pressure reading or blood test.

“Knowledge like this could empower people to make lifestyle changes or start treatment while they are still relatively young, which might reduce their risk, prevent a heart attack or stroke, and rewrite their future,” Williams said.

World.title: Stocks climb as Huang's return to Nvidia lifts investor optimism
World.content:
Technology firms rocketed on Tuesday as Asia joined a global stock surge following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia boss less than two weeks after stepping down over extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy.

 

The Silicon Valley giant's resignation on 12 November sent shockwaves through markets and dealt a severe blow to the AI trade, which was already under pressure amid worries over profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.

His role as a fixer and visionary in an industry that has fuelled a tech revolution and a global economic boom was seen as crucial to the firm's future as well as the AI buildout.

News of his return - announced soon after the opening bell Monday - lit a fire under equities, sending shares in Nvidia soaring an eye-watering 31.5% and adding more than $900 billion to the firm's market value.

Other Wall Street titans also enjoyed much-needed buying, pulling the Nasdaq up more than 6%, the S&P 500 4.7% higher and the Dow 3% higher.

And Asia, which had started the week on the back foot, followed suit.

Taipei was the standout, blasting more than 9% higher as chip titans TSMC and MediaTek added 10% each, and Seoul piled on more than 6% thanks to gains of around 8% in market heavyweights SK hynix and Samsung.

Tokyo was lifted 4% by spikes of 14% in Advantest, 11% in Tokyo Electron and 8% in Kioxia.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila also joined in the fun with healthy advances.

"Jensen's return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade," said Saxo Markets' Charu Chanana.

"He is not just Nvidia's CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate.

"(His) return is particularly welcome for Asian technology stocks, many of which suffered collateral damage from Nvidia's leadership crisis."

And National Australia Bank's Gavin Friend said: "The AI trade has been given a reprieve, with Huang's reinstatement assuaging fears of any unravelling of the circular financing activity that has been a key support for the sector."

However, analysts added that Huang's reinstatement - which President Donald Trump said followed his own direct contacts with the company's board - did not mean an end to probes or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for the past six months.

The company is still under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill.

Huang reportedly had a relationship with Alice Huang - who is not related - a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. The group is under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia's top-line chips.

Just this weekend, The New York Times added further details to the allegations, saying Alice Huang had been in touch with China's top spy agency during the secret affair.

The United States on Monday added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist that bars it from purchasing advanced chips.

Meanwhile, oil prices continued to fall after Monday's sharp drop that saw WTI back below $80 for the first time since August.

The latest selling was fuelled by hopes for an end to the Iran conflict as Axios reported US Vice President JD Vance met the prime minister of Qatar, which has acted as a mediator in efforts to resolve the near nine-month conflict.

World.title: Turkey seizes control of last major independent news channel amid fraud scandal
World.content:
Turkey's last operating independent TV news channel has fallen under state control, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan scrambles to contain a wave of public fury over a $20 billion investment fund scandal that has swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people in the country.

Advertising

Sozcu TV vanished from the airwaves before dawn on Tuesday as police enforced a court order installing a state trustee, cutting the channel's transmission as it was broadcasting a programme on the latest revelations in the investment fraud scandal.

The move echoes a similar state takeover last month of Halk TV, another major independent broadcaster.

The silencing of Turkey’s two largest independent news channels has drawn sharp condemnation from opposition parties and human rights groups. While the government maintains that the judiciary operates independently, critics argue the court orders are politically motivated.

“This is part of a process of basically closing down all independent media that might risk reaching followers of the ruling party,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb of Human Rights Watch.

“The whole tactic of the Erdogan government has been to use court orders. The court orders are so problematic in themselves, so overreaching, so disproportionate, that this has nothing really to do with the legal process. This is all about a political crackdown.”

Turkey talks green at Cop31 while cracking down on activists

Sinclair-Webb noted that television remains the primary news source for most Turks, making both networks and individual journalists who question government policies prime targets.

Four journalist have been detained or placed under house arrest for reporting on the investment scandal.

Authorities accuse Sozcu TV of ties to followers of the late cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom Ankara blames for masterminding a failed 2016 coup. Four of its executives and officials have been detained. Halk TV faces separate corruption allegations.

Both broadcasters strongly deny the charges.

Investment scandal

The closing of the channels comes amid fallout from the collapse of more than 100 investment funds, which wiped out $20 billion, stranded more than 500,000 investors and triggered a stock market crash.

The scandal has implicated numerous figures linked to Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party).

According to recent polls, 80 percent of Turks are closely following the scandal, with a similar majority blaming the government.

On Thursday, protesters demonstrated outside the Capital Markets Board, the country's financial regulator, in Ankara.

Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next

Around 500 people are under investigation and more than 100 suspects have been jailed. Erdogan vowed this week that no one would escape justice and promised to expedite repayments to affected investors.

Political analyst Sezin Oney said the government is scrambling to control the public narrative as its reputation among its own voter base unravels.

“Up to now, AK Party and government circles were able to project to their base the idea that the opposition [is involved in] all sorts of corruption. So all of a sudden, that facade, that rhetoric has collapsed. Now it’s the government circles who are massively corrupt."

Debate moves online

Atilla Yesilada, a Turkey analyst at New York-based consultancy firm Global Source Partners, warned that the scandal has exposed deep flaws in financial oversight, threatening severe economic and political fallout for Erdogan.

“Turkey is heading for a recession because the institutional structure has completely collapsed,” Yesilada said. “In a free market economy, you really need regulatory boards to do their work which clearly, as we see in this instance, they don't. In fact, they enable or incentivise thieves [and make] their jobs easier."

Yesilada added that Erdogan lacks a clear path to resolve the crisis, as opposition figures release new allegations implicating AK Party associates daily.

Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy

Following the state takeover of another broadcaster last year, the loss of Sozcu TV and Halk TV marks a grim turning point for Turkish media, Oney said. However, she questioned whether the government can successfully suppress public discourse.

“It’s the end of the road for TV journalism, you don’t have any oppositional voice or oppositional debate. But people talk, people think, one way or another. Because Turkey was a thinking and talking nation before, it's very difficult to stop [that]. It is just [being done now] on social media.”

The government has accelerated efforts to police online dissent, shutting down hundreds of critical social media accounts, although new ones are emerging just as rapidly.

Meanwhile Koza TV, a previously fringe station, has seen its ratings surge after becoming a new outlet for independent reporting on the scandal – although mounting regulatory fines make its future uncertain.

World.title: Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy
World.content:
According to a study by the Körber Foundation, a growing number of Germans now oppose providing military aid to Ukraine. The majority also believes that Germany should take a neutral position between the US and China.

For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation .

In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Growing numbers of Germans oppose international engagement

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

No longer a majority in favor of military aid to Ukraine

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

Overwhelming majority wants Germany to remain neutral between the US and China

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

If Europe wants independence, why does it keep turning to the US? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Should Germany always stand by Israel? Now only a third agree

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: India: Report warns of deepening authoritarianism under Modi
World.content:
Hasina has been in India since her ouster in 2024 Image: Daniel Leal-Olivas/AFP/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return to her country after two years of exile in India, according to her spokesperson.

That's despite the Bangladeshi government saying she can only return from the neighboring nation through extradition.

Hasina's scheduled date of return is December 16 — the anniversary of the end of Bangladesh's 1971 liberation war with Pakistan, the spokesperson said.

In June this year, Hasina vowed to return to Bangladesh while speaking at a correspondents' event in New Delhi via live audio feed.

"I know that they may put me in jail, or they may kill me, or anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she said at the time. "Fear cannot decide my duty to the people."

This, however, is the first time she has named a date, setting the stage for potential legal and diplomatic tensions.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the Government to arrange for ‌her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," the spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said in a ‌statement.

"Having ​exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th."

Hasina, having been sentenced in absentia by a Bangladeshi court last year, faces the death penalty on returning home. She was run out by angry protesters in 2024 amid a deadly government crackdown on a student-led uprising. The UN said close to 1,400 people were killed in the crackdown.

World.title: US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist
World.content:
The Trump administration has added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist after tensions over its failure to do so raised questions. The news came the same day that Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO.

The Trump administration added Megaspeed International, the firm at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist on Monday.

That means that the Singapore-based firm will not be able to obtain US technology, including semiconductors, without obtaining a license from the US government.

The news was reported by Semafor, an American news website.

US Commerce Department under scrutiny over Nvidia scandal: What to know

The US Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed was smuggling Nvidia chips into China for more than a year, according to the Financial Times.

But tensions at the Commerce Department broke into the spotlight after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive at the Singapore-based firm earlier this month.

Politicians criticized Commerce Department Secretary Howard Lutnick for not having previously added Megaspeed to the department's so-called "Entity List" despite US intelligence warnings that the company was a possible front for smuggling sensitive AI chip technology to China.

Huang briefly lost his job over the scandal as US officials said the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei in 2025 Image: TVBS/dpa/picture alliance

Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday, in a stunning reversal after his resignation just two weeks ago.

The New York Times reported last month that US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang.

Beijing has denied those claims and called the spy accusations "groundless."

Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO

Nvidia shares soared more than 30% after the company announced it reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.

Some people were happy to see him back as president of Nvidia, as videos posted to social media show.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to be the next speaker of the House, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible, and incomprehensible" and vowed Congress would reinvestigate any wrongdoing by the company and the Commerce Department.

World.title: Denmark: Top court backs hardline immigration "ghetto law"
World.content:
Denmark's Supreme Court has found that evictions of "non-Western" residents do not amount to discrimination. The government in Copenhagen argues its "ghetto law" encourages integration.

Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration.

The court on Monday upheld Denmark's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration. The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.

The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.

Denmark: Forcibly resettling 'ghettos' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Denmark's hardline immigration policies making it a role model in the EU

Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU. Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.

Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."

The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.

In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.

"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.

What is the EU-Rwanda return hub scheme? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who is a 'non-Western' resident?

Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.

The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.

According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

World.title: Tajikistan follows US call, withdraws from ICC
World.content:
Tajikistan has initiated its withdrawal from the International Criminal Court as the US calls for it to be "dismantled." The decision was made during a recent visit from Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Tajikistan has now become the fourth country to announce its formal withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, Netherlands since the US announced its intention to "dismantle" the body — joining Chad, Naoero [formerly Nauru] and Venezuela.

US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have railed against the court as abusing its jurisdiction, with Trump publicly attacking the ICC during remarks at a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin — who is wanted by the court for war crimes committed during the course of Russia's full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine.

Trump's public attacks on the world's permanent war crimes tribunal prompted an amused smirk from Putin during their meeting in Shenzhen, China.

Why is the ICC important?

The ICC prosecutes individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, crimes of aggression and war crimes in instances when national cannot or will not act.

The ICC issued an international arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023.

Tajikistan's government said it made the decision to initiate the one-year withdrawal process on Friday, when Putin made a stopover visit after leaving his trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi.

The ICC said it "regrets" Tajikistan's decision, adding that the move undermines "the collective pursuit of justice" and weakens "global efforts to end impunity."

"The ICC stands at the heart of the international system of accountability, and its effectiveness depends on sustained and unequivocal support from the international community," an ICC statement continued.

Tajikistan signed the Rome Statute that established the ICC back in 1998 and ratified it in 2000.

Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have also announced their withdrawal from the court, blasting it as a tool of "neocolonial repression."

World.title: US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035
World.content:
FIFA has confirmed the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica will host the 2031 Women's World Cup — the first to feature 48 teams. The UK will stage the 2035 edition, its first World Cup since 1966.

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

The United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

Two tournaments in seven years for the UK

The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country."

Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

The next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

World.title: Turkey: Authorities search for lioness on the loose in Istanbul
World.content:
A lioness was on the loose in northern Istanbul, with wildlife advocates demanding answers over how the animal entered the country and who was keeping it in captivity.

Turkish security forces and wildlife authorities were searching woods in the north of Istanbul on Monday for an animal believed to be a lion that was reportedly roaming free, the national parks authority said.

In an online statement, the parks authority said police officers in the Zekeriyakoy area, north of Istanbul's European side, reported spotting "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras at around 9 p.m. (18:00 GMT) on Sunday.

Grainy images published by the Turkish media showed the lioness walking through a grassy area. It was unclear where the animal came from, though some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home.

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said it launched investigation focused on identifying its owner.

Istanbul governor's office said in an online post that the location of the lion has been identified and the efforts to capture it were underway.

Turkish media published thermal images of the lioness roaming free Image: Anka

According to park authorities, the search is still underway, with specialist veterinarians also involved in the operation to capture the animal.

Outcry among activists

Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man. It remains unclear where the Istanbul lion escaped from but it sparked an outrage among activists and advocates.

Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."

"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," the organization said on X.

Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."

Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be raised about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.

Although keeping wild animals as pets are forbidden in Turkey, it has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.

In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

World.title: After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
World.content:
Japan has long-running concerns over Chinese military expansionism, and Beijing has bristled at Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan. The frosty ties were on full display at the APEC summit.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.

After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.

It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.

Sanae Takaichi was received by a mid-level Chinese Foreign Ministry official and a small guard of honor in Shenzhen Image: Bai Xueqi/Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.

Frosty China-Japan ties on full display

"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.

"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.

Yang added that the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."

China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.

Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.

Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.

Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.

Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Japan's Taiwan comments open new rift with Beijing

"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.

The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.

Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.

According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury.

China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.

And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.

"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.

"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."

Adebahr added that this left China with little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise. However, he pointed out that Beijing's reliance on coercion could backfire by prompting Japan to increase defence spending and seek closer ties with other partners.

Unlike in 2026, Takaichi did meet with Xi at the 2025 APEC summit in South Korea Image: Japan Pool/Jiji Press/AFP

Japan's leadership faces the China test

Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.

As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.

"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."

"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.

Yang added that Japan was likely to seek opportunities to signal goodwill and improve relations "in return for small-scale compromises." However, he said that a reset in the dynamics would depend on how the Trump administration shaped its foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.

"I would not be too pessimistic about the relationship, because in the medium term, trade, technology and critical minerals are now seen as security issues," he added. "Therefore, complex interdependence will prevent a return to the old pattern of keeping politics and economics separate."

"While economic interdependence alone will not be enough to stabilize the relationship, full decoupling is highly unlikely, as transaction costs would be far too high for both sides," he said.

World.title: Llega el apagón de encuestas: ¿Qué dice el promedio con las últimas?
World.content:
Esta es la última actualización del promedio de EL PAÍS, del 23 de noviembre. Además, construye tu propio promedio

Se publican decenas de encuestas en una campaña. Son el mejor instrumento para predecir unas elecciones, sobre todo cuando las miramos juntas: eso hace nuestro promedio. Combina todos los estudios dando más peso a las encuestadoras que más aciertan. En su última actualización, ese promedio sitúa al PP con el 31,5% de los votos, unos 2,5 puntos por delante del PSOE (29%), y con Vox alrededor del 18%.

En el gráfico puedes elegir entre tres promedios. El “medio” es el que usamos habitualmente; los otros dos sirven para comparar: “agresivo” (que reacciona antes a los cambios pero tiene más ruido), y otro “cauto” (que se mueve menos).

Los sondeos se han movido desde la convocatoria del 6 de octubre. El cambio más claro es la subida del PSOE, que estrecha la ventaja del PP: era de 6 puntos y ahora es de menos de 2,5, y bajando. Nuestros cálculos dicen que el PSOE tiene al menos un 25% de probabilidad de ser primero.

Algo que también ha cambiado es la izquierda del PSOE. Las últimas encuestas estiman un 6,8% de voto para lo que hemos llamado Frentes (Frente Amplio y las coaliciones con Podemos, Compromís, Ara Més o Unidad del Pueblo Canario) y un 1,1% para Podemos en solitario. Juntos rondan el 8% de voto, lejos del 12,3% que logró Sumar en 2023.

La suma de izquierdas y derechas

El número clave de las elecciones es el resultado por bloques. Al cierre, la derecha suma el 51,2% de los votos (PP, Vox y SALF) y la izquierda, el 38,7% (PSOE, Frentes, Podemos y Adelante Andalucía). Son 12,5 puntos de distancia, cuando en las generales de 2023 casi empataron, con 45,6% y 44% respectivamente. La suma de PP y Vox tendrá seguramente la mayoría si supera el 47% de votos.

La ventaja de la derecha creció entre 2024 y el verano de 2025, cuando sus votos pasaron del 48% al 52%. Pero en campaña se ha reducido unos tres puntos. Se ha cumplido nuestra hipótesis inicial: la izquierda, que partía desmovilizada, ha recuperado terreno con la convocatoria electoral, aunque siga por detrás.

El promedio también constata que las encuestadoras discrepan. Casi todas ponen al PP primero, pero con ventajas distintas: desde menos de un punto, según 40dB. o Ipsos, hasta los casi siete de Hamalgama. Solo SW Demoscopia y Cluster17 sitúan al PSOE por delante, además del CIS. Pero el dato de este último es poco informativo porque el centro sobrestima a la izquierda desde 2018.

¿Y si corregimos los llamados sesgos? Algunas encuestadoras se desvían hacia la derecha o hacia la izquierda. Nuestro promedio no lo corrige por un motivo: esas desviaciones cambian de una elección a otra y casi nunca son sistemáticas. Pero podemos ver qué pasaría si lo hiciéramos: el siguiente gráfico permite corregir cada encuesta con el sesgo histórico de su casa.

El resultado depende de qué elecciones miramos. Con los errores de todas las elecciones desde 2018, generales y autonómicas, la ventaja del PP sobre el PSOE sube de 2,5 a 3,5 puntos: en conjunto las encuestas se han quedado cortas con la derecha. Pero en las generales ha pasado lo contrario: subestimaron a la izquierda. El caso más recordado es 2023: las últimas encuestas daban a la derecha 5,4 puntos de ventaja, y en las urnas sacó solo 1,6. Si ajustamos las encuestas con sus sesgos solo en las tres generales desde 2018, la ventaja del PP baja a un punto, aunque la suma de derechas sigue claramente por delante.

Todos estos números son tentativos. Primero, porque las encuestas son una aproximación. Y segundo, porque entre las últimas encuestas y el 29-N hay seis días. La izquierda venía recortando distancia. Esa tendencia podrá seguir o no, pero ya no podremos contarlo aquí con sondeos públicos: la ley impide publicarlos en los cinco días previos a la votación.

¿Cómo funciona el promedio?

Un promedio de encuestas suele ser más preciso que cualquier encuesta aislada: suma la muestra de todas y compensa en parte sus errores, porque mezcla la “cocina” de cada encuestadora. El nuestro funciona así:

1) Todas las encuestas. Usamos las de voto al Congreso publicadas desde las generales de 2023, salvo las encargadas por partidos y las que no tienen trabajo de campo propio. La mayoría las tomamos de Wikipedia.

2) Con distinto peso. Cada encuesta importa según su encuestadora, su muestra y su antigüedad. La nota de cada casa sale de nuestro comparador, que valora su error, su sesgo y si publica sus microdatos (las mejores pesan el doble que una casa normal). El peso de una encuesta se reduce a la mitad cada diez días y desaparece a los 30.

3) Cada casa cuenta una vez. De cada encuestadora pesa su último sondeo, para que no mande quien publica más.

4) Mira hacia atrás. El promedio de cada día solo usa las encuestas con el trabajo de campo terminado hasta entonces. Si una se publica con retraso, la línea de esos días se corrige un poco.

5) Tres ritmos. El promedio central y dos para comparar: el agresivo reduce el peso a la mitad cada 8 días y corta a los 14; el cauto, cada 30 y a los 60.

6) Las listas del 29N. Desde el 14 de octubre medimos las candidaturas nuevas, y las encuestas anteriores se traducen a ellas. SALF y Adelante Andalucía entran en el promedio poco a poco, a medida que las publican las encuestadoras.

7) El sesgo, aparte. La corrección del interactivo usa el error de cada casa en la ventaja entre bloques desde 2018, entero: enseña qué pasaría si las casas volvieran a fallar como de media.

8) El promedio es sólido, pero no infalible. Lo hemos probado con 41 elecciones desde 2018: cinco días antes de votar, falla 1,5 puntos por partido de media. Cambiar la ventana o los pesos lo mejora una décima como mucho. Cuando falla es porque fallan todas las encuestas a la vez, algo que ningún promedio puede corregir: por eso nuestro modelo añade esa incertidumbre.

Todas las encuestas
