World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Colours of Ostrava official 💛 (@colours_cz)

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: Leo Express Opens Prague–Munich Train Tickets From 49 CZK
World.content:
Leo Express has started selling tickets for its new Prague–Munich express service, which will replace České dráhy on the route from December 13.

The cheapest domestic fares currently available start at just 49 CZK for journeys between Prague and Plzeň.

The new service, known as Ex36, will be operated by Leo Express for five years after the company won a public tender. It will take over the route currently served by České dráhy’s Bavarian Express trains.



International tickets are not yet available. Although German stations already appear in the booking system, passengers can currently only book journeys within the Czech Republic. Leo Express says bookings for the full Prague–Munich route will open in the coming days.

The lowest advertised fare between Prague and Plzeň is 49 CZK. The same starting price applies to journeys as far as Domažlice. Business class tickets start at 199 CZK.

Prices will vary depending on demand and availability, so not all seats will be offered at the lowest fares. A second-class ticket between Prague and Plzeň will cost up to 236 CZK, equivalent to the standard OneTicket fare.

For comparison, České dráhy currently charges between 155 CZK and 235 CZK for the same journey, depending on the time of travel. Passengers can also use the cheaper Berounka express service by combining tickets from the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) and Plzeň Region Integrated Transport (IDPK) systems.

According to the booking system, most trains will have six carriages, including two business-class carriages. The operator will use former Deutsche Bahn carriages purchased by Spanish railway company Renfe and leased to Leo Express.

The trains will include both open-plan seating and traditional compartments. Eight services will run in each direction every day, matching the current timetable of České dráhy’s Bavarian Express.

World.title: Prague’s Abandoned Vyšehrad Station Begins Its Transformation Into Apartments
World.content:
Work has begun on the redevelopment of Prague’s historic Vyšehrad railway station, set to become part of a residential complex with 138 micro-apartments, shops and two new buildings.

Developer Karlin Port Real Estate, led by Milorad Mišković and his business partner Miki Goldshtein, began preparatory work at the end of October.

The company plans to start the main renovation and construction works in March 2027.



The developer acquired the station and surrounding land in early 2024 from Cyprus-based company Miquelira Limited, which has been linked to businessman František Savov. The deal followed months of negotiations and extensive checks, as the listed historic building was in a serious state of disrepair.

The plans include the restoration of the original station building and construction of two additional buildings. The development will offer 138 micro-apartments, around 50 underground parking spaces and up to 13 retail units on the ground floor.

The apartments will be sold rather than operated as rental accommodation. According to Mišković, they could appeal to students, young professionals, investors and families looking for temporary accommodation for children studying in Prague.

The developer also wants to improve the wider neighbourhood, including the streets connecting the station with Albertov and the Vltava riverfront.

More projects planned across Prague

Karlin Port Real Estate is also preparing other residential developments in the capital. In Hostivař, the company plans to start construction of the Výhledy Košík project in 2027. It will include 228 apartments and approximately 1,500 square metres of retail space.

The company is also exploring opportunities involving former railway properties and preparing to enter Prague 9, where it plans to focus on the redevelopment of former industrial sites.

Mišković said brownfield regeneration remains his main interest, although the company is now considering projects across Prague rather than concentrating exclusively on the city centre.

World.title: 9 Czech Castles and Chateaux to Visit During Advent 2026
World.content:
Christmas markets are not the only way to enjoy the festive season in Czechia.

Across the country, castles and chateaux are preparing special Advent programmes, with decorated interiors, traditional markets, candlelit tours and activities for families.

Here are nine places worth visiting in the weeks leading up to Christmas and during the holiday season.



1. Loučeň Chateau

Located in Central Bohemia, Loučeň Chateau is hosting a Christmas exhibition titled The Story of the Christmas Tree until January 17, 2027.

Visitors can also explore the illuminated Labyrinths of Light in the castle park. One of the main highlights will take place on November 28, when the country’s largest Advent wreath will be blessed in the courtyard.

Special Advent tours and children’s programmes will run throughout December.

2. Karlštejn Castle

One of Czechia’s most famous castles will also welcome visitors with Christmas decorations.

From November 27, 2026, to January 3, 2027, selected tours of the Imperial Palace will include festive decorations and an introduction to Christmas traditions associated with the court of Charles IV.

The castle will be closed from December 21 to 25.

3. Sychrov Chateau

Sychrov Chateau in the Liberec Region will host its traditional Advent Market on November 28 and 29.

The market will feature Christmas decorations, seasonal products and food stalls in the castle courtyard.

Visitors planning a trip during the Christmas holidays can also explore the decorated interiors through self-guided tours from December 27 to January 3, 2027.

4. Křivoklát Castle

Křivoklát Castle, one of the most important medieval castles in Central Bohemia, will host its traditional Royal Advent event on December 5–6 and 12–13.

The programme includes an Old Bohemian Christmas Market, with artisan stalls selling traditional products, dried fruit, Christmas biscuits, sausages and mulled wine.

Visitors will also be able to explore the castle interiors at their own pace.

5. Hrádek u Nechanic

Built in the Windsor Gothic style, Hrádek u Nechanic will open its doors for Advent visits on selected weekends between November 28 and December 13.

The decorated interiors will feature Christmas trees, traditional ornaments, nutcrackers and nativity scenes. Guided tours will also explain how Christmas was celebrated in the past.

Special candlelit evening tours are scheduled for November 28, December 4 and December 11, while Advent concerts will take place on December 5 and 12.

The castle kitchen will also serve traditional English punch.

6. Dětenice Castle

Dětenice Castle in the Jičín area will offer a festive programme throughout December.

On December 5, children can take part in a St. Nicholas celebration in the medieval tavern. Visitors can also see Krampus performances on December 4, 5 and 12.

The castle’s medieval entertainment programme runs daily from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.

More Advent Destinations Across Czechia

Other places organising seasonal events include Třeboň Chateau, which will host Advent markets on December 5 and 6, and Jindřichův Hradec Castle, where a weekend programme of theatre, music, dance and traditional crafts is planned for the same dates.

In South Moravia, Valtice Chateau is displaying 30 Christmas trees decorated with more than 2,500 handmade glass ornaments. The exhibition runs until December 23.

Villa Stiassni in Brno is also offering special Christmas tours, featuring period decorations and an exhibition of historical toys.

World.title: Looking for a Team Challenge in Prague? This Venue Has 25 Different Tests
World.content:
Looking for something to do in Prague beyond the usual sightseeing?

TEPfactor offers an indoor adventure combining physical challenges, puzzles and teamwork, just a short walk from Wenceslas Square.

Located at Vodičkova street, the 1,500-square-metre venue takes inspiration from the TV show Fort Boyard.



Its main attraction features 25 challenges testing participants’ strength, logic, dexterity, patience and ability to work together.

Visitors compete in teams of two to six people, tackling a series of tasks that require both physical effort and problem-solving skills. The main game takes approximately three hours, making it an option for groups of friends, families and visitors looking for an alternative to traditional tourist activities.

For those seeking something more intense, TEPfactor also operates Fear House, a horror-themed attraction with several levels of difficulty. Options range from group experiences to more demanding individual challenges.

The most intense version, Hardcore + Kidnapping, includes a staged kidnapping scenario and must be arranged in advance.

The venue also caters to organised groups. Schools can book activities designed to encourage communication and cooperation, while companies can use the challenges for team-building events. Birthday celebrations, stag and hen parties and private gatherings are also among the available options.

Beyond the adventure games, TEPfactor offers event space for larger gatherings. Facilities include a theatre-style room with a stage, sound equipment and the option to arrange a DJ and catering.

Additional entertainment can include pub quizzes, stand-up comedy, mobile casino activities and theatre performances.

Reservations can also be made through its online booking system.

World.title: Prague Pride to Host Studio 54-Inspired New Year’s Eve Party
World.content:
Prague Pride will celebrate the arrival of 2027 with a Studio 54-inspired New Year’s Eve party at Slovanský dům, bringing disco music, drag performances and LGBTQ+ matchmaking.

The event, titled Disco Royale, will take place on December 31, 2026, from 8 p.m. until 4 a.m. at Empire Hall in Slovanský dům, Prague 1.



Organisers are promising a night inspired by the legendary New York nightclub Studio 54 and the disco era of the late 1970s.

Guests are encouraged to dress accordingly, with sequins, satin, colourful suits, platform shoes and extravagant accessories all part of the suggested dress code.

The programme will combine live entertainment with music and activities throughout the evening. A queer and drag cabaret will feature performances by Radek Horáček, Hugo Seneši, Lukas Illusion, Rudy Daddy, Melancholia Blackbile and Barbora Elz.

Music will be provided by DJ Jan Witek, who will play a mix of disco classics by Donna Summer, ABBA, the Bee Gees and Chic, alongside modern disco-house and contemporary party tracks. DJ Koko will also join the line-up.

Beyond the dance floor, visitors can take part in LGBTQ+ matchmaking activities, including a Traffic Light Dating System and an interactive game designed to help guests meet new people. A Studio 54-themed photo booth and a New Year’s raffle are also planned.

A dedicated chill-out area will offer a quieter space away from the music, while the bar will serve a signature New Year’s Eve cocktail.

Tickets are available in two categories. Basic admission costs 890 CZK and includes a welcome drink, a complimentary snack and access to open seating in the main hall and lounge area.

VIP tickets cost 1,390 CZK and include guaranteed table seating, access to a second-floor balcony and the same welcome refreshments.

Tickets are available through December 30, or until the event sells out. Proceeds from ticket sales support Prague Pride’s work with LGBTQ+ people in Czechia.

World.title: Black Friday in Czechia: When to Shop and How to Spot Fake Discounts
World.content:
Black Friday will officially fall on November 27 this year, but shoppers in the Czech Republic will not have to wait until the final Friday of November to find deals.

Major retailers have already turned the traditional one-day sale into a weeks-long campaign, with promotions appearing in several rounds throughout the month.

While stricter consumer protection rules have made misleading discounts harder to advertise, shoppers still need to be careful. Some retailers continue to use pricing strategies that make reductions look more attractive than they really are.



When does Black Friday 2026 start in Czechia?

Black Friday 2026 takes place on Friday, November 27. Originally an American shopping tradition held the day after Thanksgiving, the event has gradually become one of the biggest retail campaigns in Europe.

In the Czech Republic, however, the sales period now extends well beyond the official date. Many retailers begin advertising discounts in early November, gradually introducing new offers under campaigns commonly marketed as Black Week or Black Month.

The extended shopping period also serves a practical purpose. Spreading orders across several weeks helps online retailers manage warehouse operations, deliveries and payment systems, avoiding the logistical pressure that would come with concentrating all purchases into a single day.

The country’s biggest retailers are following slightly different approaches.

Alza.cz typically divides its Black Friday campaign into several stages, with different product categories and limited quantities of discounted items introduced throughout November. The final round is expected to coincide with the week of November 23–29.

Datart also rotates its promotional selection during the month. Its offers cover everything from large household appliances to smaller electronic devices, with discounts available both online and in its physical stores.

Allegro, which has incorporated the former Mall.cz into its marketplace, uses a different approach. Its platform features daily promotions from a large number of independent sellers, with special offers continuing throughout November and reaching their peak on November 27.

Notino focuses its Black Friday campaign on selected brands and promotional discount codes. Its broader offers are concentrated around the main Black Friday shopping period.

Black Friday or Cyber Monday when should you buy?

The official Black Friday date is not necessarily the best opportunity to make every purchase.

Cyber Monday, which falls on November 30 in 2026, follows the Black Friday weekend. Originally introduced as an online equivalent of traditional in-store sales, it has become another important date for retailers, particularly those selling electronics and IT equipment.

For some products, waiting until Monday could pay off. Retailers may review their weekend sales figures and introduce additional reductions on items that have not performed as expected. Televisions, laptops, monitors and computer components are among the categories worth monitoring.

How to recognise artificial discounts

Although Czech consumer protection legislation has introduced stricter rules on how retailers advertise price reductions, promotional labels do not automatically mean a product is being sold at its best price.

Under the European Omnibus Directive and the related amendment to the Czech Consumer Protection Act, retailers must generally display the lowest price charged during the 30 days preceding a price reduction.

This requirement is intended to prevent sellers from temporarily increasing prices before a sale and then advertising a seemingly substantial discount against the inflated amount.

Nevertheless, consumers should not rely exclusively on the percentage displayed next to a product.

Independent price-comparison services and historical price-tracking tools can help establish whether an offer represents a genuine saving. Checking how much an item cost in the weeks before Black Friday is often more useful than comparing its current price with the original recommended retail price.

World.title: Prague Has 2,600 Homeless People, but Shelters Cannot Keep Up
World.content:
Around 2,600 people are living on the streets of Prague, according to estimates by the non-profit organization Naděje.

While the city and its municipal districts provide various forms of assistance, social workers say existing shelters and day centres are struggling to meet demand.



Prague’s support system includes overnight shelters, emergency accommodation, low-threshold day centres, professional counselling and temporary housing programmes. The city also operates hostels, provides grants to municipal districts for homelessness-related projects and works with non-profit organizations.

One of the main forms of assistance is provided by social curators, municipal employees who work directly with people living on the streets. Prague 1 and Prague 2 both employ their own teams.

Prague 2 established a food bank distribution point in the courtyard of the New Town Hall (Novoměstská radnice). People in need can collect food and basic hygiene supplies there.

Social services struggle to meet demand

Despite these initiatives, the capacity of Prague’s existing facilities remains a major concern.

Aleš Strnad, head of services at Naděje’s Prague branch, said the number of places available in day centres and overnight shelters was insufficient.

According to Strnad, opposition from local residents is one of the main obstacles to opening new facilities. He pointed out the contradiction between resistance to new centres and public complaints about the growing number of people living in poor and unhygienic conditions on the streets.

The city also introduces additional measures during the winter months. From December until the end of March, its humanitarian programme allows people experiencing homelessness to spend the night in heated facilities free of charge.

World.title: Péter Magyar rejects EU budget proposal, compares negotiations to a ‘Marrakesh bazaar’
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has sharply criticised the European Union’s proposed 2028–2034 budget, saying Hungary will not accept making financial support for Ukraine a compulsory part of the bloc’s next seven-year spending plan. Speaking after a meeting of Visegrád Group (V4) leaders in Bratislava on Monday, he called the proposal unacceptable as a basis for negotiations.

The summit brought together the prime ministers of Hungary, Slovakia, Poland and the Czech Republic, with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker also attending. Competitiveness, migration and the EU’s next long-term budget were among the main topics.

According to Telex, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico initially avoided using dramatic language to describe the budget proposal, which the V4 countries consider unacceptable. Magyar, however, took a more forceful approach.

“I am, of course, ready for the negotiations on Thursday and Friday, but I think it would have been more useful to put forward a reasonably good proposal instead of playing a bazaar in Cairo, Tunis or Marrakesh,” he said at the joint press conference.

Hungary supports Ukraine, but rejects compulsory funding

Magyar’s main objection concerns the proposed link between the EU’s next budget and financial support for Ukraine. He stressed that Hungary, like Slovakia, Poland, the Czech Republic and Austria, stands in solidarity with Ukraine and is willing to provide assistance.

“We have done so before and will continue to do so in the future,” he said, according to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI).

However, he argued that the EU should not impose compulsory contributions on member states through an already stretched budget, threaten them over the issue or make such funding a condition in the negotiations.

The dispute is expected to feature prominently in the next round of EU-level talks on Thursday and Friday, 26–27 November.

Tusk credits Hungary’s government change for V4 cooperation

Despite their differences on individual issues, all four V4 prime ministers said the meeting demonstrated that regional cooperation remains viable.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk specifically credited the change of government in Hungary with helping the countries reach common ground.

“There are things on which we agree, and the fact that we have managed to agree now is also thanks to the change of government in Hungary,” Tusk said, as quoted by Telex. He also highlighted Magyar’s anti-corruption efforts.

World.title: Direct Budapest-Japan flights on the horizon? Transport minister holds discussion with airlines
World.content:
Hungary has held preliminary talks with Japan’s two largest airlines about launching direct flights between Budapest and Japan. Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy met senior executives from Japan Airlines (JAL) and All Nippon Airways (ANA) on Monday, although no decision or launch date has been announced.

The discussions took place at the Ministry of Transport and Investment, where a delegation representing major Japanese industrial companies and trading houses began its visit to Hungary. Vitézy described the visit as an important step in strengthening Hungarian-Japanese relations, noting that a delegation of this kind last came to the country in 2008.

In a Facebook post, the minister confirmed that the talks included preliminary discussions about establishing a direct air link between the two countries.

No launch date or airline commitment yet

The potential connection remains at an early discussion stage. Neither a launch date nor details of a possible route or flight frequency have been announced.

According to aviation news outlet AIRportal.hu, Japan Airlines operated seasonal charter flights to Budapest in the years before 2008. Neither airline currently operates a scheduled direct service to the Hungarian capital.

ANA does, however, fly from Tokyo Haneda to Vienna three times a week. JAL does not operate its own scheduled services to the region, including Vienna, Prague or Warsaw.

A direct Budapest–Japan connection could offer another travel option for passengers between the two countries, but it remains unclear whether either airline will move forward with the proposal.

If you missed it: Ryanair adds more than 70,000 extra seats on Hungarian routes for Christmas season

Japanese companies could also play a role in Hungary’s railway development

The meeting also covered potential cooperation in railway technology and investment. Vitézy presented the Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan, under which Hungary intends to spend HUF 3,550 billion (approximately EUR 9.6 billion) on railway improvements over the next ten years.

The minister argued that Japan could be an important partner in this area, given its leading position in railway technology, including high-speed rail. He said the planned investment could create significant opportunities to strengthen economic ties between the two countries.

Vitézy also outlined the Hungarian government’s new investment policy, stressing that public procurement should allow companies offering the highest quality to compete on equal terms.

World.title: Foreign minister: Hungary to host next Friends of the Western Balkans meeting
World.content:
Hungary will host the next meeting of the Friends of the Western Balkans group, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced on Monday following talks in Athens. The initiative focuses on supporting the region’s European integration, with Budapest arguing that the Western Balkans’ stability has a direct impact on Hungary.

Orbán attended the group’s meeting in the Greek capital, where participants discussed the EU accession prospects of Western Balkan countries. In a Facebook post, the foreign minister said Hungary supports bringing countries closer to EU membership as soon as they meet the necessary conditions.

She stressed that accession requires economic and institutional readiness, the rule of law, free elections and strong democratic institutions. However, she added that the EU itself must also prepare for enlargement and ensure that new member states do not end up in a second-tier position.

“Hungary consistently supports the European integration of the Western Balkans,” Orbán wrote.

Hungary joined the initiative in July

The minister described Monday’s meeting as an important milestone, noting that Hungary joined the Friends of the Western Balkans group in Rome in July and has been actively supporting the region’s EU integration since then.

The group brings together countries that support the Western Balkans’ European perspective. Hungary’s decision to host its next meeting signals its intention to remain involved in the enlargement process.

Talks with Greece, Kosovo and North Macedonia

During her visit to Athens, Orbán also held several bilateral meetings with regional counterparts, according to a statement from the Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

In talks with her Greek counterpart, she discussed EU accession for the Western Balkans, the preservation of agricultural and cohesion funding, the diversification of energy sources and the protection of the EU’s external borders.

Her meeting with Kosovo’s foreign minister focused on regional security and the NATO-led KFOR peacekeeping mission. Hungary is the mission’s third-largest contributor, according to the ministry.

With North Macedonia’s foreign minister, Orbán discussed opportunities for Hungarian companies and transport links. One of the topics was a potential corridor connecting the Budapest–Belgrade railway line with the Aegean Sea.

Security and EUFOR also on the agenda

Orbán’s talks with Bosnia and Herzegovina’s foreign minister covered the situation following the country’s elections and the EUFOR mission, the EU’s military operation in the country.

Hungary is one of EUFOR’s largest contributors, and a Hungarian officer currently serves as deputy commander, the ministry said.

World.title: How much will one euro cost in Hungary in 2027? Here’s what analysts predict
World.content:
The Hungarian forint is expected to remain relatively close to its current level against the euro next year, according to a survey of financial analysts. Their forecasts suggest an average exchange rate of HUF 366.5 per euro in 2027, although one institution warns that the currency could weaken significantly under less favourable conditions.

The figures were compiled by Világgazdaság, which asked experts from five financial institutions for their outlook on the forint. Most expect relatively limited movement, with their forecasts clustering around the current exchange rate.

What exchange rate do analysts expect in 2027?

The five institutions surveyed predict the following average euro-forint exchange rates for 2027:

Equilor: HUF 365

HUF 365 Erste: HUF 367.5

HUF 367.5 CIB Bank: HUF 365

HUF 365 ING Bank: HUF 362.5

HUF 362.5 Akcenta: HUF 372.5

This produces a consensus average of HUF 366.5 per euro. The figures suggest that most analysts do not expect a dramatic change in the forint’s value over the coming year.

If you missed it: Hungarian forint weakens further as euro approaches pre-election levels and dollar keeps marching on

Geopolitical tensions and energy prices remain key factors

According to Orsolya Nyeste, chief analyst at Erste, the forint’s performance will continue to depend heavily on geopolitical tensions, energy prices and movements in the euro-dollar exchange rate. Hungary’s strategy for adopting the euro could also influence the currency.

Following recent volatility, Erste expects the forint to strengthen below the HUF 360 level again in the medium term, provided global energy prices ease. The bank forecasts an exchange rate of HUF 360 in the first half of 2027 and HUF 355 in the second half.

Equilor, meanwhile, expects the euro to cost HUF 370 at the end of this year and HUF 365 at the end of 2027. Its chief analyst, Péter Aradványi, highlighted the interest rate policies of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) and major central banks, geopolitical tensions and their impact on oil and gas prices as important factors.

Hungary’s economic growth, credit rating outlook, budget implementation and progress towards meeting the euro adoption criteria could also affect the exchange rate, he told Világgazdaság.

ING sees the forint as an attractive regional investment

ING’s latest currency outlook for 2027 is relatively positive about the Hungarian currency. The Dutch bank considers the forint the most attractive investment prospect among the three main Central European currencies it follows, ahead of the Polish zloty and Czech koruna.

ING expects the MNB to keep its base rate unchanged at 5.5 per cent over the next nine to 12 months. Although inflation trends could theoretically create room for interest rate cuts, geopolitical risks, energy prices and high global yields are expected to encourage caution.

The bank forecasts that the euro-forint exchange rate will fluctuate within a range of HUF 350–370 over the coming quarters. It expects HUF 360 by the end of 2026, HUF 365 in the first half of 2027 and HUF 360 in the second half.

According to ING, a stronger forint could bring the exchange rate down towards HUF 350, but this might prompt markets to anticipate earlier interest rate cuts, limiting further appreciation. On the other hand, if the forint weakened sharply towards HUF 370, the central bank could intervene verbally or through market measures. An interest rate increase would be a last resort, the analysts suggest.

CIB expects gradual economic recovery to continue

CIB Bank’s analysts also anticipate a relatively stable exchange rate, despite uncertainty in the global environment. They expect Hungary’s gradual economic recovery to continue in 2027, with GDP growth reaching 2.3 per cent, compared with a forecast of 1.7 per cent this year.

Annual inflation could remain around 3 per cent, while the euro is expected to trade at approximately HUF 365 by the end of 2027.

The bank’s outlook reflects the view that domestic economic developments will continue to be shaped by external risks, even as growth gradually picks up.

Akcenta warns that the euro could reach HUF 400

The Czech financial company Akcenta is the notable outlier among the five institutions. It expects the euro to trade mostly between HUF 365 and HUF 380 in 2027, but warns that the exchange rate could exceed HUF 400 under unfavourable conditions.

According to its analysts, the budget deficit, the central bank’s interest rate policy and energy prices will be among the main factors determining the forint’s performance.

Overall, the forecasts point to a relatively narrow range for the Hungarian currency next year. However, the differences between the institutions show that the outlook remains sensitive to both international developments and domestic economic policy.

As Világgazdaság notes, traders will be paying particular attention to monthly budget figures and whether the disinflation process continues steadily.

World.title: Hungary’s guest worker U-turn: What happens next for foreign employees?
World.content:
Nearly six months after Hungary restricted guest worker recruitment, the future of foreign employment remains uncertain. While the government is considering a new regulatory framework, employers are warning about labour shortages, and trade unions are demanding stronger protections for Hungarian workers. So has the policy achieved what it promised, and what could happen next?

In June 2026, Péter Magyar’s Tisza government suspended new applications for a specific guest worker residence permit category, marking a major departure from the recruitment policies of the previous Orbán administration. The decision particularly affected nationals of the Philippines, Georgia and Armenia, although it did not amount to a complete ban on foreign employment.

Existing permit holders were not automatically required to leave Hungary, and other employment-related residence permit categories remained available. However, alternative procedures can involve considerably longer waiting times, creating new difficulties for both employers and prospective employees.

Guest workers are still an important part of Hungary’s labour market

Interestingly, the restrictions came at a time when the number of foreign employees in Hungary was continuing to rise. Approximately 112,300 guest workers were employed in the country in June, with the figure increasing to around 112,900 in July.

These numbers include workers employed under different residence categories, so they do not demonstrate whether the suspended permit system succeeded or failed. Nevertheless, they highlight the complicated relationship between immigration policy and the country’s labour needs.

Employers and unions disagree on the way forward

The government has since started discussions about restructuring Hungary’s employment-related immigration system, which currently includes around 24 different legal categories and procedures.

Employers want simpler administration and more predictable recruitment, arguing that certain industries cannot fill vacancies with domestic applicants alone. Trade unions, meanwhile, are pushing for stricter controls, better working conditions and stronger priority for Hungarian jobseekers.

The disagreement raises a difficult question: can Hungary reduce its dependence on foreign labour without making it harder for businesses to operate and attract investment?

What does this mean for guest workers?

For thousands of international employees, the debate is about more than government policy. Their ability to renew permits, change employers and continue working in Hungary depends on the rules applicable to their particular residence status.

The government has yet to complete its proposed overhaul, leaving important questions unanswered.

What changes are employers demanding, what do Hungarian trade unions want, and could the new rules put existing foreign workers at risk?

World.title: Ryanair adds more than 70,000 extra seats on Hungarian routes for Christmas season
World.content:
Ryanair is increasing capacity on flights to and from Hungary by more than 70,000 seats over the Christmas period, as the low-cost airline prepares for strong demand for holiday travel.

Ryanair prepares for the holiday season

The additional capacity is expected to help the carrier transport nearly 380,000 passengers on its Hungarian routes during the festive season, according to the company. The expansion is intended to accommodate people travelling home to spend Christmas with family and friends, as well as those taking trips during the holiday period.

Ryanair said it expects demand to remain high and is encouraging passengers to book early, warning that flights are filling up quickly, writes 24.hu. The extra seats will be available on services both arriving in Hungary and departing from the country, although the airline’s announcement did not specify which individual routes would receive additional capacity or provide a breakdown of the extra seats by destination.

Airline launches digital Christmas gift cards

Alongside the expanded holiday schedule, Ryanair has introduced Christmas-themed digital gift cards. The vouchers can be used to purchase flight tickets and are being promoted as a possible present for people who travel regularly or plan to visit loved ones over the festive period.

Jade Kirwan, Ryanair’s director of communications, said the Christmas booking season was already well under way and that flights were selling quickly. She said the additional capacity was intended to allow more passengers to spend the holidays with relatives and friends, while urging travellers to secure their tickets in advance.

Kirwan also suggested that the digital gift cards could be a way for people who are not travelling themselves to surprise family members or friends who are planning a trip.

Strong seasonal demand expected

The nearly 380,000 passengers forecast for the Christmas season would represent a substantial volume of travel on Ryanair’s Hungarian routes during one of the busiest periods of the year. The announcement comes as airlines prepare for increased demand around Christmas, when many people travel to reunite with family or take advantage of time off work.

Ryanair has not disclosed further details of the additional flight capacity, including the exact dates covered by the expansion. Passengers considering holiday travel are therefore advised to check the airline’s booking system for available services and fares.

The carrier’s announcement adds capacity to its Hungarian network for the festive period, but the final number of passengers will depend on bookings and operational conditions over the coming weeks.

World.title: Hungarian university leads regional rankings of Central and Eastern European institutes’
World.content:
A Hungarian university has been ranked the best higher education institution in Central and Eastern Europe in a new regional comparison published by the British organisation Times Higher Education (THE).

Hungarian university named the best in Central and Eastern Europe

The ranking, unveiled on 17 November, covers 155 institutions across 12 countries. Hungary secured seven places among the top 35 institutions, with two making it to the top ten. Semmelweis University took first place, ahead of Estonia’s University of Tartu and Charles University in Prague. Budapest’s Óbuda University also performed strongly, finishing seventh.

The other Hungarian institutions in the top 35 were the University of Debrecen, in 13th place; Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), joint 16th; the University of Szeged, joint 30th; the University of Pécs, 33rd; and Corvinus University of Budapest, joint 35th.

Hungarian institutions make up a fifth of the top 35

Former government commissioner for economic strategies László György highlighted the results in a Facebook post, describing them as evidence of sustained work in Hungarian higher education. He pointed out that Hungarian institutions account for one fifth of the 35 highest-ranked institutes in the region, a share he said was almost three times the country’s proportion of the regional population.

György attributed the progress to long-term planning, institutional reforms and the work of institution leaders, researchers, lecturers and students. He also linked the results to changes in the university system introduced in recent years, although his assessment represents his interpretation of the rankings rather than an explanation provided by THE.

Semmelweis also improves its global position

The regional comparison draws on data from THE’s 2027 World University Rankings. Its assessment considers a range of indicators, including teaching, research performance, cooperation with industry and international links.

Semmelweis has also improved its position in the global table, moving up from 272nd place to 247th. The latest results add to a series of international achievements reported by Hungarian higher education institutions. In October, Corvinus University of Budapest received EQUIS accreditation, an international quality label for business schools.

The regional ranking offers a positive snapshot of Hungary’s position in higher education, although individual placements reflect the methodology and indicators used by THE. The results nevertheless put Semmelweis at the forefront of the region in this latest comparison.

World.title: First widespread snowfall could arrive in Hungary this week: Here’s where to expect the most
World.content:
A cold air mass moving southwards from the north has brought temperatures below seasonal averages to large parts of Europe. Snow fell across much of the Scandinavian Peninsula over the weekend, while parts of the Baltic states and Poland could also experience snowfall at the beginning of the week, and Hungary too, might see its first more widespread snowfall of the season later this week.

Snow could cover parts of Hungary this week as temperatures fall

With north-western regions and the northern mountain ranges facing the highest probability of a white landscape, according to the latest weather forecasts. Hungary has so far experienced mostly dry conditions despite the arrival of colder air. However, the chance of precipitation is expected to increase from the middle of the week, potentially bringing snow showers to some areas.

Mediterranean cyclone could bring snow on Thursday

According to the forecast published by weather service Időkép, a Mediterranean cyclone approaching from the south-west could bring a more significant spell of winter weather on Thursday, 26 November. The combination of the incoming precipitation and cold air over the Carpathian Basin could produce snowfall not only in higher-altitude areas but also in some lowland regions.

An analysis of the ECMWF AIFS probabilistic model, based on its 22 November forecast run, suggests that the highest likelihood of snow cover by 7 PM on Thursday will be in western and northern Hungary.

North-west and northern hills face the greatest chance

The Alpokalja foothills and the Kisalföld region in the north-west could have a 70–90 per cent probability of snow cover, with the likelihood exceeding 90 per cent in some areas close to the western border. The Northern Hungarian Mountains and the Danube Bend also have relatively high chances, at around 50–70 per cent.

Further south and east, the outlook is less favourable. The Bakony and Vértes hills, as well as the wider Budapest area, have estimated probabilities of 30–50 per cent. In the Danube–Tisza Interfluve and northern parts of the Great Hungarian Plain, the chances fall to 10–30 per cent. In the southern Great Plain and Baranya County, it is currently considered unlikely for the landscape to dress in white.

Hope for the best, prepare for the worst?

The figures are probabilities rather than guarantees. The precise path of the Mediterranean cyclone and the position of the cold air mass could still significantly affect both the amount of precipitation and whether it falls as rain or snow.

HungaroMet has also cautioned that the country remains mostly dry for now, with the broader increase in precipitation chances expected only from midweek. Further forecasts in the coming days should provide a clearer picture of where snow is most likely to settle.

World.title: After ‘Propaganda’ Ban, Bulgarian LGBT Pupils Report Greater Insecurity
World.content:
After Bulgaria prohibited LGBTQ+ “propaganda” in schools in August 2024, teachers began approaching Vasil Lozanov with a question: can we still talk about it?

Thirty-three-year-old Lozanov teaches philosophy and civic education at Sofia’s Spanish High School. He also has a background in law.

“Experienced teachers, with years of experience both as people and as teachers, were in the dark about what they should do,” Lozanov told BIRN.

Lozanov did not change the way he taught. In lessons about tolerance, pupils write questions and comments on slips of paper anonymously; the papers are shuffled, selected and discussed. Sexual orientation is one of the subjects that usually comes up.

“I have never censored them and I have no intention of censoring them,” said Lozanov.

World.title: Czech PM’s Never-Ending Agrofert Saga Could Leave Taxpayers Paying the Price
World.content:
A familiar controversy

The billionaire’s alleged conflicts of interest have been a recurring feature of Czech political life, dominating public debate ever since Babis entered politics and founded his populist ANO movement some 15 years ago.

The basis of one of the country’s biggest fortunes, Agrofert was founded by Babis in 1993, a sprawling conglomerate comprising about 200 companies active in agriculture, chemicals, transport, logistics, forestry and, until recently, the media sector.

With annual revenues of over 210 billion crowns (more than 8.5 billion euros) and employing nearly 30,000 people, Agrofert is the eighth most valuable Czech company, according to the latest Czech Elite ranking.

Babis’s ownership of such a ubiquitous company – and crucially, one of Czechia’s largest recipients of state subsidies – became a focus of public debate in 2014 when the Slovak-born businessman became deputy-prime minister and finance minister. Soon he was facing calls, including from his prime minister at the time, Bohuslav Sobotka, to give up his 100 per cent stake in Agrofert.

The ANO leader has consistently described accusations of a conflict of interest between his business activities and public involvement as a targeted defamation campaign designed to undermine his political ambitions – an argument he still employs to this day.

Passed in 2017, an amendment to the Conflict-of-Interest Act – dubbed “Lex Babis” – introduced guardrails against government members’ business activities, and barred them from accessing public procurement contracts or from running media companies.

Babis, who would go on to become prime minister later that year after a landslide election victory, initially transferred his shares in Agrofert and the SynBiol holding (a separate entity for Babis’s business interests in healthcare and real estate) into two trust funds.

From the start, however, this solution was deemed insufficient by legal experts like Transparency International, who pointed out that while no longer its direct owner, Babis nevertheless remained the conglomerate’s founder and ultimate beneficiary. A 2020 European Commission audit would eventually concur with this assessment.

Compared with the much broader EU rules on conflicts of interest, “the Czech regulation is much more specific, which allows some public authorities to navigate through it, saying that in some regards Mr Babis is in a conflict of interest, while in others he is not,” explains Krystof Dolezal, a lawyer for the Czech chapter of Transparency International.

“However, when it comes to the ban on public subsidies and public procurement, the Czech regulation is actually very severe,” he tells BIRN.

From European Parliament resolutions to Czech court rulings and a so-called “Lex Babis II”, rarely a month has gone by without the issue of Babis’s potential conflicts of interests making headlines.

History, it seems, was soon to repeat itself. Having resumed direct ownership of the holding after dissolving the trust funds in 2024 and 2025 when he was out of office, Babis’s ANO party once again claimed victory in last year’s parliamentary elections.

Now facing the obstacle of President Petr Pavel, who insisted he would not appoint him to form a government until an appropriate solution was found to alleviate any conflict-of-interest concerns, Babis was eventually sworn in after promising to distance himself from his businesses.

In February, he eventually transferred his Agrofert shares into a fund called RSVP Trust, which stands for Rodinna sprava a vlastnictvi (meaning, Family Management and Ownership).

World.title: Serbia’s New Leadership Won’t Transform Old Policy on Kosovo
World.content:
The spectacular victory of the Student List has reignited policy debates in Serbia that have grown dormant in recent years, given the grasp on power exerted by Aleksandar Vucic and the Serbian Progressive Party. Chief among them is the question of Kosovo and the process of normalisation.

Whilst the incoming government’s policy is unlikely to be fundamentally different, particularly when it comes to the question of Kosovo’s status, a change in approach will create distinct possibilities – and complications.

The Student List, as with other opposition parties in Serbia, has reiterated that it considers Kosovo to be an “inalienable and integral part of the Republic of Serbia”. This should not come as a surprise, given the centrality of the constitution to their platform.

While some voices within the Student List are more open to discussion about Kosovo, not least for the sake of Serbia’s European path, they will remain marginal for the foreseeable future. A criticism of consensus-driven approaches is that they tend to favour the lowest common denominator, with polarising issues approached with a degree of conservatism.

In the current context, this is understandable. The dilution of the EU perspective in the Serbian political space has undermined one of the key drivers of compromise over Kosovo. Should the government promote a more positive posture on EU membership – and on the reforms required to achieve it – then debates on Kosovo will be framed very differently.

In the meantime, Belgrade should keep its options open. Boxing itself into a corner, by suggesting that past agreements be reviewed and revised, risks further gridlocking the normalisation process.

World.title: Serbia’s Student Movement Criticises European Parliament’s Vukovar Resolution
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbia’s student movement, which under the name Student List won the country’s recent parliamentary elections, has criticised a European Parliament’s draft resolution marking the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar in eastern Croatia, calling for adequate recognition of war crimes committed against Serb civilians during the Croatian conflict.

In a statement on the Student List – Students Win website on Monday, it said the resolution does not contribute to an “objective understanding of historical events” or to reconciliation. It argued that the draft resolution overlooks some of the suffering of Serb civilians in Croatia, including killings, persecution and mass displacement, particularly during the Croatian military operations Flash and Storm in 1995.

“Responsibility for war crimes must be individual and established on the basis of evidence and final court judgments, rather than attributed to entire nations,” the students said.

“Serbia has an obligation to cooperate in clarifying the fate of missing persons and establishing responsibility for crimes committed, but the same approach must also apply to Serb victims and crimes committed against them,” the student movement said.

The eastern border town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serb paramilitaries on November 18, 1991, during the war in Croatia, after which the remaining population was expelled. Two days after the town fell, Croatian prisoners and civilians were taken from Vukovar Hospital to a nearby farm where at least 200 people were executed.

The student movement warned that remembrance of the past should not deepen existing divisions in the region.

“True reconciliation cannot be achieved by imposing one-sided interpretations of the past, but through an honest reckoning with all crimes, regardless of who committed them or against whom,” they added.

The European Parliament was set to debate the resolution on Monday, with a vote scheduled for Thursday. The debate in Strasbourg follows the submission of two motions for a resolution on November 20, commemorating the victims of the siege of Vukovar and the atrocities that followed.

One of the motions, submitted by members of the European People’s Party, EPP, the Socialists and Democrats, S&D, the European Conservatives and Reformists, ECR, and the Greens/EFA, notes that 1,725 cases of missing persons from the war remain unresolved, including 1,341 people whose fate remains unknown and 384 whose deaths have been confirmed but whose burial sites have yet to be located.

It also calls on Serbia to grant access to relevant wartime archives, disclose information about the locations of individual and mass graves, fight against impunity for war crimes and facilitate the identification and return of victims’ remains to their families. The proposal further urges Serbia to adopt its long-announced law on missing persons.

The motion condemns the denial and glorification of war crimes, specifically referring to the public honours paid in Serbia to the convicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade in September 2026.

It further calls for educational, cultural and commemorative programmes that promote a “fact-based understanding of the Croatian Homeland War and the 1990s”, while encouraging reconciliation and respect for all victims.

The proposal acknowledges the work of the International Criminal Tribunal, ITCY, for the former Yugoslavia in prosecuting crimes committed in Vukovar, but adds that not all those responsible have been brought to justice.

The motion also highlights the peaceful reintegration of Serb-held eastern Croatian into Croatia in 1998 as an example of successful post-war reintegration and the importance of rebuilding trust between communities.

World.title: Bosnia’s Dodik Gathers Votes, Seeking Veto Over State Policy
World.content:
On November 9, Milorad Dodik, leader of Republika Srpska's governing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), handed Nebojsa Vukanovic, leader of the opposition For Justice and Order movement, a slip of paper containing the names of people who might join the governing bloc in Bosnia's Serb-majority entity.

Vukanovic had asked whose votes Dodik was counting on for his promised two-thirds majority in the new entity National Assembly.

Vukanovic read parts of the note to reporters. Three days later, Dodik said Vukanovic had skipped the name of Djordje Vucinic, a deputy elected on Vukanovic’s list. Vucinic denied that he was joining the governing parties.

By November 16, two deputies had switched sides to join Dodik's camp in the Republika Srpska assembly. Vladimir Copic, elected on the Serbian Democratic Party, SDS, list, joined United Srpska, a partner of Dodik’s SNSD.

Meanwhile Snjezana Gvozden left the Safe Srpska Movement, PSS, for the SNSD – and was elected an Republika Srpska assembly deputy speaker.

Bosnian law allows deputies who change parties to keep their seats, and Gvozden defended her move, saying that voters had given her the mandate. Whatever the outcome of complaints, people who voted for the two opposition lists have seen a seat won with their votes go to Dodik's bloc.

The governing bloc thereby grew from 54 to 56 seats in the 83-member Republika Srpska assembly. Dodik’s candidate for speaker, Nenad Stevandic, received only 52 votes, however. While his coalition in theory controlled two-thirds of the seats, it still had to show that it could deliver all 56 votes on the same decision.

World.title: Going After Protesters, Albania’s Opposition Democrats Seek Relevance, Control
World.content:
Activist Edison Lika was still in pre-trial detention, charged with throwing eggs at Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama’s car, when senior figures of the opposition Democratic Party took aim at him too.

They accused Lika and fellow activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, both regular participants in anti-government protests, of being “mercenaries paid by Soros” - a reference to the billionaire US philanthropist George Soros and a slur frequently lobbed at Albanian civil society by the Democrats.

For weeks, the Democrats have been singling out members of the protest movement and painting them as saboteurs trying to dilute the movement’s demand for Rama’s resignation with criticism of the opposition too.

World.title: Cash Scandals, Arrests, Shrinking Alliances: Can Hungary’s Fidesz Survive?
World.content:
X marks the spot

The embarrassing seizure on November 13 of 17.3 million euros in hidden cash could turn even the party’s most ardent international admirers away.

“The case and the pictures of it could cause some serious reputational damage for Fidesz,” admits Zoltan Kiszelly, director of the Centre for Political Analyses of Szazadveg, a Fidesz-aligned think tank, in an interview with BIRN.

The money – 5.07 billion in Hungarian forints, 2.65 million in euros and 1.25 million in dollars – was discovered in a forest, buried partly underground, in storage houses and even in some bird feeders. According to Finance Minister Andras Karman, 12 employees of the Treasury spent eight hours counting the money using five counting machines.

The discovery produced countless memes on social media, with some urging Hungarians to grab their spades and go treasure hunting in nearby forests for themselves. Other commentators pointed to how Orban and his foreign minister Peter Szijjarto had openly advocated for the use of cash, even at a time when much of society was switching to bank cards, speculating about whether a preference for cash was part of a general strategy to conceal the origins of stolen money.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar concluded that Fidesz is a “mafia party”, later saying in parliament: “Fidesz lived 38 years. It’s over. You are beyond redemption.”

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said the money was recovered in the framework of an investigation around the finances and business interactions of Miklos Sesztak, a national development minister in Orban’s third government, between 2014 and 2018, and is currently an MP for the Fidesz-satellite Christian Democratic People’s Party. He is under arrest in an alleged corruption case involving a bus procurement tender by state-owned Volanbusz, in which he is accused of taking more than 11 billion forints in bribes.

The discovery of the treasure trove did prompt some reactions abroad, though these have so far been limited. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk sent an ironic message to Orban: “Dear Viktor, I have always admired your creativity, but now I must say I’m impressed as never before.”

In Austria, the Social Democratic Party (SPO) was quick to use the Hungarian case to charge the far-right Freedom Party – an ally of Fidesz that is currently topping the polls in Austria – of hypocrisy. The SPO questioned how the Freedom Party could present itself as an anti-corruption party while remaining silent about the cash discovered during an investigation involving a former minister from Orban’s government. The Freedom Party rejected the criticism, arguing that no charges had yet been filed and that corruption should be prosecuted everywhere, regardless of the country or the people involved.

Most far-right parties have chosen to remain silent over the developing scandal. BIRN contacted the Patriots for Europe grouping of mostly far-right parties in the European Parliament, of which Fidesz is a founding member, for comment but received no answer back.

“Corruption cases never help a party’s image,” Vegh says, though adds that she does not believe this could herald the end of Fidesz’s international alliance network in Europe. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Spain’s Vox – both of which have benefited in the past from dubious Hungarian bank loans during Orban’s time in office – are keeping a low profile on the issue, and the case has not yet been picked up by their political opponents either.

“Most elections are decided primarily on domestic issues,” Vegh points out. “In the US, linking the governing elite’s corruption with everyday social problems was a successful narrative of the Democrats.”

World.title: Bulgaria issues warning of dangerous weather for November 23 over forecast strong winds
World.content:
Bulgaria’s national meteorological bureau has issued the Code Orange warning of dangerous weather for numerous districts for November 23 because of forecast strong winds.

The districts subject to the Code Orange warning are Vidin, Montana, Vratsa, Pleven, Veliko Turnovo, Sliven, Yambol, Haskovo, Plovdiv, Pazardzhik, Kurdzhali, Sofia city, Sofia district, Pernik and Lovech.

All other districts are subject to the lesser Code Yellow warning of potentially dangerous weather, also because of strong winds.

The meteorological bureau said that on the morning of November 23, a moderate and strong southerly wind will blow. It will be cloudy with rain in many places.

It will be relatively warm for the season, with minimum temperatures between 5° and 10° Celsius and maximums between 14° and 19°.

In the afternoon, cold air will flow in a temperatures will drop quickly and significantly.

In a separate announcement, the Road Infrastructure Agency said that from November 23, a serious cold snap with rain is expected, and in the morning hours, negative temperatures and icing conditions are expected.

“The Road Infrastructure Agency appeals to drivers to prepare their vehicles for winter conditions, to set off on the road only with suitable tyres, to drive at a reasonable speed and to keep a distance so as not to block traffic and the work of snow removal equipment,” the agency said.

The national road network has been in winter maintenance mode since November 16. The regional road departments and the involved companies are monitoring weather forecasts for timely treatment of the pavements, especially in the passes and high-mountainous regions, it said.

World.title: Gavriil, Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech, dies at 76
World.content:
Bulgarian Orthodox Church Metropolitan of Lovech Gavriil died on November 22 after a short illness, the church’s governing body the Holy Synod said in a statement.

Gavriil, who had been Metropolitan of Lovech since January 28 2001, was 76.

“His Eminence will remain in the history of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church – Bulgarian Patriarchate as a proper hierarch, a zealous monk, a fervent prayer leader, a clergyman with deep and sincere faith, and a true follower of Christ, who not only with his words, but also with his entire life and deeds proclaimed the gospel truth,” the Holy Synod said.

The statement said that the Holy Synod would meet in special session to decide on the date and time of the funeral of Gavriil, and to appoint a temporary head of the diocese.

Gavriil was born on July 16 1950 in Sofia with the secular name Tsvetan Metodiev Dinev. He took monastic vows in 1979 at the Klisura Monastery St. Petka near Bankya.

He held various clerical posts, including as head of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church in Moscow, before being elected Metropolitan of Lovech.

In 2012, a check into the Holy Synod of the time by the Dossier Commission found that Gavriil was one of only four members of the church’s 15-member governing body for which there was no evidence that he had worked for communist-era secret service State Security.

More recently, Gavriil opposed the decision of the Ecumenical Patriarchate to grant autocephaly (church independence) to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine. Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew signed the decree in January 2019.

Metropolitan Gavriil was among the three candidates for Bulgarian Patriarch both in 2013, when Neofit was elected, and in 2024, when Daniil was elected.

Gavriil’s death creates a vacancy in the church’s governing body, for which an election will be held in the coming months.

In Bulgaria’s 2021 national census, close to 63 per cent of Bulgarians said that they identified as Eastern Orthodox Christians.

(Photo via the website of the Bulgarian Patriarchate)

World.title: EC approves Bulgaria’s final payment request under NextGenerationEU
World.content:
The European Commission said on November 20 that it has partially greenlighted Bulgaria’s fifth and final payment request for 1.82 billion euro under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) of the bloc’s NextGenerationEU post-pandemic economic recovery plan.

Bulgaria submitted the payment request on September 30, the deadline set by the European Commission, which aims to wind down the NextGenerationEU programme at the end of this year.

The Commission said that its assessment found that Bulgaria “has satisfactorily completed 53 out of 59 milestones and targets set out in the Council Implementing Decision.”

As such, the EC said that it would withhold part of the funds requested, but did not give an exact figure, noting only that it would be “proportional.”

Speaking to reporters in Sofia after the announcement, Deputy PM Atanas Pekanov, the Cabinet’s senior official tasked with securing RRF funds, said that Bulgaria was slated to receive more than 1.7 billion euro under the fifth payment request.

The policy areas in which Bulgaria pursued reforms and investments tied to this payment request include decarbonising the energy sector, strengthening the anti-corruption framework, enhancing the sustainability of transport and improving social inclusion and healthcare, the EC said.

The disbursement of the payment can be made after the Economic and Financial Committee, a body composed of senior officials from national administrations and central banks, the ECB and the EC, has issued an opinion on the Commission’s preliminary approval. It has four weeks to do so.

This is the second large RRF payment request received by Bulgaria this year, following 1.1 billion euro granted by the EC in June.

Due to years of political instability and short-lived governments, the country has lagged behind other EU member states in making the requests, raising the prospect that it could miss out on a significant amount of the 6.17 billion euro allocated to it under the RRF.

Pekanov said that this year’s two payment requests would take the amount received by Bulgaria under the RRF to between 98.7 per cent and 99 per cent of the allocated funding.

World.title: Bulgarian Parliament elects 11 members of Supreme Judicial Council
World.content:
Bulgaria’s National Assembly voted on November 20 to appoint 11 members of the country’s Supreme Judicial Council (SJC), the body tasked with the appointment of senior magistrates in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

Parliament held individual appointment votes for all 21 nominees. Vote tallies showed that the candidates that secured appointment were uniformly backed by the governing Progressive Bulgaria, alongside the opposition We Continue the Change (WCC) and Democratic Bulgaria.

The three parliamentary groups have a combined 168 MPs, enough to meet the qualified two-thirds majority of 160 MPs in the 240-seat National Assembly, required for the appointment of SJC members.

Most successful candidates, save three, were also backed by the opposition GERB and Movement for Rights and Freedoms (MRF) parties. Only pro-Kremlin party Vuzrazhdane, whose sole nominated candidate was not elected, voted against all successful appointments.

Of the 11 members of the SJC appointed by MPs on November 20, seven were nominated by Progressive Bulgaria and two apiece by WCC and Democratic Bulgaria.

The council has 25 members and is presided over by the Justice Minister, who is not, however, a member of the SJC. Of the 25 members, 11 are elected by Parliament, 11 by magistrates and three are members ex officio – the country’s prosecutor-general and the heads of the two high courts, the Supreme Court of Cassation and the Supreme Administrative Court.

The 11 members elected by magistrates are voted by their respective branches – six by judges, four by prosecutors and one by investigators. This last one is part of the prosecutors college of the SJC, as the National Investigative Service is subordinated to the prosecutor’s office in Bulgaria’s judiciary.

MPs similarly elect six members of the SJC to the judges college and five to the prosecutors college.

The current SJC line-up, often criticised as being unduly under the influence of MRF leader Delyan Peevski – who is subject to US sanctions under the Magnitsky Act – has been in office nearly five years past the expiration of its five-year term.

That is because Bulgaria’s pollical instability since 2021, which saw eight parliamentary elections in five years, resulted in fragmented parliaments, some of them very short-lived, that had little appetite for tackling the issue of electing SJC members.
