World.title: Meet the shoebill: A prehistoric-looking bird that hunts baby crocodiles
World.content:
Imagine a pelican and a dinosaur had a quiet, moody child. That’s the shoebill (Balaeniceps rex) for you. Towering at nearly five feet tall, with a beak that looks carved from driftwood, this bird has something ancient, almost haunting, about it.

The shoebill’s most striking feature is, undoubtedly, its massive bill—broad and curved at the tip like a clog—and strong enough to grip wriggling catfish and even young crocodiles.

These birds are cloaked in blue-grey feathers, with a kind of regal posture that makes them seem more like swamp guardians than waterbirds. Fully grown, they can span 8 feet from wingtip to wingtip—almost as wide as a small car.

World.title: Case against Kunchacko Boban’s Officer on Duty after man’s real phone number appears in film
World.content:
Over 21 months after its theatrical release, director Jithu Ashraf’s Kunchacko Boban-starrer Officer on Duty (2025) has found itself in troubled waters. A court in Keralam has reportedly directed the police to register a case based on a man’s complaint that his personal mobile phone number was displayed in the film without permission, allegedly leading to frequent calls, some of which were abusive.

Why was a complaint filed against Officer on Duty?

The Ernakulam Chief Judicial Magistrate issued the direction on Saturday, November 21, in response to a complaint filed by one Akshay Prakash, a native of Kannur district. According to news agency PTI, he claimed his personal mobile number was displayed as the contact number for a female doctor character in one of the scenes in Officer on Duty. After the film’s release, he allegedly began receiving frequent calls from people in India and abroad, some of which were abusive in nature.

World.title: Eight injured after ‘dismantled’ body spray containers catch fire in Gujarat; 3 critical
World.content:
Eight people, four of whom are children, suffered burns from a flash fire that erupted when they were dismantling body spray containers that could be sold for scrap, in Bhavnagar city on Monday, police said.

Three of them were severely injured. One, Dalpat Devipujak, was said to have suffered 95% burns and was fighting for his life in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) of Sir Takhtasinhji General Hospital. All eight people are relatives.



The incident took place in Lane number 3 of Mill Ni Chali in the Kumbharwada area.

Chief Fire Officer (CFO) Pradyumansinh Jadeja said the extended family members were taking apart body spray cans when the flash fire erupted in the closed space of their hut.

World.title: NEET-UG reforms: Maharashtra wants exam-centres in every district; what other states told panel
World.content:
With the Centre examining a series of reforms in the conduct of national-level entrance examinations, states have called for changes to the existing admission process, including giving weightage to Class 12 board examination marks for medical admissions, allowing multiple attempts at NEET-UG and expanding examination infrastructure. The latest suggestions come amid consultations by a centre-appointed high-powered task force on exam reforms, which is examining ways to make competitive examinations more secure, transparent and accessible.

Maharashtra has also sought a bigger role in conducting national-level examinations organised by the National Testing Agency (NTA). The issue was discussed at a meeting between Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis and members of the Nandan Nilekani-led task force in Mumbai on Monday.

Also Read | AI-powered tools, new safeguards: 5 months after NEET paper leak, here’s what NTA has changed



According to an official statement, the Maharashtra government wants to make better use of its existing infrastructure to conduct national-level examinations. The discussions covered setting up adequate examination centres in every district, training personnel deployed at these centres and improving the logistics required to conduct examinations. The state also stressed the need for better coordination between state authorities and central examination agencies to ensure a secure and transparent examination process.

States seek changes to NEET-UG admission process

During consultations with the task force, several states have suggested giving weightage to Class 12 board examination marks during medical admissions. They argued that depending entirely on a single entrance examination encourages students to focus on coaching institutes at the cost of their board examination preparation. Some stakeholders have also linked this trend to the growing number of dummy schools.

Also Read | Nandan Nilekani exam reforms panel gets extension till January 2027; receives 50,000 suggestions

Other proposals include allowing students to appear for NEET-UG more than once a year to reduce the pressure of a single high-stakes examination. A majority of southern states, barring Tamil Nadu, have also supported shifting the medical entrance examination from the existing pen-and-paper format to computer-based testing (CBT). Discussions are underway on initially offering both formats to help students adjust to the transition.



Also Read | IIT Delhi to hold JEE Advanced 2027 on May 23; candidates to get on-screen calculator

The NTA conducts several major entrance and eligibility examinations, including NEET-UG, JEE Main, Common University Entrance Test (CUET-UG and PG) and UGC-NET.

States have also called for at least one examination centre in every district to reduce the distance candidates have to travel to take these tests.

What Maharashtra proposed at the meeting

The Maharashtra meeting, held at the chief minister’s official residence Varsha, was attended by task force members S Somanath and Shankar Maruwada, along with National Recruitment Agency Director Shruti Singhal, among others.



Apart from infrastructure, the discussions covered measures to make examinations more accessible to students from rural and urban areas, candidates with disabilities and those who face difficulties with English. The participants also discussed strengthening security arrangements to prevent malpractices and maintain the credibility of national-level examinations.

Reducing examination-related stress was another focus. The state highlighted the need to provide students with more opportunities to appear for examinations, design examination patterns according to the nature of the syllabus and offer adequate guidance and training to help them prepare for competitive and entrance tests.

Also Read | NTA empanels over 5,000 experts for setting, translating and vetting question papers

The Centre constituted the High-Powered Task Force in July 2026 following concerns over examination irregularities, including the NEET-UG paper leak controversy. Headed by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani, the panel is examining reforms in the conduct, security, design and governance of public examinations. Its tenure has been extended until January 2027 to complete consultations and submit its recommendations.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: 'Carrying hopes of 250m people': Zeeshan Ali to be 'first' Pakistani astronaut in space aboard China’s Shenzhou-24
World.content:
Zeeshan Ali was named a crew member of China’s Shenzhou-24 space mission on Tuesday, which is scheduled to launch on November 25, with Ali set to become the first Pakistani to undertake an orbital space mission.

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, who is in China, referred to Ali on X as “Pakistan’s first astronaut”.

Ali will also be the first foreign national to board Beijing’s Tiangong space station, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced.

“Pakistani astronaut Mohammad Zeeshan Ali is the first foreign national to visit Tiangong,” CMSA Spokesperson Zhang Jingbo said during a press conference.

He added that the Long March-2F rocket that will carry the crew into space will soon be filled with propellant. “The crew is in good condition and the space station is functioning normally, meeting all requirements for the mission,” said Zhang.

According to the CMSA, the Pakistani astronaut will serve as a payload specialist during the mission and return aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked with the Tiangong space station in May.

China’s astronaut Tang Hongbo will command the mission, with Wu Yi serving as the mission pilot and Ali taking on the role of payload specialist, according to the CMSA.

The crewed spaceship is scheduled to be launched at 8:18am (Beijing Time and 5:18am Pakistan Time) on Wednesday from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.

Ali is expected to spend around a week in space, conducting various experiments alongside the Chinese crew. CMSA said that during the mission, the crew will conduct around 90 experiments.

The Chinese space agency said the mission’s objectives included conducting an orbital rotation with the crew of the earlier Shenzhou-23 mission, carrying out routine operations and maintenance of the Chinese space station, and continuing space science research, including experiments involving space payloads.

The crew currently aboard the Tiangong space station is headed by 40-year-old Zhu Yangzhu, Lai Ka-ying and Zhang Zhiyuan, also 40.

Lai is Hong Kong’s first astronaut and the only woman currently aboard the space station.

After the new crew reaches the space station, Ali will return to Earth alongside Lai and Zhang.

Zhu will remain on board to complete China’s first full-year stay in space — a key test of endurance critical for future lunar and potentially deep-space ambitions.

Zhu will be accompanied for the next six-month Tiangong rotation by 51-year-old space veteran Hongbo and Yi, in his late thirties and making his first voyage to space.

‘We have already made history’

Speaking at a press briefing in Jiayuguan, Ali said he was “deeply grateful” to the Chinese government for helping “us realise our dream of going into space”.

He said he arrived at the Astronaut Centre of China a few months ago, carrying with him the hopes of 250 million Pakistani people.

Detailing his experience in China, he said what he gained had far exceeded his initial expectations. “First, I have acquired space flight skills. The management, staff and instructors at the Astronaut Centre of China have provided me with comprehensive training […] Day after day, I take another step upward.”

Pakistani astronaut Mohammad Zeeshan Ali. — Screengrab

Moreover, he continued, “I have learned the Chinese language and developed a friendship with my Chinese colleagues. Now, I can communicate with my Chinese crewmates in Chinese.”

“We trained side by side, and our friendship embodies the friendship between China and Pakistan: higher than the mountains, deeper than the oceans, sweeter than honey and as vast as outer space.”

He said he had come to deeply appreciate the meaning of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s words: “Exploring the vast universe, developing the space industry and building China into a space power is our unremitting pursuit of the space dream.”

“Now, this dream belongs to me and also belongs to Pakistan,” he said, adding that it would become a reality through the Shenzhou-24 space mission.

He said he believed that “what comes after this flight matters more than the flight itself”.

“This mission is not a finish line; it is a launch pad. And I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut, one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, Mars and beyond.”

Ali noted that 2026 marked the 75th anniversary of China-Pakistan space cooperation, as well as the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.

“Together with my Chinese crewmates, I will show that this friendship is real — not only on paper, but also in orbit.”

Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, Wu Yi and Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali gesture as they attend a press conference before the Shenzhou-24 spaceflight mission to China’s Tiangong space station, at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, near Jiuquan, Gansu province, China on November 24, 2026. —Reuters

Addressing Pakistanis, he said: “I now feel the true weight of the words of our Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, when he told me that we were about to write a new chapter in Pakistan’s history. I want to assure you that I am not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.

“To every child who is watching while I am in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams.”

In his message to his family, he said: “I want to say that I will travel farther from home than ever before. But I promise you one thing: whenever I look back at the Earth for the first time, I will always search for the light of our home before I look at anything else. No matter how far I fly, we will still share the same Moon, and I will still be looking back at the same Earth.”

He then thanked his teammates, those who supported him, his instructors, scientists, engineers, Pakistan’s space agency Suparco and CMSA.

“You are the reason that I am here today, and no matter who flies, we have already made history together,” he said.

Ali said the “two great nations of China and Pakistan have turned a pilot into an astronaut in a remarkably short span of time. Now it is time to show this great achievement, innovation and send the world a message that we work hand in hand for the peaceful utilisation of space”.

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal congratulated Ali and said the joint mission marked “the trust and iron brotherhood between Pakistan and China”.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted on X that a Pakistani astronaut going into space was a source of joy and pride for the entire nation.

Earlier in April, astronauts Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud were chosen to start training in China.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met the two in April, and congratulated them on their selection. He said the space mission was a “matter of pride for the entire nation” and further commended their “round-the-clock efforts” in achieving the milestone.

PM Shehbaz hoped that the space mission would “add new dimensions to the brotherly relationship between Pakistan and China”.

Beijing has invested heavily in its space programme in recent years — catching up with its main rival the United States — and aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030.

Pakistan is a natural partner, given the country’s decades-long, “all-weather” friendship. China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a major foreign investor.

In February 2025, Suparco and CMSA signed a cooperation agreement. Under the pact, two Pakistanis were to train in China, with one joining a mission on the Tiangong space station operated by Beijing.

China has been barred from participating in the International Space Station since 2011, when the US prohibited Nasa from collaborating with Chinese space agencies. Since then, Beijing has sought to build partnerships with other countries — including Pakistan — in its expanding space programme.

World.title: Petroleum dealers warn of another strike over unmet demands
World.content:
KARACHI: The Paki­stan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) on Monday warned that dealers would shut their petrol pumps unless the government fixes fuel prices for 30 days at a time, giving it 15 days to resolve the issue.

This is the latest of several strike calls by fuel retailers this year; on each previous occasion, the call was withdrawn after the government stepped in. This time too, dealers say, the issues they raised earlier remain unresolved.

At a joint press conference held at the Karachi Press Club, PPDA Chair­man Malik Khuda Bakhsh, Vice Chairmen Tariq Hassan and Anwar Kamal, Sindh Region President Ameer Khan, and Karachi Region President Saeed Khan said that daily changes to fuel prices were quickly draining pump owners’ working capital.

They said that if capital ran out, pumps would run dry, which could lead to a law and order situation.

They demanded that the dealers’ margin be raised immediately to 8pc of the retail price. They also claimed that refineries had cut supplies of petrol and diesel, and that one refinery had stopped supplying diesel altogether. According to the dealers, they collectively deposit Rs5.74 billion into the national exchequer every day.

Asked about earlier strike calls that were withdrawn after government intervention, Mr Bakhsh said this time was different. He said several issues raised with the government had stayed unresolved since the US-Iran war had changed market dynamics. With the war’s intensity now subsiding and prices falling, he said, the government should take notice of the association’s concerns.

The dealers’ first strike threat came in March this year, soon after the Mideast conflict broke out.

At the time, it wanted the dealers’ margin raised from 2.59pc to 8pc, after a Rs55 per litre increase in diesel and petrol prices. However, the association — then led by Abdul Sami Khan — had postponed their plans on the eve of the strike, citing the fragile situation caused by the Middle East war, which could disrupt oil supply chains.

The daily pricing system the dealers are opposing was introduced in July. At the time, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would be fixed daily because of volatility in international markets, with Ogra publishing prices on its website every day.

On July 22, the All Pakistan Petroleum Pump Owners Association — a separate body — deferred its nationwide strike call for two weeks after negotiations with the petroleum minister.

The association said they were told in writing that daily pricing would run for two weeks on a trial basis and could be reversed to monthly or fortnightly fixing if it caused significant difficulty.

However, the daily pricing regime has stayed in place since then.

In August too, the PPDA issued a 72-hour strike ultimatum, but backed down after the petroleum minister told a PPDA delegation that the government would continue the daily price-fixing mechanism, rejecting the dealers’ demand for monthly pricing. He said he could not commit to the 15-day timeline because the prime minister had the authority to make such decisions.

The next day, the Economic Coordination Committee of the federal cabinet approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers’ margins on petrol and high-speed diesel. The margin rose by Rs1.34 per litre, from Rs8.64 to Rs9.98, with effect from Sept 1. Resultantly, the PPDA then called off its strike.

But the ECC did not accept the dealers’ main demand. Official sources said that setting the margin at 8pc of the retail price would have meant about Rs26 per litre on petrol and Rs30 on diesel at prices at that time.

The latest pain point came in September, when the PM’s fuel subsidy scheme was rolled out, without much clarity on how pump owners would be compensated. However, that issue was settled through a mechanism managed by the State Bank of Pakistan.

In recent days, fuel prices have been falling. From Rs369.60 per litre on Nov 4, petrol is now down to Rs322, as of today. Mr Bakhsh said the daily price adjustments had become unbearable for dealers and warned that if the situation continued, they would face severe financial difficulties, forcing pumps to close and causing serious inconvenience to the public.

He urged the government to scrap the 24-hour pricing system and bring in a 30-day mechanism, along the same lines as refineries and oil marketing companies enjoyed.

While the authority to set petroleum prices should stay with the government, he insisted that dealers be taken into confidence before prices are deregulated, adding that no petroleum-related policy should be made without consulting them.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

World.title: Sheikh Hasina seeks to return to Bangladesh on December 16 on state carrier
World.content:
Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return home from more than two years of exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson told Reuters on Tuesday, though the government said she can only return through extradition.

It is the first time Hasina, 79, has set a specific date for her return, potentially raising political and legal tensions in a country where her party is banned and where violence has risen since she sought a new passport and other documents earlier this month.

In addition to seeking the paperwork, cancelled months after she fled to Delhi following the uprising against her, Hasina has urged the Bangladeshi government to arrange her return on flag carrier Biman Bangladesh Airlines.

“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” the spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said in a statement.

“Having exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th.” The government, however, reiterated that she can only be extradited by India, having been sentenced to death by a Bangladeshi court last year in her absence for ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising. Hasina has denied the charges from exile.

“She can only return home by extradition treaty; in handcuffs, and under strict surveillance,” Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s minister of state for foreign affairs, told Reuters.

India’s foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, the ministry said it was examining Bangladesh’s extradition request and wanted to “engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties”.

On the request to arrange a flight, Kobir said: “Bangladesh will not entertain any such delusional request”.

Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.

A Bangladeshi minister told Reuters on Sunday that Hasina would be arrested and jailed on return and that there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring her back.

The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced her out of power.

World.title: Collision between bus, truck kills 11 in UAE
World.content:
Eleven people were killed when a bus and a truck collided in Ras Al Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), authorities in the Gulf nation said on Tuesday.

“Investigations into the circumstances and causes of the accident are ongoing,” the Ministry of Interior stated on its X account.

According to the ministry, emergency teams were dispatched to the accident site immediately after receiving the report. They launched rescue and emergency response operations in coordination with ambulance services, Civil Defence and other relevant authorities.

The response also included securing the scene and managing traffic, it added.

The ministry said the findings of the investigation would be announced once it had been completed.

It also expressed condolences to the families of the deceased, praying for mercy and forgiveness for the victims and patience and strength for their loved ones.

The ministry urged the public to exercise caution, rely on official sources for information and refrain from circulating rumours or unverified reports about the accident.

It is the second major road accident to occur in the UAE this month.

On November 12, a multi-vehicle pile-up in Fujairah killed 14 people and left 30 others injured after a truck driver lost control of his vehicle and struck several other vehicles.

World.title: Tech firms soar as Huang’s return reinvigorates AI trade
World.content:
Technology firms rocketed Tuesday as Asia joined a global stock surge following the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia boss less than two weeks after stepping down over extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy.

The Silicon Valley giant’s resignation on November 12 sent shockwaves through markets and dealt a severe blow to the AI trade, which was already under pressure amid worries over profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.

His role as a fixer and visionary in an industry that has fuelled a tech revolution and a global economic boom was seen as crucial to the firm’s future as well as the AI buildout.

News of his return — announced soon after the opening bell Monday — lit a fire under equities, sending shares in Nvidia soaring an eye-watering 31.5 per cent and adding more than $900 billion to the firm’s market value.

Other Wall Street titans also enjoyed much-needed buying, pulling the Nasdaq up more than 6pc, the S&P 500 4.7pc higher and the Dow 3pc higher.

And Asia, which had started the week on the back foot, followed suit.

Taipei was the standout, blasting more than 9pc higher as chip titans TSMC and MediaTek added 10pc each, and Seoul piled on more than 6pc thanks to gains of around 8pc in market heavyweights SK hynix and Samsung.

Tokyo was lifted four percent by spikes of 14pc in Advantest, 11 percent in Tokyo Electron and 8pc in Kioxia.

Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila also joined in the fun with healthy advances.

“Jensen’s return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade,” said Saxo Markets’ Charu Chanana.

“He is not just Nvidia’s CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate.

“(His) return is particularly welcome for Asian technology stocks, many of which suffered collateral damage from Nvidia’s leadership crisis.”

And National Australia Bank’s Gavin Friend said: “The AI trade has been given a reprieve, with Huang’s reinstatement assuaging fears of any unravelling of the circular financing activity that has been a key support for the sector.”

However, analysts added that Huang’s reinstatement — which President Donald Trump said followed his own direct contacts with the company’s board — did not mean an end to probes or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for the past six months.

The company is still under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill.

Huang reportedly had a relationship with Alice Huang — who is not related — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. The group is under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia’s top-line chips.

Just this weekend, The New York Times added further details to the allegations, saying Alice Huang had been in touch with China’s top spy agency during the secret affair.

The United States on Monday added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist that bars it from purchasing advanced chips.

Oil prices continued to fall after Monday’s sharp drop that saw WTI back below $80 for the first time since August.

The latest selling was fuelled by hopes for an end to the Iran conflict as Axios reported US Vice President JD Vance met the prime minister of Qatar, which has acted as a mediator in efforts to resolve the near nine-month conflict.

World.title: Punjab holds over 60pc of senior federal posts, Senate body told
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Punjab holds 60.17 per cent of senior posts in the Federal Secretariat, a Senate subcommittee was told on Monday, prompting a sharp demand for immediate rectification and strict enforcement of the constitutional shares of all provinces in federal employment and natural resources.

The subcommittee of the Senate Standing Committee on Devolution, chaired by Senator Barrister Zamir Hussain Ghumro, said the over-representation was in violation of Article 38(g) of the Constitution, which requires shares of provinces to be maintained in federal services, corporations and bodies established under federal law.

Senators Jan Muhammad Buledi and Poonjo Bheel attended the meeting. The Establishment Division presented details of employees serving in the Federal Secretariat in Basic Pay Scales (BPS) 18-22, categorised by domicile for 2025-26.

Senator Ghumro observed that provincial shares must be strictly maintained in all ministries and departments. Expressing concern over the 60.17pc representation of Punjab in BPS 18-22, he stressed the need for equitable representation of the four provinces, particularly Sindh and Balochistan in the federal jobs.

Subcommittee demands strict enforcement of constitutional shares of four provinces in federal employment, natural resources

“This rectification must be made immediately,” he said. He said the rural-urban divide of Sindh was against Article 38(g), which envisages shares of provinces, and directed that the divide be done away with and only the share of the whole province, like other provinces, be maintained.

The convener expressed displeasure over the failure of the Establishment Division to submit a rectification plan for Sindh, as directed in earlier meetings.

The subcommittee reiterated its directions to submit a comprehensive rectification plan, including for posts in BPS 1-15, within two weeks and initiate the appointment process forthwith.

He also expressed concern over s designed to favour specific individuals and stressed that the recruitment process must remain transparent, impartial and free from nepotism or individual bias, ensuring shares of provinces.

The subcommittee directed the Federal Public Service Commission (FPSC) to provide details of vacant posts and appointments from Sindh and Balochistan, while ensuring strict adherence to the prescribed provincial shares.

The Establishment Division informed the committee that 5,136 posts in BPS 1-15 had recently been advertised for Balochistan to address its employment needs, and apprised it of various exemptions granted by the federal cabinet to facilitate applicants from Balochistan and its plan to create 200,000 employment opportunities for the province.

The convener emphasised that recruitment arrangements must ensure fair opportunities for candidates from deserving households and regions. The Establishment Division assured the committee that rectification shall be taken up and the process for posts of Sindh’s share shall be initiated through s.

‘Not a penny’ given to provinces The subcommittee also reviewed compliance by the petroleum ministry regarding Article 172(3) of the Constitution, which provides for joint and equal ownership of mineral oil and natural gas by the federal government and the respective provincial governments.

The convener observed that despite the passage of 16 years since the 18th Constitutional Amendment, the provision regarding joint and equal ownership and sharing of resources had not been implemented in letter and spirit.

He said that details of profits earned by only four companies — PPL, OGDCL, POL and one other — after the 18th Amendment amounted to Rs3.6 trillion, excluding SSGC, Sui Northern and other corporations, and “not a single penny has been paid to the provinces”.

Expressing serious concern over the situation, Senator Ghumro termed the situation a violation of the Constitution and said that continued deprivation of provinces from their legitimate financial share was unacceptable.

He said the total amount may exceed Rs6 trillion when details of other companies were added, as an effective mechanism for sharing profits had not been established.

The provinces, he said, are constitutionally entitled to an equal share in revenues generated from oil and gas resources produced within their territories.

The subcommittee directed the petroleum ministry to formulate a comprehensive mechanism for sharing profits equally between the federal government and the respective provincial governments, place the matter before the federal cabinet for approval on an urgent basis, and share the relevant summary with the subcommittee.

He warned that failure to comply could lead to referring the matter to auditing authorities.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

World.title: Challan submitted in Hina Javed murder case
World.content:
RAWALPINDI: Police have submitted challan to the District Prosecution Branch in the murder case of Hina Javed after completing the investigation and incorporating forensic reports into the case record.

The district prosecutor has received the challan and initiated scrutiny.

Sources said it could not be submitted on Saturday due to unavailability of the district prosecutor.

According to sources privy to the development, the initial investigation found no incriminating evidence against the victim’s husband.

Consequently, his name has been placed in Column No II of the challan, leaving the matter to the discretion of the court.

Sources in the Prosecution Branch said if any legal deficiencies or shortcomings were identified during scrutiny, the challan could be returned to the police for rectification.

After completion of the scrutiny process, it will be presented before the court of the district and sessions judge.

Hina Javed, a 45-year-old married woman, was murdered at her residence on August 20.

The murder case has been registered with Civil Lines police station.

Meanwhile, the victim’s family has already expressed a lack of confidence in the police investigation, raising concerns about the manner in which the case has been investigated.

Published in Dawn, November 24th, 2026

World.title: Used phone import surge hits industry
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Imports of used smartphones surged from 1,434 units in July to 98,383 in October, as the duty gap between locally manufactured phones and imports narrowed.

The country recorded 150,133 arrivals, including 51,750 new smartphones valued at $71.7 million in October, compared with 18,431 smartphones valued at $17.8m in July.

The Pakistan Mobile Phone Manufacturers Associ­ation (PMPMA), in a letter, has raised concerns with the Ministry of Industries and Production and the FBR about the development, noting that the most alarming issue is the sharp increase in used smartphone imports. A delegation from the association is scheduled to meet with authorities in the capital in the coming days to discuss the matter.

The association stresses that this is having a clearly negative impact on local smartphone assembly as production fell from 906,711 units in July to 752,870 units in October.

PMPMA Chairman Abdul Rehman told Dawn on Monday that the surge in CBU imports is driven by two factors: narrowed import tariff gaps, which have fuelled the ‘khepia’ business, and a downward revision in FBR taxes on imported phone sets.

He explained that the tariff gap between completely built-up smartphones and CKD kits for locally assembled smartphones has narrowed sharply, to around 11pc for a $100 phone and 14pc for a $200 phone.

“The $100-$200 category is the largest-selling phone segment, and the 11pc and 14pc gap has nearly disappeared as bulk importers use methods such as under-invoicing, leaving little room for the country’s regulated manufacturers,” he said.

Mr Rehman added that another factor driving the influx of used phones was a downward revision in FBR valuations under the Device Identification, Registration and Blocking System (DIRBS), allowing cheap imported smartphones to be registered with the PTA. Imported completely built-up units (CBUs) have captured 41.8pc of the country’s smartphone market in just a few months.

The association has said that the mobile manufacturing industry has complained about reverse cascading for the past three years, making it impossible to localise parts such as chargers, batteries, cables, and motherboard assemblies.

A charger can currently be imported duty-free as part of a CKD kit, but the cumulative duty on importing its raw materials and subcomponents is nearly 20pc.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
