World.title: Ex-OpenAI engineer vibecoded better bugs to record meetings – court filing
World.content:
BEHIND THE BUG? A man described as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device had been placed at a conference room in OpenAI offices, in a still image from surveillance video included in a charging document after US federal agents the man and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device, in San Francisco, California, USA, October 5, 2026.

Federal prosecutors are seeking to prevent ex-OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan from being released prior to his trial on a charge of illegally intercepting conversations

MANILA, Philippines – Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested in October and accused of planting a hidden bug to record office conversations, was said to have recorded a number of meetings including one held with foreign government representatives, federal prosecutors said in a court filing.

The New York Times reported on Monday, November 23, that Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and a permanent US resident, was charged with one count of illegally intercepting conversations.

Alfozan pleaded not guilty, and a hearing for his release is scheduled for November 24. He has also asked the federal judge to allow him to be released on a $1-million bond. Prosecutors opposed Alfozan’s request to be released from jail before his trial begins in January.

Making better bugs

Prosecutors said Alfozan used OpenAI’s Codex vibecoding application to improve his hidden recording device by adding voice-detection and using Codex to organize the recordings in Dropbox. The Codex account was in his wife’s name, though she has not been accused of wrongdoing.

OpenAI said many of the recordings kept by Alfozan either held confidential trade secrets, such as meetings with OpenAI customers, or were identified as having material protected by attorney-client privilege.

Prosecutors did not say in the filing that Alfozan had shared the recordings. “What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation.”

‘Less serious’ than claimed?

David Rizk, Alfozan’s lawyer, argued in a filing last week that the case was less serious than prosecutors suggested.

Rizk called Alfozan “an overly curious tinkerer,” and said the majority of recordings on Alfozan’s computer “apparently contain just random noise and silence.”

Prosecutors, for their part, outlined the timeline of the recordings, which spanned 15 folders dated September 8 to 28. It also had recordings of meetings held on 12 days in an executive conference room, with one file titled “1200-sovereign-bilateral-briefing-sep22.” The filing did not identify any foreign government.

Prosecutors added that Alfozan took photos of the printings of a confidential term sheet for a “strategic partnership” between OpenAI and another company early on October 5. That same day, a hidden camera recorded him checking behind the television where OpenAI’s security team previously found the planted listening device.

Alfozan was also said to have had contact with Saudi officials, according to the filing.

On October 6, a member of the Saudi royal family sent Alfozan a link to Echelon, a Riyadh-based AI company. Alfozan was asked, “Time to move back to KSA and join us?” Alfozan replied that he might return “after the IPO” of OpenAI, which is slated for next year.

He apparently spoke with the Saudi official through WhatsApp for 16 minutes and exchanged messages with Saudi communications ministry officials, including the minister in August, and September.

Prosecutors argued the timing of his Saudi discussions and his travel plans “appears to match the timing of his efforts to record OpenAI meetings.”

Alfozan’s lawyers said the trip was planned for paternity leave, as his wife was pregnant.

Magistrate Judge Alex Tse, who rejected the original bid for Alfozan’s release, will preside the hearing on Tuesday.

Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release if he is convicted in the January trial. .– Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Angel Ignacio, new Maharlika Investment president and CEO?
World.content:
The former finance undersecretary takes the reins of a young sovereign wealth fund with billions still sleeping in the coffers and much left to prove

MANILA, Philippines – A former stockbroker, board director, and longtime government official will now take charge of the Philippines’ first sovereign wealth fund.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has appointed Ma. Angela “Angel” Ignacio as the next president and chief executive officer of the Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC).

Ignacio succeeds Rafael “Joel” Consing Jr., whose three-year term ended on Monday, November 23. The appointment hardly comes as a surprise, with Ignacio’s name having made the rounds for months as Consing’s likely successor.

Prior to joining Maharlika, Ignacio headed the Department of Finance’s (DOF) Government Corporations and Investments Group, working closely with Finance Secretary Frederick Go, who also chairs MIC’s board.

All three previously worked at the now-defunct Office of the Special Assistant to the President for Investment and Economic Affairs, which Go headed before moving to the DOF. Ignacio served as an undersecretary, while Consing was its executive director before taking the top job at Maharlika.

Ignacio’s time in government spans several administrations. From 2011 to 2016, she served as a commissioner of the Governance Commission for Government-Owned or -Controlled Corporations (GOCC) under the Aquino administration. She also worked as a consultant for the World Bank and Asian Development Bank.

In the boardroom, Ignacio served as an independent director of Ayala Land and sat on the board of the state-owned United Coconut Planters Bank.

What’s next for Maharlika’s sleeping billions?

Ignacio said the President’s directive was to “make sure that Maharlika does what it was intended to do under the law.”

Recall that the sovereign wealth fund’s creation in 2023 drew a firestorm of criticism from economists and governance experts, who questioned its purpose in a country with little fiscal space or windfall revenues, its vulnerability to political meddling, and the wisdom of sourcing its start-up capital from state-owned banks.

Over the next 18 months, Ignacio intends to deploy more capital into power, energy, and infrastructure. She is also looking at opportunities in artificial intelligence, food security, and tourism.

Ignacio inherits a fund that has already assembled a team of around 60 professionals and established its investment policies and risk management procedures, but has been slow to put its capital to work. As of end-September, Maharlika had deployed only P24.7 billion and still held P53.67 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

Maharlika’s largest deployment under Consing was a P15-billion working capital loan to Petron Corporation, while its much-touted P19.7-billion deal that would have secured board seats in the country’s power grid operator was shelved. Only three days before Consing’s departure did Maharlika announce another strategic investment of up to P900 million in Tubig Pilipinas. – Rappler.com

World.title: Marcos appoints Lacanilao as DOTr usec, Noreen San Luis as LTO chief
World.content:
The appointment of Noreen San Luis and Markus Lacanilao comes after Vince Dizon’s return as transportation secretary

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Land Transportation Office (LTO) chief Markus Lacanilao as undersecretary of the Department of Transportation (DOTr), Malacañang confirmed on Tuesday, November 24.

Lacanilao will also serve as administrator of the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), Palace Press Officer Claire Castro announced in a news briefing on Tuesday.

Lacanilao led the LTO for just over a year. Prior to this stint, he served as a special envoy for transnational crime and played a key role in bringing former president Rodrigo Duterte to the International Criminal Court.

Noreen Bernadette San Luis will succeed Lacanilao as the new LTO chief.

San Luis, a lawyer and registered nurse, brings extensive agency experience to the role. She served as LTO regional director for the Bicol Region from 2012 to 2020, and for Calabarzon from 2020 to 2023.

In the private sector, San Luis worked for Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation’s North Luzon Expressway as vice president for road safety and quality, environment, safety, and health.

In August 2026, Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo appointed San Luis as city administrator.

Previous LTO chiefs Vigor Mendoza II and Teofilo Guadiz III both faced suspension due to their roles in allowing the continued use of an outdated IT system, resulting in motorists being charged an additional P13.3 billion in fees.

Jorjette Aquino was also appointed as the new general manager of the Philippine National Railways. She previously served as an undersecretary of the Presidential Communications Office.

The appointment of San Luis, Aquino, and Lacanilao comes after Vince Dizon’s return as transportation secretary.

In Dizon’s return as DOTr secretary, he was mandated to shorten queues at the LTO and get rid of fixers, Presidential Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano said. – Rappler.com

World.title: BARMM has a new parliament, but the guns remain
World.content:
MAJESTIC. The Grand Mosque stands in Cotabato City, the regional center of the Bangsamoro region, serving as a cornerstone of Islamic life in Mindanao and a symbol of the region’s aspirations for peace and stability under autonomous governance.

The peace process in the Mindanao region remains unfinished, with thousands of MILF combatants and weapons still awaiting full decommissioning

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – The guns did not go silent in the Bangsamoro region, where rival factions of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), feuding political clans, and competing illicit economic interests threaten to undermine a fragile peace just as a newly elected parliament took office.

The September 14 parliamentary elections brought some of these fault lines into the open, with deadly clashes between supporters of the rival Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), an independent conflict monitor said.

The rivalry runs deep within the MILF. The BFP is led by former MILF military chief and now Bangsamoro Chief Minister Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua, while the UBJP is the Front’s official political party.

Armed clashes and mob violence involving supporters of the two parties erupted during and after election day. One riot in Barangay Bagua II, Cotabato City, left three people dead on September 14.

For ACLED, the violence was a warning about the fragility of the predominantly Muslim region’s fledgling institutions. The peace process remains unfinished, with thousands of MILF combatants and weapons still awaiting full decommissioning.

“Such factionalist violence has resurfaced the urgency of completing the decommissioning process meant to get the MILF to give up its full arsenal of weapons. Coupled with intermittent political violence from other sources, such an easy recourse to arms will continue to put the region on edge,” Tomas Buenaventura, ACLED Asia-Pacific analyst, noted in a report.

The watchdog said the rivalry between the BFP and UBJP, which is led by MILF chairman and former Bangsamoro interim chief minister Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim, could subside as both camps adjust to parliamentary politics, making further armed confrontations unlikely for now. Both parties have signaled a common interest in the success of the Bangsamoro government and the peace process.

Yet the electoral rivalry is only one part of a more troubling security picture. Violence persisted across the region in October, fueled by disputes that extended beyond party politics and reached into the longstanding rivalries and illicit economies that have made peace difficult to secure.

The Critical Events Monitoring System (CEMS) of a peacebuilding monitor, Climate Conflict Action Asia (CCAA), recorded 79 conflict incidents and 47 deaths in October, compared with 74 incidents and 34 deaths in September.

The incidents included deadly clashes, ambushes and shootings across several towns. Many were driven by personal grudges, clan feuds and competition over illicit economic activities, including the illegal drug trade, gunrunning, and cigarette smuggling.

CCAA recorded 16 incidents involving personal grudges and clan feuding in October, mostly concentrated in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Sur.

In Sultan sa Barongis, Maguindanao del Sur, fighting that began on September 30 between members of an MILF base command and an armed group linked to criminal activities continued until a temporary ceasefire took effect in the third week of October. The clashes displaced around 1,100 households, killed one person, and wounded 10 others.

In neighboring Ampatuan town, a longstanding clan feud erupted into a firefight on October 15, displacing around 40 families.

Election-related tensions also spilled into clan violence. In Taraka, Lanao del Sur, a shooting was carried out on October 3, in retaliation for the killing of an individual by two UBJP supporters during the parliamentary elections, CCAA said.

Attacks on local officials also continued despite the postponement of the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections. Several shootings targeting village officials in Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte were reportedly linked to political rivalries and preparations for the 2028 elections.

Violence also affected indigenous communities. CCAA reported that a Teduray leader who was a barangay councillor in Datu Hoffer Ampatuan was shot dead on October 17, followed a day later by the shooting of two other Teduray people in Datu Unsay.

The attacks came despite the formal recognition of the Teduray and Lambangian ancestral domain earlier in October. The watchdog said indigenous communities, particularly women and children, continued to face heightened vulnerabilities, including rising reports of gender-based violence.

Competition over illicit economic activities also fueled deadly confrontations. Four people were killed in an ambush in Datu Anggal Midtimbang on October 26 in an incident allegedly linked to the illegal gun trade.

In Cotabato City, two Coast Guard personnel were killed and another wounded in an October 22 ambush involving armed men reportedly linked to cigarette smuggling. Three more people were killed in a shooting the following day in Timako Hill, although CCAA said the incidents were unrelated.

Based on ACLED’s count, Maguindanao del Sur recorded the highest number of political violence incidents in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) from January 1 to October 30, with 47 incidents.

Maguindanao del Norte ranked second with 31 incidents, followed by Lanao del Sur with 21, the Special Geographic Area with 19, and Basilan with 11.

The watchdog also identified persistent threats from the Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters and Islamic State-inspired Dawlah Islamiyah groups, although their activities did not significantly disrupt the September elections.

CCAA warned that the withdrawal of additional security forces deployed for the elections had exposed the limits of temporary security measures, allowing longstanding rivalries and illicit economic activities to continue driving armed confrontations.

The election of Macacua as chief minister comes at a critical juncture for the region, with the new parliament facing the challenge of advancing autonomy and development amid a fragile security environment.

ACLED said the immediate tensions between the BFP and UBJP could give way to a period of détente, but the continued circulation of MILF weapons and unresolved factional divisions remain concerns.

CCAA said the new regional leadership and the MILF must be held accountable for addressing persistent violence, governance issues and the incomplete decommissioning of combatants if the Bangsamoro is to achieve lasting peace and inclusive governance. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] Boardroom gymnastics, retail stakes: Unpacking the Rockwell deal
World.content:
FPH owes investors proof that nearly P16 billion in cash beats keeping a profitable property arm, just as Rockwell’s minorities deserve full clarity before deciding whether to stay put or cash out

Too often, financial reporting treats corporate dealmaking like a spectator sport for billionaires — fixating on which tycoon is buying control, which conglomerate is cashing out, and how much changes hands at the top.

Lost in the noise is what these corporate intramurals mean for the thousands of ordinary public investors whose capital sustains market valuations.

First Philippine Holdings’ (FPH) proposed sale of its controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Crème Investment Corporation for nearly P16 billion is a textbook case.

Strip away the prominent surnames, and two practical questions remain for everyday shareholders on both sides: Are FPH investors getting fair value for surrendering a profitable business, and will Rockwell’s minorities get enough hard facts to make an informed choice?

Signed on November 13, the deal carries an amended 11-month closing deadline measured from signing, down from 12 months, and awaits Philippine Competition Commission approval plus a mandatory tender offer for Rockwell’s remaining public shares. A signed agreement is only the opening act, not a finished sale.

For small investors reading the fine print, the headline numbers require unpacking. The P15.916-billion price tag covers P15.888 billion for 5.296 billion common shares at P3 apiece, plus P27.5 million for 2.75 billion preferred shares at P0.01 each.

While headlines highlight a 90.74% combined stake, measuring FPH’s common shares against Rockwell’s 6.117 billion outstanding common shares puts its common equity holding at roughly 86.58%. The combined percentage includes preferred stock; it is not the common-share stake being sold.

Equally crucial is where the money goes. Upon closing, the P15.916 billion gross consideration goes to FPH, not Rockwell. Because this is a secondary sale of existing stock rather than a capital raise, Rockwell receives zero fresh cash to build towers, pay down debt, or fund dividends. Minorities weighing whether to stay invested must recognize that the sale itself adds no cash to Rockwell’s balance sheet.

On the FPH side, small shareholders must temper expectations. Dividing P15.916 billion by FPH’s 424.5 million outstanding common shares equates to roughly P37.49 per share.

That merely measures deal scale — not a guaranteed special dividend or an automatic share-price jump. Taxes, transaction fees, and carrying value will ultimately dictate what hits the bottom line.

What public investors deserve

FPH did take visible steps to validate the P3 sale price. Adviser BDO Capital & Investment Corporation valued Rockwell’s common shares between P2.47 and P3.09 — putting the price near the top of the range — while independent directors, external counsel, and buyer adviser AlphaPrimus Advisors were brought in.

Yet governance checklists cannot replace transparent math. Public investors deserve to see how that valuation treated project spending, borrowing costs, cash collections, and recurring commercial income — and whether it included a control premium rather than pricing the block like an illiquid minority stake.

Rockwell’s latest results make this scrutiny even more urgent. FPH is not unloading a troubled unit: nine-month revenue climbed to P19.317 billion from P14.996 billion a year earlier, lifting profit attributable to parent shareholders by roughly 21.5% to P3.788 billion from P3.117 billion.

Though third-quarter attributable profit dipped about 10.7% to P1.076 billion from P1.205 billion — as nine-month non-operating expenses rose to P2.389 billion from P1.359 billion — one softer quarter hardly invalidates Rockwell’s long-term case.

At P3 per share, the deal values Rockwell at roughly 3.4 times trailing 12-month earnings of P0.88 per share. On paper, 3.4 times looks like a bargain for the buyer. While property accounting profits depend heavily on construction progress, revenue recognition, and financing costs — meaning net income rarely equals free cash — management must explain why such a modest multiple is fair to sellers.

Broker commentary underscores this tug-of-war between instant cash and lost income. Online trading platform COL Financial noted that the P15.9-billion consideration represents a 99% premium over its estimated net asset value for FPH’s Rockwell stake, raising its fair-value estimate for FPH by 11.8%. Yet COL also estimated that Rockwell accounts for roughly 25% of FPH’s net income. Unlocking asset value today leaves a sizable earnings hole tomorrow.

Bar of accountability

FPH says the proceeds will fund energy, infrastructure, and other growth ventures. Rotating capital out of mature assets makes sense, provided retail investors are told the recurring profits sacrificed, net cash left after costs, and expected returns from replacement projects — with any disposal gain reported separately from core earnings.

Meanwhile, Rockwell’s small shareholders face a pivotal choice once formal tender documents arrive. Beyond payment timelines and funding certainty, they must scrutinize the buyer’s plans. The tender price and complete terms still require confirmation. A change in control does not automatically trigger delisting, but tender acceptances could reduce public ownership below the PSE’s 10% minimum. Rockwell’s reported free float was 13.05% before the announcement. Anyone staying invested must weigh potential shifts in governance, debt appetite, and trading liquidity.

Finally, FPH’s disclosure that certain directors of the seller and buyer are related within the fourth civil degree raises the bar for accountability. Family ties do not prove wrongdoing, but detailing independent board vetting and director abstentions is essential if small investors are to trust the process.

Rockwell’s change-in-control filing left the buyer’s material relationships and directors’ transaction interests marked “to follow.” Those disclosures need completion before minorities decide whether to tender.

Public markets thrive only when everyday shareholders are treated as true stakeholders rather than passive bystanders to boardroom deals. FPH owes investors proof that nearly P16 billion in cash beats keeping a profitable property arm, just as Rockwell’s minorities deserve full clarity before deciding whether to stay put or cash out.

This analysis draws from FPH’s November 16 amended transaction disclosure, Rockwell’s ownership disclosure, its September 2026 quarterly financial report, and COL Financial’s November 13 research note. Ownership percentages, per-share proceeds, earnings growth, and the earnings multiple are our calculations; COL’s valuation and contribution estimates remain explicitly attributed.

I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

World.title: The Sky Cable paradox: From ABS-CBN’s second business to its burden
World.content:
Can Sky Cable become financially strong enough to stop depending on the company it was supposed to help?

ABS-CBN spent decades building Sky Cable into a second business that could make money outside of free television. It bought smaller cable companies, expanded into home internet and satellite TV, and borrowed billions of pesos to pay for that growth. Those choices made sense at the time, but some of the technologies Sky bet on eventually fell behind newer rivals and changing viewer habits. The bank loans, however, never went away. What started as a plan to make ABS-CBN stronger turned into another heavy financial burden for a parent company already struggling to recover from losing its free TV franchise.

Open ABS-CBN’s latest financial report and two main businesses stand out. One makes TV shows, movies, music, and live concerts. The other sells cable TV and home internet subscriptions. Both lost money in the first nine months of 2026, though they face very different problems. Content Production and Distribution—the business behind Batang Quiapo, It’s Showtime, BINI, and Star Cinema—brought in nearly P9 billion in sales, making up more than 85% of ABS-CBN’s total revenue. Still, its costs were higher than its sales, leaving it with a loss of about P2 billion. Meanwhile, the Cable TV and Broadband business—run mainly through Sky Cable Corporation and its subsidiaries—brought in only around P1.6 billion, down 41% from the same period in 2025, while its loss grew to more than P900 million. Source: ABS-CBN’s September 2026 quarterly disclosure.

Sky Cable’s problems go beyond losing subscribers and money. Between 2023 and 2025, ABS-CBN reduced the recorded the value of its Cable and Broadband business by more than P13 billion because those investments were no longer expected to earn what the company originally projected. Meanwhile, Sky Cable’s bank loans still had to be paid back, even as the business meant to pay them grew smaller.

Why Sky made sense

When ABS-CBN’s Channel 2 was the Philippines’ leading free TV network, advertising paid for much of its operations. But ad money rises and falls with the economy since companies spend more when business is good and cut their ad budgets during hard times. Cable television offered something steadier: households paid monthly subscription fees, providing a more regular source of income. Sky Cable also gave ABS-CBN a way to air its own channels, including ANC, Cinema One, Myx, and Lifestyle Network, later renamed Metro.

The Lopez group grew Sky by merging it with other cable companies, including Home Cable in 2004, Destiny Cable, Solid Broadband, and UNI Cable TV in 2012, and internet provider Tri-Isys in 2017. Each acquisition expanded Sky Cable’s reach, but also meant taking on more cables, equipment, and facilities that needed to be maintained and eventually replaced. Sky Cable brought in foreign money as well. Singapore’s STT Communications invested through Sampaquita Communications under deals that later gave it 40% of Sky’s financial returns, while ABS-CBN and related Lopez companies kept the larger share. The arrangements used Philippine Depositary Receipts or PDRs, financial certificates that gave the foreign investor a right to profits linked to shares without directly owning the shares themselves. (READ: FAST FACTS: Other businesses of ABS-CBN)

Sky Cable also borrowed heavily from Philippine banks. Its financial reports list loans from BPI, Security Bank, RCBC, BDO, and other lenders over the years. In 2018 alone, Sky signed a P2-billion BDO loan to finance new equipment and fund projects, plus a separate P762 million loan to pay off an older obligation of Pilipino Cable Corporation, the operator of Home Cable. So, some loans paid for new growth, while other loans simply replaced old debts.

Back then, borrowing was a normal and reasonable way to finance a growing cable business. Laying cables and setting up equipment required huge amounts upfront, while monthly subscription payments trickled in month after month. That business model worked as long as subscribers kept paying long enough for Sky Cable to recover its investment, cover expenses, and pay off the banks. But that plan only worked if Sky Cable’s technology stayed competitive and its subscribers stayed loyal.

Much of Sky Cable’s growth depended on three big technology bets. First, it used its existing cable TV lines to deliver home internet. Instead of replacing every single wire, Sky Cable upgraded parts of the system with fiber-optic lines while keeping older copper-based coaxial cables for the final connection into many homes. Known as “hybrid” network, this was a faster and cheaper way to offer home internet than building a brand new network from scratch.

Second, SkyDirect used satellite dishes to reach households beyond Sky Cable’s wired network. That made sense in an archipelago like the Philippines where running physical cables to every town was far too expensive. This was also one of Sky Cable’s most promising growth businesses. SkyDirect had about one million subscribers in January 2019, barely three years after it was launched, according to ABS-CBN president Carlo Katigbak. By June 2020, Sky reported 1.5 million subscribers nationwide, including families in remote communities beyond the reach of regular TV signals. Satellite technology allowed Sky Cable enter those areas without laying costly cables across islands and provinces.

Play Video

Third, Sky Cable invested in TV set-top boxes that gave subscribers more ways to watch cable channels and, later, streaming apps. By 2019, ABS-CBN’s Cable and Broadband business generated nearly P10 billion in annual revenue and reported a modest profit. The bets seemed to be paying off.

Four major blows

Between 2020 and 2024, four major setbacks derailed Sky Cable’s growth:

The June 30, 2020 NTC shutdown of SkyDirect, which ended a fast-growing satellite TV business. The rise of online streaming, which reduced demand for traditional cable subscriptions. The race to bring fiber internet directly into homes, which exposed the limits of Sky Cable’s older network. The canceled P6.75-billion sale to PLDT, which left ABS-CBN with a business it had already prepared to sell.

The shutdown of SkyDirect. On May 5, 2020, the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) ordered ABS-CBN’s free TV and radio stations off the air after its broadcast franchise expired. On June 30, the regulator issued another order shutting SkyDirect and ABS-CBN TVplus, citing the expiration of the permits they operated under.

Screenshot from ABS-CBN X posted on June 30, 2020

For Sky Cable, the shutdown was particularly damaging because SkyDirect was still attracting subscribers fast. From one million subscribers in January 2019, it had jumped to 1.5 million by June 2020. These were households paying monthly bills, or buying prepaid credits, to watch via satellite dishes. The service was especially useful in provincial areas where laying cable lines would have cost too much. Sky Cable had found a smart way to grow beyond the towns and cities covered by its existing wires, and that business was still booming when the government ordered it to stop. The order also required Sky Cable to refund unused prepaid credits, advance payments, and deposits.

The first two weakened Sky Cable’s TV business. The third showed the high cost of relying on an older broadband network while rivals built newer ones. The fourth deprived ABS-CBN of an opportunity to sell the company and use the proceeds for its other pressing financial needs.

The shutdown deprived Sky Cable of another major income source for ABS-CBN, and a fast-growing subscription business before its full commercial potential could be realized.

The shift to streaming. Netflix, YouTube, and other online apps offered programs that viewers could watch whenever, wherever they wanted, without paying for a traditional cable package. Sky Cable tried to fight back by launching SKY EVO in 2021, an Android-based TV box combining cable channels with streaming apps. But smart TVs, smartphones, and tablets were already letting people stream online entertainment without needing a cable subscription at all. SKY EVO was an attempt to adapt, but it could not stop the massive shift in viewing habits. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

The race for home internet. As cable TV subscribers left, Sky Cable needed broadband to become a stronger business. But rivals PLDT, Globe, and Converge ICT were pouring billions into “fiber-to-the-home” networks, which run pure fiber optic cables straight into customers houses and offices. Sky Cable’s older hybrid network could deliver fast download speeds, but traditional cable wires generally had less capacity for uploads, such as sending large files or joining video calls, and could slow down when too many neighbors went online at once.

These differences became more obvious during the pandemic, when families relied on home internet for work, online classes, video meetings, gaming, and streaming. Pure fiber networks offered much better upload speeds and room to handle heavy traffic. Sky Cable had made a technology bet that no longer fit the market. Extending the life of its older cable wires had saved money at first, but maintaining and upgrading that aging system grew more expensive just as rivals were building faster, brand new fiber networks. Sky Cable’s technology had not stopped working, but its earlier cost savings were no longer enough to keep up.

The aborted PLDT exit. In March 2023, ABS-CBN and other Sky shareholders agreed to sell the whole company to PLDT for P6.75 billion. The Philippine Competition Commission cleared the transaction in January 2024. Sky had already announced plans to discontinue cable television in February and focus strictly on broadband. Before that happened, however, both sides called off the deal because certain conditions had not been met and they could not agree on revised terms. Sky Cable kept running its cable TV service, which ABS-CBN remained responsible for a business it had already prepared to hand over.

The loans did not disappear

The financial consequences from these setbacks became harder and harder to handle. Sky Cable was losing subscribers and revenue, yet its bank loans still had to be paid.

Sky Cable’s money problems appeared in two ways: It was losing money from operations, and some of the businesses and equipment it had acquired were worth less than the amounts recorded in its books. When a company buys another business, for example, it may pay extra because it expects future income from customers and a well-known brand. Accountants call this additional value goodwill. If the expected future income are no longer realistic, the company must slash that recovered value.

In 2023, ABS-CBN reduced Sky’s recorded goodwill by about P4.5 billion and lowered the value of customer accounts and other non-physical assets by nearly P1.9 billion. More cuts followed for equipment and other property. Between 2023 and 2025, the Cable and Broadband business recorded over P13 billion in these value reductions, known as impairment charges. They were accounting losses rather than cash spent during those years, but they showed that Sky Cable’s past investments would never deliver the returns ABS-CBN once expected.

The decline in the business was equally striking.

Period Cable and Broadband revenue Profit or loss Full year 2019 P9.8 billion P172 million profit Full year 2023 P7.2 billion P7.1 billion loss Full year 2024 P5.4 billion P4.3 billion loss Full year 2025 P3.3 billion P776 million loss First 9 months of 2026 P1.6 billion P923 million loss

Sources: ABS-CBN annual reports and September 2026 quarterly disclosures. The massive losses in 2023 and 2024 included major cuts in asset values.

Annual revenue fell by roughly two-thirds between 2019 and 2025. Even after slashing costs, Sky Cable kept losing money.

Its debts became another major headache. By the end of 2023, Sky owed about P4.5 billion in bank loans. Because its finances were weakening, Sky Cable struggled to meet strict conditions written into those loan agreements. As a result, those loans had to be listed as short-term obligations in its financial reports, meaning the Sky Cable no longer had the automatic right to put off payments. That did not necessarily mean the banks were demanding immediate payment, but it showed how serious Sky’s borrowing problem had become.

By the end of 2025, Sky had approximately P9 billion in assets but owed around P10 billion in bank loans, unpaid bills, and other debts, meaning what it owed was roughly P1 billion more than everything it owed. ABS-CBN itself was also struggling. By September 2026, the group had nearly P12 billion in total loans and had racked up around P750 million in interest and related borrowing costs over nine months. Sky Cable was part of that debt load, while ABS-CBN’s content business was also losing money. Its auditors warned that the group’s continuing losses and money pressures created serious doubt about whether it could keep operating and paying its bills.

More time to pay, but fewer customers

In July 2024, Sky Cable made a major change in its technology strategy. Instead of spending heavily to upgrade its aging cable network, it signed a deal to use Converge ICT’s fiber optic infrastructure in Metro Manila. Converge was one of the very rivals Sky Cable had been fighting for broadband customers. Under the deal, Sky Cable could use Converge’s network to offer modern fiber connections to its own subscribers, avoiding the full cost of building those connections itself. (READ: Why Converge thinks it’s the next big thing in telco)

SCALING UP. Converge CEO and co-founder Dennis Anthony Uy speaks at the launch of the DTI AI and Scale-up Center.

The partnership gave Sky Cable a practical way to stay in the game, yet it also showed how much its strategy had changed. A company that spent decades building and upgrading its own cable network was now relying on a competitor’s infrastructure to give customers what they wanted.

Screenshot from Sky Cable Corp. statement on July 22, 2024.

Sky also needed breathing room from its banks. In February 2025, BDO, BPI, RCBC, and Security Bank agreed to change the repayment terms of P4.25 billion in loans, pushing some deadlines as far as 2032. The deal gave Sky Cable more time to pay and eased some of the financial conditions it had to meet. But the loans were not forgiven.

The debt deal produced an unusual result in Sky Cable’s 2025 financial report: an accounting gain of about P1.4 billion, even though no actual cash entered Sky Cable’s bank account. That gain came from how accountants recalculated the value of the loans after their terms changed. It helped shrink Sky’s reported loss for 2025, but the business still had to pay back every peso under the new schedule.

What the new investors wanted protected

The financial troubles of Sky Cable came up again when ABS-CBN brought in new investors in 2026. In August, the media company announced a P6 billion investment deal: P3.5 billion from I&C Holdings, P2.2 billion from three Lopez family investment companies, and P300 million from Lopez Inc. The fresh cash is meant to support operations, pay overdue bills, and cut down bank debt.

But I&C, the largest new investor, wanted protection from some of ABS-CBN’s existing money troubles. Under the agreement, ABS-CBN promised to pay for any Sky Cable worker separation costs above ₱402 million, along with certain other Sky-related bills. I&C also required that any updates to ABS-CBN’s loans with BPI and UnionBank leave the network with terms at least as good as before. Simply put, the new investor wanted a guarantee that renegotiating those bank loans wouldn’t leave ABS-CBN in a worse financial spot.

On top of that, I&C demanded protection from other identified losses worth over P3 billion. The message was unmistakable: I&C was ready to invest, but only with strict guardrails against ABS-CBN’s existing risks. Even so, those guardrails didn’t erase Sky’s debts, and they didn’t mean ABS-CBN was planning to sell or close Sky down.

That detail matters. I&C was not refusing to touch any risk connected to Sky Cable, and the P402-million threshold was not a cap on everything ABS-CBN might still have to spend on the subsidiary. Rather, the investor wanted legal protection from specific liabilities. In business, this is known as ring-fencing: drawing clear boundaries around certain financial risks so they do not automatically become an unlimited obligation for the new investor.

For ABS-CBN, this meant Sky’s financial problems were no longer just a matter of managing a troubled subsidiary. They had become a key bargaining chip in bringing fresh money into the parent company. The investment deal did not establish that Sky would be sold, closed, or separated from ABS-CBN, but it showed that Sky’s lingering debts were serious enough for a new investor to demand protection.

Sky Cable’s story shows how a company can borrow and invest in technologies that make total commercial and financial sense at the time, only to find out later that the market has moved in another direction. Its hybrid cable network fell behind newer fiber internet, its satellite TV business was shut down by regulators, and its attempt to modernize cable TV could not stop the shift to streaming. Those technology bets lost much of their expected value, yet the debts they created remained.

Sky Cable is now trying to survive by renting space on a rival’s network and taking more time to pay its banks. Neither move guarantees that lost customers will come back or that the business will make a profit again.

Sky Cable once gave ABS-CBN a way to earn steady money outside of free TV. Almost four decades later, the question has reversed: Can Sky Cable become financially strong enough to stop depending on the company it was supposed to help? – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: What does the proposed Pax Silica bill in the House contain?
World.content:
A House bill in the early stages seeks to provide the framework on how to manage the planned semiconductor hub

When US President Donald Trump visited the Philippines during the ASEAN Summit, he signed no Pax Silica agreement with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

But even as major hurdles hound a possible deal, administration-allied House lawmakers are ready to supplement a Pax Silica initiative with a bill clearing the bureaucratic and legal obstacles to an AI-native industrial acceleration hub in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac.

House Bill No. 11758, filed in October by six congressmen led by Deputy Speaker Ronnie Puno, is called the Advanced Industries Development Act.

The bill seeks to create an Advanced Industries Zone, as well as its independent government body called the Advanced Industries Development Authority (AIDA).

What the Zone is for

The Zone is envisaged to be “decentralized, self-reliant, and self-sustaining…with minimum government intervention.”

The AIDA, meanwhile, would be run by a board, composed of 11 governors, including a chairperson appointed by the President.

Based on the proposal, the AIDA would be tasked to administer the Zone and oversee persons and entities with projects in it. They would fix and collect fees, enter into contracts, and have an authorized capital of P50 billion.

If it becomes law, the AIDA would effectively be given a 25-year, renewable, franchise “to construct, operate, and maintain systems for power and water distribution within the Zone.”

Under the proposal, a person or an entity (called a locator) can apply for certification as a qualified enterprise with AIDA’s board of governors. This would allow them to do business within the Zone.

But to be a qualified enterprise, they must meet the minimum investment capital worth P15 billion, excluding land value.

Their enterprise must belong to any of the following high-tech industries:

semiconductor design, fabrication, assembly, testing, or packaging

advanced manufacturing (automation, robotics, precision engineering, or advanced materials)

data centers and computing infrastructure for AI computing

processing of critical minerals and specialty materials

scientific research, development, and technology commercialization

energy facilities

Marcos previously said the Philippine development under the Pax Silica initiative would include the construction of data centers, an issue that is at the heart of environmental groups’ opposition.

What do qualified enterprises get

Based on the proposal, qualified enterprises would enjoy exclusive financial incentives and operational privileges for their projects within the zone. These include:

income tax holiday for seven years from the start of project’s commercial operations

special corporate income tax or enhanced deductions regime in lieu of or upon the expiration of the income tax holiday

exemptions from value-added tax and customs duty

What’s in it for IPs, residents of Capas

The Pax Silica initiative has been met with intense pushback in the Philippines amid fears that hundreds of indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province would be displaced.

The House bill explicitly excludes ancestral lands from being declared alienable and disposable.

Human Rights Watch said Aeta comunities in Capas have been seeking recognition of their ancestral domain since the 1990s, but have yet to receive the title. The IPs have been informed by the government that their homes and land would be affected by the Pax Silica project, and that they would be relocated by December.

The House bill gives preferential hiring to Capas residents, members of IP communities whose ancestral domains are within or adjacent to the Zone, and potentially displaced persons due to the project.

Bill’s chances

HB 11758, whose other authors include congressmen Miguel Luis Villafuerte, Albert Garcia, Alfredo Maranon III, Rolando Valeriano, and Jolo Revilla, is in the early stages of the legislative process.

It has been referred to the economic affairs committee, but has yet to be tackled.

As with many bills, this proposal could gain further traction if backed by the House leadership — or if House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos or House Speaker Bojie Dy files their own version of the measure.

So far, the bill is not yet a Palace priority measure, and has no counterpart in the Senate. – Rappler.com

World.title: No proof of Romualdez influencing Co in alleged infra kickbacks – witness
World.content:
Former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co (left) and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez (INQUIRER file photos / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA)

MANILA, Philippines — There is no direct evidence linking former House Speaker Martin Romualdez’s influence to former lawmaker Zaldy Co in alleged budget insertions and kickback schemes in government infrastructure projects, Atty. Joshua Tan, Assistant Special Prosecutor of the Office of the Ombudsman said on Monday.

Tan made the declaration during the bail hearing of Romualdez and his co-accused on the P7.4-billion plunder case before the Sandiganbayan Third Division, where prosecutors must show strong evidence of guilt to keep the respondents detained.

READ: Witness: Romualdez used associate to conceal ownership of properties

Article continues after this 

In his judicial affidavit read by defense counsel Atty. Rashel Ann Pomoy, Tan said that Co allegedly identified projects, made budget insertions, and asked for percentages from government infrastructure projects when he was chairperson of the House panel on appropriations.

Co led the committee from July 2022 to January 2025, which was after the deliberations of the controversial 2025 national budget.

Tan, in his affidavit, also said that Romualdez yielded his influence to Co as a House Speaker.

However, during cross-examination, Pomoy asked Tan whether the Special Panel of Investigators (SPI) interviewed any individual or had explicit documents proving that Romualdez influenced Co in the alleged kickback scheme, to which Tan answered in the negative.

Pomoy further asked Tan if the team identified any substandard flood control project linked to Romualdez and if there were statements from contractors or officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways saying that the Romualdez received kickbacks from projects.

Article continues after this 

Tan once again answered in the negative.

Meanwhile, Deputy Special Prosecutor Omar Sagadal, in the redirect examination, asked Tan why the investigating team proceeded with their statement that Romualdez was the central figure of the alleged kickback plot.

Article continues after this 

Tan replied that “if you are the central figure, you will not front yourself to that scheme; otherwise, it will be pointless.”

Tan noted “three clusters,” such as the alleged delivery of cash suitcases to Romualdez, his influence as House Speaker, and the chairmanship of Co in the House appropriations panel.

Romualdez’s link to Jose Paras

On the other hand, Tan said that Romualdez allegedly used Jose Raulito Paras to conceal ownership of several properties. Paras is a lawyer and founding partner of Andres Paternal & Paras Law.

READ: Ombudsman wants Romualdez coaccused out of plunder case

Tan noted that based on their investigations, Romualdez and Paras are fraternity brothers at the University of the Philippines.

The state prosecutors earlier alleged that Romualdez’s alleged kickbacks from government infrastructure projects were funneled through companies owned or controlled by Paras.

Pomoy then cited Tan’s affidavit that properties at 30 Tamarind Street and 14 Narra Street in Forbes Park, Makati City, were not registered under Romualdez but were incorporated under Golden Pheasant Holdings Corporation and Brightnews Corporation, respectively.

Tan noted that Paras was a shareholder for both corporations.

This testimony also reiterated what Atty. Mark David Vergara, a member of the SPI, on Monday during the bail hearing.

Both Tan and Vergara said that Paras was not financially capable of acquiring the purchases that were documented under his name.

Tan added that Paras’s income tax return from 2023 to 2024 did not exceed P20 million.

World.title: NBI to subpoena comedian over ‘sexual’ playground post
World.content:
Council for the Welfare of Children Executive Director Angelo Tapales, accompanied by House Committee on the Welfare of Children Vice Chairperson Ann Matibag, on Tuesday arrived at the National Bureau of Investigation to seek an investigation into comedian Mr. JP Aguilera’s controversial post involving children. INQUIRER / MARY JOY SALCEDO

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) will issue a subpoena against comedian Mr. JP Aguilera of Pencilbox Comedy over his “sexual” playground post involving children.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said this after Council for the Welfare of Children (CWC) Executive Director Angelo Tapales, accompanied by House Committee on the Welfare of Children Vice Chairperson Ann Matibag, arrived at the NBI headquarters to seek an investigation into Aguilera’s controversial post.

NBI PROBES COMEDIAN OVER ‘SEXUAL’ PLAYGROUND JOKELOOK: Council for the Welfare of Children Executive Director Angelo Tapales, accompanied by House Committee on the Welfare of Children Vice Chairperson Ann Matibag, on Tuesday arrived at the National Bureau of Investigation to + pic.twitter.com/Qi85nqgUX9 — MJ Salcedo (@MJSalcedoINQ) November 24, 2026

Aguilera posted on Facebook: “Sabi ng doktor ko watch what you eat, kaso kumokonti na yung mga playground.”

Article continues after this 

(My doctor said to watch what you eat, but playgrounds are getting smaller.)

According to Matibag, the bureau will issue the subpoena this Tuesday, requiring Aguilera to appear on Friday or Wednesday next week.

“We’ll give the parties two options, two days na mag-attend sila, para mas may choices na sila,” he said.

(We’ll give the parties two options, two days for them to attend, so they have more choices.)

READ: Kids’ welfare group calls out comedian over ‘sexual’ playground joke

Article continues after this 

Even as the bureau is only about to start its fact-finding probe into the incident, Matibag said the post is a “clear violation” of the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children (OSAEC) Act.

“We’ll do the fact-finding, and i-submit namin sa National Prosecution Service for their preliminary investigation. And if they find probable cause with reasonable certainty of conviction, then they can file it with the proper court,” said Matibag.

Article continues after this 

(We’ll do the fact-finding, and we’ll submit it to the National Prosecution Service for their preliminary investigation. And if they find probable cause with reasonable certainty of conviction, then they can file it with the proper court.)

‘This should not be allowed’

Tapales said that after the CWC received a report regarding the comedian’s post last Nov. 20, they immediately coordinated with the office of Cong. Matibag as the vice chair of the House Committee on the Welfare of Children and the NBI for an investigation.

The CWC executive director emphasized that “these kinds of statements should not be allowed, even if they’re just jokes.”

“It might be sexualization of children under anti-OSAEC law, or it might be cannibalism of children as suggested by the other netizens,” he said.

Meanwhile, Cong. Matibag said that after receiving coordination from the CWC, she called the NBI director, who is her husband, to take immediate action.

“As a nanay, kahit hindi na po legislator, maba-bother ka eh, na bakit meron na namang ganitong malakas yung loob at bakit ang biktima ay mga bata pa,” the lawmaker said.

(As a mother, even if you’re no longer a legislator, you’ll still be bothered, why is there such a strong will and why are the victims still children.)

World.title: Quezon town declares state of calamity, prays for rain amid El Niño
World.content:
The local government of Catanauan, Quezon, declared a state of calamity due to the effects of El Niño as it appealed for divine intervention to help residents cope with the prolonged dry spell. INQUIRER FILES

LUCENA CITY—The local government of Catanauan, Quezon, declared a state of calamity due to the effects of El Niño as it appealed for divine intervention to help residents cope with the prolonged dry spell.On Tuesday, Nov. 24, the municipal government stated the declaration resulted from agricultural losses amounting to P147 million, including P95 million in damage to coconut crops.Earlier, the towns of Alabat, Jomalig, General Nakar, and Guinayangan in Quezon province also declared states of calamity due to the effects of El Niño.

READ: Provinces across Luzon ready funds, water measures for El NiñoThe Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) warned that a possible Super El Niño could bring prolonged dry spells, reduced water availability, and extreme heat to parts of the country.El Niño is expected to intensify toward the end of the year and could persist through the first half of 2027, according to Pagasa’s forecast.In its bulletin on Friday, the Department of Agriculture (DA) reported that agricultural damage and losses caused by the prevailing El Niño had reached P10.44 billion, up 4.5 percent from the P9.99 billion recorded as of Nov. 11.The DA had earlier estimated agricultural damage and losses at P8.57 billion in October, following an initial assessment of P6.87 billion in September.The prolonged dry spell has affected the livelihoods of 338,066 farmers and fisherfolk across seven of the eight regions in Luzon, all four regions in the Visayas, and five of the six regions in Mindanao.About 311,289 metric tons of agricultural produce have been damaged, affecting 332,726 hectares of farmland./coa

World.title: PNP orders probe, manhunt over death of Lanao del Sur town police chief
World.content:
Philippine National Police headquarters in Camp Crame. File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Tuesday ordered an investigation and an intensified manhunt against the individuals involved in the death of a police chief of Bubong, Lanao del Sur.

According to the PNP, Police Major Razul Guimbangan Pandulo was inside his apartment in Barangay Poblacion when two suspects reportedly shot him at about 4:30 p.m. on Monday.

READ: Police chief, driver slain in Lanao del Sur ambush

Article continues after this 

PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. condemned the attack and directed all police units in the region to launch an aggressive manhunt against the individuals involved.

“This senseless and cowardly attack on one of our officers is an affront and a challenge to the police as an organization,” Nartatez said in a statement.

“I expect swift action in this case through an in-depth investigation and aggressive follow-up operations in the interest of justice and the rule of law,” he added.

The two suspects, who were seen wearing bonnets, allegedly fled riding a motorcycle.

“We want to know everything about this incident and if it needs to form a special investigation team, so be it. What is important is we hold all those involved responsible,” Nartatez stressed. /jpv

World.title: NCRPO steps up security preparations ahead of VP impeachment verdict
World.content:
Headquarters of the National Capital Region Police Office — Photo from NCRPO/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) said on Tuesday that it had ordered all police unitsacrossMetro Manila to intensify security preparations for possible developments in Vice PresidentSara Duterte’simpeachment trial.

NCRPO chief Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano said he directed all district directors, unit commanders, and concerned personnel to heighten their security, situational monitoring, as well as ensure there is enough police visibility within their respective jurisdictions.

READ: DILG chief: PNP ‘always expects the worst’ on VP impeachment verdict

Article continues after this 

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday assured that the Philippine National Police “always expects the worst” and is ready to address possible events that may arise when the Senate impeachment court decides on a verdict against the vice president.

“Whatever the outcome may be, our mandate remains the same. We are here to serve the Filipino people, uphold the Constitution, and protect public safety. The NCRPO does not take sides in political issues. We remain committed to our sworn duty,” Abrahano said in a statement.

He further reminded the public to remain calm and respect the democratic process while awaiting the developments surrounding Duterte’s impeachment proceeding.

He added that they strengthened coordination with local government units, as well as concerned agencies for a “unified response to any eventuality.” /jpv

World.title: Families deny rebel links of 2 killed in Batangas
World.content:
The families of two men killed in Batangas City on Nov.17, 2026, denied they were communist insurgents, as claimed by the military. INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Conflicting accounts have emerged following the fatal shooting of two men in Barangay Bataan, San Juan, Batangas on Nov. 17, as authorities identified the victims as communist insurgents while their families and supporters maintain they were civilians unjustly killed.

Killed were Gilbert Orr, a known community organizer working with farmers, and Jayson Cortas, a local tricycle driver. The shooting occurred around 9 p.m. during an operation involving elements of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, Philippine National Police, and the Regional Mobile Force Battalion.

Col. Gerry Laylo, chief of the Mimaropa (Mindoro Occidental and Oriental, Marinduque, Romblon, Palawan) Police Regional Intelligence Division based in this city, stated that Orr and Cortas were members of the New People’s Army and had active arrest warrants for murder and violations of the Anti-Terrorism Act.

Article continues after this 

READ: 3 alleged NPA rebels slain in Batangas clashes

However, families, colleagues, and advocacy groups strongly dispute this version of events.

The Artists for Just Peace and the Tanggol Batangan network have called for an independent investigation, noting that Orr was on his way to meet with communities opposing mining operations in the area at the time of the incident. They described Cortas as a working father with no known political ties.

“Gilbert dedicated his work to defending farmers’ rights to their land and livelihood. Jayson was simply working to support his family. Being accused of something does not take away anyone’s right to due process,” a statement from the groups read, a copy of which was furnished to the Inquirer.

Authorities have yet to release further details on the operation. The Commission on Human Rights has been urged to look into the incident to establish what transpired and ensure full accountability if laws were breached./coa

World.title: NGCP places Visayas grid under red, yellow alerts on Nov. 24
World.content:
National Grid Corporation of the Philippines

MANILA, Philippines — The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) on Tuesday, Nov. 24, placed the Visayas grid under red and yellow alerts due to insufficient power supply.

In an advisory, the NCGP said that consumers may expect the red alert status at the Visayas grid from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m.

Meanwhile, the yellow alert will take effect from 3 p.m. to 5 p.m., and will be raised again from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.

Article continues after this 

READ: Visayas Grid on red, yellow alert anew

According to the NGCP, the red alert is issued when the power supply is insufficient to meet the consumers’ demand and grid’s regulating requirements.

On the other hand, the yellow alert is declared when the operating margin is insufficient to meet the grid’s contingency requirement.

The agency said that the Visayas Grid’s available capacity is only 2,501 megawatts (MW), while its peak demand requires 2,529 MW.

It added that the unavailability of TVI 2 due to unplanned power outage and de-rated capacity of TVI 1 and PEDC 3 may have contributed to the grid’s red and yellow alerts.

Article continues after this 

It also cited the unavailability of PCPC and KSPC Unit 2 due to a scheduled outage and the tripping of Leyte A – Mahanagdong A Unit 1 as among the factors for the alert declarations.

“Nine plants are on forced outage [since] November, 1 plant since October, 2 plants since September, 2 plants since August, 1 plant since June, 3 plants since 2025, 1 plant since 2024, 2 plants since 2023, and 1 plant since 2021,” the NGCP explained.

Article continues after this 

It added that, “21 plants are running on derated capacities, for a total of 753.3 MW unavailable to the grid.” /jpv

World.title: South Cotabato waterfall attraction gets facelift for PWDs, seniors
World.content:
One of the seven waterfalls in Lake Sebu town, a popular tourist spot in South Cotabato. Photo by Bong S. Sarmiento

KORONADAL CITY – Seven Falls, one of South Cotabato’s major tourist spots in the scenic mountain town of Lake Sebu, is being upgraded with facilities designed to be friendly to persons with disabilities (PWDs) and senior citizens.

Ray Venn Dongon, Seven Falls Project Management Unit manager, said management is working to develop PWD- and senior citizen-friendly facilities at Seven Falls to ensure visitors of all ages and abilities can enjoy the attraction.

Improving Seven Falls is one of the provincial government’s priority tourism projects, with P25 million allotted for road and facility development.

Article continues after this 

READ: South Cotabato town declared PH’s 1st FAO agrifood village

“The provincial government of South Cotabato [is working] to make the site safer, more accessible, and more convenient for visitors, especially persons with disabilities and senior citizens,” Dongon said in a statement.

He said a P15-million road concreting project is ongoing at Falls No. 1, and improving the parking area is next, all part of the efforts to make the tourist destination more inclusive for PWDs and senior citizens.

The provincial government is also preparing to construct two cable car units at the premier tourist destination, allocating P10 million for the cable car project, with construction expected to begin early next year.

Once completed, the improvements are expected to further strengthen Seven Falls as a major tourism destination in the province while promoting inclusive tourism and providing more economic opportunities for the local community, South Cotabato Gov. Reynaldo Tamayo Jr. said./coa

World.title: 14 Countries ‘Acknowledge’ ICJ Ruling on Rohingya Genocide
World.content:
LONDON—The UK and 13 other countries on Monday “acknowledged” the top UN court’s ruling that Myanmar perpetrated genocide against its Rohingya minority as London announced new sanctions.

The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, the Gambia and the United Kingdom said Myanmar had “violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”

“We underscore that the Court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court’s decision,” they said in a joint statement.

The UK separately said it “formally recognizes” genocide against the Rohingya and announced sanctions on five senior military figures.

“The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

The sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans, a Foreign Office statement said, adding that London “also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar”.

“The UK is providing an additional £5 million [US$6.5 million] in new funding to support Rohingya and other communities with essential lifesaving and life-affirming services to approximately 350,000 people who need it most in Rakhine State, where humanitarian need is most acute,” the statement added.

It said a further £3 million would “go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.”

On November 19 in a historic verdict, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

The ruling was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that it has determined that a state committed genocide.

Myanmar’s government called the ruling unfair and a “great disappointment.”

Shortly after the verdict, Britain announced it would expel Myanmar’s defence attache.

World.title: Inside the Shadow Networks Helping Min Aung Hlaing Consolidate Power
World.content:
With the help of a Russian-trained military network led by a key aide-de-camp, a team of old spooks and the military’s security and intelligence apparatus, junta boss Min Aung Hlaing now runs Myanmar with an extraordinary degree of personal authority.

Diplomats, Naypyitaw insiders and regional security specialists say the regime’s system of governance has shifted from institutionalized military junta rule toward a highly personalistic system centered on Min Aung Hlaing.

While formal cabinet ministries, the diplomatic corps and conventional military command structures remain intact on paper, The Irrawaddy has learned that substantive authority is increasingly concentrated within a narrow circle of trusted military, intelligence and informal advisers. Sources said Min Aung Hlaing has consolidated personal control since the 2021 coup, while creating three primary networks that have sidelined formal institutions and now exercise substantial influence over state and military policy.

From institutionalized junta to personalistic rule

Historically, successive Myanmar military regimes—notably the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and the State Peace and Development Council (SPDC)—operated through a degree of collective leadership among senior generals and powerful regional commanders. Since the February 2021 coup, however, sources close to the military say Min Aung Hlaing has systematically dismantled those consultative norms, concentrating executive, legislative and operational authority in his own hands.

According to insiders familiar with decision-making in Naypyitaw, major political, economic and battlefield directives now originate directly from the Commander-in-Chief’s Office rather than through cabinet deliberations or collective military council meetings. They said internal mechanisms for debate and peer review among senior generals have steadily hollowed out, leaving top brass with little room to challenge or shape core regime strategy.

At the same time, cabinet ministers and senior bureaucrats have been subordinated to the role of administrative implementers tasked with executing orders rather than formulating policy, according to people familiar with the regime’s current governance in Naypyitaw.

Within this centralized structure, access to the junta chief depends heavily on personal trust, household proximity and demonstrated loyalty, which frequently outweigh seniority or formal military rank. Insiders note that Min Aung Hlaing routinely prioritizes his own strategic instincts and the counsel of trusted informal circles over professional or technocratic assessments. They said that rather than governing through the military’s established institutional machinery, Min Aung Hlaing increasingly relies on bespoke personal networks, reducing formal state organs to instruments of execution.

Who has his ear? The three circles of influence

Sources within and close to the regime point to three distinct yet overlapping circles that exercise disproportionate sway over Min Aung Hlaing’s thinking across defense technology, foreign outreach and internal security.

Influence Circle Key Figures & Entities Primary Domain Mechanism of Influence Circle 1: Technical & Russian-Trained Network Lt-Col Kyaw Zaw Ye, aide-de-camp, DSA Intakes 46 & 47 graduates Defense procurement, drone warfare, Russia ties, strategic messaging Proximity to the leadership’s household; technical specialization bypassing general staff Circle 2: Former Intelligence Network Thein Swe, Hla Min; Paragon Institute Informal political advice, discreet foreign outreach (especially China) Reactivation of legacy Khin Nyunt-era intelligence networks; track-two diplomacy Circle 3: Security-Intelligence Core Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA) Regime security, internal surveillance, political & battlefield intelligence Direct institutional control over intelligence filtering; constant personal access

Circle 1: Kyaw Zaw Ye and the Russian-trained military network

One of the most striking shifts inside Min Aung Hlaing’s inner circle is the ascent of younger, technically specialized officers educated in Russia—particularly graduates of Defense Services Academy (DSA) Intakes 46 and 47. Some 21 personnel from the two intakes form a key part of the inner circle. Multiple sources told The Irrawaddy that Lieutenant Colonel Kyaw Zaw Ye, a DSA Intake 47 graduate, has emerged as an influential figure with direct access to the junta chief. He was appointed as Min Aung Hlaing’s aide-de-camp last year. Trained in Russia, Kyaw Zaw Ye belongs to a cohort of officers versed in Russian defense hardware, procurement pipelines and emerging military technologies.

Insiders say Kyaw Zaw Ye’s clout stems less from his mid-level rank than from close personal ties to Min Aung Hlaing and the leadership’s immediate household, giving him direct channels to the top that bypass senior commanders. The Irrawaddy has learned that this network plays an active role in bilateral defense dealings with Moscow, specialized arms acquisitions, and efforts to source and deploy unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) to counter resistance forces. Sources also link Kyaw Zaw Ye to military propaganda and strategic communications, reflecting the regime’s push to overhaul its information operations. By elevating Russian-educated technical officers through personal access, Min Aung Hlaing has cultivated an alternative source of military-strategic advice that routinely sidesteps conventional general staff hierarchies, people familiar with the matter said.

Circle 2: Thein Swe and the former military intelligence network

Facing severe diplomatic isolation and institutional deficits after 2021, the regime has turned to veteran operatives from Myanmar’s dismantled military intelligence apparatus—specifically figures formerly aligned with ousted prime minister and spy chief General Khin Nyunt. Both Thein Swe and Hla Min, prominent intelligence officers in the former military intelligence establishment under the previous regime, were arrested during the 2004 purge of Khin Nyunt’s faction and later released. Following the 2021 coup, they quietly returned to advise and assist Min Aung Hlaing’s regime.

The Irrawaddy has learned that the Paragon Institute, a policy and research platform run by Thein Swe and Hla Min, serves as an informal hub for former operatives. In 2024, they travelled to China ahead of Min Aung Hlaing’s trip to meet with organizations that promote Chinese foreign policy and work for policy research projects commissioned by major Chinese government departments.

Sources familiar with the group’s activities indicate operational overlap between Paragon-linked figures and the Office of the Chief of Military Security Affairs (OCMSA), particularly in managing discreet international contacts and backchannel outreach to key regional powers, most notably China. Through Thein Swe and platforms like the Paragon Institute, sources said, Min Aung Hlaing has effectively reactivated legacy intelligence networks to conduct sensitive political groundwork and foreign engagement beyond the constraints of formal diplomacy.

Circle 3: OCMSA and the security-intelligence apparatus

While informal advisers provide specialized channels, the OCMSA serves as the regime’s primary institutional pillar of control. Although the agency is now led by Lieutenant General Kyaw Ko Htike, its former chief—current Commander-in-Chief of Defense Services General Ye Win Oo—is widely regarded by insiders as Min Aung Hlaing’s closest confidant and principal gatekeeper, with a steady rise through the military hierarchy that reflects decades of close personal and professional alignment with the junta chief.

Since February 2021, the OCMSA’s reach has expanded dramatically. Sources say the agency oversees surveillance of resistance networks, monitors civilian political actors, vets state officials and conducts intensive counterintelligence policing inside the military itself to preempt defections and internal dissent. They said OCMSA has operated not merely as a counterintelligence service, but as the primary informational filter shaping Min Aung Hlaing’s political and strategic decisions.

The sidelining of ministers and formal institutions

As power has consolidated around these three circles, formal state institutions and cabinet ministries have seen their policymaking authority sharply curtailed. Sources in Naypyitaw say senior ministers and economic officials have repeatedly seen their warnings—particularly regarding foreign exchange controls, trade restrictions and diplomatic isolation—overruled whenever they clash with Min Aung Hlaing’s immediate political or security priorities.

Consequently, key ministries have been hollowed out of strategic influence. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has been largely reduced to handling protocol and consular affairs and defending the regime in multilateral forums, while substantive negotiations take place through intelligence and military channels. Economic ministries, meanwhile, operate primarily as enforcement arms for ad hoc directives rather than architects of coherent macroeconomic policy. Even within the armed forces, operational decision-making has become heavily centralized, limiting the autonomy of regional commanders and traditional staff departments while elevating security and procurement insiders.

While formal ministries no longer shape major strategic decisions, insiders note they remain useful to the regime for bureaucratic execution, day-to-day administration and projecting the outward appearance of state continuity.

Min Aung Hlaing’s reliance on the three circles described above has taken its toll on the country, analysts and diplomats said.

On the economic front, he has failed to listen to experts. Instead, he relies on advisers with military backgrounds, leading to misguided decisions and restrictive measures that have further undermined the economy.

As a result, Myanmar’s economic crisis has reached an extremely critical, if not its worst, point, sources said.

In foreign relations, Min Aung Hlaing appears to be counterbalancing China by leaning toward the United States, while also moving noticeably closer to Russia. He appears to be openly snubbing China, failing to recognize that antagonizing Beijing serves neither his own interests nor Myanmar’s efforts to resolve its ongoing crisis, some diplomats said.

His foreign trips have also failed to deliver tangible results. Despite reaching agreements and making commitments with international partners, few have translated into concrete action.

This likely reflects the limited capacity of those advising him, who appear to lack the understanding and expertise needed to turn diplomatic agreements into practical outcomes that serve the country’s interests, insiders said.

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Workers Have a Weapon Against Junta Abuses – Here’s How to Use It
World.content:
Representatives of the International Labor Organization (ILO) Workers’ Group for Asia-Pacific and Arab States met on the sidelines of the Governing Body’s 358th Session on Nov. 14 to discuss the junta’s demand that Myanmar migrant workers remit 25 percent of their salaries through official channels.

Among those attending the Geneva meet was Phyo Sandar Soe, Assistant General Secretary of the Confederation of Trade Unions Myanmar (CTUM), who represented Myanmar’s labor movement.

In addition to the remittance issue, participants discussed strengthening trade unions, challenges facing workers across the region, and the hardships confronting Myanmar migrant workers in the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific.

The ILO adopted its strongest constitutional enforcement measure (Article 33) against Myanmar in June 2025 following mass arrests of labor leaders and the dismantling of independent unions. At the latest meeting, member states were urged to enforce Article 33 measures demanding an end to violence, forced labor and conscription, and the restoration of union freedoms. The article also gives countries UN backing to impose trade sanctions while opening a UN channel for workers and unions to submit complaints of junta abuses, including passport extortion, forced remittance rules, and conscription threats.

Myanmar’s regime responded by dismissing the enforcement decision and rejecting the ILO’s monitoring mechanism.

Phyo Sandar Soe spoke to The Irrawaddy about the meeting, the junta’s labor policies, and recent developments at the ILO.

What were the key issues raised at the meeting?

The regime’s remittance rule is not only affecting workers in Thailand and Malaysia but worldwide.
