We told ILO regional directors for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East that Myanmar migrant workers are facing serious rights violations and requested an emergency meeting on the issue. The ILO agreed to convene a meeting with experts in attendance.

Junta labor minister Maung Myint has dismissed the ILO’s concerns about migrant workers as exaggerated and misleading. What is your response?

Looking at his social media posts, it’s clear that despite holding the post of labor minister he has no desire to defend workers.

His comments reflect a dictatorship’s mindset. They don’t care how much suffering is endured by workers. Their repression never stops even as people sink deeper into misery.

A labor ministry is supposed to protect the grassroots, the working class of the country. The situation is quite the opposite in Myanmar, which is a shame for the country.

Normally, a country that sends out migrant workers asks the receiving countries to protect its citizens. But in this case, Thailand had to ask the ILO to help protect Myanmar migrant workers. That is deeply embarrassing. The generals should reflect on their own position.

Has the situation for both migrant and domestic workers worsened under the new labor minister?

The regime faces a severe shortage of foreign currency and needs money to fund its military and purchase weapons. So, it has imposed import-license restrictions, tightened access to foreign currency, and is now milking even more from migrant workers through exchange-rate controls and remittance requirements. Regime leaders do not see migrant workers as fellow Myanmar citizens – which is not strange given that they are already killing their own people. What we are seeing is an attempt to squeeze more money from workers to finance further repression.

What decisions were made on Myanmar during the 358th session of the ILO Governing Body in Geneva on Nov. 17?

A follow-up decision on the Article 33 resolution for Myanmar was adopted by the Governing Body. It calls for an immediate end to violence, arbitrary arrests of labor leaders, and forced military recruitment. It also demands the unconditional release of political prisoners, the repeal of laws and orders restricting freedom of association, safe access for ILO missions to Myanmar, and the establishment of a mechanism to monitor labor-rights violations.

The decision further urges member states to review their relations with Myanmar authorities and calls on governments not to forcibly return refugees to Myanmar.

We will urge the ILO to enforce these by January 2027. The ILO Director-General is expected to present an update on Myanmar and progress in implementing the recommendations of the Commission of Inquiry at the 359th session of the Governing Body in March 2027.

What message do you have for Myanmar workers inside and outside the country?

Some people think ILO mechanisms achieve nothing, but a mechanism is only effective if people use it. A knife becomes sharp only when properly sharpened. The same is true of international mechanisms: the more workers make use of them, the more effective they become in protecting Myanmar workers.

Many ask why the international community fails to act despite widely publicized abuses. The reason is simple: without complaints from victims and affected workers, cases cannot move forward.

So, if workers want action and accountability, they need to file complaints and use these mechanisms. I encourage workers to make full use of them.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Says Combating Graft in Military Draft Process
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar said Sunday it has taken legal action against dozens of people, including local officials, accused of extortion and illegal detention of men seeking to avoid compulsory military service.

The statement from Myanmar’s Defense Ministry, published in state media, was a rare acknowledgement of official corruption and abuse of the conscription process in the war-torn nation.

Myanmar’s military is fighting various pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority factions in a civil war sparked by a 2021 coup that ousted the democratically elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi.

In February 2024, the military activated a conscription law, aiming to bolster its ranks. The move prompted tens of thousands of young people to leave the country to avoid forced recruitment.

On Sunday, Myanmar’s Defense Ministry said authorities had taken unspecified legal actions against 102 offenders in “financial extortion” cases and 97 others accused of unauthorized “forcible conscription”, as of the end of October.

“These forcible detentions and unauthorized collections of funds constitute unlawful acts committed by unscrupulous individuals,” the ministry said.

It said some “have impersonated officials to forcibly detain individuals, extort money, and unlawfully enlist them as public military service personnel.”

Local administrators have also collected “monthly payments under the pretext of supporting” conscripted soldiers from their areas, and illegally accepted money to “pay for substitutes on behalf of those evading service”.

The ministry said its central committee on military service conscription would continue to “prosecute offenders to reduce and eradicate the forcible conscription of travelers, nighttime arrests, paid substitution in conscription, and the unauthorized collection of funds”.

‘Afraid to speak out’

Many young people in Myanmar avoid being on the streets late at night, fearing the military or other armed groups may arbitrarily detain them or abduct them for conscription.

Local media have reported cases of young men being pulled off the streets in Yangon and other cities and taken away to undergo military training.

Authorities have previously denied the reports.

One man said Sunday that his brother-in-law was sitting in front of his own house in Yangon several months ago when a group of unidentified people grabbed him and took him away in a car.

The family later learned the detained man was at a military training base in the city of Pakokku, about 500 km north of Yangon, said the source, declining to be named due to security concerns.

“We paid a bribe [of around US$2,000] to some authorities to get him out… but he has not been released yet,” said the relative.

A Myanmar MP said some youth from his southern state, Mon, have been detained by the army and were released after bribes were paid to some officers.

Their relatives “were too afraid of the army to speak out,” said the lawmaker, who also requested anonymity.

He said he did not know the sum of the bribes.

The conscription law allows the military to draft men aged 18-35 and women aged 18-27 to serve at least two years.

World.title: Rights Groups Demand Action Against Myanmar Junta After Historic Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
Rights groups are urging governments to step up diplomatic pressure, impose fresh sanctions and isolate the military regime following Thursday’s landmark International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017.

It was the first time in its 80-year history that the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Rights advocates say the historic ruling must now translate into concrete measures to hold the regime accountable, rather than remain a symbolic legal victory.

“This is a big blow for [regime leader] Min Aung Hlaing at a time when he is trying to persuade the world to normalize relations,” Tun Khin, president of the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), told The Irrawaddy.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible, and pay reparations, as well as ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees to Rakhine State.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, although the court has no independent enforcement mechanism.

If Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling’s orders, the UN Security Council can act to enforce them, according to Article 94.2 of the UN Charter.

Tun Khin said his organization had called on the UK to organize a meeting of the UN Security Council. Though regime allies Russia and China would likely veto any resolution, they would be forced to explain such a move. London has called for a meeting.

“We hope it will result in new sanctions,” Tun Khin said.

Tun Khin expressed concern that the return of the Rohingya is still impossible due to the policies of both the Myanmar military regime and the ethnic Arakan Army (AA), an anti-regime armed group that controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships.

Lucky Karim, executive director of the group Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, said that as an initial step following the ICJ ruling, Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member countries should stop engaging with the Myanmar regime.

She noted that this year nine countries have hosted self-appointed president Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw the 2017 atrocities as military chief. She urged all countries to stop welcoming him. Despite the bilateral engagements, Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from ASEAN’s top-level summits.

“I think the regional states should apply the same rule [as ASEAN] and take a pause for now. Stop hosting him and rolling out the red carpet and engaging him,” Lucky Karim said.

The ICJ decision was welcomed by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (HRW), along with foreign ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and Turkey, as well as Myanmar’s civilian National Unity Government (NUG).

As immediate actions, London ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defense Attaché from the UK and issued an urgent call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

More than 190 local rights groups welcomed the ICJ ruling.

The regime rejected the verdict. Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for the military-appointed government, said on Friday: “The truth is we were wrongly accused.”

Emphasizing the fact that the verdict was not unanimous, she said, “Not all the judges voted for it, so it’s not a fair judgment.”

The ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Meanwhile, the AA said it would act in the best interests of the state following the landmark ruling.

“We need to wait for the regime’s report to the Court. For example, will the regime deny it, or will they say they can’t pay compensation?” Rakhine politician Pe Than told The Irrawaddy.

Backed by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Gambia brought the case in 2019, alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the Genocide Convention. It took seven years to reach a final verdict in the case.

The Myanmar regime has continued to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity across the country since the 2021 coup.

Since seizing power, the regime has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners. The group said the regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, while millions of young people have fled abroad amid forced conscription, security fears, inflation, widespread crime, job scarcity and escalating conflict.

The NUG reaffirmed its commitment to justice, citizenship, and human rights norms for the Rohingya in a statement Thursday.

It said communities across Myanmar continue to face airstrikes, killings, arbitrary detention, torture and forced displacement, while hospitals, schools, monasteries and churches have also come under attack.

“The pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by action to end the military junta’s continuing violence against civilians throughout Myanmar,” it said.

Tun Khin said the ICJ judgment is good news for everyone in Myanmar. “Now they [the regime] are officially responsible for genocide and facing renewed international pressure instead,” he said.

World.title: U.S. Sanctions Two More Myanmar Regime-Allied Scam Warlords
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two more top leaders of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) on Thursday, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

Commander-in-chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One join four other senior leaders of the regime-allied militia on the U.S. sanctions list.

Saw Steel, Saw Sein Win, San Aung and Sai Kyaw Hla were added last November as part of Washington’s crackdown on the multibillion-dollar border scam industry targeting Americans.

Also sanctioned Thursday was Cambodian national Zhao Hui and two of his scam-linked firms.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted overseas scam compounds to protect Americans from fraud,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We will continue to use all available tools to disrupt and dismantle the networks that enable scam compounds to operate.”

Thursday’s order was the U.S. latest action targeting Myanmar individuals in a crackdown on online scam compounds in Southeast Asia that defrauded an estimated $7.2 billion from Americans in 2025 alone.

The sanctions freeze any U.S.-based assets held by targets and make it illegal for Americans to do business or financial transactions with them.

Saw Shwe Wah took over protection of scam operations in DKBA-held Sone See Myaing, Kyauk Khet, Waw Lay, and Phaya Thonezu in December 2025 after replacing the blacklisted Saw Steel as DKBA’s commander-in-chief.

At least seven scam major compounds were under DKBA protection in 2025. However, staged regime raids on KK Park, Shwe Kokko, and Myawaddy in October and November last year forced a mass relocation to the DKBA’s Sone See Myaing headquarters, while others reportedly dispersed inland to villages under the group’s control.

“Shwe Wah has full oversight. The online scams are operating under his protection since he holds the highest position of the group,” a source familiar with DKBA administration told The Irrawaddy.

“Smaller scam sites are now scattered across DKBA territory. Despite their size they still have concrete buildings.”

He confirmed that DKBA-protected scam operations are concentrated in its Sone See Myaing stronghold, though others have relocated to villages in the Mulayit mountain range, roughly 20 km inside the border.

Following last year’s Myawaddy crackdown — widely dismissed as a publicity stunt — scammers reportedly flocked south to the Thai-Myanmar border town of Phaya Thonezu (Three Pagodas Pass) under the command of Colonel Saw A One.

Washington added him to its sanctions list Thursday, claiming he oversaw an expansion of scam operations and buildings.

“Tens of thousands of fraudsters flooded in here during the crackdown over there [in Myawaddy], turning this place into a large scam hub,” a resident of Phaya Thonezu told The Irrawaddy. “Since then, the scam buildings have expanded.”

He added that restrictions on movement make it difficult to determine the exact number of scam compounds and workers, though he confirmed the presence of two major compounds in the town and many more hidden nearby in restricted forest

The U.S. escalated its border scam crackdown in 2025, sanctioning leaders of the regime-allied Karen National Army (formerly the Karen Border Guard Force) including Saw Chit Thu and his two sons.

Washington has since formed the Scam Center Strike Force with Thailand to seize evidence, intercept fleeing scam bosses, and cut off cross-border supplies to compounds.

Jeanine Pirro, who oversees the Strike Force, met with Thai officials in Bangkok this week to discuss strengthening bilateral intelligence sharing, joint operations, and cross-border crackdowns against the scam syndicates.

The Irrawaddy could not reach DKBA headquarters for comment.

World.title: ‘Ungrateful and Two-Faced’: Why a Chinese Analyst Slammed Myanmar’s Junta Chief
World.content:
Following Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, a Chinese commentator responded that the junta was attempting to dodge its own political failures by simply attributing its opponent’s combat effectiveness to external assistance.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that resulted in the seizure of the Myanmar military’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and eventually left the regime stripped of control over most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State. The offensive brought about one of the most humiliating defeats in the Myanmar military’s modern history.

The regime chief insisted the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), one of the alliance members, did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” Min Aung Hlaing said, his voice filled with rage.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

On Friday, the Chinese commentator, who claims to “specialize in Myanmar and Southeast Asia”, made the comments on Chinese social media platform WeChat under the title “The Myanmar Military’s Misunderstanding of China: An Analysis of Min Aung Hlaing’s Unspoken Accusations”.

The commentator, whom The Irrawaddy has learned is knowledgeable about Myanmar affairs and familiar with Naypyitaw, argued that Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks went beyond an assessment of the military’s battlefield defeats.

“He was not explaining his assessment of the enemy; he was assigning blame. He attributed the EAOs’ victory in Operation 1027 to ‘covert support from China,’” the author says.

The commentator also said the Myanmar military has never been on the pro-China end of the country’s political spectrum. From General Aung San, the founder of the Myanmar military, to successive generations of leaders like Than Shwe, Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing, all have been full of misunderstandings and suspicions toward China, the author said.

Regarding the junta’s loss in Operation 1027, the author said the Myanmar military failed to look inward for the cause of the collapse of its combat capability after 2021. “The real collapse occurred internally: troops were replenished through forced conscription, military officers’ families enjoyed special privileges, running businesses within the military was rampant, and grassroots morale was shattered. The Myanmar military has failed to rectify these long-accumulated bad habits,” the author pointed out.

“Shoving all the blame onto ‘external assistance’ is the easiest explanation, but also the one that solves absolutely nothing,” the author added.

China mediated a ceasefire between the alliance and the military in January 2024. In April 2025, under Chinese pressure, the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio, allowing the Myanmar military to re-enter the city.

The author says these developments should have encouraged the Myanmar military to rely more on China’s mediation efforts to facilitate negotiations and de-escalation. Instead, the junta leadership interpreted them differently.

“Instead, not only were they ungrateful, but they stubbornly believed: ‘Since the EAOs listen to China and stop fighting when told to, they must also be taking orders from them to attack the Myanmar military; therefore, any military action by the EAOs must be masterminded by China behind the scenes.’”

“If China were truly covertly supporting the EAOs, Lashio would never have been returned. This is the hardest evidence to refute the ‘covert support’ theory, but unfortunately, it is never mentioned in the Myanmar military’s narrative,” the author argues.

The commentator also pointed out that whenever the Myanmar military wants China to pressure ethnic armed groups, it invokes the concept of pauk-phaw, or fraternal, ties. When it needs China to support its economy, open border ports, or buy agricultural products, it repeats the slogan “China-Myanmar Community With a Shared Future.” Yet, the moment domestic governance goes wrong, it immediately shifts the blame to China, the author says.

“This two-faced mentality of simultaneous dependence and suspicion is currently the deepest rift in China-Myanmar relations.”

World.title: Kazakhstan’s New Development Stage Opens Opportunities for Europe, Slovenia
World.content:
I am deeply convinced that our historic responsibility to future generations is not simply to leave them money in bank accounts, but to build and pass on a fundamentally different country: one that is technologically advanced, with a strong, competitive economy, modern infrastructure and a high standard of living, where every citizen has the opportunity to realize their potential.

In my view, these words from an address by Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev best capture the essence of the country’s new stage of development: the responsibility to turn today’s economic opportunities, natural resources and aspirations for progress into a solid foundation for the stability, competitiveness and prosperity of future generations.

As a Slovenian entrepreneur who has spent many years developing business ties and friendships with Kazakhstan, I see the President’s address as an ambitious yet pragmatic vision for the country’s future. Over 35 years of independence, Kazakhstan has moved beyond its role as a supplier of natural resources to become an important Eurasian hub for energy, economic activity and logistics. The country’s next challenge is to make greater use of its natural wealth and strategic geographic location to develop industry, modern infrastructure, new technologies and a knowledge-based economy.

Particularly noteworthy is the President’s emphasis on public investment to stimulate private investment. The state lays the groundwork for progress through infrastructure development, well-designed industrial policies and development institutions. Yet its full potential can be realized only through entrepreneurial initiative, innovation and long-term private investment. Combining public and private capital is therefore one of the key conditions for successful economic diversification.

In this context, I am reminded of the reflections of the great Kazakh poet and philosopher Abai Kunanbayev, who explored the relationship between reason, will and heart in his Book of Words. A country’s development requires reason to shape a vision of the future, will to turn that vision into reality, and heart to give it a human dimension. Infrastructure, technological progress and economic growth acquire their true value when they improve people’s lives and create new opportunities for future generations. This is where I see the connection between Abai’s philosophical legacy and contemporary visions of Kazakhstan’s future.

My many years of experience in international business have convinced me that turning ambitious plans into reality requires practical measures and resources: well-prepared projects, qualified professionals, reliable partners, appropriate financing mechanisms, and a stable and predictable business environment. When implementing infrastructure and industrial investment projects designed to operate for decades, honoring contractual obligations and ensuring that agreed rules remain in place are just as important as the quality of technological solutions.

This is where I see significant opportunities for cooperation between Kazakhstan and Europe. European countries can make a substantial contribution to Kazakhstan’s economic transformation by providing engineering expertise, technological solutions, experience in managing complex investment projects, and access to development finance institutions. The long-term value of such cooperation lies in partnerships that combine international expertise with Kazakhstan’s domestic potential, support local industry development and create new added value.

Slovenia also has an important role to play in this process, drawing on its industrial traditions and companies that operate successfully in international markets in energy, engineering, pharmaceuticals, logistics and advanced industrial technologies. Decades of business experience across the vast Eurasian region have given us a deeper understanding of Kazakhstan’s development needs and institutional environment, enabling us to build more effective partnerships and manage risks responsibly.

I see particularly promising opportunities in energy and transport infrastructure, including modernizing electricity grids, building power generation facilities and transformer substations, and upgrading railway and logistics infrastructure. Reliable and efficient energy infrastructure is essential for Kazakhstan to ensure a stable power supply for its population and economy, develop new industries, attract investment and strengthen its competitiveness.

The close relationship between energy and industrial development could therefore become one of the main drivers of the country’s further progress. Integrated approaches that combine engineering design, equipment supply, construction and financing play a particularly important role in implementing such projects. They allow complex investment projects to be managed more efficiently, responsibilities to be allocated more clearly, and financial predictability to improve, while also creating opportunities for local companies to participate and strengthen their capacity to deliver projects.

The Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor (TITR), connects Central Asia with Europe and is another route of major strategic importance. Beyond diversifying trade routes, it strengthens economic ties and opens new opportunities for industry, logistics and trade.

Thanks to its geographic location, railway connections and access to Central European markets, Slovenia’s Port of Koper could become an important gateway for Kazakh goods entering the European market, as well as for European exports destined for Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries. This would help strengthen both economies and deepen ties between the two countries.

New opportunities are also emerging in pharmaceuticals, digitalization, technological cooperation and joint industrial investment projects that generate high added value. Kazakh companies bring knowledge of the domestic market, local production and organizational capabilities, and established regional networks. Slovenian enterprises, in turn, can contribute technology, specialized engineering expertise and access to European business networks.

Combining these strengths makes it possible to undertake more complex projects, enhance the competitiveness of both economies and jointly expand into Central Asian markets. Beyond commercial results, such partnerships help build expertise, strengthen trust and create new development opportunities.

Economic cooperation depends not only on institutions, agreements and financial instruments, but above all on people. My experience of working with Kazakhstan has repeatedly demonstrated the importance of personal reputation, mutual respect, reliability and a willingness to build long-term partnerships. These values provide a strong foundation for agreements and joint projects.

For this reason, Kazakhstan has never been merely a market for me. My connection with the country is rooted in its people, friendships, shared experiences and a firm belief that cooperation between our nations can bring substantial benefits. I follow Kazakhstan’s economic transformation and the ambitious goals it has set for itself with great interest, respect and genuine affection.

Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar’s official visit to Kazakhstan on March 31-April 1, 2025, gave fresh momentum to bilateral relations and opened opportunities to translate the political friendship between our countries into concrete economic projects. Such projects will provide the most convincing evidence of our partnership’s strength and future potential.

This brings me back to President Tokayev’s words about our responsibility to future generations. The legacy of the current stage of development will be measured not only by investments, completed projects and economic indicators, but also by the knowledge gained, the strength of state institutions, the opportunities available to young people and the level of trust between people.

I am convinced that Kazakhstan has the capacity to turn its vision for the future into sustainable economic and social development. We in Slovenia seek to be reliable, proactive partners for Kazakhstan, focused on long-term cooperation. I firmly believe that we share an understanding that the true value of projects and partnerships is also measured by their contribution to the well-being of future generations.

The author is Janez Škrabec, president of the Riko Group and honorary adviser to Kazakhstan’s ambassador to Slovenia on economic and investment affairs.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Open Kent State University Branch to Train CA Aviation Professionals
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to establish a branch of the U.S.-based Kent State University to train pilots, aviation engineers and air traffic controllers, strengthening the country’s efforts to develop into a major regional aviation hub.

The agreement in principle was reached during a meeting between Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Assel Zhanassova and a Kent State University delegation led by Executive Vice President and Provost Melody Tankersley, the ministry reported on Nov. 21.

The discussions focused on expanding cooperation in aviation education and bringing internationally recognized training standards to Kazakhstan.

Kent State University has extensive experience in preparing professionals for the aviation industry. Its aviation programs hold international accreditation, and the university operates its own airport and training aircraft fleet, giving students practical flight training opportunities.

The planned branch is expected to serve not only Kazakhstan’s aviation sector but also the wider Central Asian region. Its programs will focus on training pilots, engineering and technical specialists, and air traffic control personnel.

Zhanassova emphasized that developing a skilled aviation workforce and adopting advanced international training standards are essential to Kazakhstan’s ambition to become a leading aviation hub in the region.

Following the meeting, the officials reaffirmed their commitment to joint educational initiatives and agreed to continue working on the project at the expert level.

World.title: Career, Family and Freedom: How Young Kazakhs Define Success
World.content:
ASTANA – For some young people in Kazakhstan success means building a career. For others, it is returning home with new skills, starting a family, becoming financially independent or contributing to society. Increasingly, it also means having the freedom to decide what a fulfilling life should look like, rather than following a predetermined path.

“Financial independence, stable employment, owning a home and the ability to build one’s life independently are becoming important benchmarks,” Aknur Turdaliyeva, chair of the Zhas Ulan youth organization, told The Astana Times.

However, Turdaliyeva, who is also a member of Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi (People’s Council), does not see money and career as the only priorities for today’s generation. She said many young people want to stay connected to family and tradition while making their own choices about work and the lives they build.

According to the British Council’s Next Generation Kazakhstan study published in 2025, 66% of respondents aged 18 to 35 identified family as their primary source of guidance. The study, which included a representative survey of 1,202 young people and qualitative research involving another 68 participants, also highlighted the importance of education, employment opportunities and economic stability.

The Kazakhstan Youth – 2025 national report similarly found that parents remained a key source of support for young people, cited by 68.8% of respondents.

“I believe the main change is that young people increasingly want to decide for themselves what success means to them, rather than meet the expectations of others,” Turdaliyeva said.

Expectations and the freedom to choose

Marriage remains an inspiration for many young people in the country, but financial security may shape when they feel ready to start a family. In a 2026 United Nations Population Fund’s survey, more than 72% of respondents ages 18 to 39 said they would like to marry. When asked what they considered important conditions for having children, 74.6% cited financial security, 71.7% homeownership and 68.4% stable employment.

Alina Kazybayeva, who spent around five years studying and working abroad before returning to Kazakhstan, has experienced how expectations around age, career and stability can differ between countries.

After moving to the Netherlands at 18, she studied business administration. She later studied economics and management at Bocconi University in Milan and worked as a social media assistant at Loro Piana.

Her return to Kazakhstan was partly motivated by the opportunities she sees in the country’s creative industries. She believes the sector offers room for young people to experiment, introduce new ideas and build projects rather than simply enter an established system.

However, having spent much of her formative years abroad, she said she sometimes feels pressure in Kazakhstan to meet major life milestones on a set timetable.

“I think there is still a fairly strong idea of the age at which you should get married, start a family, buy an apartment, take out a mortgage and build a certain level of stability. Perhaps other goals have simply been added to these expectations – a career, travel, self-realization and independence,” she told The Astana Times.

Milan gave her a different perspective. She said that in her experience high rents, salaries that did not keep pace with living costs and difficulty finding stable work can delay decisions about buying a home or starting a family. What may look like a more relaxed approach to those milestones, she suggested, can also reflect economic pressures.

“What matters most to me now is understanding what I really want, without rushing into decisions just because that is what is expected or because I feel I should have achieved something by a certain age,” she said.

Turdaliyeva said eight years of working with children and young people have shown her that success has no single measure. For some, it is career and income; for others, it is family, entrepreneurship or public service.

Education, international experience and returning home

Iliyas Marat, a digital creator studying midwifery in Greece and law at Solent University in the United Kingdom, said studying overseas has broadened his horizons. He hopes to return home as a specialist and put what he has learned to use.

“For me, the most important thing in a profession is to bring real benefit to people,” he said in a comment for this story.

His understanding of success also goes beyond professional status or financial achievement. Marat’s interest in Stoic philosophy began while he was living in Athens.

“For me, success is not money, status or a position, but the ability to appreciate the process of life itself, not only the result,” he said.

He considers financial independence important, but believes that freedom begins internally, international experience and a connection to Kazakhstan are not competing choices.

Kazybayeva has not ruled out living in Milan again, but for now wants to explore opportunities at home.

Success beyond personal achievement

The idea of success also extends beyond individual financial security and career advancement.

“Public contribution is also an indicator of success,” Turdaliyeva said. “It is not necessarily measured by the scale of a project or the position a person holds. Sometimes a small initiative that helps solve a specific problem at a school or in a community can mean much more to people than a large event.”

Youth organizations and community groups, she said, can help young people build responsibility, work with others and take part in decisions affecting their lives. That requires more than inviting them to events. Young people should also be able to propose ideas, contribute to decision-making and see the results of their work.

One example is the Youth Movement under Kazakhstan’s People’s Council. Established on Nov. 16 with 126 members from different regions and professional backgrounds, it aims to connect young participants with the council’s members, involve them in discussions and help them develop proposals on issues affecting young people.

Turdaliyeva also supports reverse mentoring, through which younger people can share their knowledge and perspectives with older generations. She said it can make cooperation between generations more reciprocal.

This emphasis on participation also connects with the broader challenges facing Kazakhstan’s youth. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, the share of young people aged 14 to 35 who were not in employment, education or training stood at 5.7% in the second quarter of 2026, while youth unemployment among people aged 15 to 34 was 2.9%. These are different indicators: the category includes people who are not necessarily looking for work, while the unemployment rate measures those actively seeking employment.

Danara Saranova, chief expert at the Regional Affairs Department of the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, said the country’s young population represents significant potential, but demographic numbers alone do not guarantee social progress.

Opportunities for education, professional development, employment and participation in public life are essential to helping young people develop independence and responsibility, she said.

A generation defining its own pace

Young people are not rejecting familiar milestones. They are wedging them alongside other ambitions: professional independence, international experiences, meaningful work and community contribution. Different perspectives suggest that success is less a fixed checklist than a personal choice, shaped by circumstances, values and the freedom to choose and decide what matters and when.

World.title: Kazakhstan Strengthens Economic Diplomacy to Attract Foreign Investment
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is looking to turn economic diplomacy into a more direct instrument of attracting foreign investment, technology and industrial partnerships as shifting supply chains, technological competition and demand for strategic resources reshape the global economy.

“Investment is no longer simply about capital flows,” Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi said at AIFC Diplomatic Day in Astana on Nov. 23, emphasizing Kazakhstan’s focus on attracting technology, management expertise and know-how alongside foreign capital.

Tileuberdi said the gathering came at a time of profound transformation in the global economy, with geopolitical uncertainty, shifting supply chains, technological competition and growing demand for energy and critical resources reshaping international economic relations.

“In this environment, economic diplomacy is becoming an increasingly important instrument of foreign policy,” he said.

He added that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs works closely with the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Baiterek National Investment Holding and other institutions to attract foreign investment, strengthen international economic partnerships and promote Kazakhstan as a reliable destination for global capital. The country’s investment agenda is tied to a broader economic transition from raw materials toward deep processing, industrialization, digitalization and higher-value-added production. The country is also seeking to strengthen its transport connectivity and position in international supply chains.

Tileiberdi noted that this strong investor confidence is closely linked to Kazakhstan’s strategic position in the global economy. The country accounts for approximately 66% of accumulated foreign direct investment in Central Asia ($156.4 billion.) In 2025, it attracted $20.5 billion in FDI, up 14.5% from 2024, while greenfield investment reached $19 billion, 2.7 times the previous year’s level. Kazakhstan’s investment policy concept through 2030 targets $100 billion in gross FDI inflows between 2025 and 2030.

Tileuberdi also pointed to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s proposal to designate 2027 as the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction, describing it as a step toward infrastructural, technological and industrial renewal.

Kazakhstan is investing in transport and logistics infrastructure, including the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, to strengthen East-West connectivity and support more diversified, resilient global supply chains, Tileuberdi said. He identified three priority areas for international cooperation: energy and critical minerals, digitalization and artificial intelligence, and agriculture. Kazakhstan accounts for about 43% of global uranium production, positioning it to contribute to international energy security and diversify strategic mineral supply chains, the minister said.

Digital development is another priority. Kazakhstan’s e-government system ranks 16th globally, according to the United Nations, while the International Data Center Valley cluster in Ekibastuz is planned to reach up to one gigawatt. Agriculture, meanwhile, offers opportunities in deep processing, advanced technologies and higher-value food production.

Alatau City is among the flagship initiatives underpinning the country’s ambitions, envisioned as a new international center for investment, innovation and advanced industries.

Tileuberdi said Kazakhstan plans to integrate KazakhInvest into Baiterek holding, combining investment facilitation expertise with financial instruments to support investment projects better. The planned integration is intended to bring investment attraction and financing capabilities closer together, allowing institutions to coordinate support for projects and investors more effectively. At the same time, protecting investor rights is a key state priority implemented through the Investor Rights Protection Committee and the Prosecutor General, who acts as the investment ombudsman.

“Transforming these opportunities into a tangible investment project requires trust, predictability, and effective institutions,” Tileuberdi said.

He emphasized the diplomatic corps’ role in strengthening Kazakhstan’s investment partnerships and turning shared ambitions into practical economic cooperation, adding that the Foreign Ministry would continue to lead international investment engagement.

AIFC seeks to connect capital with projects

AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov said the AIFC aims to strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as an international financial and investment hub connecting global capital with opportunities in Kazakhstan and Central Asia. More than 7,000 companies from over 90 countries are registered within the AIFC jurisdiction, while structured investment attracted through its ecosystem since 2018 has reached $30.5 billion.

“However, our ambitions go far beyond the results achieved to date. We strive to strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as an international financial and investment hub connecting global capital with opportunities in Kazakhstan and Central Asia,” Bekturov said.

He described diplomatic missions as strategic partners in connecting investors with projects, promoting joint initiatives and attracting international capital.

“I am confident that leveraging diplomatic networks alongside the AIFC’s financial infrastructure will help deliver tangible investment outcomes and foster mutually beneficial cooperation,” he said.

The AIFC is also developing financing mechanisms across sectors including aviation, junior mining, carbon markets, asset tokenization and creative industries.

Timur Onzhanov, deputy chairman of the management board of Baiterek National Investment Holding, presented the holding’s activities and opportunities for international cooperation. Alisher Abdykadyrov, CEO of Alatau City Authority, presented the project’s key activities and opportunities for international cooperation. Rustam Zhursunov, chairman of the Association of Investors of Kazakhstan, introduced the analytical report “Kazakhstan: An Investment Navigator,” outlining the country’s investment potential and opportunities.

World.title: Kazakhstan Prepares to Reintroduce More Przewalski’s Horses in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Preparations to reintroduce Przewalski’s horses to Kazakhstan are continuing, with a 1.5-year-old stallion named Bruno arriving at an acclimatization center in the Czech Republic ahead of a possible transfer to the country in 2027.

According to Prague Zoo, Bruno was brought from Sweden’s Nordens Ark zoo and has joined a group of stallions being prepared for potential relocation to Kazakhstan. However, his participation in the planned transport has not yet been confirmed, the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources reported on Nov. 23.

The selection and acclimatization of animals begin several months before transportation as part of the project to return Przewalski’s horses to their historical habitat in Kazakhstan.

The initiative aims to restore the wild horse population in the country’s steppe ecosystems, with preparations for the animals’ return continuing in Europe.

The reintroduction program began in 2024, when the first group of Przewalski’s horses arrived from Europe. In May, the first animals completed their acclimatization period and were released into the wild at the Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve. Kazakhstan aims to establish a sustainable population of the endangered species in its historical habitat.

World.title: Uzbek and Kyrgyz Riders Claim Top Honors at Eurasian Equestrian Final
World.content:
ASTANA – Riders from Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic claimed top honors at the Eurasian League equestrian competition in Astana, as the tournament’s final events brought together leading showjumpers from across the region and drew praise from the president of the International Equestrian Federation (FEI).

The competition concluded with two major showjumping events, including the 155-centimeter Argymak Maxima Master Eurasia Cup Final, where Uzbekistan’s Bekzod Kurbanov secured first place aboard Matts V.G. Kazakhstan’s Oleg Sokolenko finished second on Cinderella, while Ksenia Khairulina took third on Gentleman De Beaulieu.

The Kyrgyz Republic’s Rinat Galimov won the 135-centimeter Asian Equestrian Federation/Mantena Cup riding Enrique PKZ. Kazakhstan’s Ayan Gani placed second on Quattro VDB, followed by Kurbanov in third on Santos Hipica, reported the Equestrian Federation of Kazakhstan on Nov. 22.

The tournament drew FEI President Ingmar De Vos, who praised the level of competition and Kazakhstan’s potential to become a stronger regional equestrian hub.

“Kazakhstan and the entire region have great potential. The necessary infrastructure, good horses and strong riders are already here,” De Vos said, adding that he was impressed by the competition and optimistic about the future of major international tournaments in Kazakhstan.

Representatives of the national equestrian federations of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Uzbekistan also attended the award ceremonies, alongside members of the Eurasian League and the international judging panel.

The competition highlighted the growing strength of equestrian sport across Central Asia, giving regional athletes a platform to compete internationally and strengthen sporting ties.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UNODC Discuss Expanding Cooperation on Cybercrime and Rule of Law
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) have discussed expanding cooperation on cybersecurity, public safety and the rule of law, building on the outcomes of an international cybercrime conference held in the Kazakh capital.

The topics were discussed at a meeting between Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to International Organizations in Vienna, Yermek Kosherbayev and UN Deputy Secretary-General, Director-General of the United Nations Office at Vienna and UNODC Executive Director Monica Juma, the ministry reported on Nov. 21.

Juma highlighted the growing cooperation between Kazakhstan and UNODC and thanked the country for its continued support. She also emphasized the importance of the International Conference on Combating Cybercrime held in Astana, which brought together international efforts to address emerging digital threats.

Kosherbayev reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s commitment to strengthening the partnership and briefed Juma on the country’s development priorities and ongoing political and socio-economic reforms.

The discussion also focused on the government’s Law and Order policy, which seeks to strengthen the rule of law, improve public safety and promote a culture of legal compliance. Kosherbayev and Juma noted that these priorities align with UNODC’s mandate and offer opportunities for closer practical cooperation.

The meeting concluded with both officials expressing their interest in expanding joint initiatives and deepening cooperation in areas of mutual interest.

World.title: Kazakhstan Supports Opening of 2026 World Chess Championship in Geneva
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan joined international efforts to promote chess diplomacy by supporting the opening of the 2026 World Chess Championship in Geneva on Nov. 22, bringing together diplomatic representatives, United Nations (UN) officials and two of the sport’s youngest title contenders.

The opening ceremony took place at the Palace of Nations, with support from Kazakhstan’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and other international organizations in Geneva, under the auspices of the International Chess Federation (FIDE).

Ahead of the ceremony, the Kazakhstan Hall hosted a press conference attended by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Office, Yerzhan Kazykhan; FIDE President Timur Turlov; UN representatives; reigning world champion Gukesh Dommaraju of India; and challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan, the permanent mission’s press service reported.

Addressing the participants, Kazykhan drew parallels between chess and diplomacy, noting that both require strategic thinking, respect for rules and the ability to find solutions acceptable to all sides. He also highlighted Kazakhstan’s efforts to develop chess and the growing interest in the game among young people.

The championship will run from Nov. 22 to Dec. 12 at the Martin Bodmer Foundation in Cologny, near Geneva. The first game is scheduled for Nov. 24.

At 20, both Gukesh and Sindarov will make history as the youngest players to compete in a match for the world chess title.

Kazakhstan’s support for the opening ceremony reflects its engagement in international chess initiatives and comes as the country strengthens its presence in the global chess community following Timur Turlov’s election as FIDE president.

World.title: ‘Jewish question’ sparks first major criticism of South Ossetia’s new president
World.content:
The new president of South Ossetia, Marat Kambolov, has faced his first serious criticism since taking office. The controversy stems from talks with Akiva Avshalom Khudainatov, the rabbi of Kislovodsk and head of the city’s Jewish Historical and Cultural Centre, about setting up an international investment fund in Tskhinval.

Representatives of Kislovodsk’s Jewish community also proposed restoring a synagogue and a Jewish cemetery in the South Ossetian capital. This proposal has also met with strong public opposition.

Opponents of these initiatives stress that their objections are not directed at Jews as a group. Rather, they argue that these particular Jewish representatives and their projects have no connection to South Ossetia.

The meeting between Kambolov and Khudainatov took place in Tskhinval on 13 November, but neither the presidential press service nor official media reported it. Details of the talks emerged through posts by a local Telegram channel that receives inside information from the presidential administration.

Only three days later, on 16 November, Kambolov’s press service issued a statement saying:

“Another initiative put forward by the Jewish community was to establish a financial and investment centre in South Ossetia. Representatives of Jewish communities from around the world could take part in its work. The initiators believe this would help develop Tskhinval and the republic.”

South Ossetian society reacted very negatively to the proposal. However, the criticism was directed not at the Jewish community, but at the president himself.

“If Israel, like most countries in the world, does not recognise South Ossetia’s sovereignty, how does Rabbi Khudainatov intend to attract finance and investment from around the world to Tskhinval?” local bloggers and ordinary residents of South Ossetia have asked. They oppose what they see as “unrealistic” projects.

They also point out that Rabbi Akiva Khudainatov has no ties to South Ossetia or its local Jewish community. Blogger and political analyst Alan Mamiyev also notes that the Kislovodsk rabbi follows Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidism, a religious movement that Tskhinval’s Jews have never followed.

“The local Jews of Tskhinval were never followers of Chabad. Accordingly, the Kislovodsk Jewish community has no right to claim the city’s synagogue,” he argues. Many others share this view.

Social media users have also reminded Kambolov and Khudainatov that Georgian-South Ossetian conflict destroyed Tskhinval’s Jewish Quarter, which had existed during the Soviet era. At the height of the fighting, members of the Jewish community had to leave South Ossetia.

The only Jewish woman who remained there was Rybka Dzhindzhikhashvili, who died alone in April 2025. Her Ossetian neighbours supported her as best they could, while the Kislovodsk Jewish community showed no interest in her plight. Now, however, its representatives have suddenly appeared with their projects.

The ruined synagogue in Tskhinval

Under a barrage of criticism, Kambolov was forced to defend himself. His press service published a post explaining the president’s position. It turned out that he had been surprised by the public reaction.

“These people came to clean up the cemetery and asked for a meeting, expressing their intention to invest in the development of our republic. I listened to them. What is there to condemn?” Kambolov said, shrugging.

He added that listening to someone does not mean agreeing with their proposals or making any commitments. The president insisted that “all decisions will be made exclusively in the interests of South Ossetia and the Ossetian people”, saying he had no other priorities.

However, Kambolov’s belated statements failed to dispel public concerns entirely. Former president Eduard Kokoity stepped in to try to resolve the dispute. In a video address, he urged people not to politicise the issue. He stressed that the Ossetian people were known for their tolerance, that Tskhinval had been a multi-ethnic city and that local Jews had never faced persecution.

“Today, it is particularly important to distinguish reality from the information noise, assess what is happening soberly and avoid panic and rumours based on speculation and assumptions.

We should not imitate various radical movements seeking to infiltrate our society, including under external influence. Radicalism in any form is alien to the Ossetian people.”

Kokoity also advised the new government leadership, made up largely of Russian officials, to pay greater attention to the republic’s history, its armed conflict with Georgia and the consequences of that conflict. He urged them to take account of the local population’s mentality and its deeply emotional attachment to its land.

“We have shed too much blood for our land and our capital for anyone to seriously suggest today that we are ready to ‘surrender’ or ‘sell’ it, as some short-sighted fellow citizens are trying to portray it.

At the same time, attracting investment must under no circumstances run counter to national interests, let alone infringe on the rights and interests of our people – which is precisely what President Marat Kambolov has said,” Kokoity said.

The last major debate over South Ossetia’s Jewish community erupted when the previous authorities decided to demolish the ruins of Tskhinval’s Jewish Quarter, which they deemed beyond restoration.

Opinions were then divided between supporters and opponents of the demolition. But the proposal to establish an investment fund has met with unanimous rejection.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: ‘My last hope has died’: Georgia plans to ban surrogacy, prompting backlash
World.content:
Surrogacy ban in Georgia

The ruling Georgian Dream party plans to ban surrogacy completely in Georgia. Irakli Kirtskhalia, one of the leaders of the parliamentary majority, announced the initiative on Sunday, 22 November, following a meeting of the majority.

He said the party was actively discussing the issue with the Patriarchate. He also said lawmakers would submit the relevant bill in the near future.

The initiative has drawn strong criticism on social media, including from members of the medical community. Reproductive medicine specialists say that although the sector clearly needs regulation, authorities should not ban it outright.

Many believe the government is trying to win the Patriarchate’s favour. These suspicions have been fuelled by recent tensions between Georgian Dream and the Patriarchate over a debate on gambling. The Patriarchate itself has yet to issue a public statement.

How the ruling party explains its decision

Georgian Dream says it wants to ban surrogacy because of the ethical and legal risks involved. The ruling party points to threats such as human trafficking, the possible exploitation of women and violations of children’s rights.

At a special briefing, Irakli Kirtskhalia said a ban on surrogacy could have economic consequences. However, he stressed that no economic benefit could outweigh these risks:

“We fully understand that banning surrogacy could have some economic impact. However, we believe that economic benefits cannot outweigh these risks and ethical concerns.”

The parliamentary majority leader stressed that 98% of people who use surrogacy services are not Georgian citizens. As for the remaining 2%, “they will certainly understand the decision”.

“Believe me, given the specific nature of our society, our mentality, and our shared values and views, even these 2% or 1.5% [of the population] will fully understand the risks we are talking about,” Kirtskhalia added.

One of Kirtskhalia’s main arguments is that children born in Georgia are taken abroad to various destinations, after which the state loses control over their fate.

The ruling party says only five or six post-Soviet countries still allow surrogacy, and Georgia is one of them. Kirtskhalia also said the surrogacy “market” had grown significantly since 2023:

“Even in European Union member states, surrogacy is either banned or subject to very strict regulation. As for commercialisation – a problem that already existed in 2023 – the situation has unfortunately reached enormous proportions. In fact, the market is growing by 100% every year.”

He also said that although the authorities planned to ban surrogacy completely, in vitro fertilisation (IVF) procedures would not fall under the restrictions. However, they would remain subject to strict oversight.

“My last hope has died”

News of the initiative sparked an outpouring of anger on social media.

“Instead of improving the legislation, protecting the rights of surrogate mothers and punishing those who commit crimes in this sector, they are simply banning surrogacy! My last hope has died!

I want everyone – including the descendants of those who came up with this ban, those who are now pushing for it, approving it and signing the relevant law – to go through the same experience I have endured over the past seven years, both psychologically and financially,” journalist Nino Kapanadze wrote.

She published several posts on the subject.

“I wonder who the lawmakers consulted before deciding to ban surrogacy. Reproductive medicine specialists? Doctors? Agencies that organise surrogacy arrangements? Specialist clinics? And what right – or expertise – does a religious organisation have to interfere in a decision to ban surrogacy?” she asked.

Nino Tarkhnishvili, a journalist with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, has been covering surrogacy since 2022 and has published numerous reports on the subject.

In her reports on foreign women who travelled to Georgia to become surrogate mothers, she documented numerous cases of violations of women’s rights. Following the publication of these reports, Georgian authorities launched an investigation and arrested the heads of several agencies.

“I did not write these articles to call for any bans. Quite the opposite: my only aim was to ensure that Georgia introduced legislation that would properly protect surrogate mothers, children and prospective parents, leaving no loopholes for human trafficking or other serious crimes.

Banning something is the easiest option. Proper regulation, sound legislation and bringing standards into line with international norms are much harder. But the authorities have chosen the easy way – the way of bans,” the journalist wrote on social media.

Reproductive medicine specialists: “We need regulation, not a ban”

Reproductive medicine specialists have also spoken out against the proposed ban on surrogacy. They acknowledge that abuses in the sector need to be addressed. However, they argue that an outright ban, rather than proper regulation, would deprive people for whom surrogacy is the only option of the chance to become parents.

“Surrogacy is not simply a commercial activity. It is part of assisted reproductive technology and people often turn to it for strict medical reasons. For many people who cannot conceive a child themselves because of health conditions, surrogacy remains the only realistic path to parenthood,” says Professor Nino Museridze, founder of the Association of Oncofertility.

She says authorities should address the risks through clear regulations, oversight of clinics and intermediary organisations, and safeguards to protect the rights of everyone involved. Museridze hopes that the government will eventually include assisted reproductive technologies in state-funded programmes, making infertility treatment accessible to more families.

“The state should tackle the root causes of existing problems rather than trying to ban a medical option itself.”

Keti Gotsiridze, an obstetrician-gynaecologist and reproductive medicine specialist, sees surrogacy as more than just a medical procedure.

“Surrogacy is first and foremost a human story. Behind every such story lies a simple but profound dream – the dream of becoming a mother,” she says.

According to reproductive medicine specialist Nana Janelidze, work to regulate the surrogacy sector was already under way. She says experts from the International Organization for Migration had developed 33 recommendations aimed at improving the regulation of assisted reproductive technologies.

Janelidze believes the authorities should hold public consultations on these recommendations before deciding whether to ban surrogacy. Surrogate mothers, families, doctors, lawyers and government agencies should all take part. “Why should we move towards a ban without publicly discussing the recommendations that have already been developed?” she asks.

“The ruling party wants to win the Patriarchate’s favour”: reactions to the proposed changes

Tensions have recently emerged between Georgian Dream and the Patriarchate. One source of disagreement has been the regulation of gambling. In October, the parliamentary majority fast-tracked amendments allowing casinos to host international gambling tournaments and benefit from certain tax breaks.

The Patriarchate strongly criticised the decision, saying the authorities had not consulted it. Shio, the locum tenens of the patriarchal throne, also commented on the issue. He said that promoting gambling was as grave a sin as making a direct profit from the activity itself.

Against this backdrop, many have interpreted the government’s announcement of a surrogacy ban as an attempt to ease tensions with the Church.

“A shameful and disgraceful decision! In an attempt to ‘smooth things over’ with the Patriarchate, they are depriving thousands of women of the chance to become mothers. Just imagine how many children will now never be born! And this is happening in a country facing a total demographic catastrophe!” wrote Nika Gvaramia, leader of the opposition Coalition for Change.

The Georgian Orthodox Church’s opposition to surrogacy is not new. In its official statements, the Patriarchate has repeatedly described the practice as a “grave crime”.

In its 2014 Christmas message, for example, the Patriarchate asked: “Can a family truly be happy if it raises a child born to a surrogate mother?” It added that “such a child may be condemned to a life without love and in loneliness”.

These remarks sparked public criticism at the time, prompting the Patriarchate to issue a clarification.

Tamta Mikeladze, head of the Social Justice Centre, argues in a lengthy social media post that the surrogacy sector does face systemic problems and needs regulation.

However, she questions whether the government can be expected to pursue consistent policies that protect women’s rights when it has removed the concepts of “gender” and “gender equality” from its legislation:

“The timing of this decision and its political context give legitimate grounds to suspect that political interests have driven it. For years, even when various civil society groups and the Church called for surrogacy regulation, the government failed to take any effective steps in that direction.”

The surrogacy industry in Georgia

The surrogacy market in Georgia has expanded significantly, particularly since 2022. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, several international agencies operating in the sector moved their operations from Ukraine and Russia to Georgia.

A detailed article published by Deutsche Welle cites figures from Georgia’s Public Service Development Agency.

According to the data, more than 3,000 surrogate mothers were registered in the country in 2023. Since 2012, they have given birth to more than 5,000 children.

The article notes that surrogate mothers gave birth to around 300 children in 2021, but the figure exceeded 1,100 in 2023. According to Deutsche Welle, around 19 clinics in Georgia offer these services.

In Georgia, surrogacy is not simply a medical service or a reproductive option for foreign couples. It also raises serious questions about protecting the rights of women who take part in these programmes, particularly those who come from other countries.

For years, specialists in surrogacy and egg donation have highlighted the same problem. Their main recommendation is that Georgia needs a legal framework in line with European standards. It should clearly define the rights and responsibilities of surrogate mothers, couples struggling with infertility, clinics, doctors and intermediary agencies.

Previous attempt to ban surrogacy

The government has previously raised the issue of restricting surrogacy. In 2023, the cabinet submitted a bill to parliament that aimed to restrict foreign nationals’ access to assisted reproductive technologies, including surrogacy.

Irakli Garibashvili, who was prime minister at the time and is now in prison, announced the initiative:

“Our female citizens are being offered what is presented as a ‘profitable business’. Afterwards, nobody knows who takes the child born here or which couple takes the child. There are reports that same-sex couples may take these children. This could lead to a host of problems,” Garibashvili said.

Parliament officially registered the bill, but it never became law.
