World.title: Kyrgyzstan and Portugal discuss high-level visits, UN cooperation as new envoy arrives
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Kyrgyzstan and Portugal discussed prospects for developing bilateral relations, including the organization of high-level visits and the expansion of their treaty and legal framework, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kyrgyzstan.

The meeting took place in Bishkek on November 23, 2026, between Kyrgyzstan's Deputy Foreign Minister Meder Abakirov and the newly appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Portuguese Republic to the Kyrgyz Republic José de Castro Ataíde Amaral.

During the talks, the parties also addressed cooperation within the UN Security Council during their joint membership in 2027–2028.

Abakirov received copies of the ambassador's credentials, congratulated him on his appointment to the high post and wished him success in his diplomatic mission.

Diplomatic relations between the Kyrgyz Republic and the Portuguese Republic were established on August 18, 1992. Bilateral engagement develops both directly and through multilateral platforms, including the United Nations, the OSCE, and the European Union–Central Asia dialogue.

Cooperation between Bishkek and Lisbon is set to gain new momentum in 2027–2028, when both countries will serve simultaneously as non-permanent members of the UN Security Council, creating additional opportunities to coordinate positions on global peace, security, and sustainable mountain development.

World.title: Azerbaijan Banks Association signs cooperation memorandums with Central Asian partners (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. The Azerbaijan Banks Association (ABA) has signed memorandums with the Central Asia Fintech Association and the Tajikistan Banks Association in Baku on the sidelines of the 10th International Banking Forum in Baku today, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Details regarding the documents haven't been disclosed yet.

As part of its efforts to expand international ties, the ABA has been consistently developing cooperation with foreign banking associations and international financial organizations.

In 2003, a cooperation agreement was signed with the Association of Banks of Georgia. In 2004, a similar agreement was concluded with the Association of Regional Banks of Russia, followed in 2005 by agreements with the Hellenic Bank Association and the Association of Banks of Northern Cyprus.

In 2007, the ABA signed cooperation agreements with the Association of Commercial Banks of Latvia, the Association of Ukrainian Banks, the Association of Belarusian Banks, and the Moldova Banks’ Association. That same year, the organization became a member of the International Coordinating Council of Banking Associations of the CIS, Central and Eastern European Countries. Furthermore, in November 2007, a letter of intent, along with a corresponding agreement, was signed to establish a Coordinating Council of Banking Associations of the GUAM member states.

In February 2008, the ABA was granted the status of an associate member of the European Banking Federation (EBF). This provided the association with access to European expertise in organizing banking systems, as well as to databases covering European banking legislation.

In 2008, cooperation agreements were signed with the Association of Banks of Kazakhstan, the Union of Banks of Kyrgyzstan, the Banking Association of Uzbekistan, and the Banking Association of Tajikistan. These arrangements have elevated engagement with banking organizations in Central Asia to a new level and expanded opportunities for establishing mutually beneficial partnerships among their respective members.

In May 2008, the ABA signed a cooperation agreement with the Banks Association of Türkiye, aimed at strengthening interaction between the banking associations of the two countries and developing economic ties. In 2009, an agreement was concluded with the Association of Development Financing Institutions in Asia and the Pacific.

On April 17, 2009, a memorandum of understanding was signed in Istanbul to establish an international organization: the Federation of Banks of Central Eurasia. In 2010, the Federation was registered with the Ministry of Justice of Azerbaijan. Its founding members were the banking associations of Azerbaijan, Georgia, Ukraine, and Kyrgyzstan. In May 2011, the banking associations of Türkiye and Tajikistan joined the Federation.

On November 4, 2022, the Council of Banking Associations of Turkic States was established in Istanbul. A memorandum of understanding to this effect was signed by the Azerbaijan Banks Association, the Association of Banks of Kazakhstan, the Union of Banks of Kyrgyzstan, the Banking Association of Uzbekistan, and the Banks Association of Türkiye. The creation of this council marked a new stage in the coordination of cooperation among the banking associations of the Turkic states.

In January 2023, the ABA was elected as a member of the Sustainable Banking and Finance Network (SBFN) of the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Subsequently, the association’s international cooperation expanded through new agreements:

February 15, 2023 — a memorandum of cooperation was signed with the UAE Banks Federation;

April 20, 2023 — a memorandum of cooperation was signed with the Hungarian Banking Association;

June 13, 2023 — a memorandum of understanding was signed with the Association of Islamic Banks of Türkiye, aimed at supporting the development of the financial sectors in both Azerbaijan and Türkiye;

June 13, 2023 — an agreement on staff exchange was signed with the Hungarian Banking Association;

June 14, 2023 — A cooperation agreement was concluded with the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Thus, the international activities of the ABA encompass a wide range of partners across Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East, and the Turkic world, establishing an institutional framework for the exchange of expertise, the development of interbank relations, and the implementation of joint initiatives.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, Denmark consider steps to deepen bilateral relations
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Kyrgyzstan and Denmark discussed prospects for developing bilateral relations, focusing on high-level visits and trade and economic cooperation, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Kyrgyzstan.

The meeting took place on November 23, 2026, between Kyrgyzstan's Deputy Foreign Minister Meder Abakirov and the newly appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Kingdom of Denmark to the Kyrgyz Republic and Special Representative of Denmark's Ministry of Foreign Affairs for Central Asia Lars Thuesen.

During the talks, Abakirov received copies of Thuesen's credentials, congratulated him on his appointment and wished him success in his diplomatic mission.

The sides noted the importance of expanding trade and economic ties through the implementation of joint projects, as well as organizing upcoming high-level visits.

Both sides also confirmed their interest in further strengthening cooperation within international and regional organizations, including the United Nations and the European Union.

Kyrgyzstan and Denmark established diplomatic relations in May 1992. While bilateral trade turnover remains modest, both countries see strong potential for growth in renewable energy, water resource management, agri-food technologies, and digitalization.

Denmark also actively supports regional initiatives in Central Asia focused on climate resilience and green transition, working with Kyrgyzstan both bilaterally and through European Union development programs.

World.title: AzInTelecom represented at II International Conference on Cyber Diplomacy (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. “AzInTelecom” LLC, a company within AZCON Holding, participated in the II International Conference on Cyber Diplomacy (ICCD 2026), held in Baku.

The conference, dedicated to “Power and Influence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Regional Perspective on the Evolving Cyberspace Landscape,” brought together international experts, representatives of diplomatic institutions and international organizations.

Ruslan Dadayev, Director of the Cybersecurity Department at AzInTelecom, spoke during a panel discussion held as part of the conference. Addressing issues of digital sovereignty and national cybersecurity in times of crisis, he highlighted the importance of digital infrastructure resilience and the effective management of cybersecurity systems.

The conference featured discussions on key issues, including the impact of artificial intelligence on diplomatic relations, the growing role of technology companies in international processes, information warfare, and regional cooperation in cyberspace.

AzInTelecom's participation in ICCD 2026 aimed to expand the exchange of expertise in cybersecurity and digital sovereignty and strengthen cooperation with global partners.

Strengthening the country’s technological sovereignty and developing secure and resilient digital infrastructure are among AzInTelecom’s key priorities. By building the infrastructure necessary for secure data storage and processing within the country and providing advanced cloud, cybersecurity and digital identity solutions, the company aims to contribute to the development of Azerbaijan’s digital ecosystem.

World.title: Georgia's Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili to visit Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Georgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili is due to pay an official visit to Azerbaijan, the Georgian Foreign Ministry said.

During the visit, Botchorishvili is scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with Azerbaijani officials.

The talks are expected to cover various aspects of Azerbaijan-Georgia relations.

World.title: President of Indonesia expected to visit Azerbaijan for OIC summit in 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto is expected to visit Azerbaijan in 2027 to attend a summit of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Indonesian Ambassador to Azerbaijan, Berlian Helmy, said at an Indonesian business forum in Baku today, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

According to the ambassador, the visit could take place as part of events marking the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Indonesia and Azerbaijan in 2027.

The ambassador emphasized that the upcoming anniversary should serve as an impetus for further strengthening bilateral ties, including in the areas of trade, the economy, and investment.

Will be updated

World.title: Azerbaijani businesses could tap ASEAN market through Indonesia - ambassador
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Cooperation with Indonesia could open up additional opportunities for Azerbaijani businesses to enter the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) market, which has a combined population of around 700 million, Indonesian Ambassador to Azerbaijan Berlian Helmy said, according to Trend's correspondent covering the event.

Speaking at the Indonesia-Azerbaijan Business Forum in Baku on Tuesday, November 24, he said that Indonesia could serve as a gateway for Azerbaijani companies seeking to access the broader Southeast Asian market.

"Indonesia has a population of nearly 300 million. In addition, the country is a member of ASEAN, which brings together around 700 million people. This means that through Indonesia, businesses can gain access to a market with a population of 700 million," he said.

According to the ambassador, Indonesia accounts for nearly half of ASEAN's total population, making its domestic market an important component of regional economic cooperation.

He also highlighted measures introduced by the Indonesian government to support businesses.

"The Indonesian government provides benefits, various opportunities and incentives to all business participants, including both trading companies and investors. This makes business cooperation easier and more efficient," Helmy said.

Outlining potential areas of trade with Azerbaijan, the ambassador listed palm oil, coffee, cocoa, spices, rubber, vanilla, cloves, cinnamon and nutmeg.

He added that Indonesia also produces seafood, including shrimp and tuna, as well as processed seafood products.

Other goods manufactured in the country include textiles, clothing, footwear, wooden and rattan furniture, packaging materials and consumer goods.

"In addition, Indonesia produces heavy equipment for the construction industry, electronics, household appliances, pharmaceuticals, medical equipment, chemicals and plastics," he said.

The ambassador also highlighted cosmetics, fashion products and highly processed food products among Indonesia's higher value-added goods.

World.title: Uzbekistan energizes 220-kV section of new substation at Navoi power plant
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 24. Uzbekistan has energized the 220-kilovolt (kV) busbars at a new 500/220-kV substation being built as part of a project to construct a 650-megawatt (MW) combined-cycle power unit at the Navoi Thermal Power Plant.

According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Energy, the initial energization marks a key milestone in commissioning the substation, which now connects the Navoi Thermal Power Plant with a 300-MW hybrid solar photovoltaic plant.

The new facility is designed to strengthen electricity transmission links between the southwestern and northern parts of Uzbekistan's unified power grid, improve the reliability of high-voltage power transmission and enhance overall grid stability.

Modern equipment manufactured in Japan, China, India and South Korea is being installed at the substation to ensure operational reliability and meet technical requirements.

Japan's Mitsubishi Corporation and Mitsubishi Power Ltd. are participating in the project as part of a consortium serving as the general contractor, while Türkiye's Çalık Enerji is acting as a subcontractor.

The next stage will involve energizing the equipment required to transmit electricity generated by the new 650-MW combined-cycle unit to Uzbekistan's unified power grid through the substation.

This will enable final testing and commissioning procedures for the power unit, paving the way for its phased launch into operation.

World.title: Prisoner accused of fatally stabbing rapist and killer in jail faces trial
World.content:
A murder trial has begun for a prison inmate accused of stabbing a Sydney man who was serving a 45-year sentence for raping and murdering a 16-year-old.

Jayelem Cutmore has pleaded not guilty to the murder of 31-year-old Aymen Terkmani, who died after being stabbed in the chest at the Lithgow Correctional Centre on September 25, 2024.

Terkmani was serving a non-parole period of 33 years after being found guilty in 2017 of sexually assaulting and killing his friend Mahmoud Hrouk.

Crown prosecutor Carl Young today laid out the case against Mr Cutmore, which is being heard in the Bathurst Supreme Court and is expected to run for up to four weeks.

He told the court that the incident began in the afternoon when Terkmani attacked another prisoner in their cell with a sandwich maker, a type of assault described as "being brevilled".

A 14-person jury has been empanelled at the Bathurst Supreme Court. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

"Whatever his motivation, this 'brevilling' set off a chain of events that led to Mr Terkmani being stabbed minutes later," Mr Young said.

During opening addresses, the court was shown CCTV footage of the injured inmate Julal Viral entering the yard shortly after the assault.

Mr Cutmore can then be seen running towards Terkmani's cell, followed by others.

The Crown told the jury the 24-year-old stopped briefly at his own cell, where he appeared to change his shoes.

The prosecution will argue that was an opportunity to retrieve a jail-made knife or "shiv", before footage shows him standing outside the deceased's doorway for a matter of seconds.

Mr Young told the court that "during the six seconds, Cutmore stabs Terkmani once in the chest".

Terkmani died shortly later while being treated at the correctional centre's medical clinic.

No weapon was located during police searches.

The prosecution told the court it would call upon the injured inmate, who gave a police interview in which he allegedly admitted seeing the accused stab the deceased.

Jayelem Cutmore allegedly stabbed his fellow inmate Aymen Terkmani to death at the Lithgow jail in 2024. (Supplied)

Defence barrister Ian Nash told the jury several assertions were in dispute, including what was said in the prison yard and that Mr Cutmore intended to, or had time to, obtain a shiv.

He said the jury would hear evidence that Terkmani's blood was found on his client's shirt, pants and shoes, but cast doubt on how the clothes were seized for evidence and whether they proved his client caused the fatal wound, given the significant amount of blood at the scene.

Referring to CCTV footage of the incident, which runs for about 30 seconds, Mr Nash said it was unclear what occurred in the deceased's cell, and that there was a congregation of inmates gathered around immediately after Mr Cutmore walked away.

Mr Nash pointed out an "unfortunate smudge" in the video and told the jury those "few seconds will be critical".

"Fundamentally, the dispute in this trial is whether you could ever be properly satisfied that my client was the person who inflicted the single fatal stab wound," he said.

'Serious and distressing offences'

As the offence occurred in a jail, the witnesses include other inmates and employees of the male maximum-security prison in New South Wales's Central West.

Justice Peter Hamill told the 14-person jury empanelled this morning that Mr Cutmore was in jail for "extremely serious and distressing offences", as was Terkmani.

He urged them not to have prejudices against the accused, witnesses or the deceased because of that.

The prosecution will call upon the first of several witness tomorrow, including the manager of security at the jail.

World.title: Tucabia man who missed 1993 Christmas lunch is likely dead, coroner says
World.content:
It is a Christmas mystery that has spanned more than 30 years, but a NSW coroner does not expect a happy ending.

Stephen Bryant, 40, was supposed to join his friends and neighbours at Tucabia in northern NSW for Christmas lunch in 1993 but never arrived.

A coronial inquest has been told neighbours reported a "strange, strong and sickening odour" coming from Mr Bryant's house on Bellengen Street in the days that followed.

Deputy State Coroner Rebecca Hosking told the court she was satisfied Mr Bryant was deceased, but was unable to determine the place or cause of his death.

She has referred the case to the Unsolved Homicide Unit.

Fear and suspicion

The inquest was told Mr Bryant was well-liked amongst his neighbours, who held concerns for his welfare when he did not show up for Christmas lunch.

He was last seen alive on December 23, 1993.

On February 14, 1994, his neighbour Cynthia Press reported to police at Ulmarra that she feared the worst and told officers about the odour at Mr Bryant's house.

The court also heard how Mr Bryant's sister Rhonda received a call from her brother in the days before his disappearance, telling her, "If you don't hear from me, report it."

The inquest was told Mr Bryant was involved in growing and selling cannabis, and worked on a tea-tree lease for a man known as Ned Ryan, whose legal name was Edwin Ryan.

An inquest has heard that missing man Stephen Bryant was involved in growing cannabis on the NSW north coast. (Pexels: Michael Fischer)

The court heard the tea-tree leases were a front for growing cannabis.

Neighbours told police in the months after Mr Bryant's disappearance that he told people he was "really scared" and that Mr Ryan was "a good bushman" and knew "places to put me where I can't be found".

According to neighbours, Mr Bryant had cut down some of Mr Ryan's cannabis plants and kept a bag to sell.

Key suspects

The inquest heard neighbours saw Mr Ryan coming and going from Mr Bryant's house in the days after his disappearance.

Differing accounts referred to cars in the dark without headlights on, torches inside the house, and missing personal items and tools.

In the weeks over Christmas 1993 and January 1994, Mr Ryan gave neighbours different stories about where Mr Bryant had gone, including that he was on a drinking binge, was on a plumbing job in Sydney, was taking cannabis to Sydney, and was at his girlfriend's house at Grafton.

The inquest also heard about a man called "Tiny" Renshaw.

Mr Bryant's former girlfriend Roberta Rabinov alleged Mr Renshaw had beaten Mr Bryant with a plank.

Ms Rabinov told police she heard a gunshot, and saw Mr Renshaw put a body in a wheelbarrow.

The inquest heard there were several inconsistencies with Ms Rabinov's police statement including that no neighbours reported hearing any gunshots.

Ms Rabinov's mental health was later assessed, and she was diagnosed with schizophrenia.

Dead suspects and witnesses

The inquest heard how most of the suspects and witnesses had since died.

Key suspects Mr Ryan and Mr Renshaw died in 2009 and 2012 respectively, and Ms Rabinov died in 2021.

In her closing statement, counsel assisting the coroner Sian McGee said she held some hope that Mr Bryant's death could be solved because there were still some younger witnesses alive.

'Piecemeal' police investigation

During the inquest the court heard how police investigations lacked momentum since Mr Bryant was first reported missing.

At different stages since 1993, there have been years between any progress of inquiries, and police records from the early part of the investigation between January to June 1994 have gone missing.

There were also questions around why a key person of interest, Mr Ryan, was only interviewed once, in 1994.

In her findings, Judge Hosking told the court that the police investigation was "piecemeal and underwhelming".

She highlighted the delays and absence of specialist homicide investigators during the investigation, and flaws in pursuing interviews and inquiries into suspects such as Mr Ryan and Mr Renshaw.

Judge Hosking also said there was a lack of planning, continuity and oversight in the police investigation and a lack of record keeping.

But she said "it would be erroneous to judge police conduct [in 1994] by today's standards".

Missing man Stephen Bryant was last seen here on December 23, 1993. (Supplied: Google Earth)

In a statement to the court, Karen Bryant said her brother was always willing to help people.

"My brother was an exceptionally good-looking man with a quiet likeable demeanour and people who knew him appreciated that," she said.

Ms Bryant said her brother always wanted to be accepted and got in with the wrong crowd.

The coroner extended her condolences to the Bryant family.

World.title: 'Massive win' for Australia as Solomon Islands scraps China security deal
World.content:
Solomon Islands has told China it is scrapping its controversial 2022 security pact, as the Pacific Island nation prepares to sign a sweeping near billion-dollar treaty with Australia.

The move, described by one analyst as a "massive win" for Australia, comes as Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale landed in Canberra on Tuesday afternoon ahead of a signing ceremony for the new treaty on Wednesday.

Mr Wale, who came to power in May, had already flagged his government would "review" the contentious 2022 pact, which allows China to rotate its police training teams in Solomon Islands, with about two dozen permanent Chinese police in the country at one time.

Matthew Wale was given the red carpet treatment after touching down in Canberra on Tuesday. (ABC News)

On Tuesday afternoon, Nine Newspapers reported that Solomon Islands had "recently" informed China it would pull out of the pact.

The ABC has now confirmed through sources that Mr Wale's government informed Beijing that it will not renew the security agreement when it comes to the end of its five-year duration in April next year.

The ABC has contacted the Solomon Islands government, the Chinese Embassy in Solomon Islands and the Australian government for comment.

'Massive win' for Australia

Foreign Minister Penny Wong called the 2022 agreement, which was inked during the Morrison government's tenure, as Australia's "worst foreign policy blunder in the Pacific since the end of World War II".

Former Solomon Islands Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare signed the country's 2022 agreement with China. (Reuters)

Australia has long feared that China is using policing as a way of gaining a security foothold in the Pacific, and the Albanese government has said it is in a "permanent contest" with China in the region.

In her major foreign policy address to the Senate on Tuesday. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia had since offered "reliability and credibility" Pacific partners.

"We have offered partnership that is enduring, that is practical, that is respectful, that strengthens Pacific regionalism to answer the region's challenges," she said.

Lowy Institute Pacific Islands program director Oliver Nobetau described news of the scrapping of the China-Solomon Islands deal as a "massive win" for Australia.

"Getting Solomon Islands to turn their backs on China has been the holy grail of all the Pacific engagement under the Albanese government," Mr Nobetau said.

"But it begs the question: what has Australia offered to Matthew Wale to backtrack on this, has Australia offered something really significant here that we're not aware of?

"I think there must be a very big carrot on offer."

Earlier this month, the ABC reported Australian government budget assistance money meant for cyclone recovery and fuel shock assistance had been filtered into the accounts of Solomon Islands government MPs for special grants, known as constituency development funds.

Solomon Islands accuses Australia of 'chequebook diplomacy' The Solomon Islands opposition accuses Australia of "chequebook diplomacy" after Prime Minister Matthew Wale funnelled budget support from Canberra into constituency funds for government MPs.

Mr Wale is in Canberra, bringing with him a 24-strong delegation on a special chartered flight from Honiara — paid for by the Australian government — ahead of Wednesday's signing of the treaty.

The exact details of the treaty have not yet been officially released, but the ABC confirmed last month Australia will funnel $980 million in additional funding into the Pacific nation.

Leaked texts accessed by the ABC revealed $142 million would be allocated for Mr Wale's signature "free education" policy and $47.8 million to provide "visa improvements" and deal with "security requests from Solomon Islands".

Anna Powles, an associate professor in security studies at Massey University, who shared photographs in 2022 on social media of a leaked draft of the China-Solomon Islands security deal, said the move was "significant" and could potentially move the whole region in a different direction.

"It sends a strong signal about Solomon Islands foreign policy alignment under Matthew Wale and it ties Solomon Islands closer to Australia," she said.

Australia and Solomon Islands agree to new treaty Australia and Solomon Islands have reached an in-principle agreement over a new treaty.

On Monday, Solomon Islands Opposition Leader and former prime minister Manasseh Sogavare — the main architect of the 2022 agreement with China — said he believed Mr Wale was preparing to ditch the pact, which he warned could undermine ties with China.

"The country must carefully consider what it stands to lose from such a decision," he said on Monday.

Mr Nobateu warned that Mr Wale, who has already faced one motion of no confidence, was likely to face challenges in Honiara.

"He will have to be very confident that he can stay in power by doing this," he said.

"He's picking a side here, and for Australia, it's good. But it could lead to another challenge."

World.title: Drones, protests and new legal powers — what is in the new defence bill?
World.content:
Significant new legal powers to better protect Australia's defence bases have been quickly pushed through parliament, attracting some controversy in the process.

The laws respond to longstanding concerns within the government and Defence that some of Australia's most sensitive defence bases are under-protected, particularly against drones.

But the changes come with remarkable new powers, including the ability to make almost anywhere a temporary "defence zone" and to make almost anyone a "defence security official".

The changes sailed through parliament with the opposition's support, but have drawn criticism from some independents, legal experts, unions and academics.

They point to the possibility of misuse or overreach, and worry the powers could be used to crack down on legitimate protest.

They also argue the bill is massive, running to hundreds of pages, with parliament given just days to scrutinise it.

Anyone entering a special defence zone, like the joint US-Australia spy base Pine Gap, could face up to seven years in prison. (Four Corners)

The government argues that in a more dangerous and uncertain world, new powers are needed to protect Australia's national security infrastructure.

Extraordinary national security powers often draw criticism about overreach, but the government points to oversight mechanisms designed to prevent misuse.

Defence bases and defence 'zones'

The changes will not immediately mean much at most bases, but Defence argues the laws provide the capacity to respond to growing concerns about the security of Australia's defence bases.

One of the primary concerns is drones. Earlier this year, drones breached airspace over RAAF Base Williamtown, home to most of Australia's F-35 fighter jets.

There has been a surge in drone incidents at bases over the past few years, from fewer than two dozen reported in 2022-23 to 246 since the middle of last year.

Other air force bases, such as RAAF Base Darwin, have experienced security breaches in just the past few months.

The new laws dramatically expand the powers of Defence personnel to take down drones over their airfields.

Defence is concerned about drone incursions on bases. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

But they go much further than that in a few different ways.

One is the declaration of new "defence security zones", a power held specifically by the defence minister.

These new zones could, in theory, be just about anywhere, described in a parliamentary committee report as "an area of land in Australia, the sea, seabed and subsoil in or adjacent to Australia, airspace (excluding outer space) in or adjacent to Australia; a place, building or structure in Australia".

Essentially, it gives Defence the flexibility to protect its operations wherever they might be, such as training exercises, testing or manufacturing sensitive technology.

There is a requirement within the legislation to consult with anyone "reasonably likely" to be impacted by the declaration.

But it is effectively meaningless, as the minister's decision stands even if that consultation does not happen.

Anyone who enters a defence zone without permission could get two years in prison.

If it is a "special" defence zone, like Pine Gap or the Woomera testing range, the penalty is up to seven years.

Necessary flexibility or executive overreach?

The government argues defence zones are a necessary power to provide the flexibility to protect ADF operations wherever they are needed.

In a statement, a government spokesperson pushed back on criticism these powers could be misused.

"The bill does not give the defence minister power to turn almost anything into a security zone, or declare zones over arbitrary locations," they said.

"It must be based on the existence of a defence capability, activity or security requirement."

David Pocock criticised the speed and content of the bill. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

But critics of the bill argue the legislation is so broad it could be applied in a remarkably large number of ways.

Independent senator David Pocock has criticised both the bill itself and its hasty progression through the parliament.

"This is so broad it could be used for anything," he said.

"It could be used around AUKUS bases; it could be used around data centres, anywhere really where the government — or potentially at the request of the United States or someone else who's doing things here — the defence minister could just say, 'Right, no Australians can go to this place.'

"And if they do, if they protest, we can slap you with up to seven years in jail."

The bill does contain protections around the right to protest, with specific provisions stating that action cannot be taken against a person simply for protesting, unless there was a risk of serious harm to people or property.

But those provisions have been criticised by groups like the Maritime Union, who argue they contain too many loopholes.

Critics of the bill say it could be used to limit legitimate protest. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

During the brief parliamentary inquiry into the bill, a senior Defence official suggested the laws could be used to try and manage protests at events like the Land Forces defence expo.

These expos tend to attract significant protests and, as a result, a major police presence.

Defence later clarified that events like Land Forces would not meet the test for a new defence security zone.

"The bill is not intended to support the routine declaration of Defence Security Zones for general industry conferences or exhibitions … the presence of Defence personnel, assets or equipment at an event would not, of itself, satisfy [the] threshold."

Greens leader David Shoebridge argues the bill is still much too far-reaching.

"This legislation is going to war against democracy; it's going to war against our own civil rights," he said.

Criticism of speedy process

The bill was introduced to parliament on October 27, and passed (with amendments) less than a month later.

Because it had the opposition's support, the government had the numbers it needed in both chambers to stop attempts to slow its progress.

But the timeline has drawn criticism from figures like constitutional lawyer Anne Twomey, who argues it is complex legislation that needed more time.

"It is not an appropriate level of scrutiny, particularly for a bill of this kind, that does some serious things," she said.

Anne Twomey says the bill did not face sufficient scrutiny. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

"It makes significant criminal offences in relation to dealing with defence areas — and that is fine, we should have those offences — but there are also a lot of slippery definitions about mobile defence zones, emergency defence zones and special defence zones, that are not in ordinary places where a defence facility is.

"There could be areas that you just don't know [is] a defence zone, and yet you are doing something in that zone that causes you to commit a criminal offence.

" There is discussion that needs to be had around the edges of this, what the definitions are, how far they go. It went through far too quickly, and that is what people are concerned about. "

The bill has also come under scrutiny for the creation of new "defence security officials".

The new Defence officials will have a range of powers to protect defence zones, including to arrest and detain people, request identification, and search people where required.

The laws give Defence personnel more power to take down drones. (ABC Newcastle: Ross McLoughlin)

Defence says it does not want to duplicate the police force, and Defence security officials will not be tasked with carrying out the ordinary work of police.

Anyone taking on the role will have to meet minimum training and qualifications requirements, similar to military police or air force security roles.

Australian Federal Police officers would also take on the powers, where they are tasked with providing security at sensitive bases like HMAS Stirling in WA.

Defence says there is still work to do to establish how the new officials will be appointed and what sort of training they will undergo.

There have been suggestions from some, including senators Shoebridge and Pocock, that the bill would allow American officials to be appointed as Defence security officials.

But the government has pushed back, arguing that it is clearly ruled out in the new laws.

"Foreign defence personnel, including from the United States, cannot be given the powers that apply in Defence Security Zones," a spokesperson said.

Oversight of the new laws

The new laws do come with a layer of oversight to ensure the significant new powers are not misused.

The task primarily falls to the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force (IGADF), essentially the independent office that oversees all of Defence's activities here and abroad.

It is probably best known for the Afghanistan Inquiry, looking into allegations of war crimes committed by Australians abroad.

The new laws have a layer of oversight. (Supplied: Department of Defence)

There are specific reporting rules in the laws ensuring that the IGADF is told when a new defence zone is created and why it is being done.

There is a role for the parliament too, particularly the joint committee on Defence, which has the capacity to hear classified evidence.

But that committee has been criticised by crossbenchers in the past, as its membership is made up only of Labor and Coalition MPs.

World.title: Business owner banned from employing migrants
World.content:
An Adelaide business owner has been banned from employing migrant workers for three years, with a union saying a public register of approved visa sponsors would help public oversight of potential worker exploitation.

Viet Quoc Mai, who operates the Mr Viet restaurant in Adelaide CBD, has this week been banned from employing temporary migrant workers.

The NSW-based operator of another hospitality group sanctioned in an unrelated exploitation case was also handed a similar ban.

In 2025, the Federal Court ordered Mai to pay back $407,546 owed to 36 underpaid workers. He and his wife were also ordered to pay a combined $395,000 in additional court penalties.

The court found the underpaid workers were casually employed, primarily international students from Vietnam, and in some cases were paid as little as $15 per hour.

Wages owed ranged from $75 to $58,592, according to the Fair Work Ombudsman.

Mai is now listed on the government's Prohibited Employer Register and will be unable to employ migrant workers until his ban ends on November 19, 2029.

Public oversight register to help transparency

In May, a report published by the Migrant Justice Institute found two thirds of migrant workers could be underpaid, and that international students could be collectively underpaid more than $3.1 billion annually.

More than a third may also be paid below the national minimum wage, the report found.

The Department of Home Affairs recently released new resources for employers and migrant workers, including multilingual guides on reporting worker exploitation and on how to access help.

John Taylor, Commander of Field Operations and Sponsor Monitoring at the Australian Border Force (ABF), said his officers were "actively identifying and investigating employers who are doing the wrong thing, and those who exploit migrant workers should be on notice".

The ABF said it continues to investigate cases of potential migrant worker exploitation. (AAP: Dan Peled)

SA Unions want the federal government to expedite the introduction of transparency and public oversight measures, such as a register of approved worker visa sponsors as provided for in anti-exploitation legislation that took effect in October.

That legislation allows a register to be published listing approved sponsors, their ABN and postcode, the number of sponsored workers and their occupations.

A spokesperson said SA Unions was "looking forward to Home Affairs using these new powers to make a public register a reality".

"A public register which increases transparency around which employers are sponsoring migrant workers, and in which roles, will be an important resource for making sure workplace rights information and assistance can get to where it’s needed most," the spokesperson said.

ABC News has approached Mr Mai for comment.

World.title: Man accused of child abuse and drug offences in remote community
World.content:
Crown prosecutors have received an initial brief of evidence from NT police on a 48-year-old man accused of a string of child abuse and drug offences in a remote community west of Katherine.

The long list of charges detailed by police included "production, possession of child abuse material" and six separate counts of grooming.

There are also charges of indecent exposure, supplying drugs and "conduct to procure a child".

The charges involve at least one child under 14 years old and one in the 14- to 15-year-old age bracket.

The matter was briefly mentioned in Katherine Local Court today, with the prosecution given a deadline in January to serve a brief to defence lawyers.

The 48-year-old man appeared in Katherine Local Court this week. (ABC News: James Elton)

The man, whose identity has been suppressed to protect the identities of his alleged victims, has been remanded in custody, with his next appearance slated for February.

Police continue investigation

In a statement last week, Detective Senior Sergeant Michael Ordelman said police believed there had been "wide-ranging sexual misconduct to procure, groom and indecently expose children, with elements of supplying dangerous drugs to facilitate those activities".

The initial set of charges related to events over a roughly one-year period between October 2025 and November this year, which came to police attention via a tip-off on November 5.

The detective praised the assistance provided by members of the community in the Victoria Daly region — which has not been specifically named — saying the police "relied heavily on good people" in "isolated locations".

"The collaborative and discreet preliminary investigation will now broaden to focus on any potential additional children [and] continued engagement and support for those who have been impacted," Senior Sergeant Ordelman said.

Police would also "forensically examine multiple storage devices".

"Operation Helldiver has been established and is likely to reveal further offences relating to child abuse material and sexual misconduct," he said.

"That includes those responsible for engaging in, recording or distributing such content."

Senior Sergeant Ordelman said this served as a reminder for parents and caregivers to "be aware of what children are participating in on their devices".

"Police are hopeful others will be encouraged to come forward and are pursuing avenues to identify all involved individuals," he said.

World.title: Massive illegal fishing bust in northern waters alarms industry
World.content:
Border officials say a massive illegal fishing bust made in Australia's northern waters could potentially be the largest apprehension of its kind in the nation's history.

A foreign fishing vessel allegedly carrying more than 25 tonnes of fish product was apprehended by the Australian Border Force (ABF) on the Arafura Sea last week.

The crew was taken to Darwin for further investigation.

ABF said it could be the biggest apprehension of its kind ever, as the boat was allegedly equipped with commercial-scale fishing equipment, such as a gillnet, and advanced navigational systems.

It is suspected to have been operating illegally within Australia's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the Arafura Sea.

ABF said officers boarded the foreign boat following a "pursuit" at sea, which took authorities outside the EEZ and into international waters.

A map of the Australian Fishing Zone showing where fishing is allowed in the Timor and Arafura seas. (Supplied: Australian Fisheries Management Authority)

While charges have not been laid, ABF Deputy Commander Ranjeev Maharaj said the seizure represented "a significant operational outcome".

"This vessel is a sophisticated commercial fishing platform capable of spending extended periods at sea and harvesting industrial-scale quantities of marine resources," he said.

"Unlike the smaller illegal foreign fishing vessels more commonly encountered in northern Australia, this vessel was capable of extended offshore operations, carrying large quantities of catch and supporting commercial-scale fishing activity."

Authorities say the foreign crew failed to comply with directions to stop. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

An escalating issue

Grant Barker from Northern Wildcatch Seafood has been fishing in Australia's far northern waters for over 20 years and said the scale of the vessel and its alleged activity was "next level" and a real concern.

"It's quite an alarming step-up in terms of sophistication of vessel and catching efficiency," he said.

"This boat is next level and the first time we've seen a boat with this sort of power in our waters."

Grant Barker has been commercially fishing in Australia's northern waters for more than 20 years. (ABC Landline: Chris Lewis)

Mr Barker said he had seen other foreign fishing vessels take only "a few hundred kilograms" of fish product from Australian waters.

"To actually catch a boat with 25 tonnes of product on board is a big step up and big move by whoever is behind this and financing [this vessel]," he said.

Mr Barker said he recently encountered six motorised foreign fishing vessels near Browse Island, 450 kilometres off the coast from Broome.

He said the incursion of foreign boats was likely impacting fish stocks.

"I think [authorities] are doing a very good job trying to get on top of this, but it would be good to see the Commonwealth government get behind them with some serious funding, because it just gets worse year on year," he said.

"And one of the big issue is our penalties are too soft.

"They should be burning every single vessel they catch in our waters, and the guys on the boats should be jailed."

The foreign fishing vessel pictured alongside two Cape-class patrol boats operated by Border Force and the Navy. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

A joint media statement published by Border Force and the Australian Fisheries Management Authority (AFMA) said the vessel's "disposal" would be determined in accordance with Australian law.

The ABC understands the boat is currently moored in Darwin Harbour.

AFMA was contacted for comment.

World.title: Man acquitted of murdering Melbourne photographer due to psychotic illness
World.content:
A man who bashed a veteran photographer to death has been acquitted of murder because of his psychotic illness.

Victorian Supreme Court Justice Jacinta Forbes handed down the verdict of not guilty by mental impairment on Tuesday.

YF, as he is known for legal reasons, attacked veteran photographer Dominic O'Brien, 62, at an outdoor mall in Footscray in Melbourne's west on the morning of June 15, 2025.

He knocked Mr O'Brien to the ground and stomped on his head 11 times, causing catastrophic head injuries.

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander crisis support line 13YARN on 13 92 76

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

O'Brien, whose work spanned multiple news organisations, including The Age, AAP, Reuters and The Australian, died six days later in hospital.

YF was released from immigration detention in December 2023 after the High Court ruled indefinite detention of prisoners was unlawful.

He was subjected to monitoring, with Australian Border Force officers witnessing the attack as they were tracking him at the time.

When YF was arrested, he falsely accused Mr O'Brien of rape and claimed the other man had attacked him.

Two medical experts agreed YF had a schizo-affective disorder and was experiencing psychotic symptoms at the time of Mr O'Brien's death.

YF was released from immigration detention after a High Court ruling. (ABC News: Gregory Nelson)

Those symptoms included hallucinations and delusions, forensic psychiatrist Rajan Darjee told the court.

"It's clear he believed the victim had done something to him and was a threat to him," Dr Darjee said during a November 19 hearing.

" In my view, he attacked the victim as he did because of his symptoms — he believed all these things were real. "

YF first displayed psychotic symptoms as a young man in 2003 and he was subject to several involuntary treatment orders between his release in 2023 and arrest in 2025, the court heard.

YF had been overdue for his anti-psychotic medication injections at the time of the attack, forensic psychiatrist Mark Ryan told the court.

But his condition was resistant to treatment and he was still psychotic three months after the alleged murder, even though he was medicated in custody, Dr Ryan said.

In delivering her verdict on Tuesday, Justice Forbes accepted YF had attacked O'Brien as a direct result of his paranoia.

His psychotic symptoms had been present for more than two decades and were enduring even with treatment, the judge said.

Justice Forbes also noted YF's circumstances had been unstable and he had at times been turned away from treatment before Mr O'Brien's death.

She handed down the verdict of not guilty by reason of mental impairment and directed that YF be liable to supervision.

The exact orders of his supervision will be made at a later date.

AAP

World.title: WA councils face an ‘unsustainable gap’. Could it be the source of their woes?
World.content:
NationalWALocal government WA councils face an ‘unsustainable gap’. Could it be the source of their woes? Indigo Lemay-Conway November 24, 2026 — 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As councils across Perth contemplate amalgamations, Western Australia’s peak local government body isn’t convinced “putting a couple of them together” will solve anything. Instead, as part of WALGA’s 2027-28 state budget submission, they’re calling on the government to undertake an independent review of local government responsibilities, functions and funding. WALGA president Mark Irwin and deputy president Chris Antonio. Indigo Lemay-Conway The submission says that in response to population growth, demographic shifts and rising community expectations, “the sector’s role has incrementally expanded and is now significantly beyond its traditional remit”. “Today, local governments are routinely funding and delivering services – including support for healthcare, childcare, housing, community services, airports and local economic development – to address critical market gaps left by other levels of government and the private sector,” the submission reads.



“Crucially, the sector’s funding arrangements have not evolved to match these expanded responsibilities. “Local governments continue to rely heavily on rates and user charges to fund this widening scope of work even as the demand and cost of delivering core infrastructure escalate. “This has created an unsustainable gap between state policy objectives, community expectations and the actual resources available to councils.” WALGA president Mark Irwin said ratepayers often don’t know what tier of government handles community services and even council members are starting to get lost when making decisions. “The stories we’re hearing [from councillors] are about increased expectations on their delivery of community safety programs, the increase in cost of doing business to provide community infrastructure for children playing sport,” he said.



“Many things that are happening right throughout our state, most people wouldn’t even have an understanding that local governments are responsible for them. Related Article Local council State government and coastal council clash over who pays $100,000 for merger study “Almost 90 per cent of our road network is under the care and control of local governments. The emergency services provision of volunteer fire brigades right throughout Western Australia, the GP services in our communities, the economic development contributions they make.” Irwin said WALGA would like to see the independent review commence at the start of the next financial year and would be a great first project for the proposed 2050 Commission – a new productivity commission created to strengthen the state’s economy and delivery of public services. But he believes it should happen in conjunction of investigations into amalgamations and not after.



“The reality is, you can’t have a solution to a problem you don’t know what it is. That body of work will understand the scope of all of those projects, all of the services that our local governments provide,” he said. “It can have a look at what those sticking points are and what the actual big problems in local government in sustainability are. “But until we have an understanding of what local governments are delivering right throughout our state, what it costs to deliver them, and how they’re delivering it, I find it hard to believe that putting a couple of them together is going to be a solution to anything.” Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Irwin addressed local government dysfunction across Perth and the negative connotations around council monitors. “The monitors were seen as a real positive from the sector. There is no reason that local governments shouldn’t have access to skill sets to be able to assist them to provide good governance for their districts,” he said.



“It is unreasonable to expect that when you grab 12 people untrained from their community and sit them around the table and tell them to fight for what they believe in and fight for their community under that increasing pressure and expectation, that there won’t sometimes be conflict, especially when all of those conversations are live-streamed. Related Article City life Sex, planning and the city: Adult store owner lashes Perth council’s ‘poor governance’ after second rejection “The monitor is supposed to assist that. It shouldn’t be negative.” He said that 90 of the 139 councils have had some interaction with Local Government Inspector Tony Brown this year. “The inspector’s role is to interact with local governments. [But] to say the absolute majority of local governments are dysfunctional, the inspector having a relationship with the local government isn’t a sign of dysfunction,” he said.



“It’s a sign of the regulator doing their job, and it’s a sign of 139 local governments who are operating in an increasingly complex legislative environment, trying to work out what they should be doing under the element of reform, which has been going on for a number of years now.” Other key priorities in the WALGA submission include waste management, rural and remote health, emergency management and roads. They are requesting the state government invest $350,000 to develop a state waste infrastructure plan and $41.1 million to clear the backlog of unfunded capital grant requests for emergency management. Almost $10 million per annum from 2027-28 to establish a local government primary healthcare support fund for the regions and commit to fully funding the $250 million regional road safety program to improve regional roads if the federal government contribution is not secured.

World.title: Liberals vow to shut Richmond safe injecting room
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian election Liberals vow to shut Richmond safe injecting room Patrick Hatch November 24, 2026 — 6:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victoria’s only safe injection room would be permanently closed under a Coalition government, with Opposition Leader Jess Wilson confirming she does not intend to open an alternative facility elsewhere in the state. An independent review found the medically supervised injecting room in North Richmond has been successful in reducing heroin-related deaths, safely managing nearly 650,000 visits and more than 12,000 overdoses without a single fatality at the facility. The medically supervised injecting room in Richmond (pictured) has been operating since 2018. Penny Stephens But its location next to Richmond West Primary School has made it a lightning rod for controversy, with residents citing concerns about antisocial behaviour and discarded syringes nearby. The Coalition has long wanted to move the facility and in 2023 called for laws to ban injecting rooms within 250 metres of schools.



Wilson said on Tuesday the Coalition would shut down the North Richmond facility if it forms government after Saturday’s election. Related Article Exclusive

City life Injecting room admits failure to address community concerns “I’ve heard from families … with kids at that school that they turn up there in the morning and there are people shooting up outside a primary school. It’s unacceptable,” she said. Asked at a press conference if Victoria should have any safe injecting rooms, Wilson said: “That is not our policy. Our policy is to look at how we can provide that break of drug addiction.” When asked if the facility had saved lives, Wilson said that was “a matter for the community health facility”.



Wilson said instead of the safe injecting facility, the Liberals would focus on providing access to hydromorphone, a relatively new treatment for people dependent on heroin or other opioids. Related Article Victorian election The Liberal Party’s secret election weapon: One Nation and Labor voters The Department of Health is preparing to launch a trial of hydromorphone at Flinders Street Health in the CBD next year, which Labor announced after rejecting expert advice to open a second supervised injecting room in the CBD. Victorian Alcohol and Drug Association acting chief executive Scott Drummond said that with 632 fatal overdoses in Victoria last year, now was not the time to shut down a service that was saving lives. “There is an assumption that should it be closed down, that drug use will go away. If it does [close down], drug use will go elsewhere and the harms will continue to increase,” Drummond said.



“If the Coalition is committed to not opening other supervised injecting rooms, that would be a concern to us, but we would also like to understand what they propose to do instead.” An independent evaluation in 2023 found the facility had saved an estimated 63 lives – or 16 every year – while also reducing the spread of blood-borne diseases like hepatitis C and linking drug users to health and social support services. The evaluation noted community concern about drug use, discarded syringes and antisocial behaviour near the facility. A Monash University and Turning Point study published in July this year found heroin-related ambulance call-outs in Richmond fell from around 48 each month when the centre opened to 36 a month by December 2023.

World.title: Trump’s Nvidia intervention confuses foreign policy and private gain
World.content:
November 24, 2026 — 5:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

President Donald Trump turning a blind eye to his intelligence agencies’ reports that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang was having an affair with a Chinese spy sits uncomfortably with Australia’s AUKUS security partnership with the United Kingdom and the United States. The pact exists primarily to counter China’s growing military modernisation and regional influence in the Indo-Pacific. Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Washington on October 8. AP Trump has been urging America to stay ahead of China on AI, but he pushed for Huang’s reinstatement even though his administration was informed the tech boss’s paramour, Alice Huang, had been in touch with an official of Beijing’s Ministry of State Security. She was chief executive of a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that acquired huge volumes of Nvidia’s most advanced chips and deployed them in data centres in South-East Asia, where Chinese companies may have used them to train their artificial intelligence models. Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling some chips directly to China in breach of US export controls.



Also muddying the water, Trump holds shares in Nvidia through his investment accounts and trust structure, and has reportedly bought and sold the AI company stock with a combined transaction value of up to $US100 million. The value of his Nvidia stock rose $US15 million on Monday’s Huang news. As his stocks roared back into life, Trump immediately took credit for Huang’s rehabilitation. “I’ve been speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly,” he said. “I believe my intervention was very important.” Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs – in his case temporarily – over personal misconduct. But by pandering to another philandering rich man, Trump has saddled his presidency with an enduring problem. A social media post by Donald Trump shortly after Jensen Huang was reinstated. The AI-generated image references the assassination attempt on Trump in 2024. TruthSocial The perception of corruption heavily influenced voters in this month’s midterm elections. The result should have been enough to give Trump pause for thought, but he ambled on. For good measure, he even stooped to posting an insouciant meme on Truth Social depicting Huang holding up a red bra, parodying a photograph of the Pennsylvania assassination attempt on Trump in July 2024.



Now, as the Herald’s North America correspondent Michael Koziol reports, a rabid US Congress, including many Republicans who are absolutely incensed by what has transpired, means the Nvidia scandal could consume the administration in its remaining two years. Related Article Updated

AI Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after direct lobbying by Trump Trump’s presidencies are synonymous with feints and retreats. But this time he has overstepped. Trump has also trashed corporate independence and created confusion about governance and the reputational risks facing companies dealing with conduct unbecoming. As a president who spent much of his time in office attacking China, he prevailed on the board to reverse its decision about its CEO and his liaison with a suspected modern-day Mata Hari. His myopia has ramifications for Australia too.



Nvidia’s technology already reaches the Australian Department of Defence. The corporation’s involvement with Western governments and aerospace companies carries the potential to compromise defence systems. Trump’s bundling together of foreign policy and private gain has resulted in a horrifying and dangerous debacle. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: CFMEU official cleared of death threats, police chief intervened in probe
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCFMEU CFMEU official cleared of death threats, police chief intervened in probe Cameron Houston and Erin Pearson November 24, 2026 — 5:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The high-profile case against a CFMEU official accused of making death threats has failed, amid evidence that the former police chief intervened in the investigation and instructed officers to raid his home at 5am. Melbourne Magistrates’ Court heard Joel Shackleton, 41, was home with his three young children when major crime detectives arrived before dawn to question him about alleged threats made in March 2022 at a building site in Clyde North. Joel Shackleton leaving the Melbourne Magistrates Court. PENNY STEPHENS Shackleton, a Koori organiser for the CFMEU, was charged with three offences in September 2024 over alleged threats to kill Danny Miller, who was managing director of Indigenous labour-hire firm Marda Dandhi. A video played in court showed Shackleton telling Miller: “I’ll f---ing take your soul and rip your f---ing head off.”



Shackleton’s barrister Jason Gullaci, SC, described the case as “politically motivated” and baseless, before asking Magistrate Simon Zebrowski to throw out the charges. Gullaci said the interaction was part of a protracted dispute between the pair, which had been inflamed when Shackleton’s mother was contacted by an associate of Miller regarding the workplace feud. On Monday, Miller told the court he was intimidated and traumatised by the alleged threats from Shackleton, who had previously told him that his firm would not have its enterprise bargaining agreement renewed by the union. “He told me to f--- off and go back to Sydney where you belong, and you will never get an EBA,” Miller told the court. Zebrowski was highly critical of the prosecution case, repeatedly standing the hearing down to allow for private discussions between the parties.



Under cross-examination from Shackleton’s defence barrister, Detective Senior Constable Branka Jurilj agreed the trigger for the charges, two years after they allegedly occurred, was the airing of a video on 60 Minutes in July 2024 as part of the Building Bad series with The Age. Those articles revealed that Miller raised a complaint about the incident with then-minister Jacinta Allan and then-premier Daniel Andrews. Loading Allan responded a year later, saying industrial relations and subcontractor selection were contractor responsibilities. The project’s builder raised the matter with the state infrastructure authority but no action was taken. The failed prosecution, which also comes after an unsuccessful blackmail case against bikie Joel Leavitt and a fraud case that ended without a conviction against controversial company BK Labour Hire, further demonstrates the difficulty law enforcement has faced in its efforts to clean up Victoria’s building industry.



Jurilj agreed pressure had been put on investigating officers, by command, to take action, with diary notes revealing she’d been told the arrest must take place when it did, before Shackleton had left for work. “Matter needs to be resolved by end of the week per Chief Commissioner’s instructions,” Jurilj wrote in her diary. The chief commissioner at the time was Shane Patton, who resigned in February 2025 after more than 45 years with the force. Jurilj conceded it was unusual for the chief commissioner to become involved in a matter regarding threats in a workplace. She also confirmed that on September 4, 2024, she pushed back and advised that it would be more appropriate to arrest Shackleton, who has no criminal history, by appointment.



On Tuesday, Zebrowski struck out one charge of making a threat to kill, while finding the other two charges had not been proven. “No doubt the language is violent and colourful and on first blush could be viewed as threatening. But this is a court of law, not a court of morals and certainly not a court of etiquette,” Zebrowski said. He ordered Victoria Police to pay Shackleton’s legal costs. Shackleton and another official are still facing Federal Court action by the Fair Work Ombudsman over the incident. The workplace regulator claims the CFMEU pair breached laws on industrial coercion.

World.content:

An 80-year-old woman spent eight days in hospital after being bitten by a dog in the office of Wynnum Manly councillor Alex Givney, a meeting of Brisbane City Council has been told. The shocking claim came to light on Tuesday afternoon as Labor leader Jared Cassidy asked the lord mayor what investigation was under way into the matter. The victim, a representative of the local Quota Club, met with Givney in her office earlier this month as part of the local Australia Day Organising Committee. LNP councillor Alex Givney with her dog, Tillie, in her Wynnum Manly ward office in 2024. Facebook “After that meeting had concluded, Councillor Givney’s dog bit this constituent without warning and drew blood. The dog was unrestrained at the time,” Cassidy said.



“The victim sought medical care that afternoon, and the next morning was referred to the Mater Hospital for emergency care, where she stayed for serious treatment for eight nights.” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said he was not aware of the allegation but was happy to have it investigated. The woman said she spent eight days in hospital after the dog attack. “Obviously, the claims that have been made are serious, and as we investigate any kind of dog bite or situation such as this, we will absolutely take this very seriously and investigate,” he said. Cassidy said Givney responded to the dog attack by telling the victim: “It’s never bitten a woman before, only men.”



Later on Tuesday, Givney released a statement saying she had been trying to reach the constituent to apologise personally. “I’m so sorry this happened and can only imagine how frightening and upsetting it must have been for the community member involved,” she said. Alex Givney with her dog, Tillie. Councillor Alex Givney's Facebook page “As a dog owner, I know it is my responsibility to make sure others feel safe around my dog. “I take full responsibility for my obligations as a dog owner and just want the woman involved to know how genuinely sorry I am.”



Labor distributed photographs of the victim’s injuries, and a copy of her complaint, which was emailed to the Brisbane City Council chief executive on Monday, November 23. The victim also contacted the council call centre on Monday, and council officers were in contact within about three hours. In the email complaint, the victim formally requested that the matter be investigated “independently, impartially and transparently”. “It is essential that the investigation is conducted without any actual or perceived conflict of interest, and that Councillor Givney has no involvement in determining how the complaint is investigated or resolved,” she wrote. “At 80 years of age, I should be able to attend a meeting with my elected local representative without fearing for my personal safety. No member of the public, regardless of their age, should be exposed to such a risk when visiting a council office.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Accused double murderer ‘was not broken down’ by cross-examination, defence says
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial Accused double murderer ‘was not broken down’ by cross-examination, defence says Michaela Whitbourn November 24, 2026 — 5:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Accused killer Beau Lamarre-Condon was “not broken down” over six days of cross-examination and the jury should accept his testimony as truthful, his barrister has submitted in his criminal trial. Defence barrister John Stratton, SC, concluded his closing address on Tuesday in the NSW former police officer’s trial over the alleged murders of Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon during Justice Natalie Adams’ summing up. Rocco Fazzari NSW Supreme Court Justice Natalie Adams delivered a summing up to the jury after the conclusion of Stratton’s address. On Wednesday, the court will conduct a ballot to reduce the number of jurors from 15 to 12 before the jury retires for their deliberations.



Stratton told the jury that Lamarre-Condon could have told prosecutors, in effect: “Do your worst, see if you can prove this against me, but I’m not going to help you; I’m going to stay out of the witness box.” Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Judge delivers summing up to jury after defence closing Instead, in Stratton’s submission, the accused “took that long walk from where he is now to the witness box, and he did that voluntarily”. “He subjected himself to a detailed, fierce cross-examination by a very experienced Crown prosecutor … over six days,” he said. “My submission to you is that after that searching cross-examination by the Crown … he was not broken down.”



Stratton argued that “the Crown did not establish that he was telling you lies” and the jury should “accept his testimony as truthful”. Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Baird, 26, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024. The Crown alleges the former NSW police officer plotted to kill Baird after the former TV presenter ended their non-exclusive relationship in November 2023, and that he killed Davies to eliminate a witness. Beau Lamarre-Condon’s barrister, John Stratton, SC. George Chan The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon shot Baird in self-defence with his police-issued Glock pistol, and that Davies shot himself by accident after he grabbed the gun.



Lamarre-Condon testified that he went to Baird’s Paddington home to collect some of his belongings. He said he was disguised as an Uber Eats rider because he was concerned Baird might accuse him of harassment or seek an AVO if he saw him at the door. Stratton said the defence case was that the accused honestly believed he had to shoot Baird in self-defence. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial ‘Love makes fools of us all’: Defence closing address in Lamarre-Condon trial Lamarre-Condon testified that he shot Baird once in an attempt to disarm him after the former TV presenter lunged at him with a knife. He said a second shot, to Baird’s temple, was accidental as the men fell to the ground during a struggle. Stratton said that “the accused asks you to return a verdict of not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter” in relation to Baird’s death.



Adams said in her summing up to the jury that Lamarre-Condon was seeking to rely “on the partial defence of excessive self-defence, manslaughter” on that count. The judge said the Crown had to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Lamarre-Condon’s acts were not done in self-defence. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Rainbow Sexual, Domestic and Family Violence Hotline (1800 497 212) and Lifeline (13 11 14).

World.title: AFP ‘layered secrets upon secrets’ to conceal underworld figure’s illegal deportation, court told
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime AFP ‘layered secrets upon secrets’ to conceal underworld figure’s illegal deportation, court told Riley Walter November 24, 2026 — 5:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Australian Federal Police “layered secrets upon secrets” and concealed its involvement in the illegal deportation of Sydney underworld figure Masood Zakaria, the NSW Supreme Court has heard, as the alleged kingpin’s unprecedented legal challenge to have murder charges against him thrown out enters its final days. In her closing submissions on Tuesday, Zakaria’s barrister, Julia Roy, SC, told the court the AFP had tried to conceal the nature and extent of its involvement in Zakaria’s deportation – which prosecutors concede was illegal under Turkish law – and colluded with NSW Police to circumvent extradition and secure the 31-year-old’s return to Australia to face charges. Masood Zakaria was deported from Turkey in December 2023. Wolter Peeters Roy said the AFP had facilitated Zakaria’s deportation despite knowing it was unlawful because of his pending appeal against his removal from Turkey.
