World.title: WA councils face an ‘unsustainable gap’. Could it be the source of their woes?
World.content:
NationalWALocal government WA councils face an ‘unsustainable gap’. Could it be the source of their woes? Indigo Lemay-Conway November 24, 2026 — 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As councils across Perth contemplate amalgamations, Western Australia’s peak local government body isn’t convinced “putting a couple of them together” will solve anything. Instead, as part of WALGA’s 2027-28 state budget submission, they’re calling on the government to undertake an independent review of local government responsibilities, functions and funding. WALGA president Mark Irwin and deputy president Chris Antonio. Indigo Lemay-Conway The submission says that in response to population growth, demographic shifts and rising community expectations, “the sector’s role has incrementally expanded and is now significantly beyond its traditional remit”. “Today, local governments are routinely funding and delivering services – including support for healthcare, childcare, housing, community services, airports and local economic development – to address critical market gaps left by other levels of government and the private sector,” the submission reads.



“Crucially, the sector’s funding arrangements have not evolved to match these expanded responsibilities. “Local governments continue to rely heavily on rates and user charges to fund this widening scope of work even as the demand and cost of delivering core infrastructure escalate. “This has created an unsustainable gap between state policy objectives, community expectations and the actual resources available to councils.” WALGA president Mark Irwin said ratepayers often don’t know what tier of government handles community services and even council members are starting to get lost when making decisions. “The stories we’re hearing [from councillors] are about increased expectations on their delivery of community safety programs, the increase in cost of doing business to provide community infrastructure for children playing sport,” he said.



“Many things that are happening right throughout our state, most people wouldn’t even have an understanding that local governments are responsible for them. Related Article Local council State government and coastal council clash over who pays $100,000 for merger study “Almost 90 per cent of our road network is under the care and control of local governments. The emergency services provision of volunteer fire brigades right throughout Western Australia, the GP services in our communities, the economic development contributions they make.” Irwin said WALGA would like to see the independent review commence at the start of the next financial year and would be a great first project for the proposed 2050 Commission – a new productivity commission created to strengthen the state’s economy and delivery of public services. But he believes it should happen in conjunction of investigations into amalgamations and not after.



“The reality is, you can’t have a solution to a problem you don’t know what it is. That body of work will understand the scope of all of those projects, all of the services that our local governments provide,” he said. “It can have a look at what those sticking points are and what the actual big problems in local government in sustainability are. “But until we have an understanding of what local governments are delivering right throughout our state, what it costs to deliver them, and how they’re delivering it, I find it hard to believe that putting a couple of them together is going to be a solution to anything.” Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Irwin addressed local government dysfunction across Perth and the negative connotations around council monitors. “The monitors were seen as a real positive from the sector. There is no reason that local governments shouldn’t have access to skill sets to be able to assist them to provide good governance for their districts,” he said.



“It is unreasonable to expect that when you grab 12 people untrained from their community and sit them around the table and tell them to fight for what they believe in and fight for their community under that increasing pressure and expectation, that there won’t sometimes be conflict, especially when all of those conversations are live-streamed. Related Article City life Sex, planning and the city: Adult store owner lashes Perth council’s ‘poor governance’ after second rejection “The monitor is supposed to assist that. It shouldn’t be negative.” He said that 90 of the 139 councils have had some interaction with Local Government Inspector Tony Brown this year. “The inspector’s role is to interact with local governments. [But] to say the absolute majority of local governments are dysfunctional, the inspector having a relationship with the local government isn’t a sign of dysfunction,” he said.



“It’s a sign of the regulator doing their job, and it’s a sign of 139 local governments who are operating in an increasingly complex legislative environment, trying to work out what they should be doing under the element of reform, which has been going on for a number of years now.” Other key priorities in the WALGA submission include waste management, rural and remote health, emergency management and roads. They are requesting the state government invest $350,000 to develop a state waste infrastructure plan and $41.1 million to clear the backlog of unfunded capital grant requests for emergency management. Almost $10 million per annum from 2027-28 to establish a local government primary healthcare support fund for the regions and commit to fully funding the $250 million regional road safety program to improve regional roads if the federal government contribution is not secured.

World.title: Liberals vow to shut Richmond safe injecting room
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian election Liberals vow to shut Richmond safe injecting room Patrick Hatch November 24, 2026 — 6:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victoria’s only safe injection room would be permanently closed under a Coalition government, with Opposition Leader Jess Wilson confirming she does not intend to open an alternative facility elsewhere in the state. An independent review found the medically supervised injecting room in North Richmond has been successful in reducing heroin-related deaths, safely managing nearly 650,000 visits and more than 12,000 overdoses without a single fatality at the facility. The medically supervised injecting room in Richmond (pictured) has been operating since 2018. Penny Stephens But its location next to Richmond West Primary School has made it a lightning rod for controversy, with residents citing concerns about antisocial behaviour and discarded syringes nearby. The Coalition has long wanted to move the facility and in 2023 called for laws to ban injecting rooms within 250 metres of schools.



Wilson said on Tuesday the Coalition would shut down the North Richmond facility if it forms government after Saturday’s election. Related Article Exclusive

City life Injecting room admits failure to address community concerns “I’ve heard from families … with kids at that school that they turn up there in the morning and there are people shooting up outside a primary school. It’s unacceptable,” she said. Asked at a press conference if Victoria should have any safe injecting rooms, Wilson said: “That is not our policy. Our policy is to look at how we can provide that break of drug addiction.” When asked if the facility had saved lives, Wilson said that was “a matter for the community health facility”.



Wilson said instead of the safe injecting facility, the Liberals would focus on providing access to hydromorphone, a relatively new treatment for people dependent on heroin or other opioids. Related Article Victorian election The Liberal Party’s secret election weapon: One Nation and Labor voters The Department of Health is preparing to launch a trial of hydromorphone at Flinders Street Health in the CBD next year, which Labor announced after rejecting expert advice to open a second supervised injecting room in the CBD. Victorian Alcohol and Drug Association acting chief executive Scott Drummond said that with 632 fatal overdoses in Victoria last year, now was not the time to shut down a service that was saving lives. “There is an assumption that should it be closed down, that drug use will go away. If it does [close down], drug use will go elsewhere and the harms will continue to increase,” Drummond said.



“If the Coalition is committed to not opening other supervised injecting rooms, that would be a concern to us, but we would also like to understand what they propose to do instead.” An independent evaluation in 2023 found the facility had saved an estimated 63 lives – or 16 every year – while also reducing the spread of blood-borne diseases like hepatitis C and linking drug users to health and social support services. The evaluation noted community concern about drug use, discarded syringes and antisocial behaviour near the facility. A Monash University and Turning Point study published in July this year found heroin-related ambulance call-outs in Richmond fell from around 48 each month when the centre opened to 36 a month by December 2023.

World.title: CFMEU official cleared of death threats, police chief intervened in probe
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCFMEU CFMEU official cleared of death threats, police chief intervened in probe Cameron Houston and Erin Pearson November 24, 2026 — 5:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The high-profile case against a CFMEU official accused of making death threats has failed, amid evidence that the former police chief intervened in the investigation and instructed officers to raid his home at 5am. Melbourne Magistrates’ Court heard Joel Shackleton, 41, was home with his three young children when major crime detectives arrived before dawn to question him about alleged threats made in March 2022 at a building site in Clyde North. Joel Shackleton leaving the Melbourne Magistrates Court. PENNY STEPHENS Shackleton, a Koori organiser for the CFMEU, was charged with three offences in September 2024 over alleged threats to kill Danny Miller, who was managing director of Indigenous labour-hire firm Marda Dandhi. A video played in court showed Shackleton telling Miller: “I’ll f---ing take your soul and rip your f---ing head off.”



Shackleton’s barrister Jason Gullaci, SC, described the case as “politically motivated” and baseless, before asking Magistrate Simon Zebrowski to throw out the charges. Gullaci said the interaction was part of a protracted dispute between the pair, which had been inflamed when Shackleton’s mother was contacted by an associate of Miller regarding the workplace feud. On Monday, Miller told the court he was intimidated and traumatised by the alleged threats from Shackleton, who had previously told him that his firm would not have its enterprise bargaining agreement renewed by the union. “He told me to f--- off and go back to Sydney where you belong, and you will never get an EBA,” Miller told the court. Zebrowski was highly critical of the prosecution case, repeatedly standing the hearing down to allow for private discussions between the parties.



Under cross-examination from Shackleton’s defence barrister, Detective Senior Constable Branka Jurilj agreed the trigger for the charges, two years after they allegedly occurred, was the airing of a video on 60 Minutes in July 2024 as part of the Building Bad series with The Age. Those articles revealed that Miller raised a complaint about the incident with then-minister Jacinta Allan and then-premier Daniel Andrews. Loading Allan responded a year later, saying industrial relations and subcontractor selection were contractor responsibilities. The project’s builder raised the matter with the state infrastructure authority but no action was taken. The failed prosecution, which also comes after an unsuccessful blackmail case against bikie Joel Leavitt and a fraud case that ended without a conviction against controversial company BK Labour Hire, further demonstrates the difficulty law enforcement has faced in its efforts to clean up Victoria’s building industry.



Jurilj agreed pressure had been put on investigating officers, by command, to take action, with diary notes revealing she’d been told the arrest must take place when it did, before Shackleton had left for work. “Matter needs to be resolved by end of the week per Chief Commissioner’s instructions,” Jurilj wrote in her diary. The chief commissioner at the time was Shane Patton, who resigned in February 2025 after more than 45 years with the force. Jurilj conceded it was unusual for the chief commissioner to become involved in a matter regarding threats in a workplace. She also confirmed that on September 4, 2024, she pushed back and advised that it would be more appropriate to arrest Shackleton, who has no criminal history, by appointment.



On Tuesday, Zebrowski struck out one charge of making a threat to kill, while finding the other two charges had not been proven. “No doubt the language is violent and colourful and on first blush could be viewed as threatening. But this is a court of law, not a court of morals and certainly not a court of etiquette,” Zebrowski said. He ordered Victoria Police to pay Shackleton’s legal costs. Shackleton and another official are still facing Federal Court action by the Fair Work Ombudsman over the incident. The workplace regulator claims the CFMEU pair breached laws on industrial coercion.

An 80-year-old woman spent eight days in hospital after being bitten by a dog in the office of Wynnum Manly councillor Alex Givney, a meeting of Brisbane City Council has been told. The shocking claim came to light on Tuesday afternoon as Labor leader Jared Cassidy asked the lord mayor what investigation was under way into the matter. The victim, a representative of the local Quota Club, met with Givney in her office earlier this month as part of the local Australia Day Organising Committee. LNP councillor Alex Givney with her dog, Tillie, in her Wynnum Manly ward office in 2024. Facebook “After that meeting had concluded, Councillor Givney’s dog bit this constituent without warning and drew blood. The dog was unrestrained at the time,” Cassidy said.



“The victim sought medical care that afternoon, and the next morning was referred to the Mater Hospital for emergency care, where she stayed for serious treatment for eight nights.” Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said he was not aware of the allegation but was happy to have it investigated. The woman said she spent eight days in hospital after the dog attack. “Obviously, the claims that have been made are serious, and as we investigate any kind of dog bite or situation such as this, we will absolutely take this very seriously and investigate,” he said. Cassidy said Givney responded to the dog attack by telling the victim: “It’s never bitten a woman before, only men.”



Later on Tuesday, Givney released a statement saying she had been trying to reach the constituent to apologise personally. “I’m so sorry this happened and can only imagine how frightening and upsetting it must have been for the community member involved,” she said. Alex Givney with her dog, Tillie. Councillor Alex Givney's Facebook page “As a dog owner, I know it is my responsibility to make sure others feel safe around my dog. “I take full responsibility for my obligations as a dog owner and just want the woman involved to know how genuinely sorry I am.”



Labor distributed photographs of the victim’s injuries, and a copy of her complaint, which was emailed to the Brisbane City Council chief executive on Monday, November 23. The victim also contacted the council call centre on Monday, and council officers were in contact within about three hours. In the email complaint, the victim formally requested that the matter be investigated “independently, impartially and transparently”. “It is essential that the investigation is conducted without any actual or perceived conflict of interest, and that Councillor Givney has no involvement in determining how the complaint is investigated or resolved,” she wrote. “At 80 years of age, I should be able to attend a meeting with my elected local representative without fearing for my personal safety. No member of the public, regardless of their age, should be exposed to such a risk when visiting a council office.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Accused double murderer ‘was not broken down’ by cross-examination, defence says
World.content:
NationalNSWLamarre-Condon trial Accused double murderer ‘was not broken down’ by cross-examination, defence says Michaela Whitbourn November 24, 2026 — 5:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Accused killer Beau Lamarre-Condon was “not broken down” over six days of cross-examination and the jury should accept his testimony as truthful, his barrister has submitted in his criminal trial. Defence barrister John Stratton, SC, concluded his closing address on Tuesday in the NSW former police officer’s trial over the alleged murders of Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies. A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon during Justice Natalie Adams’ summing up. Rocco Fazzari NSW Supreme Court Justice Natalie Adams delivered a summing up to the jury after the conclusion of Stratton’s address. On Wednesday, the court will conduct a ballot to reduce the number of jurors from 15 to 12 before the jury retires for their deliberations.



Stratton told the jury that Lamarre-Condon could have told prosecutors, in effect: “Do your worst, see if you can prove this against me, but I’m not going to help you; I’m going to stay out of the witness box.” Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Judge delivers summing up to jury after defence closing Instead, in Stratton’s submission, the accused “took that long walk from where he is now to the witness box, and he did that voluntarily”. “He subjected himself to a detailed, fierce cross-examination by a very experienced Crown prosecutor … over six days,” he said. “My submission to you is that after that searching cross-examination by the Crown … he was not broken down.”



Stratton argued that “the Crown did not establish that he was telling you lies” and the jury should “accept his testimony as truthful”. Lamarre-Condon, 31, has pleaded not guilty to murdering Baird, 26, a former Network Ten producer and presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024. The Crown alleges the former NSW police officer plotted to kill Baird after the former TV presenter ended their non-exclusive relationship in November 2023, and that he killed Davies to eliminate a witness. Beau Lamarre-Condon’s barrister, John Stratton, SC. George Chan The defence case is that Lamarre-Condon shot Baird in self-defence with his police-issued Glock pistol, and that Davies shot himself by accident after he grabbed the gun.



Lamarre-Condon testified that he went to Baird’s Paddington home to collect some of his belongings. He said he was disguised as an Uber Eats rider because he was concerned Baird might accuse him of harassment or seek an AVO if he saw him at the door. Stratton said the defence case was that the accused honestly believed he had to shoot Baird in self-defence. Related Article Lamarre-Condon trial ‘Love makes fools of us all’: Defence closing address in Lamarre-Condon trial Lamarre-Condon testified that he shot Baird once in an attempt to disarm him after the former TV presenter lunged at him with a knife. He said a second shot, to Baird’s temple, was accidental as the men fell to the ground during a struggle. Stratton said that “the accused asks you to return a verdict of not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter” in relation to Baird’s death.



Adams said in her summing up to the jury that Lamarre-Condon was seeking to rely “on the partial defence of excessive self-defence, manslaughter” on that count. The judge said the Crown had to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Lamarre-Condon’s acts were not done in self-defence. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Rainbow Sexual, Domestic and Family Violence Hotline (1800 497 212) and Lifeline (13 11 14).

World.title: True crime pages at heart of Lloyd Rayney’s Meta court fight
World.content:
NationalWADefamation True crime pages at heart of Lloyd Rayney’s Meta court fight Carla Hildebrandt November 24, 2026 — 5:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Unmoderated social media comments made on three Facebook pages, including an Indian news site and a small Perth crime watch group, are at the centre of legal action launched by a West Australian lawyer acquitted of murdering his wife more than a decade ago. Former criminal barrister Lloyd Rayney launched legal proceedings against Meta in the Federal Court last week in an attempt to have the social media firm reveal the identities of users who had allegedly defamed him. Lloyd Rayney with his wife, Corryn, who was killed in 2007. Perth law firm Cove Legal, who act for the Como resident, filed three documents, including an affidavit and an originating application. This masthead understands the father-of-two has taken issue with a post by local group, Inglewood 6052 Crime Watch, which boasted of a “worldwide exclusive” after a user allegedly spotted Rayney in public.



The post, which has since been deleted, included a picture of Rayney and referenced his wife Corryn, 44, who disappeared after a boot scooting class in August 2007. Related Article Exclusive

Courts Rayney pursues broke detective to recoup more than $400,000 A week later, her body was found in a bush grave at Perth’s Kings Park. The second allegedly defamatory instance was a Facebook page, State Stories – an independent Indian-media news website – which published a post in July with details about Corryn’s death. It is understood the post itself was not considered defamatory, however some of the more than 200 comments below the post allegedly were.



The Missing, Murdered & Unsolved Crimes of Australia Facebook page, which posts information on true-crime stories, is the last page alleged to have received defamatory messages after sharing a post on Corryn’s death last September. Rayney’s lawyer Roger Blow said the legal action stemmed from “unpleasant mob attacks” occurring more than a decade after his client was acquitted of Corryn’s murder. Rayney was charged with murder in 2010 and acquitted in July 2012 after a three-month trial. He received a record $2.6 million compensation payout by the state government after being named the “prime and only suspect” of his wife’s murder by a WA Police officer. State Stories editor Zishan Ali told this masthead the page took the defamation concerns “seriously” and had removed the post.



“We are a small independent true crime page, and we take concerns of this nature seriously,” Zishan said. “We regret any distress the comments may have caused and have no wish to be involved in any legal dispute.” An admin for the Inglewood 6052 Crime Watch page did not specifically comment on the post at the heart of Rayney’s court action. The Missing, Murdered & Unsolved Crimes of Australia page has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Beef mince sold at Auckland supermarket recalled over possible metal pieces
World.content:
Beef mince that was sold at an Auckland supermarket is being recalled over concerns it may contain small pieces of metal.

New Zealand Food Safety says Pak'nSave Highland Park is recalling made-in-store beef mince and prime beef mince as the products may contain foreign matter.

"The concern with these products is that they may contain small metal pieces, which could cause injury if consumed," said New Zealand Food Safety deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle.

The affected products have a 'PACKED ON' date of 23.11.26 and a 'BEST BEFORE' date of 26.11.26.

Arbuckle said the mince products can be returned to the supermarket for a refund.

"If that's not possible, throw them out."

The affected products were sold only at Pak'nSave Highland Park. They have been removed from sale and have not been exported.

There have been no reports of any injuries from the mince, said Arbuckle.

A social media creator says overseas online casinos are offering him thousands of dollars to advertise their platforms, even though it's illegal.

With Aotearoa moving to license online casinos, there's concerns operators will keep flouting the law on social media.

Advocates say it's time for tougher advertising restrictions and bigger fines for those who break the rules.

Auckland-based social media content creator Jackson Francis posts photos and videos he's taken of cars and his overseas travels. On his Instagram page he's followed by just under 20,000 people, a large number being men aged between 18 and 21.

From the middle of this year, he said he had been getting weekly messages from overseas-based online casinos, asking him if he would advertise for them.

Checkpoint has seen some of the offers, sent through emails and private messages.

One of the casinos offered him $3500 for 10 Instagram stories. Another sent a script for him to follow and said they would supply video for him to post, so it would appear as though he had won money.

All up, Francis told Checkpoint he's been offered around $35,000.

"It would probably be the easiest money you'd ever get too, you'd just film a quick iPhone video, takes you five minutes then you post it to your story."

But Francis turned the offers down, as he didn't want to sell his followers out.

"It's not worth it, [the online casinos] are just preying on the smaller influencers, the ones out there posting and they don't have hundreds of thousands of followers."

"They're probably the most likely ones to say yes to a quick, easy couple thousand dollars."

Online gambling 'normalised' for young people

Since May last year, nine social media influencers have been given infringement notices by the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA).

Jackson Francis' Instagram page. RNZ

Each infringement costs $5000 each, with four influencers slapped with $20,000 worth of fines.

Frances Russell, clinical lead of support service Touchgrass said online gambling has become normalised for young people, through advertising on social media and in sport.

"Seeing it pop up like that can be a real trigger for young brains - you might struggle a little bit with impulse control.

"They might be having a bit of a wobbly day and that can lead them into paths of gambling that they hadn't intended to do, so I don't think that it is harm-free."

Russell said she's seeing teenagers as young as 17 seeking help for problem online gambling.

"What I see with young people is a lot of feelings of shame and guilt around the kind of destruction that it causes in their lives, young people losing quite significant amounts of money.

"I'm also seeing young people who originally started out as having really well-rounded lives, being members of sports teams and going out with friends, [now] making active choices to stay home and gamble, because they're chasing losses."

Calls for steeper fines

Problem Gambling Foundation's Andree Froude said despite it being illegal, some social media influencers are still taking up offers because the fines aren't hefty enough.

"For those operators, it's like a cost doing business, it's not really a penalty.

"I know in some situations the operators probably covered the costs of these fines for the influencer."

From next year, the Online Casino Gambling Act will take effect, granting 15 offshore online casinos licences to operate in Aotearoa.

Andree Froude. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

But Froude said the bill still allows licensed online casinos to advertise, but with restrictions.

"We need to make sure that if they are breaching our laws, or they are using influencers to promote their products, their sites, then they need to be held to account from the get go."

Vicki Scott, DIA director of gambling, told Checkpoint as part of the new system they're carrying out public education and awareness activities.

Licensed operators will also have to pay their share of the problem gambling levy once they begin generating revenue.

If a licensed online casino breaks the rules, they could face take-down notices, formal warnings and penalties of up to $5 million.

World.title: RNZ Chief People Officer Sarah Neilson leaves amid financial crisis
World.content:
RNZ's human resources boss Sarah Neilson is leaving the public broadcaster, the third senior executive to depart amid its financial crisis.

The Crown entity confirmed on Tuesday that Neilson, its chief people officer, would finish on Friday.

Her departure follows those of chief executive Paul Thompson and chief financial officer Hilary Parker, as an independent inquiry looms into RNZ's shock $11.8 million loss this last financial year.

Parker unexpectedly quit in October, while Thompson exited last Monday, six weeks earlier than planned.

Checkpoint last week revealed increased scrutiny on Neilson's involvement, including that she had acted as an intermediary ​between Thompson and Parker after a breakdown in their communications earlier this year.

About $3.2 million of RNZ's deficit was due to an overspend on personnel. Neilson also led the group overseeing RNZ's Auckland office relocation, which ran $1.85 million over budget.

In a message to staff, acting chief executive Mark Stevens thanked Neilson for her contribution and wished her well.

Neilson said it had been a privilege to work at RNZ.

"The past few weeks have been really tough for the organisation and for the great people that work here," she said.

"I have always been proud to work at RNZ and believe in its purpose to deliver the important services and exceptional content it does day in and day out to New Zealanders.

"I look forward to seeing that important work continue from afar."

Asked for more details, the broadcaster declined to say whether Neilson had resigned, taken voluntary redundancy or been fired, or whether she had received any financial payment on leaving.

"RNZ does not comment on individual employment agreements," a spokesperson said.

Taxpayers' Union spokesperson Ella Dickson said RNZ should disclose whether Neilson or any of the other departing executives had or would receive an exit payment.

"Taxpayers shouldn't have to prise this information out through Official Information Act requests," Dickson said.

"RNZ makes a taxpayer-funded living asking questions, now it's their turn to answer."

In October, RNZ chair Brent Impey said Parker had not received any special exit payment beyond what was usual for staff.

Repeated questions about Thompson's salary and exit package have so far gone unanswered.

The latest development comes as politicians from both sides of the aisle harden their stance on RNZ's board and executive leadership.

Associate Finance Minister David Seymour, who has shareholding responsibility for RNZ, asked the board to "toughen" the terms of reference for the independent inquiry into the saga.

Labour's media spokesperson Reuben Davidson also stepped up his rhetoric, calling for the entire board to be sacked and replaced with interim directors while the inquiry took place.

World.title: Is Black Friday looking dark for retailers?
World.content:
It has been a rocky year for retail in New Zealand, but it is not all doom and gloom in the shopping centres, says the head of the Newmarket Business Association.

There have been a growing pile of retail casualties in recent weeks, with department store David Jones and Australian clothing brands General Pants Co, Cue and Veronika Maine all in voluntary receivership.

All have branches in the upmarket Auckland shopping precinct of Newmarket, but the head of the local business group says an increase in leases being taken and stores being fitted out was a good sign for the future.

Audio player for " Is Black Friday looking dark for Newmarket’s fashion retailers? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2764376%2Fis-black-friday-looking-dark-for-retailers

Is Black Friday looking dark for Newmarket’s fashion retailers? Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

Newmarket Business Association chief executive Mark Knoff-Thomas told Checkpoint that it had been a "bumpy" 2026 for retailers so far.

"We've had good periods and bad periods throughout the whole year, and that's across the board, across the country."

Mark Knoff-Thomas. supplied

But he said he felt New Zealand was coming out the other side of an uncertain period.

"Some of the anecdotal numbers we've had recently, just in the last couple of weeks, foot traffic has been pretty phenomenal and trade has been amazing."

He said retailers had been "very, very busy" in Newmarket today, with one athletic clothing brand having a Black Friday sale that had "gigantic queues snaking around the ground floor" of the mall.

"So there is demand there for people to spend money, but it is fair to say everybody is looking for a deal - a good deal - and Black Friday has tipped us into the sales mentality, leading into the Christmas rush period."

Knoff-Thomas said retail had always been a tough business.

"Retail has never been a strawberries and cream industry, it's always been tough for some operators.

"But we've been through worse periods than this over the last six years, where it was really dark and some of the trades were just very, very gloomy. But what we're seeing now is a kind of shakedown where some retailers... may be coming through very weakened, and they're having some very real conversations around the boardroom table."

But he said other retailers were talking about double-digit growth year on year.

"So it's a very mixed bag and not everybody is having the same experience but I think there is still some good life left in it yet."

The Westfield mall in Newmarket. Google Maps

While the proportion of empty shopfronts in Newmarket peaked at 39 percent a few years ago, that was now down to 12 percent, said Knoff-Thomas, with the demand for leasing a shop "really picking up for some".

"For every brand doing it tough, there are other brands lining up to give it a go."

The New Zealand dollar has slumped to its lowest levels since the global financial crisis, hovering under 55 US cents - making imported goods more expensive - and Knoff-Thomas said this was putting more pressure on everybody - except exporters.

But he said the new City Rail Link was creating more foot traffic through Newmarket, notably on weekends, and that stores in the business precinct racked up $56 million in sales for October, down just 1.4 percent on last year "which is respectable, all things considered".

He said he expected business to pick up once the next Government had been formed, saying it did have a real effect on overall sales with an air of uncertainty.

"There is this paralysis that creeps in on decision-making and that does trickle down into consumer spend.

World.title: RMA expert questions Fonterra's application to dump 22m litres of milk
World.content:
Audio player for " Fonterra insists permission to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk only used in emergency " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/environment/2764606%2Frma-expert-questions-fonterra-s-application-to-dump-22m-litres-of-milk

Fonterra insists permission to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk only used in emergency Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A resource management expert is questioning Fonterra's rationale in applying for consent to dump up to 22 million litres of raw milk in Canterbury.

The dairy giant has applied to the regional council to vary the conditions of seven consents, arguing approval is needed because of a forecast milk surplus due to processing constraints in the South Island.

Fonterra director of NZ Manufacturing Chris Kane told Morning Report the company had the capacity to process the milk, and the dumping would only bever happen if there was a major event like a power cut or a natural disaster.

"We'd only have surplus milk if we couldn't process it, and we couldn't process it because we had a power shortage or we had some other force majeure event," he said.

"It's highly unlikely we'll ever have to use that because we have a network of 24 sites."

There is no mention of a force majeure event in the application to the regional council.

Kane said there was no issue of surplus milk, and the repeated use of the phrase in the company's consent application was a "technicality."

Resource management practitioner Greg Carylon said there were already provisions in the Resource Management Act that allowed for emergency milk dumping from unforeseeable events.

References being made now to the consent being sought in case of a natural disaster seemed to be a "retrospective response," he said.

"They would have had a gap there and would have been trying to close it on a responsible basis, but the reality is they're overproducing at times across a number of plants around the motu and the cost of that is being externalised to the environment and community where it should not be."

Carlyon referenced the Kaikoura earthquakes as an example.

"There was all sorts of outcomes from that earthquake that were unanticipated, and it drove all sorts of exercises, emergency road building, sewage discharges into the moana.

"Whatever it might be, there's an avenue for those reasonable, necessary undertakings, but in this case, Fonterra could simply take the steps that it knows it could and provide capacity for overproduction in its own plants in a more responsible way."

Fonterra was able to predict the surge in milk and constraints on processing capacity because it was inevitable, Carylon said.

"[Fonterra] has deliberately designed and built the system that we're seeing now, and it's been occurring over two and a half decades.

"It's easy to anticipate, it's just expensive to resolve and it's obviously from their perspective a lot easier if someone else resolves it at someone else's cost."

He said Fonterra's strategy was once producing boutique products, but it had become a bulk supplier to the world.

"It means that when we're working in bulk, we have these massive peaks that come through, and to process it all into one product at one time is problematic."

Fonterra exports 95 percent of its milk, primarily as milk powder.

Future Farmers spokesperson and contract milker Daniel Judd said he did not think Fonterra would dump milk unless it absolutely had to.

He puts the supply surge down to dairy conversions allowing for tens of thousands more cows on the Canterbury plains in the last two years, and shifts in supply from other milk processors.

Judd said not all of the approved dairy conversions would have taken up all of the stock they were consented for, especially as stock was expensive at the moment.

But those that did would likely mean a further increase in milk supply next season.

Judd said there had been a lack of clarity from Fonterra in its application and subsequent comments, especially on the reasons behind the surplus.

Some of that may be down to issues in the RMA and consent applications, that he said showed the system was not working.

"With the combativeness and lack of clarity in the way that [regional council] ECan processes these consents, Fonterra may see it as advantageous to provide as little information as necessary, so as that information becomes required in the consenting process, they will allow some of that contextual information to be let in."

He said there were other possibilities for the surplus, such as stock feed.

"There's an opportunity for a system to have improved circularity to it."

Judd said it was up to the regional council to ensure Fonterra's proposal was environmentally sound.

"A consenting process should outline the best practice option for engaging with that activity. Fonterra have identified something that's missing from their consent, so they need a best practice plan for how to engage with that activity.

"If the best option for what they should do is not to apply to land, then the council needs to offer them a solution for what to do in that scenario," Judd said.

Environmental Law Initiative researcher Anna Sintenie said Fonterra's comments were not in line with the applications it had lodged, which made no mention of emergencies, extreme weather events or other unforeseen circumstances.

She said the 2.3 million litres of milk specified in the application was given as a conservative estimate of anticipated surplus, not a maximum, and if granted, the variation amounted to a blank cheque.

"If approved, the proposed changes would remain attached to existing consents for many years, with some consents not expiring until 2045. That's unacceptable."

World.title: Vehicle importer wound back odometers by almost 50 million kms
World.content:
By Milly Matthews, student journalist

An Auckland vehicle importer has been jailed for nearly two and a half years for winding back odometers by almost 50 million kilometres.

The man was also ordered to pay $27,000 in reparation, while his company was ordered to pay a further $315,000.

A Customs investigation - in collaboration with the NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi - looked at 174 used vehicles imported from Japan and found the importer had been intentionally winding back odometers between August 2020 and January 2024 to make the vehicles appear more valuable.

In total, 48,674,800 kilometres in mileage was wiped from odometers.

Individual vehicles had between 60,000 and 840,000 kilometres wound back, and Customs estimated the profit was close to $5.6 million.

The imported trucks had rolled-back odometers and forged documents. Supplied

Customs acting investigations manager Nigel Barnes said the man's actions were not an error.

"This was deliberate and calculated fraud. The man wound back odometers and forged export certificates to conceal the vehicles' true histories and inflate their value.

"Accurate mileage helps people assess a vehicle's value, safety, and maintenance needs. The deception denied buyers the information they needed to make informed decisions."

Some forged certificates contained false information about their year of manufacture or carrying capacity.

World.title: ACT MP calls for law changes after woman forced to travel overseas for assisted dying
World.content:
Warning: This story contains details of assisted dying and may be upsetting for some readers

Audio player for " Loosening of assisted dying law could put vulnerable at risk " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/health/2764338%2Fact-mp-calls-for-law-changes-after-woman-forced-to-travel-overseas-for-assisted-dying

Loosening of assisted dying law could put vulnerable at risk Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

An MP calling for changes to New Zealand's assisted dying law says people should not be forced to leave the country in order to die with dignity.

The ACT Party's Todd Stephenson has drafted a private member's bill which would remove the rule that people could opt for assisted dying only if they were terminally ill and had six months or less to live.

The bill would have to be drawn from the parliamentary ballot before it could be debated by MPs and have any chance of becoming law.

However, opponents of a law change say broadening the criteria could put disabled people at serious risk.

They fear disabled people could ask for assisted dying not because they wanted to end their lives, but because they could not get the support, housing and care they needed.

Criticism of New Zealand's existing End of Life Choice Act - too restrictive for some, a moral anathema to others - is back in the spotlight after a 93-year-old woman had to travel overseas to fulfil her wish of assisted dying.

Brothers Justin and Peter Topzand said they took their mother Margaret to Switzerland so she could end her life on her own terms, rather than suffer a long, slow decline into dementia and dependence.

Margaret Topzand, seen here with son Peter, enjoying the sun during one of her last walks in the Swiss countryside. Supplied

They said she was not eligible for assisted dying in New Zealand because she was not expected to die within six months from a terminal illness.

Justin Topzand said it was "ridiculous" the current law forced people to travel halfway across the planet for a medically simple procedure; while Peter Topzand said it was "appalling" people who could not afford to travel to Switzerland were unable to access assisted dying.

'Dignity at the end of life'

The End of Life Choice Act started as a private member's bill introduced by ACT leader David Seymour in 2017.

It became law in 2021 after passing a conscience vote in Parliament and gaining roughly two-to-one support in a referendum held alongside the 2020 general election.

Act MP Todd Stephenson said his party was proud of getting an assisted dying law across the line, but many people were still missing out.

"I've heard from many, many New Zealanders who have loved ones who are sick and who want to access the end-of-life choice regime, but unfortunately, they are still not eligible."

Stephenson said his bill, if passed, would adopt all 25 recommendations made in a health ministry review of the existing law.

More importantly, he said, it would remove the "arbitrary" six-month rule.

"We think people being able to make decisions around how they die - and having that dignity at the end of their life - is really, really important. It's not an option for everyone. It's actually people's individual decisions about whether they apply," he said.

"But when they're living with a terminal illness, we want them to have that option so they don't have to leave New Zealand and seek other ways of getting assisted dying."

'Not a real choice'

Disabled Persons Assembly chief executive and former Green MP Mojo Mathers has grave concerns about what an expanded assisted dying law could mean for disabled people. Supplied

When the law was last reviewed in 2024, religious and disability groups were among those who spoke out against any move to broaden the criteria.

Disabled Persons Assembly chief executive Mojo Mathers, a former Green MP and New Zealand's first deaf Parliamentarian, said she had "grave concerns" about the potential effect on people with disabilities.

She said her fears had been borne out in Canada, where a 2021 law change had made assisted dying available to people with non-terminal conditions.

Mathers said between 2019 and 2023, 42 percent of assisted deaths in that country were of people who required disability services - and more than 1000 of those people required disability services but did not receive them.

"So essentially they are euthanising disabled people who need disability support services and are unable to access them," she said.

"When we see that happening overseas we are incredibly concerned, particularly in the current political environment where access to disability support and accessible housing is being withdrawn or becoming harder to get, and political parties are talking about cutting access to funding for disability support services even further."

Mathers said disabled people needed a chance to live well first, before any conversation around expanded criteria for assisted dying could even start.

If the disabled were opting to die because they lacked support, that also raised questions about whether they were genuinely exercising free will.

"If we can't access housing, if we can't access the disability support services we need, and the only option is assisted dying, then that is not a real choice," she said.

CCS Disability Action had similar concerns.

National leadership advisor Debbie Ward said she supported the rights of everyone, including disabled people, to choose - as long as they had a chance to give genuine informed consent, in a way that was accessible and meaningful to them.

Simply signing a form written in legal jargon was not enough, she said.

She also worried recent cuts to disability services could affect people's quality of life, which could then influence their long-term decisions.

"In our current economic and political environment disabled people, and their whānau, may feel more pressure as the supports to help them live their best lives are harder to get," Ward said.

'Not everyone is going to have a straightforward death'

Voice for Life, a national organisation that campaigns against abortion and euthanasia, is also opposed to any broadening of the criteria.

President Lydia Posthuma said the group wanted to see the current law repealed but accepted that would be challenging.

Posthuma questioned whether people really had freedom to choose when one option, assisted dying, was fully government-funded while the other, hospice or at-home palliative care, was not.

Also, hospice services were not available everywhere in the country.

Posthuma said her group had heard alarming stories about people asking for assisted dying because they had reached a point where they needed full-time care.

Moving into a rest home would, however, require selling the family home - leaving the other spouse, or any dependent adult children, with nowhere to live.

"We're concerned that people are choosing it not because they are necessarily wanting to die, but because financially they're finding that's maybe the only way, in their mind, that they can care for their loved ones. So are they choosing it because it's actually a choice or because that's what they feel like is their only choice?"

Posthuma said it was important to understand why people were choosing assisted death.

"Is it because they don't have adequate access to palliative care or don't know about the support palliative care can provide them? Death has a lot of unknowns and people are scared of dying, so they want to be able to control it," she said.

"But we can educate them around what good death looks like, and acknowledge pain and suffering and that not everyone is going to have a straightforward death. We also acknowledge the dignity of walking alongside someone until the end and giving them a death with compassion and care."

One of the last photos of Margaret Topzand was taken as she enjoyed the view from a hotel balcony just outside Zurich. Supplied

'It's got to be around suffering'

The Topzand family respected their mother's wish to choose the time of her death but did not want to be directly involved.

Instead, they hired a "death doula" to take care of the paperwork, doctor's visits and psychiatrist's appointments demanded by the Swiss authorities.

Doula Deb McCullough likened her role to a midwife's, but at the other end of life.

She said she was often contacted by people who wanted an assisted death but did not meet the legal criteria.

"It's great that we have the ability for people to look at assisted dying here. It's just that so many people don't fit the very strict criteria. There's a lot of people suffering with illnesses, they're not always age-related, but the people I get contacted by are largely elderly looking for a way out," McCullough said.

"They've had enough. They're sick of suffering whatever it is that they're suffering with, but they don't fit into that criteria, and they don't know what to do."

Getting approval for Margaret Topzand to go to Switzerland took seven months, she said.

"It's a big process. I think we could have probably done it in four or five if there wasn't the Iran war in the middle of it all, but there are a lot of hoops to jump through. It's not straightforward, but at least their criteria are broader."

McCullough said the law "absolutely" needed changing.

"It's got to be around suffering, not timeframes, in my opinion. You can suffer with some illnesses for years and the suffering's awful. It's intolerable in many cases, but because you can't get a doctor to say you'll die within six months, that's it, you're out the door, you haven't got a choice."

"Death doula" Deb McCullough guides people through the end of life. Supplied

'A fundamental failure of politics'

Dignitas, a Swiss not-for-profit organisation, offers physician-assisted death to foreign nationals, as long as they meet certain criteria.

Figures from the Dignitas website show the organisation recorded 4179 assisted deaths between 1998, when it was founded, and the end of 2025.

During that period the highest number of assisted deaths were for German citizens (1462), followed by French (654), British (651) and Americans (301). Five New Zealanders had died with help from Dignitas.

A spokesperson from the organisation said people from New Zealand should not have to turn to Dignitas.

"The fact that they, and others, reach out to us in Switzerland, and some make the journey to us for assisted dying is a fundamental failure of politics on the part of countries with no or with restrictive end-of-life-choice laws. They are abandoning their citizens in a desperate situation," the spokesperson said.

'People are still missing out'

Central government funds 50 percent of hospice costs in New Zealand, with the rest covered by op shops, grants and fundraising events.

Hospice New Zealand chief executive Wayne Naylor said better funding was needed for end-of-life care, before assisted dying was expanded.

"We know that across New Zealand there are people who are still missing out," he said.

"We have some fantastic hospice services out there and some great hospital palliative care teams. But the further you get away from a main centre, the less services are available. So we need better funding for equitable access to good-quality palliative and end-of-life care services so whoever needs them can get them."

He believed the current law was working as designed, but great care had to be taken with any changes to avoid unintended consequences.

Naylor wanted the debate to focus on the almost 99 percent of New Zealanders who did not have an assisted death.

"There's a huge number of people who die, who don't choose assisted dying, who are probably missing out on a good death. And we should be focusing more of our attention there."

* According to the Ministry of Health, in the year to 31 March 2026, 486 New Zealanders had an assisted death, making up just under 1.3 percent of all deaths during that period. The total number since the law came into force is 1696.
