World.title: Newspapers delayed as Allied Media hit by cyber attack
World.content:
Audio player for " Community newspapers latest victims of cyber-attack " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business_media/2762284%2Fnewspapers-delayed-as-allied-media-hit-by-cyber-attack

Community newspapers latest victims of cyber-attack Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

The head of New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre says AI is accelerating the speed and scale of cyber threats after several Allied Media newspapers - including the Otago Daily Times - were affected by an attack.

Catriona Robinson, who is also the deputy director of General Cyber Security, told Checkpoint AI tools intended to help check for cyber vulnerabilities were now being used to conduct cyber attacks.

"So these tools were available on a public repository... They're being repurposed by cyber criminals, and that's accelerating the pace and scale at which those criminals are able to launch cyber attacks."

This comes after Allied Media confirmed on Tuesday it had been the target of an attack that had "disrupted several of our production systems".

It said community papers that were due out on Wednesday - including the Blenheim Sun, Southern Rural Life and The Ensign - will now be delivered on Thursday.

"Our teams are working to restore access to our systems so that we can produce tomorrow's Otago Daily Times."

Greymouth Star's deputy editor Brendon McMahon confirmed today' edition could not be published and Wednesday's Hokitika Guardian could also not go ahead.

"The internet issue has impacted the entire Allied Media group South Island-wide..." McMahon said

"We hope to provide an update later in the day on the timing to solve what is a complex issue , and hopefully tomorrow will be a new day!"

He thanked readers for their patience. Allied Media said there was no evidence that customer information had been accessed.

Attacks on the rise

More recently Top Ten Holiday Parks Group said it was hacked, leading to phishing scams that targeted guests.

Last week, the Defence Force shut down some of its public websites after a cyber attack and Forrest and Bird also confirmed it had been hacked.

Robinson said the National Cyber Security Centre was helping these organisations deal with the attacks, which don't appear to be linked.

She said attacks were on the rise and the centre had seen the highest quarterly total of cyber incidents being reported in two years.

"We're talking about 1700... It concerns me a great deal, you know, that the environment is getting more turbulent."

The centre was working with critical infrastructure companies in New Zealand to help them prepare, including those in telecommunication and finance.

A cyber criminals motivation was financial, Robinson said, and they tend to go for sectors rich in sensitive and personal information.

"On the dark web, you can absolutely purchase a cyber criminal service to go and steal information for you... which you can then launch attacks against other organisations with."

She also said it was highlighted in their recent cyber threat report that international state actors were another documented threat, including those from China, Russia and Iran.

"We assess that China is the most persistent and capable state sponsored actor acting against New Zealand... when we see state sponsored activity in New Zealand, it seems predominantly to be aimed at espionage purposes and other forms of information theft, intellectual property theft, for example."

Robinson said there was one case with a North Korean IT worker scamming their way into a role with a major New Zealand company and putting it at risk of breaching sanctions legislation.

She urged everyone to be cautious of any links or attachments that might be sent to them and avoid clicking on anything.

On the other hand AI also created opportunities for defenders, Robinson said.

World.title: Hobart's new $1.23 billion stadium price tag explained
World.content:
It has become a familiar — verging on cliché — line when discussing anything regarding the Macquarie Point stadium.

The devil is in the detail.

When Premier Jeremy Rockliff revealed the updated cost of the stadium had risen from $1.13 billion to $1.23 billion via his Facebook page this morning, the number was met with a mix of relief and surprise from those who expected a much higher spike.

But here comes that devil.

A simulation of the internal concourse at the proposed Macquarie Point stadium. (Supplied: MPDC)

Hobart's stadium and precinct costs rise to $1.54b The state government blames high oil, materials and labour prices for the blowout from a $1.13 billion budget set last year.

For the stadium to actually function, it requires broader precinct works at Macquarie Point to be completed.

They are works that sit outside the core construction of the stadium but are vital to its functionality.

Energy. Water. Landscaping. For those things, an extra $132 million has been allocated by the government.

It is true that that infrastructure will serve a broader purpose — TasPorts, and future developments (hotels, restaurants, shops, housing) on the site will all draw on the energy and water upgrades that will happen as part of the stadium development.

But it is also true that for the stadium's lights to turn on and for its toilets to flush, those things must be built and therefore must be included as a cost.

Doing so sees the price lift from $1.23 billion to $1.36 billion.

The developer cited the war in Iran as a major factor behind the cost increase. (Supplied: MPDC)

Then there are the costs of facilitating that extra work, as well as costs already incurred by the Macquarie Point Development Corporation.

That spits out at $183 million.

Now we are at $1.54 billion for the stadium and the precinct works that let it operate.

And that's if everything goes to plan across the life of the build.

The roof was a condition of the contract with the AFL. (Supplied: MPDC)

One crucial number that's missing from the update is the contingency price, with the government and Macquarie Point Development Corporation opting to keep that number secret ahead of penning a building contract with construction partner BESIX Watpac.

Previous estimates included this figure, with $174 million making up part of the stadium's last cost estimate of $1.13 billion.

That is 14 per cent of the budget.

Applying this number to the new overall cost adds another $215 million to the total, for a total budget of $1.76 billion.

How much contingency the Macquarie Point Development Corporation keeps up its sleeve depends on the contract it signs with BESIX Watpac.

Jeremy Rockliff (right) says the "cost has changed, but the opportunity for Tasmania has not". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

At a recent public accounts committee hearing, department secretary Kathrine Morgan-Wicks spoke of assurances made before the "final investment decision".

"This includes understanding the proposed relationship between MPDC and the lead contractor," she said.

" For example, the contract cost will be higher as risks are transferred to the contractor, or lower if the state accepts risks. "

The MPDC cited the war in Iran as a major factor behind the cost increase, as well as Australia's competitive infrastructure pipeline, which includes the upcoming Brisbane Olympics.

In a bid to keep costs low, the MPDC also confirmed it had "value managed" the project by $100 million, mainly through the design process and the process in which the stadium is delivered.

So, let's break down the numbers even further.

Many elements of the project have not been factored into the new cost. (Supplied: MPDC)

Included in the $1.2 billion stadium cost is the core construction of the stadium building, seats, roof, grass and fit-out.

Everything that makes a stadium a stadium.

It also includes the cricket test rig, which was constructed earlier this year, dilapidation surveys, environmental monitoring equipment and bulk excavation works currently occurring at the Macquarie Point site in anticipation of the build.

A smaller-scale roof was constructed to test if the shadows were a problem for cricket play. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The $132 million in precinct costs will cover stormwater and water upgrades, power upgrades and landscaping.

A car park has also been included, but MPDC chief executive Anne Beach said it "absolutely wasn't required" for the stadium; rather, it would act as an "enabler" for the precinct.

The $183 million in project delivery costs are the costs to deliver the precinct — It includes paying for consultants, the Macquarie Point Development Corporation staff, incidentals like personal protective equipment, computer software, training, headworks and building insurance.

Not included? The Northern Access Road, which is priced at $78.9 million and, while necessary for the stadium to function, is a long-existing project which will be headed up, and funded by, Building Tasmania.

The cap on state funding of $875 million, agreed to by Jeremy Rockliff in exchange for support, is essentially scrapped. (Supplied: MPDC)

The updated budget also does not account for interest on the additional borrowings which will be required to cover the increased cost, which will flow through a new "funding facility" being set up for the MPDC.

In other words, the MPDC's borrowing limit will be increased in order for it to pay for the project, and $1.29 billion of the total project cost will currently be borne by the Tasmanian taxpayer through capital and borrowings.

That means the state funding cap of $875 million agreed to by Premier Jeremy Rockliff in exchange for the upper house vote of Bec Thomas is essentially scrapped.

But there does still remain the possibility for more funding from external sources, with the premier today confirming ABC reporting that conversations had begun with the federal government, AFL, cricket and private sector regarding increased financial contributions.

Jeremy Rockliff says "every generation has a couple of rare opportunities to change their future … for us, this is a golden one". (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

The new budget will be presented to cabinet by November 30 and is expected to be approved, with a construction contract to be signed in the coming weeks.

"We've had our commercial and legal team, as well as our technical team, look at the detail submitted by [BESIX] Watpac," MPDC's Anne Beach said.

"We've undertaken an analysis, and we're confident that we can deliver within that budget," she said.

World.title: Munster calls Storm contract offer 'disappointing'
World.content:
Cameron Munster has declared all options are on the table after officially rejecting a deal to stay in Melbourne and labelling the Storm's latest offer "disappointing".

With Melbourne already facing a battle to retain Harry Grant, the Storm is now officially fighting a retention war on two fronts after Munster's decision.

The Melbourne superstar admitted on Tuesday that Grant's future could play a role in his own call, as well as Craig Bellamy's impending retirement at the end of 2027.

As it stands, Munster will not take up an offer from the Storm that is understood to have been for one year with an option for a second.

"I have declined it," the Queensland State of Origin captain said.

"I am not saying I am going to leave Melbourne. Just with the terms and conditions that they put out to me, it is probably something that is a little disappointing.

"But it's a business, I am not stupid."

Munster admitted his own form had not been good enough for the Storm last season as they missed the finals for the first time in his career.

The Storm did not enjoy a good NRL season, missing the finals. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

And in turn, the 32-year-old conceded the offer may have been as a result of that.

"That [offer] just makes my job a little bit harder. But it's also a bit of a challenge saying I am not where I need to be," he said.

"Maybe I need to be a little bit better to earn that contract that we're looking for.

"And maybe it is a little bit of a kick up the bum from them. I am not too sure where we'll go from here but all options are open at the moment."

Munster's rejection comes after Grant met with Gold Coast officials last Friday and officially received an offer to join the Titans.

It is understood Melbourne's offer for the Queensland dummy-half will either be worth similar or more than the Titans.

But Gold Coast are hopeful of luring the hooker north, given his relationship with ex-Maroons assistant coach Josh Hannay and prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui.

Harry Grant may also be moving away from the Storm. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

NSW prop Stefano Utoikamanu is also off contract at the end of next year and has also been linked to the Sydney Roosters.

At the same time, Bellamy's retirement at the end of next season is proving a challenge for the Storm, given he is like a father figure to Munster.

"When you look at someone like Craig as a coach, he is a great coach and I have so much respect and have admired him for such a long time," Munster said.

"It's going to be different at the club. I'm not too sure where the club wants to go with all that stuff.

"I don't know who they are going to get and I'm sure it will be a daunting job coming after him."

Munster also confirmed he will likely follow the Cameron Smith route and give away representative football at some point to focus on club duties.

"It definitely has [crossed my mind]," Munster said.

"The hard thing for me is giving up the captaincy.

"Once I start declining [I will look at it] and I thought I was declining. But after my last few games for the World Cup I am pretty confident I can get back to that."

AAP

World.title: Why there's no time to waste for Matildas ahead of World Cup
World.content:
With no time to waste as the Matildas hurtle towards next year's Women's World Cup, Mary Fowler and Kyra Cooney-Cross's respective returns cannot come quickly enough for captain Sam Kerr.

Australia play world No.19 Colombia in Canberra on Saturday, then again in Geelong next Wednesday.

Fowler missed the last window through personal reasons while Cooney-Cross returns to camp having spent time away for personal reasons since the Asian Cup.

"We only have six games left, so to play together as a team is most important," Kerr said.

Sam Kerr recently joined American club Gotham FC. (Getty Images: Dustin Satloff)

"And of course you want to see new faces and you want to see the new talent coming through.

"But you also want to build cohesion and play with the people that probably are mainstays on the team. And Mary, Kyra, all of those girls are.

"And it's obviously harder when you go into a World Cup with less minutes together.

"So we need as many minutes as we can with everyone, and while breeding the new talent."

This month's games mark the final window before the December 11 World Cup draw as the clock ticks down to next year's tournament in Brazil.

Kerr said she had not spoken to Fowler, nor many of her other teammates this window, but was keen to have her back in the fray.

Mary Fowler will return to Matildas camp after missing matches due to personal reasons. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"Of course, Mary's an important part to the team," she said.

"Hopefully she can play well for us."

Facing Colombia, who have established themselves as the second-best South American team behind hosts Brazil, serves as crucial preparation.

"I know it sounds like six months, but we probably spend a month of that together. So we've got to make the most of every game," Kerr said.

"And Colombia is a really good team and a team that we could face at the World Cup.

"They're a different team. We don't normally face teams like this. They play hard. They play a different style of football than we're used to, similar to Brazil and those countries.

"But personally, I want to win the games."

Kerr famously missed most of the 2023 World Cup, where Australia made the semi-finals, with a calf injury.

Sam Kerr missed much of the 2023 World Cup through injury. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

A horror protracted return from a knee reconstruction wiped her out for almost two years.

"When you see the draw coming up, all of those things, the last few teams of qualifying, this camp over in Europe, it starts to feel real," Kerr said.

"Six months will go like that. The last 3.5 years has gone really quickly, so it seems crazy that 2023 was nearly four years ago, it's gone really quick.

"Just really excited but taking it day by day, kind of focusing game by game. Getting excited though."

Kerr crossed from English powerhouse Chelsea to NWSL team Gotham FC last season and is confident she is primed to deliver for the Matildas.

"I feel good. Obviously, would have liked to have scored a few goals in the play-offs recently, but it didn't work out like that.

"But I've been going for 18 months, so I'm looking forward to a break and a refresh before starting up next season, but two more games to go.

"And I feel confident every time I play for the Matildas because it feels like a really comfortable space for me to come and perform."

AAP

World.title: Cameron Smith keen on PGA return following LIV collapse
World.content:
Moving quickly on after LIV Golf's demise, Cameron Smith has revealed a burning desire to return to the PGA Tour as his Australian peers welcome the end to the sport's bitter civil war.

With LIV filing for bankruptcy and being liquidated, Smith has joined the DP World Tour on an invite basis, but has no full-time status.

But for the first time since joining the Saudi-backed league a month after winning the 2022 British Open, Smith conceded he hoped to find a permanent home back on the PGA Tour.

"I guess that's the path. That's where I want to be now for sure," the one-time world number two said ahead of this week's Australian PGA Championship in Sydney.

"DP's given us a chance to kind of fulfil that. We'll see how that goes. There's plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it's going to be difficult.

"But for sure that's where I want to play."

Cam Smith is playing on the DP World Tour. (Getty Images: Hector Vivas)

Only the top 10 from the DP World Tour's season-long points race qualify for the PGA Tour.

But Smith can greatly enhance his chances of getting back to the US big time by at least gaining a full DP World Tour card by winning the PGA Championship, next week's Australian Open in Melbourne or topping the summer-long Australasian order of merit.

At the very least his intention to return to the PGA Tour is a major revelation.

In January, Smith flatly rejected an offer to come back under strict guidelines, insisting he had "no" temptation to follow Brooks Koepka and make a $5 million charity donation.

While he remains disappointed at how LIV collapsed, the 33-year-old ex-Ripper GC captain is relieved a resolution has finally come so he can open a new chapter in his decorated career.

Smith signed with LIV Golf in 2022. (Reuters: Imagn Images/Dennis Schneidler)

"There were lots of rumours floating around throughout the year. There was a lot of uncertainty and then in a way it was good to just like get the noise over and done with," Smith said, maintaining he has no regrets about ever joining LIV.

"It was a big move to go LIV at the start for sure, and I think everyone that was close to me and all my friends saw why I was doing it and why I made the decision.

"So I didn't lose many friends over it — I didn't lose any friends over it, really. I still talk to the same people, I still have the same conversations. I've always tried to do the right thing."

Compatriots Min Woo Lee and fellow major champion Adam Scott said they'd love to see Smith back excelling in the States again.

Smith is the biggest star in Australian golf. (AP: Alastair Gran)

"He's a good friend and we want to see a short-game [star] around the PGA Tour, so it'll be very exciting to see him play on the PGA Tour again," Lee said on Tuesday.

"Whenever we get Aussies on the tour, it's a good time. When we see each other, it doesn't seem like we've missed a day and it's nice.

"Hopefully the golfing world is coming back together. Even just yesterday I was in the locker room with Cam and it's just 'welcome back'.

"I don't pay attention too much to it — (the LIV rivalry) but, yeah, hopefully it all comes back together and we're all happy."

Scott dismissed the notion that Smith couldn't be a success again in America after losing his mojo on the so-called less competitive LIV league.

"Cam's incredibly talented and hell adjust to his new environment and he'll be just fine," Scott said.

"There's no doubt about it."

AAP

World.title: Teenager threatened with violent sexual assault after losing tennis match
World.content:
An 18-year-old player has been subjected to death threats and graphic abuse after losing her tennis match during an Adelaide international tournament.

Adelaide's Taylah Lessue was competing during the City of Playford Tennis International on Sunday, winning the first set 6-4 before succumbing to an ongoing illness and losing 6-4, 0-6, 0-6.

According to her mother, Rachelle Lessue, the singles player had been bed-ridden for three weeks with glandular fever before giving the tournament "everything she had".

"Only eight days ago she was in hospital on a drip and lost 6 kilograms in a week unable to eat or swallow anything," Ms Lessue wrote in a social media post.

"But what breaks my heart is, 15 minutes after walking off court, the disgusting, hurtful and sick messages she received on social media."

The online abuse arrived within 15 minutes of Taylah Lessue's match ending. (Supplied)

Lessue is number 647 in the ITF World Tennis Junior Girls Singles rankings and her match, which was streamed live, had apparently been subject to betting.

She received a torrent of violent, sexually explicit death threats shortly after her loss, even as she recovered from the "fatigue, chest tightness and muscle spasms" her mother said had affected her performance.

"These people have no idea what Tay has battled the last few weeks, and the huge amount of courage and fight she showed to play today," Ms Lessue said.

The abuse started as Lessue stood courtside after the match with City of Playford Mayor Glenn Docherty, who described it as "too graphic" to repeat.

"I know that she's a pretty resilient young lady, but she should not be putting up with this type of abuse," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"It's just absolutely scary.

"To see the content of those messages … I'm sickened by it.

"Hopefully this person or persons can be unmasked and can be dealt with appropriately by law enforcement."

Taylah Lessue was courtside with Glenn Docherty when the abuse started. (Facebook)

Police said they were investigating after a victim received messages of an inappropriate and offensive nature on social media.

"Northern District Police are investigating and will determine if there is evidence to sustain any criminal charges," a spokesperson said.

Tennis Australia responds

Tennis Australia head of integrity Dan Stuk said it was disgraceful that people would go online and "target individuals that they don't even know simply because of their sporting performance".

He said social media was an "overwhelmingly positive space" that gave a lot of "support and love for a number of athletes".

"But there are small numbers of abuse taking place and what we're finding is that it has, as you would imagine, very deeply personal impacts and it can have a real effect on the athletes."

Mr Stuk said the abuse could be targeted at anyone from experienced players to junior athletes, and was "circumstance-specific".

"I would say that online abuse can come from a number of different areas and it can be betting-related, but it can also be related to any other aspect of society," he said.

"Our job at Tennis Australia is to be ready to respond to that, regardless of the abuse.

He said that included educating players about social media use and their privacy settings, how to manage and report any online abuse, and options to monitor and moderate online content with a third-party provider so "they don't even see this in the first place".

It also included providing support for players and family in response to abusive content.

Taylah Lessue won the first set in her match but succumbed to illness. (Facebook)

Ms Lessue said tournament doctors examined her daughter after the match and she had been ruled out of any competition for the next seven to 10 days.

"But the way she conducted herself and fought until the end, when most other people would be bedridden or retired mid-match, fills me with immense pride," she said.

"While it's a loss on the scoreboard, it's another step in her journey and she learned many valuable lessons.

"Above all else, she can hold her head high knowing she fought her heart out and gave the match everything she had."

World.title: Hobart's stadium and precinct costs rise to $1.54b
World.content:
The total estimated cost of the Macquarie Point stadium precinct has risen to $1.54 billion, the Tasmanian government has revealed.

The 23,000-seat roofed stadium, which is a condition of Tasmania's AFL deal, was approved by the Tasmanian parliament last December.

The premier says the stadium and its new cost will not be headed back to parliament for approval. (ABC News: Owain Stia James)

A new estimate revealed today has put the cost of stadium delivery at $1.23 billion.

But that figure does not include the wider precinct infrastructure costs needed to support the project that the government also announced today.

A car park and power supply for the precinct was budgeted at $132 million, while project delivery costs add another $183 million.

This brings the total to $1.54 billion.

The government had previously estimated the stadium cost at $1.13 billion. (Supplied: MPDC)

Contingency costs not included

There is also a "client contingency" amount, which has not been revealed or included in costs.

It will cover any potential rise though the final stage of procurement negotiations and, if needed, would bring the project cost even higher.

Until today, the most recent stadium cost estimate had been from September, when the government priced the stadium at $1.13 billion, however this figure included project costs and contingencies.

The government will break its promise to cap its spending at $875 million. (Supplied: MPDC)

Last week, the lower house of the Tasmanian parliament passed a motion calling for the "current estimated cost" of both "stadium delivery", and "the broader Macquarie Point precinct-enabling infrastructure", including power upgrades and a centralised car park.

In order to win over the votes needed for the approval order to pass the Legislative Council, the government made a number of commitments, including to limit the state's contribution to $875 million.

Treasurer and Minister for Macquarie Point Urban Renewal Eric Abetz said the government would cover the shortfall from state funds, breaking the promised state contribution cap.

Tasmanian Treasurer Treasurer and Minister for Macquarie Point Urban Renewal Eric Abetz said the government would cover the shortfall. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

He said the state would then "look to what opportunities there are to gather the funding, and as a result reduce the borrowings that are necessary".

Parliament grills government on costs

In parliament this morning, Tasmanian Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff asked Mr Rockliff if he would keep his promise of a $875 million taxpayer funding cap.

Mr Rockliff responded that the spending cap "was the best estimate at the time".

"I couldn't foresee the conflict in Iran," he said.

"I acknowledge we have to borrow more to see the project through, and we had the best estimate back in September last year so now we're 14 months on with the Iran conflict and cost escalation in everything we do."

Ms Woodruff asked Mr Rockliff if there was "any limit to how much you're prepared to spend or commit of Tasmanians' taxpayer money to get the stadium built".

He did not answer the question, instead saying the government had been "up-front with the Tasmanian people".

The stadium will have a roof, which was a requirement of the agreement with the AFL for a state team. (Supplied: MPDC)

A Greens' push for the government to "honour its commitment to cap taxpayer funding for the stadium at $875 million" did not get enough support to pass the lower house.

Treasurer Eric Abetz described it as a "motion designed to kill the stadium". Labor also voted against it.

"We support scrutiny, but we don't support sabotage," Labor leader Josh Willie said.

" The stadium is going ahead and it will be a good thing for Tasmania. "

Independent Clark MP Kristie Johnston, who, along with independents Helen Burnet, Craig Garland and George Razay, voted with the Greens and was scathing of Mr Willie and Labor.

"They might as well move across the government benches because they provide no opposition at all," Ms Johnston said.

The federal government has committed $240 million to the Macquarie Point precinct, and the AFL is chipping in $15 million for the stadium.

Despite the US–Iran war pushing up construction costs worldwide, the government has only recently admitted the stadium would likely cost more than estimated last year.

During question time, Ms Johnston asked Mr Abetz whether the government had calculated what the loan financing would cost.

"How much interest will we be paying on the stadium borrowings over the next 10 years?" she said.

But Mr Abetz criticised Ms Johnston and "those that have opposed the stadium each and every step of the way".

"Have you written to federal Labor, have you written to the AFL, have you written to Cricket Australia asking them to make a bigger contribution for the stadium so our borrowings may be less?"

Mr Willie, speaking after question time, said the federal government should pay more, and he called on the state government to go back to the other funding partners.

Oil, material and labour costs blamed for price increase

Premier Jeremy Rockliff called the increases "unavoidable", pointing to high oil and materials prices, higher labour costs and the "complexities driven by the parliamentary-driven order".

Loading...

He said the state was in conversation with its funding partners about them making larger contributions.

While some MPs had been calling for the parliament to be required to tick off any cost increase, Mr Rockliff said it would not be doing so.

"The parliament had its say last year in early December," he said.

He remained committed to the project.

"Every generation gets a handful of opportunities to shape the future, and the stadium is one of those opportunities," he said.

Ms Johnston told 936 ABC Hobart this morning that the state would be "on the hook" for significant amounts of borrowing.

"We will be borrowing $1.29 billion to cover the cost of the stadium … that's a significant impost onto the state's finances, particularly when we are in a budget crisis," she said.

" That's taxpayer's money that will need to be paid back and remembering that the stadium will not be generating sufficient income to even cover the interest payments, let alone the principle. "

She said the government needed to explain the different contingencies regarding the estimated costs of the project.

Independent economist Saul Eslake said $1.29 billion would either need to be borrowed directly by the government or by the Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC), which is owned and underwritten by the government.

"The interest cost on that $1.29 billion will, if the interest rate is about 5.5 per cent on average over the period for which that debt is outstanding, is about $71 million per annum, so that's a significant cost," Mr Eslake told 936 ABC Hobart.

"And the government has acknowledged, and I'm not criticising them for this, that there may well be some further increases that are currently still to be negotiated with the company before a contract is finally signed."

Final contract negotiations

MPDC is in the final stage of negotiations with preferred tenderer BESIX Watpac, and hopes to sign a contract for the build by Christmas.

It submitted its final price to the government earlier this month.

Macquarie Point Development Corporation head Anne Beach said about $100 million had been saved through "value management" already. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

MPDC chief executive Anne Beach said a "intensive, rigorous process" had been run to sign a contract this year.

"There are some risks that are carried by us, and some by the builder," she said of the contract.

She said about $100 million had been saved through value management already, and that MPDC would keep looking for efficiencies.

Our Place Hobart, a community group opposed to the stadium project, said the $1.54 billion project figure was not the full picture.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff at the sod-turning ceremony for the stadium earlier this year. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

"That's not including a massive interest bill, the northern access road and contingencies," the group's Roland Browne said in a statement.

He said the government was hundreds of millions of dollars above the maximum state funding figure it promised parliament's upper house.

"This is extraordinary. The government and MPDC have lost control of this project," he said.

World.title: Legal battle looms over potential Russian return to international sport
World.content:
Russia's return to international sport after being excluded over its invasion of Ukraine is facing mounting opposition in Europe, drawing the world's biggest sports organisations into a legal quagmire.

The International Olympic Committee barred Russia from Olympic and international competitions following Moscow's February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It lifted the ‌suspension in July this year and several sports federations are now allowing Russians to compete.

With qualifiers across dozens of sports for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles kicking off in earnest next year, the IOC's recommendation to allow Russia's return to international competition is now being put to the test, with some European countries putting barriers in front of Russian athletes' renewed participation.

Russian athletes were permitted to compete at the 2024 Games as individuals. (Getty Images: Raemon Haazen)

Spyros Capralos, president of the European Olympic Committees umbrella body, said there were concerns the stand-off with Russia could affect key LA 2028 qualifiers, including the European Games in June 2027.

The multi-sport event in Istanbul will offer places at the Olympics across several sports and will likely be the biggest test of how Europe will react.

"It is a massive problem facing Europe because Europe is divided on this matter, with governments which sometimes forget the autonomy of sport," Capralos said.

"They forget that ⁠the most important thing is for all athletes to take part."

The dispute is already before the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the sporting world's top arbitrator. CAS said that the Russian Olympic Committee had filed an appeal against the EOC over conditions on Russian athletes' participation in the Winter European Youth Olympic Festival, to be held in Romania in February.

Russian athletes competed as Individual Neutral Athlete at the 2024 Olympics. (Getty Images via Xinhua: Sun Fei)

Russian athletes were told to compete under their national Olympic committee's logo rather than with their flag and anthem, amid strained relations between Romania and Russia.

Romania, a European Union and NATO member, shares a land border of more than 600 km (370 miles) with Ukraine. President Nicușor Dan, a centrist, has said his country is the target of a hybrid war waged by Russia to destabilise nations that support Kyiv. Russia denies these accusations.

CAS said both parties had agreed to an accelerated procedure, with a ruling expected by December 15 at the latest.

The IOC is eager to have Olympic powerhouse Russia fully back in the games after its athletes competed at the Paris 2024 Summer Games and the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics as neutrals, without their flag or anthem.

Some international sports federations, such as World Athletics, which oversees a showpiece Olympic discipline, still have restrictions in place.

Furthermore, with the war in Ukraine, Europe's biggest conflict since World War II, about to enter its sixth year, many European ‌nations are ⁠not eager to facilitate Russia's sporting return.

The IOC has recommended Russian athletes be allowed to return to competition. (Getty Images: Kadir Caliskan)

Norway, Sweden and Poland have denied visas to Russian athletes, while some national teams have refused to play them.

Some have said they will not compete against Russia even in junior events, as Norway's ice hockey team has done. Event organisers, meanwhile, are weighing the costs of hosting Russian competitors.

Next year's ice hockey World Championships in Germany are already in focus after CAS ruled that Russia was eligible to compete, overturning an International Ice Hockey Federation decision to exclude the team.

German organisers have said a Russian presence would require heightened security arrangements that could stretch budgets.

Russia, however, is not planning to back down. After briefly considering a switch from the European to the Asian sports federation system several ⁠years ago to give its athletes better access to competitions, it is now taking cases to CAS to secure places in events.

Earlier this year, it succeeded at CAS in securing places for some of its winter sport athletes at the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics.

Russian athletes were permitted to compete at the 2026 Winter and Winter Paralympic Games. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Russia's sports minister and national Olympic committee president Mikhail Degtyarev has criticised restrictions on Russian athletes, saying his country would consider all legal options.

"We are waiting for a legal statement to proceed with all our complaints to authorities. The [Russian} Hockey Federation follows its own ⁠line, and we would go through the IOC," Degtyarev told Russian television on November 12.

The IOC, which says entry visas are a sovereign responsibility, wants Russia back in the fold.

"Athletes' access to international competition should not be limited by the passport they hold or affected by the involvement of their governments in a war or conflict," an IOC spokesperson told Reuters.

However, it has made clear that outside the Olympic Games, it is for international sports federations to ⁠deal with the issue of Russian participation at their events.

"The international federations have to navigate the complex and evolving reality — and concrete consequences — of the current geopolitical context, in particular for events they have already awarded and planned," the IOC said.

Those consequences could, however, end up affecting the IOC's own events, including the Olympic Games.

"There is, of course [concern]," Capralos, who is also a member of the IOC Executive Board, said, when asked whether the arguments could affect Olympic qualifiers.

"One of the reasons we wanted to have Russians competing was to allow them to qualify for the Games," he said.

Reuters

World.title: W Award winner Georgie 'not anymore' in older sister Maddy's shadow
World.content:
With the league best and fairest medal around her neck, Georgie Prespakis looked down at her sister Maddy from the stage.

"To think that she's been up here and been able to achieve this. I'm full of emotion and trying to hold back some tears for sure," the Geelong star said into the microphone.

"I've always wanted to follow in Maddy's footsteps, and at times, I probably felt a little bit in her shadow."

The camera then panned to Essendon's Maddy, who mouthed "not anymore" with a face wet with tears. The room erupted with laughter before focusing back on Georgie.

Georgie presented Maddy with the W Award in 2020. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"It's obviously a hard game. It's a hard game at times, so to be able to lean [on] and support one another is something that's meant a lot to me, particularly this year," she said, after the Cats finished in the top two but exited the finals in straight sets.

When asked what made the pair so good, Georgie replied: "Certainly some good genes. I'll take those for sure.

"[But] no, no doubt my family, my parents particularly, are feeling super proud, and yeah, I can't wait to obviously share this moment with them."

The Prespakis pair became the first sisters in AFLW history to both win the league's highest honour, the W Award.

When Georgie and Maddy play each other, it's subbed "the Prespakis cup". (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

The only brothers to win the men's equivalent, the Brownlow, were Albert and Harry Collier, back in 1929 and 1930 respectively.

Maddy won it back in 2020. With the awards held via Zoom due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Maddy was presented with the medal by Georgie in their shared backyard.

A year later, Georgie was drafted to Geelong.

In her early years at the Cats, Georgie was constantly being compared to her older sister. When Geelong and Essendon (or Carlton when Maddy was still there) played each other, it was referred to as "the Prespakis cup".

As the years went on, Georgie burst out of that shadow, as she does from stoppages, and began to represent a new era of AFLW talent.

Inaugural player Jasmine Garner was the favourite on Monday to take out the W Award, a medal that has eluded her over her career despite long being regarded as the best player in the competition. She earned her ninth All Australian blazer this week, the most of any player in the history of the competition.

Garner polled 24 votes, falling behind the other two frontrunners, Charlie Rowbottom (28 votes) and Georgie (30 votes).

Georgie Prespakis is the first Geelong player to win the AFLW W Award. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

Charlie and Georgie were drafted in the same year, with picks one and two respectively. They are the first players not to have played in the first two seasons of the competition to poll so high.

"I've always set really high standards for myself," Georgie said.

"And I've always wanted to be the best that I can be, and I will always work incredibly hard to kind of get myself in that position. And no doubt, my first season of AFLW was a real eye-opener just as to how difficult it is.

"That was something that I really struggled with, and knew that off the back of that, I had to lose a little bit of chubby, baby fat and get to work, and that was something I did.

"It was really difficult to move out of home and go up to Geelong and start a life down there. And I think that's why I feel so grateful to have landed at such an amazing club… [that} allowed me to become not only a better person but a better footballer."

Tech.title: Google alternative Kagi launches an email service
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Kagi, which already offers a paid alternative to Google Search and its own Orion browser as a rival to Chrome, is taking on another Google service: Gmail. Today, Kagi announced a public beta of Kagi Mail, a new email service that has “no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.”

With Kagi Mail, you get an @kagimail.com address, but the service also supports unlimited aliases and domains. It also offers 50GB of storage and a built-in calendar. On the roadmap, you can expect contacts and an address book in Q1 2027, but native mobile apps aren’t expected to arrive until Q3 2027.

“Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once,” Kagi says. “There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.”

Kagi Mail is available now with a 60-day free trial before you have to pay $99 per year. The service is available as part of a $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription.

Rockstar launched GTA VI last week to positive reviews. The studio said the game made $3.79 billion in its first day of sales.
